en: Preface to the Essentials of the Vinaya, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Xuanyun of Hongfa Monastery in Chang’an.

Now, the scriptures of the Vinaya are vast and their principles profound; it is because they adapt to the changing times that the teachings of the Prātimokṣa flourish and the era of the Muni’s dispensation prospers.
That the Bhikṣuṇīs have been able to prolong their lives is truly due to the fact that the precepts serve as the mainstay of the True Dharma and the pivotal mechanism of compassionate instruction.

Thus we know that those who weary of worldly life and seek the Reality are said to be endowed with the "White Dharma" (śukla-dharma) and the support of the precepts; through these, concentration arises, which is described as the "Cooling Category.

It is indeed the natural course of principle that like follows like. Since the Buddha Śākyamuni appeared in the world and first inaugurated this school, he propagated the Five Sections of the Vinaya to exhort people toward goodness.

By establishing the seven groups [of precepts] to punish evil and prevent the arising of outflows, those who first returned to the faith and extinguished their mental delusions were guided by the Sage.

Among all who offered prayers, who was not moistened by this grace? When the Tamer of Men (the Buddha) laid down his burden, the Arhats protected and sustained [the Dharma]; yet as the lingering influence gradually declined, it could no longer match the traces of former times.
Reaching the age of the Semblance Dharma, the days became increasingly turbid; the doctrines of the hundred schools surged like waves, while the myriad virtues [of the true teaching]...

The profound essence has thus become obscured; consequently, various records have been recounted, differing in their brevity or detail. Some are arranged inconsistently, while others present historical events with gaps or omissions.

Monks and nuns are conflated despite their distinct offenses, and they are mixed together in the same category. Competing citations of flowery rhetoric cause the colors red and purple to be usurped by one another, as names and terms are erroneously constructed and divergent paths are artificially distinguished.
Thus, those who practice toil in vain with little merit, and those who study are broad in knowledge yet lack true realization.

Originally, my intention was to assist in propagating these sublime instructions; yet that you would come to destroy the fundamental patterns of human relations is something for which one must deeply sigh and for which many must shed tears.

However, the Way relies on people to be propagated, and principle is made manifest through teaching. In propagating the Way and establishing teachings, nothing is more esteemed than adapting to the capacities of beings and responding to circumstances according to the times.
One’s practice should consist of maintaining frugality and simplicity, relying upon and repeatedly studying the texts so that their meaning may be clearly sought. I, Yu, [have thus composed this].

Although I lack intelligence, I have had the honor of participating in the academy; having devoted myself to these teachings without slackening, I have gained some understanding of the fundamental path.

Thus, during the intervals between my studies, I have applied my mind to compiling this record. Whenever a single phrase was worthy of praise, I would immediately reflect upon it three times with deep consideration.

Having fished through the sūtras and vinayas and gathered from various records, I have laid bare my sincerity and refined my research, hoping to preserve the essentials. This work consists of forty chapters and is completed in three volumes. Presented above.
Chapter Thirty-Five: On the Commonalities and Differences in the Precepts for Monks and Nuns. This section includes five chapters that specifically exhort the assembly of nuns.
The present compilation takes the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) as its primary authority; where this text is insufficient, it supplements it with other sections from various schools.
Throughout, I have clarified the underlying meanings and refined the phrasing with colloquial expressions so that readers may easily understand the contents upon perusal.

Upholding the Dharma without hesitation, I respectfully follow the ancient precedents; it is not that I dare engage in forced interpretation or arbitrarily establish headings, but rather to guard against my own shortcomings.
May the discerning gentlemen not reproach me.
*Vinaya-taoyao*, Volume One (Correctly explaining the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* while collating other schools).

This chapter has two main sections: first, a general discussion of the benefits gained by following the teachings of both transformation (*nirmāṇa*) and discipline (*vinaya*);
second, a specific discussion clarifying the resulting harm caused by violating these two types of teachings.
Within the first section concerning transformation, there are four parts. The first is the *Hīnayāna* sūtras, such as the *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, which states that the Buddha was about to...

When the World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa and there was no teacher remaining, Ānanda requested of the Buddha, saying: "Bhikṣus, if you are able to uphold the precepts, they shall be your Great Teacher;
it would be no different from my remaining in the world. The *Śāsanānuśāsanī-sūtra* states: "If one lacks pure precepts, all wholesome merits will fail to arise.
Furthermore, it is because of these precepts that concentration and wisdom are obtained. Another sūtra says: "As for the precepts..."
The root of practice abiding and sustaining is metaphorically likened to the great earth, for it is able to generate and sustain all things; thus it is called "abiding and sustaining.

Second, regarding the Mahāyāna sūtras: as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states, "Fully receiving and upholding the teachings on dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), practicing the six points of harmonious respect (*ṣaḍvidha-sāmīcī-kriyā*), skillfully guiding the great assembly with a mind free from sorrow or regret, and preaching the True Dharma without contradicting its teachings—for these reasons, one is able [to abide and sustain]."
It ensures that the Three Jewels are not interrupted and that the Dharma may abide for a long time. Furthermore, a verse states: "Precepts are the foundation of unsurpassed Bodhi;
one should fully maintain pure precepts. If one can firmly uphold the prohibitions, this is what the Tathāgata praises.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says: "The Bodhisattvas requested the Buddha to establish prohibitory precepts, so that the Dharma might endure for a long time, as it does in other Buddha-fields."

Therefore, the Buddha permitted this; as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If I do not maintain the precepts, I shall fall into the three evil realms and will not even obtain a human body, let alone be able to bring sentient beings to maturity, purify a buddha-field, or perfect all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The *Satyaka-nirgrantha Sūtra* states: "If one does not maintain the precepts, one will not even obtain the body of a mangy jackal, let alone [a human body]."

One shall attain a body of merit. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If one wishes to see the Buddha-nature and realize Great Nirvāṇa, one must cultivate and maintain the pure precepts with a profound mind.
If one upholds this sūtra yet violates the pure precepts, such a person belongs to the retinue of Māra and is not my disciple;
I do not permit them to receive, uphold, or recite this sūtra. The *Candrapradīpa Samādhi Sūtra* states: "Though one possesses form and longevity..."

Furthermore, even one who is widely learned but lacks ethical discipline is like a bird or beast; though they may dwell in a lowly position, one who has little learning or insight yet can maintain pure precepts is called a superior person.
Third, as for those who propound the Hinayana, such as the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it says: "The pavilion of the factors of enlightenment takes ethical discipline as its courtyard;
the city of meditative concentration takes ethical discipline as its pillars. One must wear the seal of ethical discipline to gain entry into the assembly of the virtuous. *Vibhāṣā* (or *Viśeṣa*).
The *Vibhāṣā* states that *śīla* means "coolness," referring to the absence of the heat of broken precepts as well as the heat of the three evil realms;
it is also called "concentration" (*samādhi*), for one who abides in the precepts finds concentration easily; it is also called a "pool," because it is where the assembly of noble ones bathes;
and it is also called a "mirror," because when the precepts are pure, no image of a self appears. Fourth, regarding the Mahāyāna treatises, such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
The treatise says: If one seeks great benefit, one should firmly uphold the precepts as if cherishing precious treasures or protecting one's own life.
The precepts are the dwelling place of all wholesome dharmas; it is like one who wishes to walk without feet, fly without wings, or cross over without a boat—it is impossible.
If one lacks pure precepts yet desires to obtain good fruits, it is likewise so. If one abandons them...

Although this person who observes the precepts may dwell in the mountains, taking medicine and eating grass no differently from birds and beasts, if they can maintain the precepts, their fragrance will be heard throughout the ten directions and their fame will spread far and wide; gods and humans will love and respect them, and all their wishes will be fulfilled.

When such a person who maintains the precepts reaches the end of their life, the "sword-wind" (kṣurapra-vāyu) dismembers the body and the sinews and veins are severed, yet their mind feels no fear. As the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra* states: [The third...]
The twelve marks [of a Great Man] are attained through the cause of non-differentiation, all of which are obtained by upholding the precepts;

if one does not uphold the precepts, one cannot even obtain the body of a lowly person, let alone the retribution of the marks of a Great Man. Next, regarding the regulations within the Vinaya, there are two parts. First, concerning the sincere text of the original Vinaya:
the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states, "If one wishes to obtain the five benefits of material offerings, one should receive and uphold this Vinaya. What are these five?
First, to establish the Buddha-dharma; second, to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time; third, not wishing to harbor doubts or regrets, one seeks instruction from others;

fourth, to act as a refuge for monks and nuns who have committed offenses; fifth, desiring to travel and transform beings in all directions without hindrance—these are the five benefits for a faithful son of good family.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that one who upholds the Vinaya obtains [these benefits].
There are five merits: first, the quality of the precepts is firm and solid; second, one is able to overcome all adversaries; third, one is certainly fearless in the midst of the assembly;
fourth, one is well able to resolve all doubts and regrets; fifth, one skillfully upholds the *vinaya*, causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "For how long will the Buddha-dharma remain in the world? The Buddha replied: "It shall remain as long as pure bhikṣus recite the *prātimokṣa*."

"Decay" refers to the duration of the Dharma remaining in the world; this applies even to the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Next, regarding the explanation according to the treatises, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Vyākaraṇa*) states:
"The original sound is called *vinaya*, which is abbreviated as *vini*. This means the conduct practiced by superior persons (*viśiṣṭapudgala*).
Both the Buddhas—whether Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas—and ordinary persons who practice it are superior persons. [This is the view of] the Sarvāstivāda school.
The Treatise says: The Buddha told the bhikṣus that because the precepts possess four meanings, violating them is more serious than in other sūtras:
(1) The precepts are the level ground of the Buddha-dharma, from which all myriad virtues grow; (2) All sons of the Buddha rely on the precepts for their abode;
if one lacks the precepts, they have no basis; (3) All sentient beings exist by virtue of the precepts; (4) The three [kinds of] precepts are the path leading to nirvāṇa.
The initial gateway of the *pāṭha* (path) is that if one lacks the precepts, there is no means by which one can enter the city of *nirvāṇa*.
These four precepts are the jeweled ornaments of the Buddha-dharma, capable of adorning the Buddha-dharma. The *Saddarśana-śāstra* (*Shan-jian lun*) states:
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "After my parinirvāṇa, there shall be five dharmas that cause the Dharma to abide for a long time: first, the *vinaya* is your great teacher; second, down to..."
1. Five persons who uphold the Vinaya remain in the world; 2. if there are ten persons in the Middle Kingdom or five in the borderlands, they may receive the precepts according to the Dharma;

3. up to twenty persons may expiate offenses according to the Dharma; 4. because of the presence of masters and those who uphold the Vinaya, the Buddha-dharma shall abide in the world for five thousand years;
5. as stated in the *Five Hundred Questions*, the Buddha has two bodies: although his physical body has departed, his Dharma-body remains.
In this world, those who revere the Dharma and keep the Dharma in mind revere the Buddha and keep the Buddha in mind; those who uphold the precepts see the Dharma-body;
and those who protect the Dharma protect the Buddha. Just as when the *Poṣadha* is recited every half-month, one sees me.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* asks: "Why was the Vinaya first compiled? Because it is supreme and because it is secret, unlike the various Sūtras which are not restricted by time."
In the *Ren shuo ming de jing lü* (The Sūtra and Vinaya Spoken by a Layman), it is not so; because the Buddha himself taught that the essentials must be within the Saṃgha, it is superior.
The *Fenbie gongde lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merits) states: "Because it is supremely secret and not the practice of worldly people, it is not permitted to be seen."

Second, specifically regarding the two teachings, a detailed explanation of the causes for decline due to transgressions is as follows. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that during the age of the Semblance Dharma (*saddharmapratirūpaka*), five phenomena lead to the extinction of the Dharma:
first, a bhikṣu who has attained only minor realizations claims to have realized the state of an arhat;
second, laypeople are reborn in heaven while monastics fall into hell; third, some people abandon worldly occupations to leave the home life but then break their precepts; fourth... [text continues].
Many people assist those who have broken the precepts, even up to Arhats being beaten and reviled. Furthermore, there are five kinds of fear:
first, not cultivating the body, morality, mind, and wisdom oneself, and furthermore teaching others not to cultivate the dharmas of the body, morality, and so forth;
second, keeping śrāmaṇeras; third, providing dependence to others; fourth, living together with lay attendants and śrāmaṇeras without knowing [how to manage them]; [fifth, ...].
The three characteristics refer to digging the earth, cutting the grass, and watering [the seeds]. Although the five [factors] are recited from the Vinaya-piṭaka, they are disordered in sequence.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that there are five ways in which the True Dharma is rapidly extinguished: first, there is a bhikṣu who does not carefully receive or recite the Vinaya, delights in forgetting its phrases, and furthermore teaches others;
since the text is incomplete, its meaning is deficient. Second, he is a preeminent person within the Saṃgha...

The Elder was honored by the entire nation, yet he mostly did not uphold the Vinaya but practiced what was unwholesome; later generations emulated him, leading them to abandon the precepts and conduct themselves within the three realms of existence.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who upheld the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā, yet they failed to instruct either the clergy or the laity, and thus passed away suddenly, causing the Dharma to be extinguished.
These four types of bhikṣus are difficult to instruct; they do not accept wholesome words, and other virtuous bhikṣus likewise find it hard to guide them.

The Buddha set aside five ways of mutual reviling and seeking out each other's faults that cause the True Dharma to perish quickly. Furthermore, there are five transgressions for one who violates the precepts:
first, self-harm; second, being censured by the wise; third, the spread of an evil reputation; fourth, giving rise to regret at the time of death;
and fifth, falling into the evil realms after death. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Though one has received the precepts for many years, if one does not know [the rules]..."
The five qualities [of one who should not be relied upon] are: first, ignorance of what constitutes an offense; second, ignorance of what does not constitute an offense;
third, ignorance of what is light; fourth, ignorance of what is heavy; and fifth, failure to recite the precepts extensively and with full mastery.

Furthermore, when various bhikṣus neglected the study of the Vinaya and instead devoted themselves to reciting the Sūtras and Abhidharma, the World-Honored One rebuked them in various ways, even stating that because of this...
Because the Vinaya and the Buddha-dharma abide in the world, there are many senior elder bhikṣus who study the Vinaya. The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states:

"There are elder bhikṣus who do not study the precepts nor praise the precepts; yet there are other bhikṣus who delight in studying the precepts, but they are unable to exhort or praise them at the proper time.
Seeing such faults in these elders, I do not praise them, fearing that others [might follow suit].
People who practice and study [the Dharma] endure suffering throughout the long night. The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states:

"One who has attained one hundred years of seniority (*vassa*) but does not know the Dharma should rely upon one with ten years of seniority who knows the Dharma. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If one does not understand the Vinaya but only understands the Sūtras and Śāstras, one may not ordain a śrāmaṇera nor act as a preceptor (*upādhyāya*). The *Māyā-sūtra* states: "Those who delight in fine clothing and indulge in wanton play..."

To treat a slave as a bhikṣu or a maidservant as a bhikṣuṇī, to take no pleasure in the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), to slander the *vinaya*, and to commingle the property of the Triple Gem—these are called the signs of the extinction of the Dharma.

The *Buddhabhāṣita-samādhi-sūtra* states that those who commit the four grave offenses and consume the offerings of the faithful in vain incur sins exceeding those of killing eighty-four thousand parents. The *Brahmajāla-sūtra* states that if a Buddha...

Because one has left the household life with faith and received the Buddha’s true precepts, should one give rise to the thought of violating those holy precepts, they shall not receive the offerings of any donors, nor shall they be permitted to walk upon the ground of the king;

they shall not drink from or use the water and soil of the king, and five thousand great ghosts will constantly block their path. These ghosts will cry out: "A great thief has entered our village, city, town, or house!"
The ghosts there further swept away his footprints, and all the people of the world reviled him, saying, "He is a thief within the Buddha-dharma;
no sentient being wishes to see such a person who violates the precepts, for he is no different from a beast or a block of wood. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Because the bhikṣus do not uphold the precepts, they possess the eight kinds of impure wealth, yet they claim, 'This is permitted by the Buddha. How can this be?

This person’s tongue does not curl back. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: What is meant by a person who has broken the precepts? A person who has broken the precepts is not loved or respected by others;
their home is like a cemetery that people do not approach. The evil mind of a person who has broken the precepts is fearsome, like a *rākṣasa*.
A person who has broken the precepts is not sought out by others, just as a thirsty person does not go toward a dried-up well.
The mind of one who has broken the precepts is constantly filled with doubt and regret, just as a person who has committed a crime is perpetually afraid that punishment will arrive.
A person who has broken the precepts is like a field struck by hail; it can no longer be relied upon. A person who has broken the precepts is like a bitter gourd;

though its shape resembles its seed, it is unfit for consumption. A person who has broken the precepts is like a village of bandits; one cannot take refuge there. Thus is the breaking of the precepts.
Such a person is like a gravely ill man who does not wish to draw near one who has broken the precepts; he cannot escape suffering.
Like a perilous path that is difficult to traverse, one cannot dwell together with one who has broken the precepts.

Like a wicked thief who is difficult to approach, one who has broken the precepts is like a pit of fire which the practitioner must avoid; it is difficult to associate with one who has broken the precepts.
One who dwells in such a state is like a venomous snake; one who violates the precepts is not to be approached or touched, being like a great conflagration.
One who violates the precepts is like a broken ship, unfit for crossing over. One who violates the precepts is like vomited food, which cannot be eaten again.
One who violates the precepts among a virtuous assembly is like a vicious horse in a herd of fine horses. Thus is the violation of the precepts.
Such a person, though in form resembling a bhikṣu, is like a corpse among those who sleep;
a person who has broken the precepts is like a counterfeit pearl among genuine pearls; a person who has broken the precepts is like an eranda tree in a sandalwood grove.
Such various and immeasurable offenses of breaking the precepts are beyond description; the practitioner should therefore maintain single-mindedness.
The *Jie Chui Zui Qingzhong Jing* (Sūtra on the Lightness and Heaviness of Violating the Precepts) states:

The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana, "If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, lacking a sense of shame and remorse, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt and violates the *śaikṣa-dharmas*, they shall fall into hell for a lifespan equal to five hundred years of the Cāturmahārājika devas, which, by human reckoning, is nine hundred thousand years.
[Private Note: If calculated using the small number system, this would be nine million years; if using the large number system, it would be ninety million.]

[For a thousand lifetimes, some have secretly doubted that there was a textual error. The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "If one lacks a sense of shame and conscience, and with a disrespectful mind treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, they commit a *pātideśanīya* offense.
They shall fall into hell for a lifespan equal to a thousand years by the reckoning of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which corresponds to three hundred and sixty million years by human calculation.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "If one lacks a sense of shame and conscience, and with a disrespectful mind treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, they commit a [pātideśanīya offense]."
One who has committed a *yātti* (wrongdoing) falls into hell with a lifespan equal to two thousand years in the Yāma Heaven;

in human reckoning, this is twenty-four billion and forty thousand years. The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "If one lacks a sense of shame and conscience and treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, they commit a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
One who has committed a [wrongdoing] equal to a lifespan of four thousand years in the Tuṣita Heaven falls into hell..."
[In the plow-drawing hell], they remain for fifty billion and sixty thousand years by human reckoning (*note: seven characters are missing after "fifty," which can be determined by calculation*).
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "If one lacks a sense of shame and remorse and treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;
such a person falls into hell for eight thousand years by the reckoning of the Tuṣita Heaven, which corresponds to two hundred and thirty billion years by human reckoning."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "If one lacks a sense of shame and remorse and treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, they commit a *pārājika* offense.

Such a person will fall into hell for a lifespan equal to sixteen thousand years as measured by the gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven—which, in human reckoning, is nine hundred twenty-one billion and sixty thousand years.
In total, this applies to both monks and nuns regarding the five categories and seven groups of offenses."

If one were to calculate the total duration of these offenses by treating each individual transgression separately, according to the reckoning of human days, months, and years, it amounts to a total of one trillion two hundred and sixty-one billion five hundred million years spent falling into hell. The holy teaching is not false;

therefore, one must be especially reverent and cautious. One should cultivate skillful means, examine one’s own body and speech, exert one’s will with single-minded devotion, and aspire to emulate those who have gone before.
The Sages may not allow themselves to be indolent, for they do not disparage the Buddha’s words; thus the Sūtra says: "The True Dharma abides, the True Dharma perishes"—the meaning lies herein.
Chapter Two: On the Causes for the Arising of the Teaching.
This chapter has two main sections: first, clarifying the intent behind the emergence of the teaching; second, clarifying the sequence of its exposition.

Regarding the first, the intent behind the emergence of the teaching: Question: For what reason did the Buddha establish these five divisions of the *vinaya* for his disciples, with their varying degrees of gravity, thereby causing sentient beings to mutually give rise to disputes over right and wrong? Answer: The Buddha established them for the sake of the bhikṣus.
Even a single division of the Vinaya does not possess two names, let alone five;

yet the Tathāgata, governing the world, thoroughly understood the dispositions of sentient beings and established precepts according to their transgressions, opening or closing them as required by the occasion.

From the time he was under the twin śāla trees until his final traces were exhausted, the Venerable Upāli assisted in proclaiming this teaching—truly a preeminent figure among both teacher and disciple, encountered but once throughout the entire Bhadrakalpa.

Since the Tathāgata’s disappearance and Upāli’s withdrawal from view, there have been five arhats—Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Madhyāntika, Śāṇakavāsin, and Upagupta—who have successively maintained and transmitted [the teachings].
Although they did not equal the achievements of their predecessors, they were nonetheless secondary sages;
they are known as the "Eighty Reciters of the Vinaya," who briefly recorded the titles of the chapters but had not yet divided them into sections.

In the latter days of the era of Kāśyapa Mātanga, there was a sagacious king known as Aśoka. From his youth, he revered the profound and mysterious, and with a sincere mind, he sought the fruit of Buddhahood.
He then summoned from afar those of renowned virtue and re-edited the Tripiṭaka.

Subsequently, five men, including Dharmagupta and others, each relied upon their own teachers' traditions and vied with one another over points of agreement and difference; thus, the single Piṭaka of Vinaya was divided into five schools.

Although the articles and clusters [of the precepts] differ and the permissions and prohibitions vary, even if one examines the texts they appear divergent, there is no loss in their underlying meaning.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Though the five schools are each distinct, this does not hinder the Buddhas or the Great Nirvāṇa."
Regarding the sequence of the second translation (the following is based on the *Sanbao ji* by Fei Changfang, a scholar-translator of the Kaihuang era, in Chengdu):

*The Ten Recitations Vinaya*, fifty-eight fascicles (translated at Zhong Temple on the seventeenth day of the tenth month in the sixth year of Hongshi of the Qin dynasty; see the two *Qin lu* catalogs). This single work originally consisted of fifty-eight fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra, Puṇyatāra, [arrived] in the Qin...
Regarding the one known as Guṇabhadra (translated as "Virtue-Flower"), who was renowned for his observance of the precepts and his travels in spreading the teachings:

when he arrived at the capital, Yao Xing immediately summoned over six hundred monks of established virtue and merit, including Chang’an (the character "Chang" was changed due to the taboo name of Yao Chang), and invited Guṇabhadra to rest at Zhong Temple.
There, Guṇabhadra recited the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which Kumārajīva translated into the Qin language; three parts were successfully completed.
Before the second [volume] was finished, Tāranātha suddenly passed away; the assembly all lamented his loss deeply.

After Kumārajīva, they continued the translation together with Dharmaruci (translated into Chinese as *Fǎlè*) until the *Vinaya* was completed in three fascicles (these are the "Excellent Recitations" following the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, as seen in the two Qin records).
Furthermore, during the reign of Emperor An, there was the Tripiṭaka Master and Vinaya Master Vimalākṣa from Kaśmīra (translated into Chinese as *Wúgòu*).

In the eighth year of the Hongshi era of the Yao Qin dynasty, [the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*] arrived at Chang’an; it remained there until the passing of Kumārajīva, after which it was taken to Shouchun and housed at Shijian Temple.

There, a multitude of disciples specializing in the Vinaya gathered, and he extensively propagated the *Vinaya*. Originally, Kumārajīva’s version of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* consisted of fifty-eight fascicles;

later, under the direction of Saṃgharakṣa, it was expanded to sixty-one fascicles. Furthermore, the title "Ten Recitations" (*Shisong*) was changed to "Vinaya Recitations" (*Pinisong*), and thus it exists today as such.

Two schools of the Vinaya-piṭaka spread to the East: first, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations); then, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* in forty-five fascicles—“Dharmagupta” being the name of a person who was the master of this school;
it has now been expanded to sixty fascicles, as seen in the *Jìnshì zá lù* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jìn Dynasty). This one school originally consisted of forty-five fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Ān of the Jìn dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas from Kapiśī—“Buddhayaśas” meaning “Awakening Fame” in the language of Qín—[translated it].
It was recorded that in the eighth year of Hongshi, Kumārajīva arrived at Guzang; however, he had already been in Chang’an for some time.

Originally residing in the Western Regions, he had taken up the teachings of Buddharakṣa as his master. Upon hearing that [Buddharakṣa] had reached Guzang, he felt great joy and urged Yao Xing to send an envoy to welcome him.
Yao Xing had not yet granted permission when he commanded Kumārajīva to translate the scriptures, and Kumārajīva furthermore...
He said: "One who wishes to propagate the unsurpassed Dharma teachings should ensure that the words, meanings, and underlying principles are perfectly integrated.
Although I have recited these texts, I am not yet proficient in their underlying principles; only Dharmayaśas has a profound mastery of the scriptures' intent. He is currently in Guzang.

I pray that you issue an imperial decree to summon him so that he may examine the matter three times for thoroughness before we commit it to writing. Only then shall the subtle words not fall into oblivion, and our work gain the trust of the world."
When Yao Xing heard that [Kumārajīva] had been well-received, he immediately dispatched envoys with generous gifts, all of which Kumārajīva refused.

He laughed and said, "Since Your Majesty’s gracious decree has been issued, I ought to set out at once. However, as the Patron treats scholars so generously, if my treatment were to match that accorded to Kumārajīva, I would not dare accept such an order.
Yao Xing sighed in admiration of his prudence and sincerity; only after repeated and earnest exhortations did he finally arrive in Chang’an. Yao Xing himself...
Upon his departure, a separate provincial administration was established at the Xiaoyao Garden to provide him with the four requisites of monastic life, yet he accepted none of them;
when it was time for almsround, he would take only a single meal. His hair was red, and he was skilled in the Vibhāṣā; thus, his contemporaries called him "Red-bearded Vibhāṣā.
Since Kumārajīva took him as his teacher, he too was referred to as the "Great Vibhāṣā," and the four requisites were provided for him.
His robes, alms bowl, and bedding filled three rooms, yet he did not set his heart upon them; instead, he devoted himself to building the Xuansi monastery.
Previously, when he had recited the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya), he had suspected there were omissions or errors and had attempted to have it recited again.

He found that the text contained approximately fifty thousand words of medicinal prescriptions and formulas. After one day of review, he recited it without a single error, whereupon the assembly all bowed in submission.
From the twelfth year of Hongshi until the fifteenth year, when the translation of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other sūtras and vinayas was finally concluded, he offered a distribution of alms.
He presented ten thousand rolls of silk to Buddhayaśas, but he would not accept any of it.
To the two śramaṇas Daohan and Zhu Fonian, who served as scribes, he bestowed one thousand rolls each; to the remaining five hundred śramaṇas of renowned virtue, he gave generous donations of cloth.

Later, he returned to the West, and his final whereabouts remained unknown. Regarding the transmission of the Vinaya teachings to the East, there is the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), the second of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Twenty-section Vinaya), in forty fascicles (translated in the eleventh month of the twelfth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty by Faxian and others; as seen in the *Zhudaozu lu* and the *Bielu*, some versions contain thirty fascicles).
This particular recension originally consisted of forty fascicles. During the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra from the country of North India...

Dharmakṣema (translated as Juéxián in Chinese) translated [this work] at two locations, Yangdu and Mount Lú, with the śramaṇas Fǎyè, Huìyì, Huìyán, and others serving as scribes. The Vinaya teachings spread eastward.

This is the third part of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Míshīsē lǜ), consisting of thirty-four fascicles (the *Jiàozōngqílù* and *Biélù* state it was twenty-four fascicles; this is likely an error). This single recension originally consisted of thirty-four [fascicles].
In the reign of the deposed Emperor Yingyang Wang, the Tripiṭaka Master Vinaya-ācārya Buddhayaśas from Kaśmīra arrived at the capital of Yangdu.

His name means "Awakened Longevity" in the Song language. In his youth, he received his training in the Mahīśāsaka school, specializing in the categories of the Vinaya while also attaining mastery in the essentials of Dhyāna.
He arrived in the seventh month of the first year of the Jingping era. Previously, Faxian had obtained [the text] in the Kingdom of Siṃhala.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* had originally not been translated when [Guṇavarman] passed away.
When the monks in the capital heard that Buddhayaśas was well-versed in this field of study, they deliberated together and requested him to produce a translation.

Consequently, in the eleventh month of winter in that year, they gathered at Longguang Temple to translate it into thirty-four fascicles; Yaśas held the Sanskrit text while the Yuezhi śramaṇa Huìyán acted as the scribe.
They took turns receiving the dictation and collating the text and principles; Wang Lian of Langye, serving as Palace Attendant, acted as the patron (*dānapati*).

It was not until the twelfth month of the second year that it was completed. This is the first fascicle of the *Sifen lü jieben* (The Four-Part Vinaya Precept Manual), the fourth part of the *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya), which transmits the teachings of the Vinaya to the East.
[Note: The *Jiaye pi lü da ben* (Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya Great Text) has not yet arrived. This single fascicle reached the era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty.
The Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci— translated into Wei as Zhīxī (Wisdom-Longing)— a native of the city of Vārāṇasī in the Southern Indian kingdom of East Wei,
arrived at Yecheng from the beginning of the Yuánxiàng era until the end of the Xīnghé era. During this time,

although there was also Bodhiruci who produced translations both before and after him, the various catalogs transmitted by successive scribes omitted [the latter] and placed [Prajñāruci’s works] above.
Regarding the mention of the *Prajñā* [sūtras], it is only said to have been translated by "Liu Zhi," yet it is unknown which Liu Zhi this refers to.

To this day, as various catalogs intersect and cross-reference one another, errors and redundancies have become so intertwined that it is difficult to establish a definitive determination. I hope that future scholars, drawing upon broad research, will investigate this matter.
This concludes the fifth section on the liberation brought about by the transmission of the Vinaya teachings to the East.
Chapter Three: Explaining the Names of the Sections and Aggregates.
This chapter has two main sections: first, enumerating the numbers and explaining the names; second, distinguishing their functions according to their nature.

Regarding the first, enumerating the numbers and explaining the names, there are five sections and seven aggregates. When differentiated according to their meanings, they are explained as having seven names. Thus it is concluded.

Regarding the treatise on offenses, although it actually restricts itself to designating six categories of dharma, we shall first explain the seven groups (*sapta-varga*) and subsequently interpret the five sections (*pañca-vastu*):
(1) *pārājika*, (2) *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, (3) *sthūlātyaya*, (4) *pāyattika*, (5) *pratideśanīya*, (6) *duṣkṛta*, and (7) *durbhāṣita*.
These seven names have no direct translations in the Vinaya; they are provisionally rendered here by inferring their meanings.
Briefly explaining the initial path, the term *pārājika* (defeat) has the meaning of "extreme evil" according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which provides three interpretations:
first, it is called "retrogression," because by committing this precept, one becomes ineligible for the fruits of the Path;

second, it is called "not living together," meaning that one has not merely lost the Path but further ceases to belong to either of the two types of Saṃgha—the *karmadāna* (formal ritual assembly) or the *poṣadha* (confessional assembly); third, it carries the meaning of "falling away."

After casting off this body, one falls into the Avīci Hell; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one falls into an undesirable place, while the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* says that by fighting with Māra and violating this precept, one immediately falls into defeat.
In this Vinaya, a *pārājika* offense is like severing a person's head, from which they cannot rise again; if one violates this precept, one no longer constitutes a bhikṣu.
It is named from the practice of the dharma; it is also called "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*) because it is named from the complete severance of the various dharmas.
Thus the verse says: "Those who perform evil deeds are like corpses, not tolerated by the assembly. For this reason, one must maintain the precepts;
it is also called "not living together" (*asaṃvāsa*), as previously mentioned in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. Regarding the two names for *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *vaśeṣa* means...
"Saṃgha" means "community. "Saṃghāvaśeṣa" means "remainder. If one commits this offense, the practitioner is defiled by entanglements and is not entirely pure in their conduct;
because there remains a residual offense that must be extinguished through the community (saṃgha), it is called "Saṃghāvaśeṣa" (Community Residue).
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "It is like a person who has been struck by another; because a throat remains, it is called 'residual' (*avaśeṣa*). The *Sudarsana* states: "'Saṃgha'..."
*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* means "belonging to the Saṃgha" (saṃgha-bhava), referring to the initial stage when the *paryuṣitaparivāsa* rite is first granted;
*avaśeṣa* means "remainder," referring to the subsequent stage when the *āvarhaṇa* (expiation) rite is granted. Regarding the offense of *sthūlātyaya*, the *Samantapāsādikā* states:
*sthūla* means "great," and *atyaya* means "obstruction"; it refers to that which subsequently obstructs the path of wholesome qualities.
The nature of falling into the evil destinies is base and defiled; this name is established based on what is unwholesome. The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states:

"Sthūlātyaya is 'gross obstruction' (*sthūla-vāraṇa*) or 'gross transgression' (*sthūla-aticāra*). There are two kinds: first, the preliminary stage (*prayoga*) of a grave offense; second, that which can sever the roots of goodness.
As for "transgression" (*aticāra*), it refers to acting in a manner that does not conform to the precepts established by the Buddha; hence it is called a "transgression. This is the fourth name.
*Pāyattika* is translated as "falling" (*pāta*). Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one falls into the hells of burning, boiling, and concealment;
therefore, it is called "falling. In the first section of this Vinaya, the thirty rules concerning forfeiture (*niḥsargika*) involve offenses arising from material things;

because greed and arrogance arise, one is compelled to relinquish them to the Saṃgha, hence they are called *niḥsargika*. The remaining *pāyattika* offenses involve transgressions arising from specific circumstances, which are expiated by confessing alone before another person.
Furthermore, as these offenses are equal in grade, they are all subsumed under the third category. Regarding the *naiḥsargika*, the old translation is "abandonment and falling" (*she-duo*).
The *Sheng lun* (Treatise on Sounds) states that *nai* is translated as "exhaustion" (*jin*) and *sargika* as "abandonment" (*she*).

Regarding the *pāyattika*, its original name is *pāyatti* (the *yi* in *pāyatti* is pronounced with the *e* tone). It has five names; regarding the *pratideśanīya*, the meaning is translated as "confession."
That [offense] is named "repentance" (*pratideśanīya*) because it is established based on the object of its remedy; the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] states that this offense should be confessed.
This very point is clearly explained in the words for repentance found in the *Dharmaguptaka* (*Catuḥpariṣatka-vinaya*). The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states:

*pātideśanīya* is translated as "that which should be confessed individually," meaning one confesses the committed offense before another person. Sixth, regarding the name *duṣkṛta*, it is good... [text ends].
It is said that *dukkaṭa* means "evil" and *pācittiya* means "to do. In this Vinaya, *śikṣākaraṇīya* is translated as "that which should be studied";

the monks of the Western Regions say it is translated as "guarding the precepts. Because these offenses are subtle and extremely difficult to maintain, they are named according to what is studied and guarded as one proceeds.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One sees the commission of the offense with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)."
"O Bhikṣus, when rain falls heavily, is it not by focusing one's mind exclusively upon it that one is said to be 'guarding the precepts'?

Seventh is the "evil speaker. This is subsumed under the sixth category (*ṣaṭka-nikāya*) of this Vinaya; its meaning is divided into two parts: first, "evil conduct" (*duṣkṛta*) by way of the body, and second, "evil speech" (*durbhāṣita*) by way of the mouth.
Therefore, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense, and with the subsequent addition of "evil speech," there are seven in total. This is discussed according to their essential nature.

The actual definition of the *pārājika* offenses is sixfold, yet they are divided into seven based on differences in their karmic consequences. Regarding the question of why the five categories (*pañca-pārājika*) and seven groups (*sapta-saṃghāvaśeṣa*, etc.

are distinguished: the answer is that there are three types of uniformity. They are subsumed under the categories because of this uniformity: first, uniformity of name; second, uniformity of substance; and third, uniformity of completion.

As for the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses), they are called "uneven" in both name and meaning. Various offenses, being mixed together, are collectively gathered into "groups" (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). This is the second point.

Regarding the indeterminate offenses (*aniyata-āpatti*): if discussed in terms of their objective basis (*ālambana*), they encompass all seven classes of offenses; however, if one considers their essential nature (*dravya*), they consist merely of a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) arising from doubt or lack of faith.

As for the texts that specify three or two offenses, these are merely brief mentions of instances where doubt arises; other meanings are not fully exhausted and are described in detail in the commentaries (*śāstra*).

Among the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptadharmā vinayasya samathāḥ*), these offenses are also present; however, this is because there has been no mutual contention regarding the four types of disputes (*caturvidha-adhikaraṇa*).

Because they are harmonious, these seven medicines are prescribed to eradicate sinful disputes; as the textual meaning is extensive, it is not the essential point here, but should such matters arise, one hopes to seek them in the original texts.

Second, regarding the classification of medicines according to their nature (*svabhāva*): Question: Within the three natures of mind, does the sense of transgressing the precepts exist in all of them? Answer: It does.

Regarding the transgression of the precepts with a wholesome mind, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that a young bhikṣu, being ignorant of the characteristics of the precepts, committed an offense by sweeping away the grass on top of a stūpa, whereby he obtained both merit and sin.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that a bhikṣu in charge of monastic affairs, being ignorant of the precepts, misappropriated the property of the Three Jewels;
or, seeing someone offering their body [as an act of devotion], he felt compassion and sorrow, assisting them in gathering firewood; or, seeing his parents or teachers...
If a monk violates the laws of the state and is subjected to corporal punishment, such as being sought for execution by sword or rope, he may pray to be quickly freed from suffering.
Although such acts are performed with a virtuous intention, one cannot escape liability through ignorance; all constitute grave offenses (*pārājika*).

Since the Dharma is something that can be learned, the fault of ignorance—failing to learn it—is even more severe, applying even to minor infractions (*duṣkṛta*) down to the *dūṣaṇa* level. As for the retribution received in future lives, the resulting suffering is likewise [severe].

If one treats the original precepts with negligence and compliance, and the mind does not further increase in merit, thereby violating the essence of the original undertaking and failing to escape hell, this is called an offense committed with a virtuous mind.

Second, regarding offenses committed with an unvirtuous mind: this refers to those who, either knowing the characteristics of the precepts or being ignorant of them, treat the holy teachings with contempt, disparage the words of the Buddha, and thus violate prohibitions; lacking shame and remorse, their intention becomes increasingly perverse.
When a wicked mind gradually intensifies, it is called an unwholesome transgression of the mind. Thus, the *Abhidharmadīpa* states that there are four kinds of grave mental offenses:
first, turbid and heavy greed, hatred, and delusion; second, lack of faith in karmic retribution; third, disregard for the precepts one has received;
and fourth, treating the Buddha’s words with contempt. Therefore, if one acts with such a state of mind, one incurs a grave offense and achieves [the result] as described in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
The treatise states: "It is more harmful to kill an ant with a mind of malice than to kill a human being with a compassionate mind and commit a *pārājika* offense.

This person commits an offense that will certainly result in suffering, because both the time and the retribution are fixed. Even if one merely gives rise to the intention and establishes a remedy, one may avoid the single offense of violating the disciplinary rules (*śikṣāpada*), yet this does not prevent the karmic path from remaining;
it ultimately cannot be eliminated. As the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: 'Devadatta committed a *sthūlātyaya* for breaking the Sangha.'"
The Buddha commanded that such offenses be confessed before the Saṃgha; yet regarding the path of karma, one still falls into Avīci Hell, while other matters remain beyond words.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states that there are two types of karmic action: first, the certainty of the action itself; second, the certainty of the resulting retribution.

That which cannot be altered even by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas refers specifically to transgressions committed with an unwholesome mind. Third, those who transgress the precepts with an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind are said to lack protection.
When the mind that observes the precepts flows along with the current and forms intentions that are neither good nor evil, arising suddenly, it is called an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state of mind.

An offense occurs when, like a foolish bhikṣu who does not recognize the characteristics of the precepts, he lets his body and speech run wild, harming living beings, cutting down grass and trees, acting as a matchmaker for laypeople, or misappropriating communal property;
thus, his physical conduct is ruined, and he defiles the pure vessels of the Sangha. Such is the case.
These examples are all included within the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If one follows the tenets of this treatise, they also possess the sense of producing retribution (*vipāka*).

Question: Since the indeterminate is not karma, how can it produce retribution? Answer: There are two ways in which retribution is produced: 1. First, there is a preparatory effort (*prayoga*), and subsequently, one enters into an indeterminate state;

because the karma is completed while the mind remains in an indeterminate state, it is said to "produce retribution," yet in reality, the indeterminate itself is not the fruit of a determinate mark (*vyākṛta-phala*). 2. [The second type involves]... (the text continues).

It is not that one does not experience a collective retribution while there is no distinct individual experience; as in the sutras, a *dhūta* bhikṣu did not perceive he was killing a living being, yet later he was killed by a pig.
Furthermore, the *Pañcaśata-praśna* states that a steward bhikṣu who inadvertently touched a vessel containing pure food later became a ghost that eats excrement.
As for the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it explains that karma formed during sleep is also an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) retribution. Question: How is this so?

Question: Is there an indeterminate offense that does not entail retribution? Answer: It is said that for one who knows the characteristics of the precepts, is well-versed in their observance and violation, and whose mind is constantly diligent—yet who, being indifferent and forgetful, commits a transgression against a prohibition through unintended circumstances—this is an opening where there is no offense. This includes cases such as: keeping extra robes beyond the allotted days without declaring them pure (*śuddhi*);
failing to properly guard the sense gates; nocturnal emissions due to sleep; or accidentally falling from a roof beam and thereby killing a human life. Such instances as these are not offenses.
This example is not intended as a definitive limit. Furthermore, regarding these three types of mind, there are two ways of confronting an object:

if one commits a *prakṛti-sāvadya* (natural transgression), such as killing or stealing, one incurs both types of offenses—namely, the offense of the path of action (*karmapatha*) and the offense of violating the precepts. This is because it involves harming sentient beings, and thus it is grave.

If one commits a *pratikṣepa-sāvadya* (prohibited transgression), such as damaging plants or trees, one incurs only the offense of violating the teaching and does not incur the offense of the path of action, because there are no sentient beings to be harmed.

Therefore, if one disparages the retribution of ordinary beings while harboring such thoughts in one's breast, who could avoid transgression? Once a transgression has occurred, one must perform repentance to restore purity and return to the ranks of the Sangha.
What is the meaning of harboring malice and defiling one’s own mind and conduct, thereby failing to join the pure assembly?

This is a great error in principle. The Vinaya states that one whose head is severed loses the Way in the present life; however, when discussing the essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*), it is actually inherently pure. In the world today...

When a person violates the precept against sexual misconduct, they are initially filled with fear and dread; yet later, through concealed reflection, they conclude that the precepts are utterly nonexistent.

Consequently, they conform to this view and fail to restrain their faculties, allowing their minds to run wild and indulge their passions as they commit transgressions. Is this not because they themselves were ignorant of the precepts, thereby leading the common world astray?

This is true even when violating the precept against sexual misconduct; how much more so for the other grave offenses such as killing and stealing, which one must always keep pure, let alone lesser ones.
In other sections, the principle is that words are transcended; thus, the Sarvāstivādins say, "It is better to simultaneously give rise to all precepts than to simultaneously break all precepts.
This statement is verified and its evidence is clearly known.
Chapter Four: Essentials of the Karmavācanā.

This chapter has three main sections: first, distinguishing the intent and explaining the name; second, the ritual procedure and its requisite conditions; third, the establishment of the rules regarding their scope and application.

First, regarding the clarification of the intent and the explanation of the name: As for the term *karma*, its meaning is "to accomplish a matter. That which is not the accomplishment of a matter is not called *karma*.
Because it possesses the efficacy to successfully complete a preceding matter, it is termed a "matter" (*vastu*); thus, the *Śata-śāstra* translates it as "matter.

Furthermore, since *karma* in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* refers to the activity (*karman*) of vocal instruction, the commentary on the *Abhidharma-samudaya-viniścaya-śāstra* translates it as "activity. However...

The Sangha is the person who performs the ritual, and the *karmavācanā* (formal act) is the dharma that is performed. Regarding the preceding matter, it must further be supported by the three methods according to reality;
only then will the matter be successfully accomplished. If even one method deviates, it will be difficult to bring to completion. Therefore, the Vinaya states:

"If one performs a *karmavācanā* that does not accord with the method of the *jñapti* (motion), or performs a *jñapti* that does not accord with the method of the *karmavācanā*, or performs a *karmavācanā* [that does not accord with the preceding steps]—if it proceeds in such a gradual manner..."
This gradually leads to the destruction of the True Dharma.

Second, the general clarification that all *karmas* (ritual acts) must necessarily have a gradual process; thus, there are ten distinct conditions: first, describing the matter; second, regarding the location;
third, assembling the Saṃgha; fourth, harmonizing the Saṃgha; fifth, selecting the assembly; sixth, stating the intention; seventh, granting... [the text continues].

Section Eight: Questions on the Fundamental Principles; Section Nine: Answers on the Matters; Section Ten: The Administration of the Dharma. The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it must have a specific purpose. What is that purpose?
It refers to matters such as the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*). If these matters did not exist, how could the Dharma alone be elucidated? Therefore, one must first describe the matters.
Furthermore, although the matters exist, if there were no location, those matters would have nothing to rely upon. Hence, the second section follows.

Regarding the discussion on the basis of location (*sthāna*): this refers to the establishment of the *saṃgha-sīmā*. With the exception of the formal ritual of boundary-establishment (*sīmā-bandhana-karman*), all other matters must rely upon a physical location.
Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "In a place where no ritual has been performed, one may not carry out monastic affairs.

Furthermore, one must also understand the origins, formation, and dissolution of the established boundaries; otherwise, if there is no formal establishment, the rite will not be accomplished, and human effort will be wasted in vain.

If one’s efforts reach their end without accomplishment, it is because although the proper place exists, the Dharma relies upon people for its propagation; if there were no Saṃgha, who could uphold the Dharma?

Therefore, next, the mallet is struck three times to assemble the assembly, to measure the number of monks, to observe the timing and regulations, and to universally recognize the distinctions in the functions of the four types of Saṃgha.
Even if they have gathered in body, if their minds are at variance, the Dharma will likewise be difficult to accomplish; hence, next—
The Elder of the fourth assembly briefly harmonized the sentiments of the community and addressed the Saṃgha, saying: "Virtuous ones, do not be offended by this gathering;
there is now a matter that requires the performance of a *karmavācanā*. I pray that the Saṃgha, out of compassion, will collectively uphold this procedure.

One must then clearly understand the fifteen kinds of silence according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, for matters may be right or wrong, and people may either acquiesce or resist, being of differing views.

Therefore, it is necessary to clarify that although the assembly is harmonious and silent, there may be individuals who do not belong to the same class; if such persons were to dwell together in confusion, it would contradict what is appropriate.

Thus, the fifth section sequentially excludes those in the assembly who have not yet received full ordination. Furthermore, one must know the number [of members] and the characteristics of right and wrong, as detailed below.
Once the assembly is pure, one should properly express the original intent; therefore, the sixth section correctly sets forth the fundamental matter.
The meaning is as follows: regarding the acts of formal accusation (*ukkhepana*) and calling to mind (*sāraṇīya*), there are four types of requests for permission from the Saṃgha.
First, when one’s own inclinations are followed and one requires much, one must request permission, such as in the cases of the two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Second, when one’s will is opposed and a disciplinary measure is established, or when one accepts [the penalty] without intention, there is no need to request permission, such as in the case of the seven *karmas* of disciplinary expulsion (*pravāsanīya*) or those who are insane.

These three types of *saṃghakarma*—the initial establishment of the Dharma, the formal demarcation of boundaries (*sīmābandha*), and that which is clarified here [the ordination]—do not require a formal request (*yācanā*).

Furthermore, the four types of *saṃghakarma* that are performed regularly, such as the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, the *Pravāraṇā*, and the distribution of voting sticks (*śalākā*), likewise do not require a formal request. However, the essence of *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action) lies in its meticulous adherence to the prescribed form;

thus, even if physical circumstances present obstacles, there is no hindrance so long as the mind is present. Therefore, the seventh [category], the granting of consent (*chanda*), should follow accordingly.
It should be understood that once harmony has been established by discussing what is right and wrong, it remains unknown what specific matter the assembly intends to perform;

Because there is an inquiry from the former [the master], there must logically be an answer given to dispel [the uncertainty]; hence, this follows in sequence.

The ninth [type of response] is answering according to the specific matter (*vastu*). When performing a particular *karmavācanā*, one must record both the formal act and the matter at hand, informing the Saṃgha of both;

one may not answer by mentioning the matter alone. For example, if one were to answer simply "the *poṣadha* and the recitation of the precepts" (*śīla-deśanā*), this is merely answering the matter itself and does not apply to a formal act (*karmavācanā*).
However, if one answers "the *śīla-deśanā* *karmavācanā*," this constitutes both the matter and the formal procedure.
Having announced that the aforementioned conditions are now complete, from this point forward it is appropriate to set forth the original intent;
therefore, the ten formal acts (*karmavācanā*) are performed in succession. These ten conditions generally indicate the sequence, though not every *karman* necessarily possesses all ten.

For instance, in rituals such as the delimitation of a boundary (*sīmā-bandhana*), there are no conditions such as a formal request (*yācñā*) or the declaration of consent (*chanda*). Similarly, this is also the case for the observance of the day (*poṣadha*) and the recitation of the precepts (*pravāraṇā*).

Regarding the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) and other rites, although there is no formal request (*yācanā*), it does not preclude the necessity of such reciprocal exchanges; one should perform them according to the requirements at the appropriate time.

Third, concerning the distinction between the general and the specific regarding the establishment of the rules, this is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the scope of the encompassed dharmas; second, citing specific examples.
The *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure) explains its formation and dissolution; this is divided into four sections: first, the *dharma* (rule); second, the *vastu* (matter);

To list these three positions, one must know their respective names. First, regarding the *cittānuvartana-dharma*: this refers to matters that are minor and for which no person is present within the boundary.

To cause one’s own practice to achieve the state of being free from transgressions of the precepts, one generates the thought, attends to the object, and communicates it verbally through one's own mind;

hence it is called "mental recitation" (*cittānuvāda*). Within this, there are four types: first, single mental recitation; second, face-to-face mental recitation; third, communal legal mental recitation;

and fourth, universal mental recitation. Regarding the first, single mental recitation: this refers to the boundaries, whether internal or external, where one speaks of the matter oneself according to the occasion, even if [the assembly] is absent.

It is so that there may be cases where the formal method for persons (*pudgala-dharma*) can still be accomplished. Because there are no people within the boundary (*sīmā*), the mental recitation rule was established; thus, as stated in the Vinaya, even in this way the precepts and the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) are successfully accomplished.

The *Samantapāsādikā* states that there are eight kinds of boundary characteristics: first, mountains; second, rocks; third, groves; fourth, trees; fifth, roads; sixth, anthills; seventh, rivers; and eighth, water.

Next, regarding the shape of the boundary, the *Samantapāsādikā* states that there are five kinds of boundary shapes: first, square; second, circular; third, drum-shaped; [fourth, half-moon-shaped]; and fifth, irregular.

Nowadays, those who perform the ritual mostly do so on open ground or within four-sided cities; wherever there are natural curves, one must first identify the limits and then announce them.
What is meant by "transgression"? It refers to a situation where the preceding student has not yet reached [the goal] and the succeeding student has not yet clarified it;

if one merely announces the boundaries, errors and contradictions may arise. For example, if one announces from outside a wall, saying, "From the southeast corner to the southwest corner," and continues until the circuit is complete at the south gate of the monastery, this constitutes a separate assembly (*bhedasaṃgha*). This is because when announcing the boundary, one passes directly over the gate from the base of the wall.

If the boundary were established outside, then those inside the temple would be excluded; even if the door were closed and a *karmavācanā* performed, if there were people outside the threshold who had not been summoned to assemble, would this not constitute a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*)?

Furthermore, if one were to chant directly from within the wall, there would again be the faults of a separate assembly, such as [the invalidation of] the summer retreat (*varṣā*) or the separation from robes (*cīvara-vipravāsa*).
Since the boundary arises according to the interior of the wall, if one now chants directly alongside the wall, the ground within the threshold is indeed [included].

If one performs a formal ritual outside the boundary or within a monastery, and someone sends their consent (*chanda*) by crossing the threshold of the gate to join the assembly, must they not re-enter the boundary?
Is this not then a separate gathering (*pṛthag-saṃgha*)? Furthermore, regarding the violation of the summer retreat (*varṣā-bheda*):

if someone is in residence within the boundary and the dawn light has not yet appeared, but before they have returned to the edge of the threshold, the dawn light has already broken, they are then outside the boundary; is this not a violation of the retreat?

Regarding the summer [retreat], what constitutes the loss of one's robes? There is a person who has established a "boundary for not losing robes" (*acīvarāpatti-sīmā*). Before the appearance of light (*āloka*) has arisen, he goes inside the threshold without his robes. If the appearance of light arises, does this not constitute the loss of the robes? Therefore, it is necessary to delineate the boundaries with precision;

only then may the boundary be proclaimed. One must not proclaim it by passing through directly and vaguely. Should such an error occur, it would cause others to spend their entire lives in vain. Thus, it is said:

"If one were to pass through directly and proclaim the boundary without first defining it, and if there were such a mistake, it would cause others to spend their whole lives in vain. Therefore, one must first define the area and then proclaim the boundary. It is not permissible to pass through directly and proclaim it in a general or haphazard manner. If there were such an error, it would cause others to waste their entire lives. Hence, the necessity of careful definition before the proclamation.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "After my parinirvāṇa, bhikṣus who lack the precepts will fill Jambudvīpa. These words are indeed true.

The person appointed to proclaim [the boundary] should rise, pay homage at the feet of the Sangha, and stand while proclaiming: "Venerable Sisters (or Venerable Brother), may the Sangha listen!

If the boundary is being established within a village, a walled city, a moat, or a monastery, it is generally proclaimed from within the walls, starting from the interior of the southeast corner of the monastery’s great wall.

Regarding the three ways of assembling the Saṃgha—whether the boundary markers are distant or near, narrow or naturally wide—one should assemble within the natural limits of the area.

If the boundary markers are wide and the natural area is narrow, one should assemble within the markers; therefore, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one avoids the difficulties within the boundary.
Within a distance of three *yojanas*, any monks present must be summoned; however, once they have already left the boundary, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) may be performed to establish it.
Various masters explain that even if one acts only upon those who have gathered naturally, this is permissible;

I fear that such matters might create obstacles; therefore, it is necessary to assemble everyone now. My understanding is not otherwise: "To mark [the boundaries] completely" means, first, to provide deep protection, and second, because there is a textual authority in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

If there is a village within the marked area that lies inside the natural limits (*prakṛta-sīmā*), and one does not wish to include it, one should circumambulate the four sides of the village and announce the inner boundary-mark (*anta-sīman*), followed by announcing the outer boundary-mark (*bāhya-sīman*), and only then perform the formal act of establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) for the bhikṣus within the village.
There is no need to assemble from outside; if there are *bhikṣuṇī* boundaries both inside and outside, they do not obstruct one another.

There is no need to call for an assembly if there is a formal act (*karmavācanā*) that encompasses the boundary of the Saṃgha; it is sufficient simply to ensure that the *bhikṣus* do not exit the boundary.

It is also permissible to establish a connection by taking everything within [the area], such as the circular enclosure (*maṇḍala*) or the separate residence (*pṛthagvāsa*) mentioned in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*. This asks: why is it that one cannot receive [the precepts] through the establishment of a boundary?

The reason for establishing the desire [to define] boundaries is that they possess three essential meanings, and thus one must accept them: first, the boundary is the fundamental basis for the communal assembly (*saṃgha*), and it is logically necessary to establish it urgently;

second, the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*) is weak and cannot sustain formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*), as the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One may not perform monastic affairs on ground where no formal boundary has been established";

third, it allows for the recognition of boundary limits, thereby preventing transgressions such as those regarding the summer retreat (*varṣā*), the protection of robes, the protection of food, and the performance of separate assemblies.

Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: When a bhikṣu performing the *karmavācanā* dies and the others do not know the boundaries of the precinct, the Buddha commanded that they first dissolve [the boundary] and then re-establish it;

thus, everyone must assemble. Next, while formally performing the *karmavācanā*, the presiding elder asks: "The Saṃgha has assembled in harmony. He asks again: "Those who have not yet received full ordination, depart! Then he asks:

at the outer corner of the southeast corner, one should pierce through the small wall, enter to the west, proceed along the southern wall of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) until the inner corner of the southwest corner, then proceed along the inner western wall of the great boundary, go straight north, and pierce through the small wall.

Afterward, one should mark it with winding lines. For the "natural ground" outside the boundary of the precept-platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*), the two eastern and northern sides should be demarcated using small walls as the natural ground;
the two southern and western sides should be demarcated by marking them with a cord one cubit (*hasta*) long.
If there were no prior markers within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), one should erect stakes and connect them with cords; this should be done at the site of the precepts.
Eight chi from the southern wall of the Great Boundary at the southeast corner of the site, drive a large stake into the ground beneath the foundation of the small wall.
From there, go straight west until you are eight chi inside the western Great Wall, where you again drive a stake.
Proceed straight north to the foundation of the small wall and drive another stake there as well, ensuring it remains one chi and eight inches distant from the Great Wall. Then, using a cord...
Beyond these three markers is the natural ground (*prakṛtistha-bhūmi*). Regarding the boundaries of the *sīmāmaṇḍala*:

on the two eastern and northern sides, the inner edge of the small wall constitutes the boundary of the *sīmāmaṇḍala*; on the two southern and western sides, the inner edge of the cord-markers constitutes the boundary of the *sīmāmaṇḍala*.
Answer: If these cord-markers remain firm and do not decay, a person within the natural ground does not violate the *sīmā*.

Within the precincts, the ritual proceedings can be successfully accomplished because the characteristics of the boundary (*sīmā*) are clearly recognized. If these boundary markers, such as the cord, are destroyed or absent, then later when visiting monks arrive, they may not know the limits of the boundary.
Consequently, they might sit or stand within the natural ground (*prakṛtistha-bhūmi*), or their movements may become indeterminate;
fearing that this would disrupt the monastic legal proceedings (*saṃghakarma*), the situation would be perilous and extremely terrifying. Such ignorance is comparable to being like a child.

If the foundation of this great boundary wall is more than two chi wide, it is most secure and prudent to announce that one cubit of natural ground shall recede into the interior of the great boundary wall;
since the boundary is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*), there is no hindrance to its entering into reality.
Calculating one cubit of natural ground as being equivalent to eighteen inches, with the remaining two inches, the substance of the great boundary wall itself is sufficient for identification.

Regarding the characteristics of the two boundaries (*sīmā*) explained above, we have provisionally used a single object as the substance of these boundaries; however, since the characteristics of the boundaries are numerous, they may not necessarily correspond exactly to the diagram.

At the time of the ceremony, one should adjust them according to the actual facts and supplement this section accordingly. Within the gate of the *śīla-kṣetra* (precept field), one should also chant the boundaries with appropriate curvature;
fearing that it would become overly cumbersome, I cannot describe it further here. If one is to establish two boundaries, one should first establish the boundary for the precepts (*śīla*).
Because the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) is established after the site boundary (sīma), the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* also requires that the site boundary be established first.
If the Great Boundary were established first, one must relinquish it and subsequently establish the site boundary before establishing the Great Boundary.

Furthermore, the *Vinayamātṛkā* states that if one does not establish a Great Boundary outside [the site] but establishes only a Small Boundary (khuḍḍaka-sīmā), one may not receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Question: If the Great Boundary is established first and the site boundary is established later, is it valid?
Because it is not answered that one should abandon the fivefold [boundary] and re-establish it, we know that [the previous boundary] is successfully established;

since the subsequent dharma cannot be accomplished, it must be dissolved. The *Wubai wenshi* (Five Hundred Questions) states: "Regarding the subsequent establishment of a *sīmā* (monastic boundary), if one receives the precepts within it, there is fear that nothing will be gained.

It further states: "If one does not know [the rules], it is the same as when the regulations were not yet enacted; relying on this path, one may pass through by chance. The *Yi* (Exegesis) says: "In the present time, the *sīmā* is established..."
The instances where the rules are conflated are numerous and cannot be recounted in full; however, once the formal text is established, the meaning will reveal itself.

As clarified in the previous sacred teachings, the boundary for the *śīma* (precept site) must first be fixed. Knowing this to be so, if one wishes to proclaim the formal act of binding [the boundary], it must be done for each respective realm;

one may not perform it remotely from one side to another. Thus, the monks of the natural boundary (*jñapti-prakṛti-sīmā*) shall all assemble at the location of the *śīma*, and one person shall be appointed to do so.
The resident bhikṣus arise, assume their proper deportment, and stand while proclaiming: "Venerable Sisters (or Bhikṣuṇīs), may the Saṃgha listen!
I, the bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī) [Name], for the sake of the Saṃgha, proclaim the marks of the four sides of the small boundary of the *śīma*:
from the inner mark at the southeast corner, following the cord westward to the inner mark at the southwest corner; from this cord, following it northward to the inner mark at the northwest corner."
Furthermore, following the small wall, descend eastward to the inner corner of the eastern boundary; from there, proceed southward to the inner marker at the southeastern corner.
This completes one circuit of the boundaries of the *sīmā* (precept field). (One recitation. Once the Elder has asked whether the Saṃgha is assembled and in harmony, he asks again:
"Those who have not yet received full ordination, depart. Now that the Saṃgha is in harmony, what shall we perform? The answer is: "We shall perform the *karmavācanā* for delimiting the *sīmā*."
Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! This resident [monk or nun], so-and-so, announces the marks of the small boundary (sīmā) on all four sides.
