If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent. The Saṃgha now establishes a *śīlākṣetra* (precept-field) within these marks of the small boundary on the four sides.
Thus is the motion (*jñapti*). Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! This resident [monk or nun], so-and-so, announces the marks of the small boundary on all four sides.
The Saṃgha now establishes a *sīmā-kaṭhina* (boundary enclosure for the observance of the precepts) within these four boundaries of the small *sīmā*.

Those of you, Venerable Elders and Sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha’s establishment of this *sīmā-kaṭhina* within these four boundaries of the small *sīmā*, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
Since the Saṃgha has consented and remains silent, it is understood that the Saṃgha has completed the establishment of this *sīmā-kaṭhina* within these four boundaries of the small *sīmā*.
Maintain the matter thus.

Next, regarding the explanation of binding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), there are three stages for proclaiming the characteristics: first, proclaiming the inner characteristics; second, proclaiming the outer characteristics;

third, the final summary after the proclamation is complete. Now, first, we proclaim the inner characteristics of the great boundary, saying: "Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! I, [the Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī]..."
I, [Name], shall proclaim for the Saṃgha the internal boundaries of the great boundary of the four directions:

starting from the outer corner of the southeast corner of the small wall, one passes through the small wall to the west; proceeding along the inner side of the large wall to the inner corner of the southwest corner, one then descends northward along the wall, passes straight through the small wall, and reaches the outer corner of the northwest corner of the small wall; from there, one descends eastward along the small wall.
Reaching the outer corner at the northeast of the small wall, one proceeds south along this small wall until returning to the outer corner at its southeast;
this completes one circuit of the inner boundary (one recitation).
Next, in proclaiming the outer boundary, one should begin from the outer corner at the southeast of the monastery’s outer wall: "Venerable Sisters, listen to me, [I, the Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī]..."
[Name], for the sake of the Saṃgha, proclaims the external boundaries of the great boundary in the four directions:

starting from the outer corner of the southeast corner of the monastery’s outer wall, one proceeds straight west along the wall; then, following its curves, one goes out to the earth-ridge on the eastern side of the south gate;

from there, one proceeds westward to the earth-ridge on the western side of the gate; from there, one proceeds southwest to the outer corner of the southwest corner; from there, one proceeds northward to...
From the outer corner of the northwest, go eastward down to the outer corner of the northeast; from there, go southward back to the outer corner of the southeast.
This completes one circuit of the outer boundary marks (one recitation). Having finished the third proclamation, the summary states:
"This constitutes the outer boundary marks, and that constitutes the inner boundary marks; this completes one circuit of the inner and outer boundary marks of the Great Boundary."
Having finished the conclusion, one should inform the Saṃgha, saying: "The proclamation of the internal and external boundaries of the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) is complete.

The assembly of monks should then perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā). Once the proclaimer has returned to his seat, the Elder asks: "Is the Saṃgha assembled and in harmony? He asks again: "Have those who have not received full ordination departed?
[The response is: "The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall it do? [He replies: "To perform the formal ritual for establishing the Great Boundary. Venerable Sisters, may the Saṃgha listen!"
In this residence, [the monk/nun] so-and-so announces the marks of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) in the four directions.

If the Saṃgha is ready and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now establish a great boundary within these marks of the four directions as a single residence with a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). Venerable sisters, may the Saṃgha listen: in this residence, [the monk/nun] so-and-so announces the marks of the great boundary in the four directions.
Venerable sirs, the Saṃgha now demarcates a great boundary within these four markers for a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa.

Those of you, Venerable Elders (or Sisters), who consent to the Saṃgha’s demarcation of a great boundary within these four markers for a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak. The Saṃgha has consented to this demarcation of the four markers.

The internal great boundary (mahā-sīmā) has been established; because the Saṃgha remains silent in approval, this matter is thus maintained. Regarding the meaning: one should simply recite the text as it stands without alteration, saying:

"The Saṃgha now establishes a great boundary within these four sides, both inside and outside the markers. This is because when the body is taken as the reference point relative to the markers, it naturally encompasses both the interior and exterior;
furthermore, when the boundary itself is taken as the reference point relative to the markers, the entire boundary lies within the markers. Thus, by means of the markers, they are mutually defined.
Since the characteristics of the boundary (*sīmā*) are all outside the boundary, there is no need to alter the text according to it.

Next, regarding the supplementary explanation of the method for dissolving the boundary: first, concerning the method for dissolving a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) that lacks a designated precinct (*sīman-maṇḍala*), the Elder asks once the Saṃgha has assembled in harmony;
he further asks those who have not received full ordination to depart, and whether those who have not come are present. Then, the bhikṣus announce their *chanda* (consent) one by one.
Having answered, he asked again: "The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall it perform? He replied: "The *karmavācanā* for dissolving the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).

(From here on, the number of conditions for the various *karmavācanā* sections is the same as these four; they differ only according to the specific matter being recited, as found in the procedure for producing the *kaṭhina* robe.

"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! At this residence, the monks and nuns dwell together in one place and perform the *poṣadha* together. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent to dissolve the boundary."
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen to this: the bhikṣus residing at this monastery share the same dwelling place and perform the *poṣadha* together.

Now, the boundary is being dissolved. Those Venerable Sisters who consent to the dissolution of the boundary for those sharing the same dwelling place and performing the *poṣadha* together, remain silent.
Those who do not consent, please speak. The Sangha has consented to the dissolution of the boundary for those sharing the same dwelling place and performing the *poṣadha* together."

Since the Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. If there is a *sīmā-kaṇḍa* (boundary for the precepts), one must first dissolve the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary) and afterwards dissolve the *sīmā-kaṇḍa*;
this is the standard procedure. Regarding the questions and answers of the *sthavira* (elders), they are designated differently according to the specific matter;
unlike the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for receiving the precepts where a single response suffices for many acts, here [the boundaries] are separated by natural features.
Because the ritual procedures for the two boundaries are distinct, they do not apply to one another.

Next, regarding the explanation of the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (precept-field): when formally dissolving the *sīmāmaṇḍala*, one must still remain within the *sīmāmaṇḍala*; it is not permitted to dissolve it from afar while remaining in the *mahāsīmā*.

Although the Vinaya contains no text specifically on dissolving [the boundary], we now follow the precedent of dissolving the boundary due to difficult circumstances; by simply reversing the procedure for "binding" (*bandhana*), the principle of dissolution is universally applicable.
Wen Shun asked: "Monks, now that you are in harmony, what is to be done? He replied: "The *karmavācanā* for dissolving the *sīmā* (boundary). "Venerable Sisters, may the Saṃgha listen.
The Saṃgha has assembled at this place to dissolve the *sīmā*. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha permits, I shall now announce the dissolution of the *sīmā*.

This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Venerable Sisters, may the Saṃgha listen. The Saṃgha has assembled at this place to dissolve the *sīmā*. Which of you, Venerable Sisters, approves of the Saṃgha's dissolution of the *sīmā*?"
Those who have gathered here to dissolve the *sīmā* (boundary) remain silent; whoever does not consent, let them speak. The Saṃgha has consented to the dissolution of the *sīmā*.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "One must not build a dwelling upon a *sīmā*, even if a king should so command.
A conscientious bhikṣu should dismantle it; the remaining timber and grass should be sent to the bhikṣus residing in the monastery."

Regarding the construction of the Buddha hall and the trees: the meaning is that in the Western Regions, the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (precept platform) is mostly situated in the open air, similar to a worldly sacrificial altar or a site for suburban sacrifices.
The Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang, Śīlabhadra (*Bopō*), and others all refer to it as a *maṇḍala*;

therefore, it is frequently termed a "precept maṇḍala" (*jìtán*) in the Vinaya. The *Wǔbǎi wèn shì* states: "If it rains while receiving the precepts, if one moves the precept platform to a building..."

For those of inferior capacity, one must first dissolve the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), then re-establish the monastery precinct (*sīmā-kuṭika*) and subsequently re-bind the great boundary; only then is it accomplished.

Fourth, regarding the determination of the formation and dissolution of boundaries: according to this Vinaya, because it is governed by the monastery, the purity of the ground is not lost. If there is doubt, one should relinquish it and re-establish it. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"Once the boundary has been established based on its physical marks, even if the boundary marks are later lost, the boundary itself is not lost, provided it was small."
The *Dharmakṣaya-sūtra* states that when the kalpa-ending fires arise, places where a monastery once stood are not consumed by fire, even becoming earthen platforms for the Vajradhātu.
Even if one harbors an evil mind, the boundary (sīmā) established within it is not lost.
Chapter Six: Striking the Gavel to Assemble the Assembly.
This chapter has three main sections: first, preparing the seats and striking the gavel; second, gathering the monks from near and far; third, the number of monks in the assembly.
Now, first I shall explain the initial gate: before striking the *kīla* (gong), one must first prepare the seat;

thus the Vinaya states, "One should spread out the seat and strike the *kīla* so that everyone assembles in one place. The *Vinayamātṛkā* quotes the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra*, translating *kīla* as *jūchuí* (巨槌); its phonetic transcription is *dì* (音地), which here refers to a *qing* (stone chime), also known as a bell.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "At that time, there was no one in the monastery to strike the *kīla*."

When the bedding was being spread in succession and people were cleaning fruits and vegetables, the assembly spoke in a chaotic manner; at that time, there was no one to snap their fingers [to signal silence], so the Buddha ordered the *karmadāna* (the *weina*) to stand.
The term for "sound-theory" (*śabda-vidyā*) is translated as "succession. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Strike three times.

Later, it was only upon the invitation of others that the "long-strike" (*dīrgha-ghaṇṭā*) came to be used. The *Dharmaguptaka-dharmapada-śāstra* (or *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-dharmapada-śāstra*, *Fufa zang zhuan*) says: "In the past, there was a king named Kaniṣka."
Having committed acts of cruelty, he was reborn in the great ocean as a thousand-headed fish. A wheel of swords revolved and severed his heads;

as soon as they were cut off, they would immediately grow back again, and he was severed in this manner repeatedly. This process continued until, in the space of a mere moment, his severed heads filled the great ocean.
At that time, an Arhat *karmadāna* struck the *gandi*; upon hearing it, the swords ceased and his suffering subsided slightly.
The King then addressed him, saying: "I only pray that, O Virtuous One, when you strike the *ghanṭā*, you may do so for a long duration;

having struck it for a long time, once the seven days have passed, one's suffering will be brought to an end. Because he struck it for a long time until now with the intention of benefiting all beings, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"When the bell is struck, the sufferings of all evil realms are simultaneously suspended. It further speaks of two [types of striking].
This verse removes the heavy sins of birth and death from five hundred billion kalpas; it subdues the enemy of Māra’s power and eliminates all fetters without remainder.
When the ghaṇṭā is struck in the open air, monks shall assemble upon hearing it.

Those who wish to hear the Dharma and cross the flood of the ocean of birth and death, upon hearing this wondrous sound, should skillfully gather themselves here. Since such is known, the *karmadāna* (venerable of duties) is about to strike the bell.

Having first prepared the ritual deportment and paid homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, one should then with utmost sincerity manifest the intention of summoning both the ordinary and the holy for the sake of sentient beings.

Thereafter, one should gradually strike the mallet, proceeding from the subtle to the manifest; one must not act with negligence by striking too forcefully, as this would startle and disturb the minds of the assembly.
Since the ritual applications are numerous and cannot be described in full, I have briefly set forth this meaning; practitioners should take note. As stated in the *Five-Part Vinaya*:

The Buddha said that when the time for the *poṣadha* assembly approaches, it hinders the practice of the Path. He declared: "One should announce that the time has arrived by striking a *gandī*, beating a drum, or blowing a conch.
A resident *śrāmaṇera* or a lay attendant (*karmadāna*) shall strike it; they must not strike it too many times, but rather three times. The same applies to blowing the conch.
With the exception of trees with lacquer or poisonous sap, one may use other wood, copper, iron, or clay to produce sound for the monastery; however, one must not make it too loud."
If it is heard everywhere but no one knows to assemble, one should shout from a high place; if they still do not know to assemble, they should speak to one another until it is known.
If there are no śrāmaṇeras or lay attendants (karmadāna), a bhikṣu may also strike [the gong]. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"When a layperson invites the saṃgha, he himself strikes the mallet within the monastery, even up to announcing that 'the time has arrived,' and the woman who delivers the food also strikes the mallet herself; the same applies to those who offer midday meals. This refers to such cases.
The Vinaya states that there are seven methods for summoning the Sangha: measuring shadows, splitting bamboo, making sounds, emitting smoke, blowing a conch, beating a drum, and striking a *gandi*;
it also says that a *śrāmaṇera* may perform these when the time has come. (In the present day, there are still some monasteries that do not permit *śrāmaṇeras* or laypeople to ring the bells;
this is a profound misunderstanding of the teachings.)

Regarding the second [topic], the gathering of the Saṃgha according to distance, there are briefly two types: first, the formal boundary (*karmabhūmi*), and second, the natural boundary (*prakṛtisthā*).

If the gathering of the Saṃgha is conducted within a formal boundary, all members must assemble within the limits of that area. If the gathering is conducted within a natural boundary, there are four distinctions based on the varying distances of the respective locations:
first, the village; second, the forest hermitage (*araṇya*); third, the path; and fourth, the water boundary. These four types are all... [text ends]
Because they are established for the sake of beings according to where people reside, there are distinct divisions; therefore, it is called the "first natural village.
Regarding the measurement of a village (*grāma*), there are two types to be distinguished: distinguishable villages and indistinguishable villages. First, to clarify the distinguishable:
these refer to villages and hamlets outside city walls, as well as frontier towns and cities, where the population is sparse and can be easily counted.
Regarding the establishment of names according to their meaning, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"In a village where no monastery exists, when a monastery is first built and the boundary has not yet been established, the village boundary itself constitutes the monastery boundary. The text below specifies that within the area where monks may walk back and forth, one must not perform a formal act separately from the assembly;
this should be understood as a village that can be demarcated. This Vinaya takes the village boundary (*grāma-sīmā*) as the standard.
Regarding the two types of "indistinguishable clusters" (*grāma*) mentioned in the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*: the latter refers to places where the population is so dense that they cannot be distinguished.
To establish a name according to its meaning, one should follow the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which states:
"If the boundaries of a city or a village cluster cannot be discerned, use a bow of five cubits; plant a tree every seven bows, ensuring that the trees are spaced apart at intervals of seven."
When the assembly sees one another, they do not commit the offense of being a separate group, and each attains accomplishment;
this should be understood as an "indistinguishable village" (*agrāma*). According to the general definition, seven trees with six intervals between them equal sixty-three paces (*krama*).

If one takes the two ends of the trees, each having half a shadow, then with seven trees and six intervals, there are seventy-three and a half paces. [Question: What constitutes a forest hermitage (*araṇya*)?
When one wishes to establish a boundary (*sīmā*) for a monastic residence (*saṃghārāma*), where should the monks assemble? The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shisong lü) answers:

"The boundary of the monastic community follows the boundary of the village (*grāma-sīmā*), such that the perimeter of the enclosure and the characteristics of the village are not distinct; therefore, it is not necessary to assemble people from five *li* away.

Thus, the text below states that when a monastery is first established in a wilderness (*araṇya*) where no village exists, it says "one *krośa* boundary. From this, we know that [the former refers to cases where a village already exists].

If there is a monastery (saṃghārāma), it shares the same village boundary (*grāmamaryādā*) as defined in the Vinaya; the four characteristics of a village and the two types of boundaries are not distinct.
Only when the enclosure (*prākāra*) is incomplete does one obtain the status of relying on an *araṇya* (wilderness) for the assembly of the Saṃgha. Second, regarding the *araṇya* boundary:

this generally clarifies that there are many kinds of *araṇya*, namely, the *dhūta* [observances], the entrusting of robes, the precept against stealing, the Saṃgha boundary (*saṃghasīman*), and the robe boundary (*cīvarasīman*). For now, we shall clarify the remaining boundaries.
Regarding the definition of an *araṇya* (forest hermitage) within the monastic boundary (*sīmā*), there is no textual authority in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü).

While the various schools offer differing and inconsistent accounts, they all refer to an *araṇya* as being one *krośa* or similar measure; for instance, the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* states that one *krośa* is five *li*.
It is traditionally held that this serves as the definitive standard. Furthermore, the *Yaśas-ācārya-śāstra* (Yesheshi zhuan) states that a *krośa* is the distance at which a large bull bellows.

It is sound; its sound is heard for five *li*. If there is an obstacle such that it cannot be heard for five *li*, then according to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the smallest *araṇya* boundary is seven *paṇḍa* square, with one *paṇḍa* being twenty-eight cubits (*hasta*).
If those who do not consent [to the boundary] are outside the seven *paṇḍa*, one may perform ritual acts [within]; calculated, this amounts to one hundred and ninety-six [cubits].
Each cubit (*hasta*) is one foot and eight inches; in total, this amounts to fifty-eight paces and four feet and eight inches.

Since it is stated that the assembly of monks must be gathered, those who disagree should find it difficult [to comply]; therefore, this is permitted as an exception. Regarding the third, the boundary for traveling (*cārikā-sīmā*):
the Sarvāstivādins say that when a bhikṣu travels, wherever he stays, there is a boundary of one *krośa* in length and breadth; within this area, one may not eat separately.

The separate *poṣadha* (observance) also does not clarify whether it is large or small; this treatise explains the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, stating that six hundred paces constitute one *krośa*.
Regarding the fourth water-boundary (*udakakhandasīma*), the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says:

"That which is natural within the water—if one is walking in the water, the area reached by the water sprinkled by a strong person among the assembly is called a boundary. The *Sudarśana-vibhāṣā* says: "Whether by throwing water or scattering it..."
Outside the sand, where it does not obstruct monks from gathering water and where water flows constantly, one may perform the *poṣadha* at any depth; however, one must not do so in natural tides.
If the *poṣadha* is held on a boat, one should drop a stone anchor; one must not tie the boat to the shore or to the roots of trees in the water, as these are connected to the boundary of the land.
All wood, stones, and trees within the water constitute the natural water boundary (*udaka-sīmā*).
Regarding "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*), it means that one who has left the ground may ask about the preceding statement regarding the "indivisible cluster" (*asaṃvibhakta-grāma*) being sixty-three paces.
Does this mean taking sixty-three paces for each of the four sides of the body, or taking thirty-one and a half paces for each side?
Answer: If there are people on all four sides, one takes sixty-three paces from each; therefore, that text states that there are seven trees with space between them.
Question: If members of different assemblies see one another, does this constitute the offense of performing legal acts separately? Answer:

If both parties are presiding over a communal legal act (*saṃghakarma*), how wide or narrow is the extent of the natural boundary (*prakṛtisthāna*)? Answer: Various teachers offer differing explanations;

however, according to our own interpretation, each of the two assemblies has its own boundary of sixty-three paces. This is because the boundary is always fixed, regardless of whether a legal act is being presided over or not. Thus says the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
Regarding the phrase "different groups" (*visabhāga*), this refers to the bodies of monks from two distinct locations.

Since it is stated that if one encounters a member of a different group within the space of seven *ru* (bow-lengths), there is no offense of *pṛthaktva* (separation), this text is consistent with reason and its meaning is complete; there is nothing to doubt.
Question: If the two groups are mutually related by using a distance of sixty-three steps, then the two boundaries would overlap. If...

To distinguish their boundaries, the answer is as follows: if these were demarcated by formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*), one must necessarily leave a clear interval between them so that the two boundaries do not intersect;
however, since this is a naturally designated area for the gathering of the Saṃgha, it may be used universally without hindrance.
Third, clarifying the number of monks required for an assembly: this generally explains that there are four types of assemblies. First, regarding the assembly of four monks:

this refers to the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and the confession of *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses, and so forth. Second, regarding the assembly of five monks: this refers to receiving the full ordination and performing the *Pravāraṇā* ceremony in border regions, and so forth.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the confession of a *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense also falls under the category of the assembly of five monks, as the presiding confessor acts [as the fifth].

When one performs a *śuddhaka-śveta-vācanā* (a formal announcement) for oneself or another, one does not count toward the quorum of the Saṃgha; however, when receiving a confession (*pratideśanā*), one is included in the count.

This is analogous to the *pravāraṇā*, where members take turns mutually fulfilling the required number. Because the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) is not explicit on this point, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) is consulted:
"A Saṃgha of ten persons" refers to the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*) and so forth in the Central Kingdom; "a Saṃgha of twenty persons" refers to the same in the Four Border Regions.
The term "Sangha" refers to those who perform the confession of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and the subsequent rehabilitation from guilt (*āpatti-vyutthāna*).

For the nuns' community, the Sangha required for such rehabilitation must consist of twenty members, which differs from that of the *bhikṣu* (male monastic) Sangha. The commentary explains that the first four types of Sangha are each described in terms of their individual practice;

they must all be pure, because one who has committed a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) is not eligible for formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*). However, if categorized according to the communal legal procedures (*saṃghakarma*), there are two types. If [the procedure] is for...
In the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the confession of offenses, purity is essential. One who has committed an offense is not permitted to recite the precepts, nor may they hear them;
one may not confess an offense to another who has likewise committed one, nor may such an offender accept the confession of another.

If the purpose is to receive the precepts as a gateway for generating wholesome states, it is not strictly necessary to grasp the substance [of the precepts] itself; rather, it suffices that the outward form be pure so as to inspire a sense of reverence in others.

Regarding the accomplishment of the ritual for receiving the Dharma, the Vinaya states that although a disciple may know that their preceptor has committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), if they do not know [the preceptor] is such a person, the reception of the precepts is still accomplished;
thus, it is permitted that the reception is valid. One should understand that this concerns only the formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and does not depend upon the actual substance (*bhāva*).
Chapter Seven: On Completing the Quorum for the Arising and Ceasing [of the Saṃgha].
This chapter has two main sections: first, on the validity of completing the quorum; second, on the invalidity of a separate assembly.

Regarding the first, on the validity of completing the quorum: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, eleven persons do not constitute a sufficient quorum for the Saṃgha; this refers to a monk who is asleep.
If one falls asleep after hearing the formal announcement (*jñapti*), they can still become a person subject to expulsion;

therefore, it is known that prior to the announcement, those who speak incoherently, those who cause a commotion, those who have entered meditative absorption, the mute, the deaf, those who are both mute and deaf, the insane, those with distracted minds, those whose minds are impaired by illness, monks on trees, and so forth, are all not counted. This is stated in three places in the *Mātṛkā*.

Those who do not count toward the quorum are: those who are gravely ill, people from border regions, and those who are dull-witted; conferring precepts upon them or performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony with them does not constitute a valid assembly (*saṃgha*).
There are six types of persons who do not count toward the quorum: namely, if there are fewer than ten including the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), the conferral of precepts is not accomplished;
or if one has given their consent (*chanda*) [to another]; or if there is a physical barrier; or if there is a partial covering and partial exposure with an intervening obstruction.

In cases where one is half-covered and half-exposed such that the hands cannot reach each other, or on bare ground such that they cannot reach each other, and so forth—even when performing *karmavācanā* while walking, if one sits, one commits the offense of *parivāsa*;
the same applies when sitting and lying down are mutually inconsistent. By extension, those who are intoxicated need not be counted;
laypeople (*avadātavasana*) need not be counted; and even the Buddha, according to the Sarvāstivāda, need not be counted. The above summarizes the various schools.
There are twenty-three types of persons who do not suffice for the quorum of a *saṃgha*. According to this Vinaya, there are twenty-eight types of persons who do not suffice for the count;
these include: a *bhikṣu* performing a *karmavācanā* who is supplemented by a *bhikṣuṇī*; as well as *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*; those subject to the thirteen *antarāyika-dharmas*;

those subject to the three types of *utkṣepaṇīya-karman*; those subject to *pravāsanīya-karman*; and those who ought to be subjected to *pravāsanīya-karman*. These twenty-two types [of the latter group] are excluded because they are of a different class (*visabhāga*).

Therefore, they do not count [toward the quorum]. Those who dwell separately, those on the boundary of the *karmavastu*, those with supernormal powers who remain in the air, and those who have vanished from the range of sight and hearing—these five types of persons, though belonging to the same class, do not count because they are separated from the community of monks (*saṃgha*) and thus discordant with it.
Furthermore, the person for whom the *karma* is being performed does not count, as they are measured by the standard of the *saṃgha*. Finally, the *upādhyāya* alone does not count.

The number of *karmavācanā* (formal acts) for receiving the precepts is determined by the measure of others; [the formal acts] of censure (*tarjanīya*), banishment (*niḥsaraṇa*), dependence (*niśraya*), and prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople (*apravāsanīya*) may be performed by four persons.
Furthermore, all *karmas* such as the concealment period (*parivāsa*), the *mūlāpakarṣa*, the *mānatva*, and the rehabilitation from offense (*āvarhaṇa*) may be performed by four persons;
this is also the case for those who have completed the concealment period, the *mūlāpakarṣa*, and the *mānatva* according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

In total, there are seven individuals; they are insufficient for the four types of *karmavācanā* (formal acts) such as concealment (*paticchādana*), yet they are sufficient for other monastic legal procedures (*dharmakarma*).

Master Daoshi states that because the monks Uvāha, Kuḷa, and Taṭiṭṭha were punished by the monastic officials according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, they are only insufficient for the *pravāsanīyakarman* (act of banishment). This interpretation, however, likely does not apply to all cases.

By what intention does the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) community know that the person who has been expelled by the performance of the dharma is already established [in that status]? Why, then, is it insufficient for them to be counted?

Furthermore, one’s own performance of a *karmavācanā* is different from that of a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), as one does not perform the rite for oneself but is measured by another as a *karmācārya* (ritual master);
thus, the meaning is that they are insufficient for counting. Regarding the thirteen grounds of defeat (*pārājika*) and so forth, prior to their self-accusation, they are the same as the Saṃgha.
Dharma-affairs shall all be accomplished; even if one speaks for oneself when performing the ritual and no one else knows it, the monastic procedure (*saṃghakarma*) is still established.

Since there is no violation within the formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the preceding matter is successfully transacted. As the Vinaya states: "One must not observe the purity or impurity of others with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*);
one should observe them with the fleshly eye. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "If a person who has committed a grave offense (*pārājika*) feigns being a fellow monk..."
When I was formerly a layman, if those who had broken the precepts spoke first of their transgressions before the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) was performed, it would not be valid;
if they did not speak, all the rites were valid. Furthermore, one is not even permitted to use the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) to observe whether others uphold or violate the precepts.
The meaning of "speaking for oneself" is that one must inform the person present, saying, "I have committed sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth," so that the person clearly understands.

Knowledge and understanding alone constitute a formal declaration; even if one does not declare it oneself, if the Saṃgha collectively knows that one has committed a grave offense such as the thirteen *antarāyika-dharmas*, and this is known and heard throughout the land, being fully understood by all people—such individuals do not require a formal declaration to be excluded, nor are they fit to be counted [in the assembly].
Even if a ritual is performed within the assembly, there is no fault if they are not summoned. If this is so, why does the Vinaya state "all"?

Regarding the requirement that one must speak for oneself and so forth, it is further asked: "Should one not observe the purity or impurity of others with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), but rather with the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*)?

Answer: The requirement that one must speak for oneself refers to those who do not know [of their own transgression]. Since one now knows that they have committed an offense, why wait for them to speak for themselves?
Furthermore, observing others with the divine eye is not permitted; one should observe them with the fleshly eye. I, too, shall observe with the fleshly eye and not with the divine eye.

Regarding what constitutes a quorum for the formal act: if a *rāṣṭrapāla* (or one who has committed a grave offense) is known by the Saṃgha to have transgressed, there is no need for him to confess it himself or for the matter to be presented before the assembly; he is to be directly expelled and cast out.

The meaning is that if it is thoroughly known that a person has committed such a grave transgression and that person is so wicked as to be beyond distinction, then the one who presides over the legal procedure, if they are in an open space...

When performing the ritual of the site (*bhūmi-karman*), one must sit in a circle with shoulders and knees touching one another; it is not permitted to sit with gaps between individuals or to sit in a single file.

Since the body itself does not count as a sufficient quorum, if one sits separated from others who are "good persons" (qualified monks), then even if one is within arm's reach on open ground, is this not the fault of forming a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*)?
Knowing this, when presiding over the ritual, one must discreetly attend to these matters.
If one attempts to inform others beforehand, it conversely results in an increase of misfortune and the ritual procedure becomes difficult to accomplish;

since such occurrences are frequent nowadays, this is recorded separately: unless it is an open space, if all are within the hall, even if good and evil persons are mixed together, the rite is accomplished without fault.
The second point regarding the fault of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*) refers to being at variance within the same boundary (*sīmā*), thereby differing from the Saṃgha;
hence it is called a "separate assembly. The Vinaya states: first, those who ought to come must come—this means the assembly of body, speech, and mind together;

second, those who ought to grant their consent (*chanda*) must grant it—this means the assembly of speech and mind, though the body does not assemble; third, those present who are entitled to reprove must not reprove—this refers to the body.

If the mouth is assembled but the mind is not assembled, even if one remains silent and does not voice a reproach, it is still called "harmony" (*sāmagrī*); thus the Vinaya states: "One should not fail to reproach those who ought to be reproached.
Furthermore, the text below states: "If one sees another performing a *karmavācanā* in accordance with the Dharma, yet one's own mind does not agree, one should remain standing in silence;

this is called 'acting in accordance with the Dharma'. Additionally, when the group of six bhikṣus went to the place where the *poṣadha* was being recited and stood instead of sitting, the Buddha said:

The *Wufen lü* (Five-Part Vinaya) states that when a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed behind the back of a sick person, the Buddha declared it a violation of the rules for a separate assembly (*biezong*). The meaning is as follows:

When discussing the dharma of the community (*saṃgha*), one takes only the outward signs of deportment (*īryāpatha*) and does not rely on the sincerity of the mind. Provided that the outward forms are in conformity, even if the mind is contrary, the legal act is nonetheless established.
Thus, the Vinaya says: "If one witnesses a formal act that is in accordance with the Dharma, yet one's mind does not agree with it, it is still termed 'in accordance with the Dharma'."

One should know that one merely takes up the formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) without deliberating on the mind; this is not like when one intends to uphold the Dharma, where all must wait for the respondent to be seated before proceeding, though there are also cases where it is accomplished while standing.

With the exception of the person for whom the *karmavācanā* (formal act) is performed—who, being under disciplinary treatment, does not count toward the quorum—the act is accomplished even if standing.
However, for requests such as receiving the precepts or performing repentance, it is best to sit while making the request.
According to the meaning of the formal text, it is established that among those presiding over the *karmavācanā*, the procedure is valid for all except two persons:
the *vinayadhara* (preceptor of deportment) who presides over the *jñapti* (single motion) as an agent of the Saṃgha and must not sit down arbitrarily;
and the one who recites the *poṣadha* standing, which is done so that the assembly may hear. Aside from these, all others must necessarily preside while seated.
Chapter Eight: On the Formation and Destruction of Sensual Enjoyment.

This chapter consists of four main sections: first, defining the intent and explaining the name; second, opening the conditions for attainment; third, determining the right and wrong regarding the conditions for enjoyment;
and fourth, expounding the dharma of sensual desire.

Regarding the original intent and the explanation of the term for the initial formulation: Generally, the word *chanda* (desire/intention) is mostly defined as "longing" or "requisition," meaning that when the mind and speech accord with the Dharma, the matter can be successfully accomplished.
However, if there are circumstances that prevent the fulfillment of one's wishes, the Noble One [the Buddha] permits the expression of *chanda* to show that there is no discord.
Thus it is called *chanda*. The *Mātṛkā* asks: "What is meant by *chanda*? It means taking pleasure in following the matters to be performed.

One should take joy in participating together in the monastic affairs conducted according to the Dharma. Next, to distinguish the essential nature of the *chanda* (consent), there are generally two types of requirements for it:

those required by both the Saṃgha and the individual, such as the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) and the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults); these are matters for which the Buddha has established formal regulations, and to violate them constitutes an offense.

There are also those required solely by the Saṃgha, such as the conferral of ordination (*upasampadā*) and the determination of the date for the rains retreat (*varṣā*); these are referred to as "matters required by the Saṃgha. As for those required by myself...
It is not necessarily because the Buddha did not establish a formal prohibition that the second opening condition cannot be obtained;
as the Vinaya states: "Except for the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*), the acceptance of delegated consent (*chanda*) is permitted in all other cases."

The third [point], regarding the invalidity of the *kṣānti* (consent) based on conditions: if there is an offense against the precepts or if the conditions are contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*), because the matter is improper, it is in no way permissible to grant *kṣānti*.
However, if one refers to the permitted matters, all such acts are successfully accomplished. Therefore, the Vinaya states:

"The Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, a stūpa, tending to the sick, and the sick—these six conditions are the Buddha’s formal regulations by which the granting of *kṣānti* is valid. Yet, the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*)...
A bhikṣu engaged in the work of making robes may also convey the *chanda* (consent), yet this is not the formal rule; its meaning is as follows:

nowadays there are many bhikṣus who treat the Buddha’s words with contempt and perversely practice the holy teachings. Claiming they are truly not ill, they declare themselves ill; claiming they do not wish to speak, they express their consent (*chanda*);
claiming what is impure is pure, they cause others to transmit these falsehoods while speaking before the assembly. According to the number of monks present, each individual [must act accordingly].
Regarding the three *pāyattika* offenses incurred when speaking to each individual who knows [the truth] but speaks falsely:
if one conveys what was transmitted to the person to whom it should be conveyed in a general manner, one does not incur a *pāyattika* offense, though one may incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Question: Since it is improper to speak [of such matters] when one is not ill, can the formal ritual (*dharmakarma*) still be accomplished? Answer: It can be accomplished; the preceding person [remains valid].

There is the offense of speaking falsely. Fourth, regarding the one who conveys the *chanda* (consent): [In this original text of the Vinaya, the specific matter is not recorded; what is written today has been added by later authors. Furthermore, because it was not recorded within the *karmavācanā*, it lacks the formal wording for declaring one's inability to attend;

thus, the current meaning is stated correctly as follows: "Venerable Sister, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name]—a Bhikṣu or Bhikṣuṇī—convey my consent (*chanda*) for the legal business of the Saṃgha."

[This section] clarifies that through purity (one obtains it by a single recitation). The upper part clarifies the Dharma taught by oneself; the lower part clarifies the turning over of desires, encompassing the methods for others.
That is to say, having received the desire of another, if one has personal business requiring the matter to be turned over to someone else, the holy teaching also permits this.

Question: How many times may one turn it over? Answer: According to the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, one may turn it over seven times. "Venerable sister, please attend to me: I, [Name], a bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī), receive..."
[Question: "I, [Name] (a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī), wish to purify both that person and myself through the formal act of the Saṃgha; I grant my consent (*chanda*) and purification (*viśuddhi*).

What is the difference between granting consent (*chanda*) and purification (*viśuddhi*)? [Answer: Consent (*chanda*) should be granted for a formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), while purification (*viśuddhi*) should be declared during the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).

When the recitation takes place, both must be formally announced. This rule was established later in this Vinaya; it differs from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which prescribes the former and discards the latter.

The Vinaya teachings state: If a gravely ill person is unable to express their *chanda* (consent) at length, it is permitted for them to say, "I give my *chanda*," or "Give me your *chanda*," or "Bestow your *chanda* upon me," or to manifest signs of their body and so forth; in all such cases, the transmission of *chanda* is accomplished.

Conversely, if they do the opposite of these, it is not accomplished. The remainder of the text may be understood through inquiry. Regarding the response by means of manifesting signs, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The patient..."
If one cannot speak, one may convey the expression of the body or the sign of purity by raising a hand, a finger, shaking the head, or even by raising the eyes;

this is termed the meaning of conveying the expression of purity (*śuddhacitta*). Although the Vinaya states this, if one is to receive the expression of purity, it must necessarily be understood that the signs of anger or joy are present for it to be accomplished.
If the mind is in a state of anger yet the eyes are raised [as a sign], [it is not valid].

Although [the formal act] is not accomplished if [the names] are not taken, it ultimately constitutes a separate assembly. The Vinaya states: "If one does not remember the [given] name, calling out the clan name (*gotra*) is also permissible.

If many bhikṣus can each remember [their own names], they may speak them all at once together, and the response will be accomplished. Regarding the words for declaring one's consent (*chanda*) before the Saṃgha, if the speech is confused and everyone speaks simultaneously, it is accomplished.
Since there is no explicit text in this Vinaya regarding whether or not [this constitutes a response], it is not difficult to know [that it does]. Although...

Regarding the *samyakprahāṇa* (right exertions): if there are obstacles, it must certainly be accomplished; if there are no obstacles, according to the external Vinaya, I fear it may not be accomplished.
Therefore, the *Pañcavargika* and *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinayas] require one to go before the Saṃgha and announce one's name.

If one does not do so, each individual case will fail. Question: When many people are present to declare their consent (*chanda*) and few are present, is it accomplished? Answer: According to the *Dharmaguptaka*, it is accomplished.
The text is not clear; it merely states that one may accept [the *chanda*] according to one’s discretion as to its quantity, yet does not say whether the rite is accomplished or not.

If one were to follow the various schools, I fear it would likely not be accomplished. Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "If the number of those who give their *chanda* is equal to or greater than [those present], one may perform the *poṣadha*, but one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says: "It is permitted for many to assemble and bring the *chanda* of those who are few. Next, the method for addressing the *saṃgha* through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is explained.
The *mala-ācārya* (preceptor) says: "If one does not come, one must state the *chanda* (consent). It should be said: 'Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
I, [Name] Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī, have received from him the *chanda* for purity. He, like the Sangha, gives the *chanda* and purity. (This is stated once.

According to this Vinaya, if one has received the *chanda* from another but has a personal matter that prevents one from going, one should say to the Sangha: "Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen! I, [Name]..."
[The donor] (a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī): "That [person], so-and-so (a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī), has entrusted their consent and purity to me.

For that person and myself, regarding the formal monastic business (*dharmika saṃghakārya*), I grant the consent and purity" (one recitation). If one has a personal reason and must convey it to the Saṃgha, one should say: "Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
I, so-and-so (a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī), regarding the formal monastic business, grant my consent and purity" (one recitation). This is from the Vinaya.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is stated that when a sick bhikṣu conveys his *chanda* (consent) to a bhikṣu in the adjacent room, he may enter the assembly himself to declare it.
The Buddha said: "Do this well according to the Dharma; one who does not convey it incurs an offense. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there is no text regarding the threefold proclamation of *chanda*;

rather, it is obtained by a single proclamation. Therefore, among all the *karmans* and various legal procedures in the Vinaya, those that require the addition of three proclamations [are so specified].
All say that the second and third [recitations] are also spoken in this same manner; one who does not cling [to these views] will certainly know that a single recitation suffices.

Nowadays, those who do not study the Vinaya engage in frivolous disputes throughout the world, causing others to recite three times. Even if the *Mahāsāṃghika* contains a text for three recitations, it is nonetheless improper to suppress others;
the *Dharmaguptaka* likewise maintains three recitations. Furthermore, the texts for the recitations in the *Dharmaguptaka* and the *Mahāsāṃghika* differ from one another.

How can one take the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika* and equate it with the explanation in the *Dharmaguptaka* regarding the loss of the *chanda* (consent) procedure? This Vinaya enumerates twenty-one types of persons who lose the *chanda* after having received another's consent:

namely, the eighteen types consisting of the thirteen *anantarya* offenders, those subject to the three kinds of *ukkhepanīyakamma* (formal acts of suspension), those subject to *pabbājanīyakamma* (acts of banishment), and those subject to *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* (acts of reconciliation).

These eighteen individuals, having received the consent of others, lose that *chanda* by declaring themselves to be among the thirteen *anantarya* offenders and so forth; such is the characteristic of this Vinaya.

If one who has previously consented to hold the *chanda* (consent) for the five-part procedure dies, travels elsewhere, renounces the path, joins a non-Buddhist group, or enters a separate sect, or if he reaches the boundary of the *sīmā* (ordination site) at dawn, his *chanda* is lost;

this is contrary to the case where one who does not hold the *chanda* becomes one who holds it through such actions. Furthermore, this Vinaya mentions seven types of persons [who lose their *chanda*]:

if they die, travel to another place, renounce the path, join a non-Buddhist group, enter a separate sect, reach the *sīmā*, or if dawn breaks—all these result in the loss of the *chanda*. The rest of the phrasing can be understood as explained above.

What is meant by "going elsewhere" (*anyatra-gamana*)? It refers to one who, having taken another's *chanda* (consent) with the intention of going out of the boundary, subsequently returns to join the assembly;

this does not constitute the formal holding of *chanda*, and is thus termed "going elsewhere. In the text concerning the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), the term "going elsewhere" is changed to "going outside the boundary. Furthermore, this Vinaya mentions two types [of "going elsewhere"]:

first, using supernatural power (*ṛddhi-pāda*) to remain in the air and become invisible, thereby departing from the range of sight and hearing; second, physically departing from the range of sight and hearing. Regarding the latter, "departing from the range of sight and hearing": [text follows].

Question: Does "being apart" mean being separated from both [seeing and hearing], or does it mean being separated from one or the other? Answer: It means being separated from both; that is, with respect to the person sitting nearby, one is separated from both seeing and hearing.
Therefore, in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is said that even if one is in the same location, if they are separated from one another, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) is not established.

Furthermore, there are seven types of persons for whom the transmission of consent (*chanda*) is not established: the four types of nuns mentioned below, the three types including those who are insane, and so forth, as recorded in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
The five ways of losing a formal consent (*chanda*): (1) being outside the boundary while granting consent; (2) the person holding the consent going outside the boundary;
(3) having granted consent, one’s own self going outside the boundary; (4) having granted consent, arriving at the assembly and then silently departing from the group;

(5) the person holding the consent reaching the assembly and, due to a disturbance or alarm, rising up so that not a single person remains—this is called "destroying the assembly" and losing the consent. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is also lost when granted to one who is undergoing a period of separate residence (*parivāsa*).
Regarding the forfeiture of the *chanda* (consent): this refers to cases where the period of concealment has ended, the period of *mūlaparivāsa* has ended, or the period of *mānatva* has ended.

The meaning is that for such persons, the giving of *chanda* is not valid, nor is the holding of *chanda* valid; for if one knows [the situation] yet acts intentionally, one incurs an offense against oneself.
Thus, the Vinaya states: "In such cases, all constitute the giving of *chanda*; one should further give the *chanda* to another. If, however, one is too ill to bear it...

Regarding the procedure for the *saṃgha* when receiving *chanda* (consent): if there are many sick persons and they cannot be assembled, the *saṃgha* shall go outside the boundary to perform the *karmavācanā*.
Once the *chanda* has been received, if one encounters an obstacle while on the way to the *saṃgha* and returns from outside the boundary, the legal act of *chanda* remains valid.

However, if an obstacle exists and one does not go to where the *saṃgha* is performing the legal act within the boundary, the act is not accomplished. Therefore, the Vinaya states: "There was a bhikṣu who performed a *karmavācanā* without the [necessary] perception."
Question: Is it not established that one who has accepted the *chanda* (consent) fails to communicate it when encountering circumstances? Answer:

The Vinaya states that if the person who has accepted the *chanda* falls asleep, enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*), or fails to communicate it due to forgetfulness or error, it is still established [as having been communicated]. Question: If one intentionally fails to communicate it, does one incur an offense? Answer: Yes, one incurs an offense. Question: Is it established [that the act is completed]? Answer: It is established. Question:

If, after the matter has already been concluded, one gives the *chanda* but does not come back, does one commit the offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*)? Answer: One does not commit an offense, because [the assembly] is already complete through me.
When the mind is harmonious and one has reached the state of a monk, it is unrelated to the conditions of desire; therefore, the Vinaya states: "If the matter has ceased, one should go;
if one does not go, one shall be dealt with according to the law. However, it does not say that [the act] is accomplished regardless of whether the principle is fulfilled.
The Essential Compendium of the Vinaya, Part One:
The Final Section of the Essential Compendium of the Vinaya, Chapter Nine:
On Receiving the Full Ordination.

This chapter has thirteen main sections: 1. The requisites for receiving the precepts; 2. The ritual for requesting a teacher; 3. The conditions for generating the precepts; 4. Arranging the location; 5.
Appointing a person by means of a *jñapti* (formal motion); 6. Leaving the assembly to inquire about impediments; 7. Calling [the candidate] back in by means of a *jñapti*;
8. The procedure for requesting the precepts; 9. Reconciling with the Sangha by means of a *jñapti*; 10. Questioning the candidate before the assembly; 11. The formal reception of the precepts.
The Dharma of the precepts is explained in twelve parts, and the characteristics of the recitation of the precepts in thirteen.

One may encounter circumstances that lead to the relinquishment of the precepts. First, regarding the person receiving the precepts: they must receive the ten precepts before receiving full ordination.

Therefore, the Vinaya text below states that if one does not receive the ten precepts yet obtains the precepts [of full ordination], the assembly of monks incurs an offense. The Sarvāstivāda school explains that this is why the reception of the ten precepts is prescribed.

This is for the purpose of cultivating and training in the Buddha-dharma (for the *śikṣamāṇā*, six additional rules must be added; the specific regulations for her intention are slightly different and are detailed below).
Second, the request for the three masters and seven witnesses. First, the method for requesting the *upādhyāya*. As for why one must request one:

because the *upādhyāya* is the root of obtaining the precepts; if this person were absent, one would lack instruction, and there would be no means by which to advance on the Path. This is the principle.
One must request [a preceptor]; thus, the *Sudarsana-vinaya-śāstra* states that because they did not request [one], they committed many unrighteous acts.

When the teacher rebuked them, they replied in turn, "Who requested that you, Venerable Sir, act as my upādhyāya? Consequently, the Buddha established this rule: if one does not request [a preceptor], one may not be granted ordination.

In this Vinaya, regarding the request for a teacher, it does not specify that it must be done before the Saṃgha; rather, one may request [the preceptor] within a period of one month or five months in advance.

What harm is there in this? The Great Principle is further established, and good people will now mostly be found among the assembly. As for those who request [ordination] within the community, this is based on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya).

Its text states that the person receiving the precepts must first enter the Saṃgha and be instructed to perform prostrations at the feet of each member of the Saṃgha in succession with their head to the ground;
only after that may they make the request. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is also like this; one should fully cultivate dignified deportment and proceed to the harmonious assembly.
The Preceptor (ācārya) standing before him instructs, saying: "The reason you must request [the precept] is that this teacher is the root of the attainment of the precepts;
if you do not request them, there is no way for you to obtain them. You should give rise to a mind of earnest devotion. Having finished these instructions, he says:
"Regarding this text of the request, it should issue from your own mouth. Because you did not understand, I have taught it to you. You should receive my words with single-minded attention."

The instruction for the response is as follows: "Venerable Sister, attend with one-pointed mind to me, [Name]. I now request the Venerable Sister to be my Upādhyāyī; may the Venerable Sister act as my Upādhyāyī.
Relying upon the Venerable Sister, I shall receive the full ordination (Upasaṃpadā). Out of compassion, please grant this. (Recite this three times. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"After the candidate has made these three requests within the assembly, the Upādhyāyī should speak to arouse joy in her heart."

In the Vinaya, the response is given as "So be it," or "I shall instruct you," or "I shall instruct you; do not be negligent. The disciple replies, "I shall receive and uphold [these instructions] with the highest reverence.
Next, regarding the invitation of the two *ācāryas*, there is no explicit text in the Vinaya. However, in the Buddha’s Abhidharma, both teachers have methods for being invited;
because those texts are not elegant, they have not been transcribed here. Now, following the principles of the *upādhyāya*, I shall set forth the invitation.

If one wishes to request a *karmavācanā* master (*karmācārya*), it is permissible to request them in advance. One should then prepare oneself with proper deportment and approach the preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
The preceptor shall instruct: "The *karmācārya* is the primary condition for receiving the precepts.
If this person does not preside over the *karmavācanā*, the dust and sands of the precept-dharma cannot arise; therefore, you must arouse a superior resolve."
With a mind of profound reverence toward the preceptor, after being thus instructed in various ways, one should then request:
"Venerable Sister (or Elder Sister), please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], now request the Venerable Sister to serve as my *karmācārya*.
May the Venerable Sister act as my *karmācārya* for me. Through the Venerable Sister, I shall receive full ordination. Out of compassion, [please grant this]. (Recite three times.)
Next is the ritual for requesting the Preceptor of Dignity (*vinayācārya*). Having fully cultivated the dignified deportment, one approaches the preceptor. The *ācārya* instructs:
"By means of this Preceptor of Dignity, you shall be guided and led into the midst of the assembly; he will bring about the conditions for the arising of your full ordination (*upasampadā*) precepts.

Because it is due to this master that [the ordination] must be requested with a mind of profound reverence, [one says]: "Venerable Sister, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [name], now request the Venerable Sister..."
"I request the Venerable Ācāryā to act as my Ācāryā for the observance of proper deportment (*airyāpathika*). Through the Venerable Ācāryā, may I receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Out of compassion, [please grant this]. (Recite three times. Question: Why is the *upādhyāyī* addressed as "Ācāryā" in the Vinaya? Answer:

When the Buddha was in the world, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī was the Buddha’s maternal aunt. It was because of her that the other bhikṣuṇīs were able to [receive ordination]. Thus, she is called "Ācāryā."

Because they subsequently studied the Buddha’s words and all addressed [their preceptors] as "Aunt" (*yí*), this tradition has been passed down without interruption until the present day, just as in secular society one refers to the Emperor’s aunts, uncles, and so forth.

In the lower section of this Vinaya, it states that if a disciple knows his preceptor (*upādhyāya*) has committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), and knows that he should not receive the precepts from such a person, and further knows that although he may receive them, he will not obtain the precepts—such a case constitutes a failure to properly receive the precepts. This is the reverse [of the proper procedure].
The above thus establishes the remaining nine masters; although there is no explicit text in the Vinaya, it is interpreted by analogy with the meaning of the *upādhyāya*. It is said:

"If the *upādhyāya* commits a grave offense (*pārājika*), and the *karmavācanā* master knows of it, the ordination is not valid, because the candidate [to be ordained] is not a *bhikṣu*. If the ten masters know of one another’s offenses, the ordination is likewise not valid.
If they clearly know that he is not [a *bhikṣu*], they should not perform the *karmavācanā*; at the very least, they must know that he exists."
Because a group of four who are pure can fulfill the function of a *saṃgha*, the *Mātṛkā* states:

"In border regions, five persons who uphold the Vinaya may confer [ordination]; one should know that in the Middle Kingdom, this principle is not mentioned. (For a *bhikṣu* preceptor, ten years of seniority are required; for a *bhikṣuṇī* preceptor, twelve years. One must strictly limit this to nine years of seniority according to this Vinaya;

although the preceptor may be permitted to confer [ordination] if the requirements are met, it constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). (The case of a *bhikṣuṇī* preceptor with eleven years of seniority is to be judged accordingly.)

One should admit two types of preceptors (ācāryas)—those who have been a full monk for five *varṣas* or more, and those who have been a nun for six *varṣas* or more—before one may receive the precepts; therefore, the text of the Vinaya below mostly specifies "five years.
Other teachers hold that there is no hindrance depending on the number of years, whether more or less. Regarding the *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu*:

if a bhikṣu with less than five *varṣas* ordains a disciple and knows it is improper yet proceeds to ordain him, he commits a *pāyattika*; however, if the disciple does not know right from wrong, [the teacher is not at fault].
Regarding the attainment of the precepts (the principle that for *bhikṣuṇīs* with less than six years of seniority is likewise applicable):
Third, instructing them on the conditions for generating the precepts. First, clarifying the objects of focus; second, demonstrating the distinctions between superior and inferior states of mind.
Regarding the first point, clarifying the conditions: the precepts thus generated are immeasurable according to their respective objects; however, to summarize them generally:

However, as for sentient and insentient beings, the two retributions of the primary and secondary, the two truths of existence and non-existence, the principle of cessation, nirvana, the Buddha’s holy teachings, written scriptures, physical images, stupas and temples, earth, water, fire, wind, space, consciousness, the myriad objects of the six sense-fields, and the dharmas of the dharma-realm—it is impossible to describe them all in detail.
Why is this? Because by virtue of non-acceptance, within a single [moment]...

Regarding a single sentient being, regardless of whether they are ordinary or noble, if one were to commit as many evils as there are grains of dust, now by transforming them into goodness, one thereby accomplishes as many precepts as there are grains of dust.
Thus, the *Śūramgama-sūtra* (or *Shansheng jing*) states: "Because sentient beings are limitless, the precepts are also limitless. Next, to clarify [the case of] non-sentient things:
according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, one may also obtain immeasurable merit and virtue from the precepts regarding non-sentient objects, as in the case of the ten [precepts].
If all the great earth within the world-system, from its base down to the realm of space, were reduced to fragments as small as motes of dust, one would incur a corresponding amount of sin;

yet, by virtue of having received the precepts, all these become merits of the precepts. For example, if one destroys a single blade of grass, beginning from its sprout through each of its flowers and leaves, one incurs a certain amount of sin;
now, by reversing that, one obtains a corresponding number of precepts. Thus, the *Shansheng tian* (Heaven of the Birth of Goodness) says:
Because the earth is immeasurable, the precepts are also immeasurable; this extends even to space, which possesses the sense of being subject to theft and damage.

Thus, *Śīlasaṃbhava* states: "Because space is boundless, the precepts are also boundless. The *Sarvāstivāda* school maintains that a person newly receiving the precepts is equal in merit to the Buddha.
Inferring from this, the renunciant is truly a locus for the accumulation of the merit of wholesome dharmas.
The reason why humans and devas are benefited by this is that regardless of whether one maintains it, even a person who has violated the precepts can obtain the boundless benefits of the precepts.

How is this known? Therefore, the *Daśacakra Sūtra* states: "A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts, though he be a dead man, through the residual power of these precepts, can greatly benefit both the human and celestial realms, as well as the laity and the clergy, just like the *go-rocanā* of a cow or the musk of a musk deer."
Then he spoke in verse: "Though the *campaka* flower has withered, it surpasses all other flowers; A bhikṣu who violates the precepts still surpasses all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Therefore, if a practitioner who has received the precepts gains such merit even while breaking them, how much more so when they maintain them purely according to the Dharma—this is inconceivable and beyond description!
You should take these aforementioned objects as your mental focus; once you know what [is required]..."
Having focused on the object of meditation, one should next broaden the mind’s scope so that the recipient may increase their resolve for the Path.

One should say: "Son of good family, daughter of good family, listen! You should give rise to a superior-grade mind to obtain superior-grade precepts; if you give rise to a middling or inferior-grade mind, you will obtain middling or inferior-grade precepts.
Even if the Path were perfected through the four fruits of realization, these precepts would still be only middling or inferior. How, then, can they be called superior-grade minds?"
If one says, "I am practicing for the sake of heading directly toward Nirvāṇa; for the sake of entering the three gates of liberation; for the sake of fulfilling the three groups of precepts;
for the sake of causing the Dharma to abide for a long time; for the sake of rescuing and gathering sentient beings from all their sufferings and afflictions;
and for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way to deliver sentient beings"—then such a person is truly a disciple of the Buddha who has obtained the pure precepts of the Buddha. Thus it is asked.
Question: If the teaching is small, how can it give rise to the great resolve? Would this not contradict your own school’s tenets? Answer:

It is likely incorrect that many masters of antiquity judged the Four-Part Vinaya (*Caturvargika*) to be Mahāyāna. In reality, although the teaching is small, it does not hinder one from giving rise to the great resolve.

For example, even though the Buddha taught the Mahāyāna, there were those who gave rise to the mind of the Hīnayāna; what prevents one from saying that by teaching the small, the great resolve may be attained?
Having aroused the great resolve and understood this, one must recognize that there are superior and inferior levels within the mind regarding the sphere for receiving the precepts.

It is essential that a wise person, prior to the reception of the precepts, recites each item individually for the candidate; only when the mind has clearly perceived and understood the Dharma so that it becomes pure and luminous may the precepts be conferred.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) states that one should place the person seeking ordination in a location where they are within sight but not within hearing;

for if they are placed in a location where they are neither seen nor heard, or outside the boundary (*sīmā*), it is not called receiving the precepts. Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wufen lü) says that because of the potential for transgressions, one is permitted to place them outside the ordination platform (*kṣetramandala*) in a place where they can be seen.
Fifth, the single formal motion (*jñapti*) for appointing a master of decorum (*airyāpathika-ācārya*) to inquire privately regarding the impediments (*antarāyika-dharma*).

Because this Vinaya prescribes that one must remove one's robes outside the boundary (*sīmā*) to examine [the candidate], it causes the recipient to feel shame and delays the reception of the precepts. The Buddha said: "One must not examine [the candidate] while they are naked;

rather, one should appoint a person to inquire privately regarding the impediments. According to this Vinaya, that Preceptor (*śikṣācārya*) should ask within the assembly: "Who among you is able to act as the [master of decorum] for so-and-so?"
The Preceptor replied, "So-and-so can. The Teacher asked the Saṃgha, "Now that you are in harmony, what is to be done?
He replied, "We appoint a Preceptor; this is a *jñapti-karman* (a formal motion). If he had answered in this way, only one procedure could have been performed.

However, if he had answered generally by saying, "The *karman* for receiving the full ordination," then subsequently there would be no need for formal harmony (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*), even if the ordination were received again later.

Because one answer suffices for many people, the Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen: that [candidate], so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor and preceptress, so-and-so.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha grants its consent, let it be announced that so-and-so shall serve as the instructor.
Thus is the motion.

Sixth, the explanation for why one must ask questions from within the assembly. The reason for questioning is that one fears the candidate may become terrified upon seeing the multitude, leading to confusion regarding what exists or does not exist, errors in speech, or untruthfulness in their responses; thus, by questioning them in private, one ensures they are thoroughly examined and certain.

Furthermore, if these thirteen points of difficulty are not questioned, the precepts are not obtained; likewise, if there are questions but no answers, the reception of the precepts is also not accomplished. Therefore, the text says: [as cited above].

If one does not inquire after self-restraint has been undertaken, the precepts cannot be obtained. Furthermore, the nature of such inquiry must involve analyzing the phrasing of the text so that the gravity of the various characteristics is understood;
one must not ask directly, "Have you not committed a pārājika offense? without first knowing what constitutes a pārājika offense.

Unless one is well-versed in the Vinaya, how could one comprehend this? If one does not inquire thoroughly, there is a danger that the candidate may actually possess one of the thirteen impediments (*antarāyikadharma*).
(Śrāmaṇera; Śikṣamāṇā): If one was originally a layperson who once received the five precepts or eight precepts but violated any one of them seriously, the precepts are not generated.

Or, if one previously received the full ordination (*mahāśīla*) but did not formally renounce it, or if one renounced it without clarity, or if one returned to lay life and failed to understand the characteristics of the precepts—claiming to be without precepts—if such a person now receives the precepts again, there is no fault provided they receive them alone.

If one were to receive the precepts at the same time as another virtuous person, yet allow that other to receive them first while placing oneself later—thereby remaining outside the altar as a fully ordained *bhikṣu*—would this not violate the ritual procedures of the preceding individual? Since such an error would exist, one must have a master thoroughly versed in the Vinaya inquire into these matters in detail.
Now, as you emerge from the assembly to pose questions regarding the ritual deportment (*īryāpatha*), the Preceptor shall rise and pay homage.
Once the monk has reached the place where the practitioner is sitting, he says to the recipient: "Sit down; let us spread out the great seat-cloth for you to stretch it out within arm's reach.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, he should comfort them by saying: "Do not be afraid; in a moment I shall take you and place you in a high and secure location.
He should then take up the robe and bowl and examine them, because of these various [impurities] associated with the robe and bowl.
Having enticed her and made her take hold of the five strips [of cloth], he said: "This is the *antarvāsaka* (the lower garment worn on the body); this is the *uttarāsaṅga* (the upper robe).
Having made her take hold of the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), he said: "This is the *saṃghāṭī*. [The nun asked: "What is the *saṃkakṣikā*? [He replied: "It is the shoulder-covering garment.

"These three [types of] robes—these five [robes] in total—are names for garments that none of the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders possess; therefore, I now show them to you, and I also give you the alms bowl."
Having said, "This is the *pātra*; do you have these robes and bowl? he should reply, "Yes.
Then, having packed away the robes and bowl, he should say: "Listen well, [son or daughter of good family]. Now is the time for truth; now is the time for speaking the reality.
I shall now question you; answer me according to my questions. If it is not true, you must speak the truth. Why is this so?"
Since beginningless time, many have uttered false speech to deceive both ordinary people and noble ones, causing them to sink into the cycle of birth and death.
Now, desiring to abandon the false and realize the true, I require you to answer truthfully.

If you evade my questions with prevarication and do not answer honestly, you will merely suffer in vain and shall ultimately never attain the precepts. First: Have you not committed a pārājika offense? If you do not answer, it is improper speech.

they shall never again become [a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī]. Can you maintain this, refraining from doing such a thing for as long as life lasts? He replied: “I can.”

Because one is unable to avoid all [transgressions], if one intentionally takes the life of a human being—even down to an ant—if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes the life of a human being with their own hand;
or praises death, hands over a knife to another, teaches or exhorts another to die; or gives another non-medicinal substances;
