because they are named after the duration of the days, they are called "seven-day. Regarding "lifelong medicines," because their potency is weak, it is permitted to store and take them for as long as one lives until the ailment is cured.
There are three kinds of "life": namely, the life of the medicine, the life of the body, and the life of the illness.

Regarding the physical form as the basis for the report, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states: "As long as there is a body, there will inevitably be illness; even if a slight recovery occurs, it will certainly recur severely later.

Consequently, one undergoes the ritual by accepting its observance until the end of life. Although the conditions [of the body] may perish, the ritual itself is not lost; this is what is meant by "lifelong" (*yāvajjīvam*).

Regarding the second [category], the substance of the four medicines, it is divided into four parts. First, concerning the substance of *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for the proper time), there are ten types according to the Vinaya:
namely, boiled rice, parched flour, cooked rice, fish, meat, stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, and ground powders. This Vinaya does not exhaustively distinguish them all;

fearing that people might not recognize them and eat them after the proper time has passed, we shall now further identify them according to various schools to resolve difficulties, beginning with the *Mahāsāṃghika*.
Regarding "timely food" (*kālabhojana*): it includes radish roots, scallion roots, turnip roots, and the roots of poisonous plants (such as *caimai* roots).
Regarding "timely beverages" (*kālapāna*): this refers to all rice gruels, flour gruels, milk, curd-liquor, and so forth. This meaning is found in the Vinayas of all schools;

however, the practice of including fish and meat as timely food was previously abolished and not followed, which is for the best. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* state: [omitted].

There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which eating meat is not permitted; these various prohibitions and restrictions are fully detailed in that text. Second, regarding "non-timely drinks" (*vikālabhojana*):
the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that all grains, legumes, or wheat that have been boiled but not broken apart may have their juice extracted and drunk.

This applies to ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, the juices of the fourteen kinds of fruits, and the juices of raw fruits, provided they have been purified with water if the bottom of the vessel [has come into contact with impurities].
Residual water used for rinsing and the like are also termed "pure. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If grapes have not been purified by fire and their juice has not been purified by water, or if they are mutually impure, one should not drink them; however, if they are pure, one may drink them.

Following this principle, it applies generally to the four types of medicine; they are purified to alter the flavor and eliminate greed. The *Samantapāsādikā* states that "juice of śālūka fruit" refers to the root of the lotus.

Clarify the juice of the fermented drink so that it is clear enough to drink. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If one has various fruits and cannot finish eating them all, one is permitted to break them open, extract the juice, and drink it.
However, if by nightfall it has turned into *kaṣāya* (bitter wine), it must not be drunk, because its alcoholic potency is about to be realized.
This rule concerns the eight kinds of fermented drinks (*aṣṭavidha-pāna*) which were consumed by the ancient desireless sages (*ṛṣi*); these include the sourness of pears (*li*).

Regarding dates, sugarcane, *mṛdvīkā* fruit, grapes, *śāluka* fruit, and the like: if they cause intoxication, one should not drink them. If one drinks them, one is to be dealt with according to the Dharma. The principle is as follows:
when preparing a fermented beverage (*mantha*), it is essential that the liquid and the dregs be separated;
one must strain and clarify it until its appearance is like water before it may be drunk. If there is turbid liquid mixed with solid food, for every swallow, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding the seven-day medicinal substances for *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses, the Vinaya states: "Ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar—these five kinds are recognized by the world as both food and medicine;
they should be treated like rice or parched rice, and one must not let them appear coarse.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, sugar syrup may also be accepted for seven days, because its essential nature has not yet been relinquished. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* adds fat as one further kind.

In this Vinaya, Śāriputra suffered from a wind-disease (vāta-roga). Following the physician’s instruction, he was taught to consume five kinds of fats—namely those of the bear, the brown bear, the pig, the donkey, and the fish.
The Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states: "This medicine is pure and free from the odor of food; it may be accepted at one time and consumed for seven days.

There are four hundred and four diseases: one hundred and one are treated with animal fats, those caused by the heat of the fire-element are treated with ghee (sarpis), and those caused by the water-element are treated with oil."

Honey treats miscellaneous illnesses; for these, use the three aforementioned medicines to treat them. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that stone honey (*śarkarā*) must not be consumed indiscriminately, except by five types of persons who are permitted to eat it:
those traveling on long journeys and those who are ill. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that one is permitted to drink it with water during the two times of hunger and thirst.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if much curd is obtained at the beginning of a meal and cannot be finished, one may prepare fresh butter (*navanīta*) from it. 7.
One may accept [ghee] for seven days; if one accepts it for a long period and cooks it into mature ghee (*sarpis*), one may accept it for seven days.
If, at the time of begging for food, one obtains much ghee, a poor or sick bhikṣu may strain it through fine cloth and take the ghee; he may accept it for seven days.

If there is a necessary reason and he cannot perform the ritual before midday, he should make a formal declaration in the presence of another bhikṣu, saying: "This is pure substance; having received it, I shall prepare it within seven days."
If one receives [medicine] daily but forgets it, or if one does not receive it or purify it (pariṣkāra) when the time has passed, this is called "impure.

Regarding medicines for as long as life lasts (*yāvaj-jīvikāni*), the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Black pepper, long pepper, ginger, harītakī, and so forth—when these various medicines are mixed with food that may be eaten at any time, they must be received [as medicine].
A sick bhikṣu may consume them for as long as he lives. This Vinaya further records the Buddha’s words: "All bitter, pungent, salty, and sweet [medicines]..."
Regarding those things unfit to be used as food, it is permitted to consume them for as long as one lives. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"All trees, fruits, roots, stems, branches, and leaves that are unfit to be used as food may all be accepted and consumed for the duration of one's life.

The meaning is that, regarding everything listed above, the essential nature has been briefly explained according to the various sūtras and vinayas; however, people in the present day frequently consume food outside of the proper time.
What is meant by "eating at the proper time"? It refers to eating dates or the juice of various raw fruits that are not clarified;
or eating raw lotus roots, rice gruel, and the like; or, when one does not have a serious illness, consuming rock sugar, ghee, oil, apricot-pear soup, and so forth at an improper time.
All of these are contrary to the Dharma. For every swallow of such food, there is a *pāyattika* offense. Therefore, the Vinaya says: "Seven."
If one consumes it after seven days have passed, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense. Regarding why the *akṣa* (apricot) decoction is not permitted for consumption:
the answer is that the Vinaya merely states, "Sick bhikṣus are permitted to consume *akṣa*," but it does not explicitly permit it as a decoction.

Furthermore, because the potency and flavor of this decoction are so great, it differs from things such as clarified butter (*sarpis*). The Great Master said: "It is not permitted to eat or consume it at an improper time."

Regarding the powder of dried *huang* (Rehmannia) and *fuling* (Poria cocos), as well as various delicious decoctions and the like, it is now ruled that these may be eaten. How is this known? For the Vinaya states:
"Butter, oil, honey, and fine foods are considered 'proper food' (*bhojana*) and 'proper medicine' (*bhaisajya*); even for these, it is permitted to eat them at improper times if one is ill.

How much more so for these medicinal substances, which are not of heavy flavor; if one has an illness requiring treatment, why would their consumption not be permitted? Now, let us further discuss their admixture.
Regarding the clarification of the characteristics of transformation and the identification of the substance, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"Just as grape juice may be drunk by one who observes the precepts, if it transforms into wine it should not be drunk; if it transforms into sour wine (kṣaudra), it may be drunk again.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Sugar cane is a 'timely medicine' (*kālabhaiṣajya*); its clear juice is a 'non-timely syrup' (*vikāla-pāna*); when made into stone honey (*śarkarā*), it is a 'seven-day medicine' (*saptāha-bhaiṣajya*); when burned to ash..."

Roasted [grains] are medicines for as long as one lives (*yāvajjīva*), and sesame seeds are likewise. The *Sarvāstivāda* school states that when these four types of medicines are mixed together, one should take them according to whichever is most potent.

If a medicine for a specific time (*kālika*) is supplemented by a medicine for as long as one lives to constitute a seven-day medicine (*saptāhika*), it is taken for seven days because the power of the seven-day medicine is predominant and it serves as a supplement.
This is like using molasses and pepper to supplement ghee, oil, and so forth, which is permissible.

If one prepares a seven-day medicine for consumption, or if one uses time-medicine (*kālika-bhaiṣajya*) or seven-day medicine to assist in the preparation of a lifetime medicine (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*), it may be taken as a lifetime medicine.
For example, this applies to cases such as making pills by mixing *iṅguda* seeds with ghee and milk;
likewise, when using poisonous substances such as *atīsa* or *akarkoṭaka* to soak beans or wheat, these may all be consumed throughout one's life. If [the substance] is a lifetime medicine...
Medicines that are seven-day medicines and assist in the formation of "timely medicines" (kālabhojana) are those consumed during the proper time,
such as food made by mixing ghee, oil, ginger, pepper, tangerine, and so forth with flour. If the proportions are equal and their potencies are balanced,
they may be designated and categorized under a single name.

Regarding the third section, the distinctions between the two types of formal acceptance (*pratigraha*)—those by hand and those by mouth—there are five points: first, the restriction on the two types of mental acceptance;

second, the differences in the methods of acceptance; third, the different ways of declaring purity (*śuddhi*); fourth, the general applicability or restrictions of acceptance; and fifth, whether multiple acceptances may be obtained or not.

As for the restriction on the fivefold acceptance by hand, the Sarvāstivādins state there are five reasons: first, to prevent the causes and conditions for theft; and second, to serve as a witness to the act.
Third, to stop slander; fourth, to accomplish fewness of desires and contentment; fifth, to give rise to a mind of faith and respect in others. The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* states:
"Because the precepts had not yet been established, each gave rise to transgressions. Laypeople rebuked them, saying:
'We do not rejoice in seeing these evil people wearing robes of cut and dyed cloth, yet they eat food that should not be eaten. This is called [the fault of] eating.

Regarding the sequential explanation of "receiving by mouth": this is for the purpose of preventing "receiving by hand. If there were no such rule concerning the mouth, [the food] would be lost after noon;

because this rule exists, it remains until the limit is reached before it finally ceases to exist. Furthermore, it is to prevent the seven offenses of eating at improper times, eating what has been stored overnight, receiving what has been touched by others, cooking inside [a monastery], storing overnight, and cooking for oneself; whereas "receiving by hand" prevents only the offense of not receiving and the offense of being touched by others.

Regarding the two offenses: second, concerning the distinctions in the formal reception of the Dharma, the Vinaya states that if one intends to receive oil but mistakenly receives ghee (*sarpis*), the reception is not valid;
in all cases, the object and the intention must correspond, and there must be mutual understanding between the mind and the circumstances for it to be termed a "reception. This is the sole exception:
those with impaired vision or those who dislike seeing renunciants may receive the substance by placing it on the ground. Knowing this, prior to receiving [the substance], one must necessarily...

One must first form the intention to receive [the food] and then receive it. Regarding the method for receiving food at the initial reception, it is as explained below in the section on the *pratimokṣa* rules.

Next, to clarify the method for receiving non-timely liquids (*vikāla-pāna*) by mouth: among the various methods for receiving medicines and the rules for "purification" (*viśuddhi*) that follow, the Vinaya contains only the names of these receptions but lacks the specific procedures for receiving them.
Now, I have set forth these procedures based on their underlying principles; it would be beneficial to practice accordingly.
[Approaching] a [Bhikṣu or Bhikṣuṇī], one should fully observe the proper deportment and, with a sincere mind, speak these words: "Venerable Sister (or Venerable Brother), please attend to me.

I, [the Bhikṣu or Bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so, because of this cause and condition of thirst, now receive from you, Venerable Sister (or Venerable Brother), this ginger-honey decoction for the purpose of consuming it during the night.
[This is to be recited three times. If it consists of various fruits such as grapes or pears, etc., [the formula is adjusted accordingly].

Regarding fruits, syrups, and so forth, one should record the specific medicinal name according to the patient's illness and include it within the ritual procedure; simply changing the name constitutes the formal act.

If one receives and drinks them all at once, there is no need for the formal addition [of the ritual]. The oral procedure for receiving seven-day medicine says: "Venerable Sister (or Brother), please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī) [Name], now, on account of the cause and condition of fever, receive this ghee as seven-day medicine."
[This is] divided into seven days for taking [medicines] while staying together; therefore, one now receives [them] from the Venerable Sister (three times).
Just as one takes oil for wind-diseases (*vāta*), honey for cold-diseases (*śīta*), and rock-sugar (*śarkarā*) for miscellaneous diseases, each should be taken according to the specific ailment.

The procedure for placing the written notice into the mouth may be understood by analogy with the following: The procedure for receiving medicine for life (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*) is as follows: "Venerable Sister, please attend to me. I, a bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī]..."
"I, [Name], now for the cause and condition of wind-disorder (vāta), receive this *śu-yū-wán* (暑蕷丸) as a medicine to be taken for life, because I wish to take it regularly and for long-term use.

I now receive it from the presence of the Virtuous Sister" (recite three times). Or, according to whatever ailment one has—such as ginger, pepper, cinnamon, or other of the nine powders—one names the specific remedy appropriate to the disease, taking each medicine as the primary one in accordance with the ritual procedure for the mouth; the meaning is as stated above.

If one purchases medicine that is not yet sufficient, as soon as it is obtained, one should perform the *mukha-dhāraṇa* (oral consecration) ritual; however, if the substance is a medicine for life (*yāvaj-jīvikam auṣadham*), one should prepare it according to its original name.

If it is a medicine for the time (*kālika-auṣadha*) or a seven-day medicine (*saptāhika-auṣadha*) that has been included within the category of pills or powders, it should be taken as a medicine for life.
If circumstances prevent [the preparation] from being done together, one may combine it with a medicine for life and prepare them at the same time.

Regarding the Dharma procedure for responding to one [person]—whether a *bhikṣu* or a *bhikṣuṇī*—the ritual formula is as follows: "Venerable Sister (or Venerable Brother), please attend to me with a single mind.

I, the *bhikṣu* (or *bhikṣuṇī*) [Name], now, for the sake of the causal condition of a certain illness, take these fermented soybean products, clarified butter, and other medicines suitable for lifelong use, in order to divide them for storage and long-term consumption.

Therefore, I now receive them from you, Venerable Sister (or Venerable Brother). (Recite this three times. Other items such as oil, honey, and dates should be declared according to this same principle.

If one knows [the rules] now but does not know the Dharma, and upon obtaining even a single piece of ginger or cassia, immediately hides it away without applying the ritual treatment (*mukha-dhāraṇa*), and subsequently consumes it, then with every swallow one incurs many *thullaccaya* offenses. It would be better to perform the ritual procedure at once and then consume it;
thus, the matter will be purified and free from fault. If one wishes to purchase medicine, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) negotiate the price.
Once the determination has been made, the bhikṣu himself selects [the portion] so that it exceeds his original share; having done so, he sends it to be weighed.
Once weighed, he receives it, but must not set it down on the ground; he must immediately apply the oral formula (*mukha-dharma*) before one [other person], whether a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī.

If he does not do so, or if more than a moment passes, the acceptance is lost and an improper touch (*duṣṭa-sparśa*) arises. If he obtains it from a layperson to take back home, he must pound and mix it together.

Thereafter, it is most excellent to receive [the food] and apply the rite of adding it to the mouth. When first receiving medicine, if one forgets to perform the *śuddhi* (purification) rite, it does not constitute an impure contact (*duṣṭa-sparśa*).

Therefore, the text below in the Vinaya states: when one has received raw fruit but forgets to perform the purification, the Buddha said that one should set it down on the ground, have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to prepare food) perform the purification, and then wash one's own hands and receive it again. Thus, we know that this is for the purpose of receiving.

Receiving [medicines] does not constitute an unwholesome touch. Regarding the third point, the difference in the method of *śuddhi* (purification): for the seven-day type of medicine, once the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been completed, one may privately appropriate it for oneself;
however, one must perform *śuddhi* before storing it. This is because the substance of the medicine is precious, and there is a danger of excessive greed or hoarding.

Furthermore, since it remains unchanged over long or short periods of time and its potency is exceptionally superior, it sustains the body’s strength; therefore, one is strictly required to perform *śuddhi*.

If one does not perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification) and exceeds the time limit, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. Regarding the remaining three medicinal substances, there is no method for relinquishing them because they do not possess the aforementioned intention;

therefore, it is unnecessary to perform the purification. The wording is as follows: "Venerable Sister, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī] named so-and-so, have this surplus medicine which has not yet been prepared.
For the sake of purification, I give it to you, Venerable Sister," etc., following the same procedure as the discourse on surplus robes (*atireka-cīvara*).
Purity consists solely in changing the name to "different. Regarding the fourth point, the two types of receiving—by hand and by mouth—their permissibility and prohibition are as follows:

Receiving by hand is permitted for one person to prevent theft; once that person has completed the reception, it is common to other bhikṣus who may eat it together. It is argued that receiving by mouth is also common to others, because the ritual of the mouth extends to others.
Furthermore, there are two ways in which medicine is common: first, the commonality of flavor; second, the commonality of receiving by hand. Thus, these two are mutually pervasive.
If one relinquishes [medicine] to another person who accepts it according to the Dharma, why is it not lost? How is this known? For the Vinaya states:

"If on the seventh day medicine is given to the bhikṣus for them to eat, if it is given to someone else, the recipient loses [the status of] what was received; the medicine is not pure, and the Buddha does not permit it. He encourages its relinquishment and encourages its consumption.
Based on this principle, we know that [the status] is generally lost. Fifth, regarding whether one may receive [medicine] again after having received it once: [one may not].

The *Yi* (義) commentary states: Regarding manual acceptance (*pāṇisamādāna*), if one loses the original acceptance through contact with another, one must accept it again; although this constitutes a repetition, there is no fault.

Regarding oral acceptance of the Dharma (*mukhasamādāna*), the Sarvāstivādins say that if, within five days, a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things permissible) comes and touches the medicine, and one accepts more without having finished the previous period, the seven-day rule applies once again.
This is not based on the two-day rule, but is accepted strictly according to the nature of the Dharma itself, rather than following other [procedural] rules.
Once six days have passed since the initial administration of medicine, one may not add more medicine, as it will enter the state of purity (*śuddha*).

Therefore, one should follow the power of the original medicine and not perform the ritual of addition. If there are many medicines and one does not know which is the primary medicine, one should undergo the two-fold reception (*paribhoga*) by hand and mouth before consuming them.
If the illness is severe and one is unable to perform the oral reception, one may consume the medicine directly without needing to perform the ritual procedure.

If a monk who is nursing a patient receives the formal consent (kammavācā) on behalf of that patient through both hand and mouth, it constitutes a valid reception of the rite; one should receive it while pronouncing the name of the sick monk.
Chapter Fifteen: On the Mutual Support Between Teacher and Disciple.
This chapter has seventeen major sections: 1. Explaining the name of the preceptor; 2. The intention of the *upādhyāya* upon whom one relies; 3. Persons exempt from relying on a preceptor;

4. Persons who must rely on a preceptor; 5. The general rules for the *upādhyāya*; 6. The procedure for the disciple’s formal announcement; 7. The method for requesting the transmission of the scriptures;
8. The method for repaying kindness; 9. The intention of the *ācārya* upon whom one relies; 10. The period of dwelling without a teacher.
Section Eleven: On the Virtue of the Preceptor; Section Twelve: On the Method for Requesting a Preceptor; Section Thirteen: On the Method of the Preceptor’s Guidance;

Section Fourteen: On the Method of Rebuke; Section Fifteen: On the Method of Punishment; Section Sixteen: On the Method of Reprimanding for Losses; Section Seventeen: On the Method of Reprimanding for Repentance.

Regarding the first [section], explaining the names of the teachers: Question: What are the names "Teacher" (*śāstṛ*), "Preceptor" (*upādhyāya*), and "Instructor" (*ācārya*)? Answer: These have no direct translation;
by inferring from their meanings, one may roughly understand their scope. The *Sudarsana* states: "To see what is faultless and to reprove one for seeing faults is called 'my Teacher.
To instruct and cause one to know within the shared wholesome dharmas is my 'Instructor' (*ācārya*). It further states: "As for the Preceptor (*upādhyāya*..."
In the language of the Western Regions, this is translated into Chinese as "knowing whether there is an offense or no offense," which is why he is called an Upādhyāya (Preceptor).

Thus, the text below in the Vinaya states: "Whether I have committed an offense or not, the Teacher does not know. The meaning is that an Upādhyāya is one who provides the power for birth (*balotpādaka*), while an Ācārya is one who provides correct practice (*samyak-caryā*).

A *śiṣya* (disciple) is so called because they study after me; they are my younger brother (*dì*) and their understanding arises from me, thus they are my son (*zǐ*). This is found in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
The non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also address their teachers as *upādhyāya*.
Regarding the second point, the intention of reliance, the *Śikṣānanda-ṣaḍdig-gamana-sūtra* states that there are five intentions with which a disciple serves his teacher:
first, to revere and honor him; second, to be mindful of his kindness; third, to follow all his verbal instructions; fourth... [text continues].
There are five reasons why one should not grow weary of thinking about [the teacher], and five subsequent reasons for praising the teacher’s instruction of disciples:

first, to cause them to understand quickly; second, to cause them to surpass the disciples of others; third, to ensure they do not forget what they have learned; fourth, to provide explanations for all doubts and difficulties;
and fifth, to cause the wisdom of the disciples to exceed that of the teacher. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The teacher ordains the disciple."
One must not ordain others for the sake of providing for oneself; to do so incurs an offense.
Rather, one should cause that person to attain ordination through one’s influence so that they may cultivate various wholesome dharmas and achieve the fruits of the Path. This Vinaya states:

"A preceptor should regard his disciple as he would his own child, and a disciple should regard his preceptor with the thought of a father. The meaning of "regarding him as one's own child" is that one must...

Possessing four intentions: first, training and instructing as a master craftsman; second, compassionate mindfulness; third, sympathetic love; and fourth, gathering [others] through clothing and food.

The meaning is that one should regard them as a father would look upon his son. Conversely, one should possess four states of mind: first, affectionate love; second, respectful compliance; third, fear of transgression;
and fourth, reverence and veneration in providing support—just as a minister serves a sovereign. Therefore, the Vinaya says: "In this way, they successively respect and honor one another."
By observing [these rules], the True Dharma shall abide long and flourish.

Third, there are eight persons who are exempt from the requirement of formal dependence (*niśraya*); this Vinaya lists six, while other schools list two. The Vinaya states: first, those who delight in solitude;
second, those who guard their dwelling place; third, the sick; fourth, those who nurse the sick; fifth, those who have already completed five years [of seniority]; and sixth...

One should naturally abide in a place where one’s own conduct and wisdom are unsurpassed by others; this is because there are seven types of places of famine and lack of food. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If one fears dying of starvation, one should dwell in a place where one sees one's upādhyāya every day.

If one fears that this cannot be done, one should stay within fifteen days' distance, or two and a half yojanas. When the time for the *pravāraṇā* arrives, one must come to see the upādhyāya and perform the eightfold path of service."
Regarding the "place that accords with one's wishes," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The bhikṣus each diligently cultivated the Path;
as there was no one to serve as their *upādhyāya*, they relied upon the senior monk (*sthavira*) within the assembly, honoring him according to the dharma of a teacher. The *Mātṛkā* states:
"When first arriving at another place, if you do not know the people well, listen for two or three days and then make your selection" (this rule is the same in this Vinaya).

Regarding the fourth category, those who rely [on a teacher] collectively comprise ten types of persons. As stated in the Vinaya: first, when the preceptor has passed away; second, when the preceptor has abandoned the path (renounced the monastic life);

third, when the preceptor has resolved to go beyond the boundary; fourth, when the preceptor has relinquished the right to have followers; fifth, when the disciple’s circumstances have separated them from another region;

sixth, when the disciple no longer finds satisfaction in the dwelling place and seeks superior conditions elsewhere; seventh, when less than five years have elapsed since ordination; and eighth, when one is not proficient [in the precepts].

Regarding the framework of the teachings, the *Vinaya* states: "If one is foolish and lacks wisdom, one must rely upon another for as long as life lasts. This refers specifically to the practice of the teachings.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that even if one has received the precepts for many years, if one does not know the five dharmas, one must rely upon another for as long as life lasts:

(1) not knowing what constitutes an offense; (2) not knowing what does not constitute an offense; (3) not knowing what is light; (4) not knowing what is heavy; and (5) not having extensively recited [the scriptures].

Regarding the universal application of the *vinaya* for those who have attained mastery, the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "One who has reached one hundred years of seniority (*vassa*) but does not know the Dharma should rely upon one who has ten years of seniority and knows the Dharma.
Whether foolish or wise, this refers to those who repeatedly commit various offenses. The *Vinayamātṛkā* further states that there are three types of persons who do not recite the precepts:

those who intentionally do not recite them; those who previously recited them but later forgot them; and those whose faculties are dull such that they are unable to master the recitation through study. These are the three kinds.

A person may not be separated from their preceptor (*niśraya*). Furthermore, because the first seven types of persons have not yet completed five years of summer retreat (*pañca-varṣa*), they must rely on a preceptor;

if they have completed them, such reliance is no longer required. As for the latter three types of persons, once they have passed the five-year mark and possess the capacity for independent practice, they cease relying on a preceptor.

However, regarding the loss of reliance after five years, this is discussed from the perspective of formal instruction; according to their own practice, they ultimately still require the teacher’s guidance—thus it is stated in the Vinaya.

It is said that only when the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*) is established is one truly free from dependence; furthermore, according to various teachings, even a Buddha has a teacher, namely the Dharma.
Regarding the fifth teacher and the seven kinds of common practices for disciples, the Vinaya states: "First, the Sangha acts as the teacher..."
When a disciple is being punished, the preceptor should intervene to reconcile them with the Sangha, ensuring that the proceedings are conducted according to the Dharma without opposition;

he should seek the removal of the offense so that the Sangha may swiftly grant absolution. Second, if the preceptor commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, the disciple should exhort him in accordance with the Dharma to confess it;
having done so, he should assemble the Sangha and perform the six-night *parivāsa* for concealment.
Regarding the three types of offenses and so forth: if the preceptor falls ill, the disciple shall attend to him, or have another person care for him until he recovers or passes away.
Regarding the four types of preceptors: if the disciple does not find the dwelling place agreeable, he shall move himself or instruct others to move it. Regarding the five types of preceptors:
if there is a matter of doubt, the disciple shall instruct according to the Dharma and the Vinaya in accordance with the law. Regarding the six types of preceptors: if they are wicked... [text ends].
Upon seeing a newly ordained disciple, one should instruct them to abandon wrong views and abide in right view. Regarding the seven types of disciples, they should be protected by two things:

namely, the Dharma, and food and clothing. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or instructor (*ācārya*) engages in unrighteous conduct, the disciple must not speak harsh words;
rather, in accordance with the method of admonition, they should use gentle speech to counsel the teacher, saying: 'This should be done; this should not be done.'"

If the preceptor does not accept the words, the disciple should leave and go far away. If it is the teacher upon whom one relies, one should take the robes and bowl, go beyond the boundary for one night, and then return.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the teacher commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and seeks the Saṃgha to request a formal act (*karmavācanā*), the disciple should sweep and sprinkle the area, arrange the seats, assemble the Saṃgha, and request the master of the formal act and the others [to proceed]."
Regarding the sixth disciple’s procedure for reporting a matter: in this Vinaya, whenever one intends to perform any action, one must inform the teacher so that they are aware.
At the time of reporting, one should fully assume the dignified posture, kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and say:

"Venerable sir, please take note. I, the disciple [Name], for a certain reason, must go to a certain place. I have a companion named [Name]; I inform the Venerable sir so that he may be aware. (One need only state this once. The teacher should then weigh the propriety of the situation.

That is to say, if three conditions are met—the companion is suitable, the destination is suitable, and the business to be conducted is suitable—then one may be permitted to go according to the regulations.

If these matters are contrary [to the requirements], one should not be sent; however, the companion must have a clear understanding of the Vinaya teachings before they may depart. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"When intending to travel, one should inform the teacher two or three days in advance so that he may be aware of it, with the sole exception of attending to the needs of nature (defecation and urination)."
Regarding the use of a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that for all actions one must inform one's teacher, with the sole exception of three things:
paying homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, defecating or urinating, and chewing a tooth-stick; these do not require informing the Saṅgha.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one may take half a thread or half a morsel of food without informing the teacher. However, if one sews a full thread without informing [the teacher], it constitutes an offense.
The *Za zang jing* (Saṃyukta-āgama) states: "If one cannot inform the teacher individually, it is permissible to report the matter collectively.
Furthermore, if a barber arrives while the Upādhyāya is absent, one should inform an elder bhikṣu so that he may be made aware.

When the teacher returns later, one should explain the prior circumstances, saying: "I have already informed bhikṣu [Name]. Other beneficial matters should be handled according to this general principle.

When one intends to travel a long distance, one must not inform the teacher at the last moment; rather, one should inform him in advance, one month or half a month prior, so that the teacher may deliberate upon it.
The *Sudarsana* states: "A disciple traveling with a teacher must not go too far from him;
[the distance] may be limited to seven feet. The *Śrāmaṇera-Ācāra-sūtra* states: "A disciple following a teacher must not step on the teacher’s shadow, nor should he follow behind the teacher."
There are five further matters regarding walking: first, one must not pass through or frequent people's homes; second, one must not stop along the way to converse with others;

third, one must not look left or right; fourth, one should keep the head lowered while following behind the teacher; fifth, upon arriving at the house of a donor, one should stand to one side, and only sit when the teacher instructs one to do so.

Regarding the seventh point, "Requesting the Sūtras and Inquiring about their Meaning," the Vinaya states: "At dawn, he should enter the preceptor’s room to receive the sūtras and inquire about their meaning.
The *Śrāmaṇera-ācāra-sūtra* states: "If one enters the teacher’s room, one should snap one’s fingers three times.

The commentary explains: "In general, when a disciple visits his teacher, he should avoid six places: first, he must not stand directly in front; second, he must not stand directly behind; third, [he must not stand directly to the left]..."
1. One must not stand too far away; 2. one must not stand too close; 3. one must not stand in a high place; 4. one must not stand upwind.

Regarding the eighth [requirement], the *Prātimokṣa-vinaya* states that at dawn one shall enter the preceptor’s room to remove the vessels for excrement and urine, announce that the time has arrived, and so forth;
three times each day—at morning, midday, and evening—one shall inquire after the preceptor’s well-being. Furthermore, one shall report to him on two matters:
When performing laborious tasks, one must not decline or make excuses; first, one should repair the rooms and dwellings, and second, one should mend and wash the robes.
One must fully carry out all matters as instructed by the teacher according to the Dharma. If sent elsewhere, one must not feign reasons or causes for delay. The *Śrāmaṇera-Ācāra-sūtra* states:
"When the teacher speaks to you, you must not respond with words, nor should you attend to your own affairs; if there is something to be done, it is because the teacher has dispatched you."

There are seven matters that must not be transgressed: first, one must go directly; second, one must return directly; third, one must remember what the teacher says and also remember the responses given by others;
fourth, one must not forget anything said; fifth, if one cannot obtain what is sought, one must not remain overnight; sixth, one must not engage in frivolous or mocking speech;
seventh, when going out, one must follow the proper regulations. The *Saṃghāṭi-vinaya* states: "A disciple should [rise] at dawn..."

First, having entered the preceptor’s room with the right foot foremost, one should prostrate at his feet and inquire whether he has slept well; the rest is as described in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Even a bhikṣu of a hundred years’ standing must rely upon a bhikṣu of ten years’ standing who maintains the precepts, or at least one who knows the two divisions of the Vinaya.
Rising early, one should inquire after his welfare and provide a vessel for the evacuation of excrement and urine, no different from the manner in which a disciple serves his teacher.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "A great bhikṣu may receive dependence (*niśraya*) from a junior bhikṣu and receive all offerings;

he is no different from a junior toward a senior, with the sole exception that he must not perform prostrations at the feet; otherwise, he should do everything as prescribed. The *Vinaya* further states:

"If a disciple perceives five kinds of unrighteous conduct in his preceptor (*upādhyāya*), he should apologize and depart, saying to the preceptor: 'First, I act according to the Dharma, yet my preceptor does not.'"

1. One does not know that one's two types of self are inferior to those of the preceptor; nor does one know 2. that one has committed a transgression of the precepts, such that the preceptor abandons one and fails to instruct or reprove them;
nor does one know 3. that one has not committed a transgression; nor does one know 4. that although one has committed a transgression, one has already repented it.

Regarding the ninth point, the reliance upon the *ācārya*: generally, those who have newly received the precepts and have just entered the Buddha-dharma are ignorant regarding all matters, as if wandering in the darkness of night.

In whatever they undertake, their actions invariably deviate from the Holy Teachings. If they do not rely on the guidance of a teacher, what will their mental and spiritual faculties, their Dharma-body, and their life of wisdom have to depend upon?
Thus, the Vinaya states: "Those who have not yet completed five years of summer retreat, or those who, though having completed them, are still ignorant..."
This means causing one to rely upon a person of virtue so that they may receive and inherit his Dharma teachings, thereby perfecting their own benefit.
Tenth, regarding the duration of dwelling without a teacher: the *Vinaya* states that after first washing one's feet and drinking water, one may then rely [upon others];

the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if there is no excellent teacher, one is permitted to do so for five or six nights, but if there is an excellent teacher, it shall be for even as little as one night.

Regarding those who do not rely [on a preceptor], the *Five Hundred Questions on Matters of Offenses* states: "If one does not rely [on a preceptor] while drinking water, eating rice, or sitting or lying upon a bed or mat, one commits the offense of theft every day.
If one has passed ten years since full ordination (*daśavarṣa*) and does not recite the precepts, the offense is the same as that of not relying [on a preceptor]."
Eleventh, regarding the virtue of the preceptor (*ācārya*), the Vinaya states that there are five types of *ācāryas*:

first, the *pravrajyā-ācārya*, which refers to one upon whom one relies for receiving the ten precepts; second, the *upasaṃpad-ācārya*, which refers to one who presides over the *karmavācanā* for the purpose of receiving full ordination;
third, the *anuśāsaka-ācārya*, which refers to one who instructs in the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*); fourth, the *śrutoddeśaka-ācārya*, which refers to one who... [text continues]
Regarding those from whom one receives the precepts, there are five types of *niśraya-ācāryas* (preceptors providing dependence).
While the aforementioned four are collectively termed *ācāryas*, what is clarified here concerns specifically the *niśraya-ācārya*, as this serves to illustrate the position of the *upādhyāya*.
One must thoroughly master the Sūtras and Vinaya and possess clear, comprehensive understanding before one may assume this role; one must not hastily provide dependence according to mere convenience.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one must not arbitrarily seek formal reliance (*niśraya*); rather, one should rely on a teacher who has accomplished five qualities: first, affection; second, respect; third, shame (*hrī*);

fourth, dread of blame (*apatrāpya*); and fifth, delight in dwelling [with him]. In the subsequent section of this Vinaya, it is recorded that various bhikṣus arbitrarily relied upon others, which could not long benefit their practice of the śramaṇa path.
The Buddha therefore commanded them to select and accept a formal reliance. The *Mātṛkā* states: "In general, those who wish to..."
One who seeks to rely upon another should carefully weigh what is appropriate: whether that person can cause wholesome dharmas to increase;

whether one has asked others how this bhikṣu’s virtue of precepts (*śīla-guṇa*) compares and whether he is able to provide instruction; and whether his followers are of such a nature that they do not engage in disputes.

Only if all these conditions are met should one rely upon him. This Vinaya clarifies that there are three kinds of qualifications for the two types of teachers (*ācārya*): first, the exclusion of those who are immature.
Regarding the selection [of an ācārya]: first, one must be at least ten years old; second, although the two summer retreats may have been completed, one must possess wisdom;

third, even if one possesses the above two virtues, one must be able to diligently instruct disciples and be capable of mutual support as an ācārya. Furthermore, there are seven kinds of rules for co-residence, as previously explained in the section on the upādhyāya.

Twelfth, regarding the method for requesting a teacher: because this Vinaya was damaged in many respects due to the passing away of preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and the resulting lack of instruction, the Buddha permitted the practice of having a *niśraya-ācārya* (reliance teacher).

They were to provide mutual guidance and training according to the rules of a preceptor, honoring one another in succession so that the Buddha-dharma might increase and spread widely. When making the request, one should fully observe the proper deportment and proceed to...
That preceptor shall say: "Venerable Sister, please attend to me. I, the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī] named so-and-so, now request the Venerable Sister to act as my *niśraya-ācārya*.
May the Venerable Sister grant me the status of *niśraya-ācārya*; by relying upon the Venerable Sister, I shall abide in accordance with the Dharma.
(This is to be recited three times. That preceptor shall reply: "So be it; I shall grant you *niśraya*. Do not neglect it."

Yìsuí (Yishui) further stated that for each matter, one obtains five points [of merit], saying: "If the preceptor does not respond with his consent, the rite of dependence (*niśraya*) is not established.

Regarding the thirteenth, the rite of formal acceptance (*parigraha*), it is largely the same as what was explained previously in the section on the *upādhyāya* (preceptor); however, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Day by day..."
Regarding the inability of the teachings of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) from the distinct teachings of the three periods to be extensive:

at the very least, one should have a rudimentary knowledge of the gravity of the *prātimokṣa* precepts and the meaning of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*). Whether during the time of receiving the scriptures, the time of communal recitation, or the time of seated meditation, this is what constitutes "instruction" (*avavāda*).

If it is not so, then at the very least one must not be negligent. (Based on this text, when lecturing nowadays, explaining [the text] twice daily suffices; this itself serves as the exhortation (*anuśāsana*), making it unnecessary to provide further separate instruction.)

The meaning is that in requesting the teacher, one must possess four intentions: First, the intention to request that he take me under his care, thinking, "I shall request that he regard me with compassion and pity.
Second, the intention to request the Dharma of the Path to nourish the spirit, so that through his instruction, practice may be perfected and wisdom may arise.

Third, the intention to express one's own purpose, declaring that one is capable of relying upon him—meaning one possesses affection and reverence, regarding him as a father. Fourth, the intention to manifest one's own capability.

To act in reliance [upon one's teacher] means that the two mental states of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) must both be present; only when these qualities are possessed is one free from fault.
If it were otherwise, one’s practice would be in vain and no good would be accomplished. As the *Sudarsana* states: "The preceptor often has many disciples;

he may retain one person to provide for him, while the others may be allowed to engage in recitation and study as they wish. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The two teachers (preceptor and instructor) must not detain a disciple for even minor matters."
If a disciple utters vulgar or unrefined words in the presence of a layperson, he should ensure that the person is made aware of it.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a disciple faces danger from a king, the teacher must manage the situation; if there is plundering by bandits and so forth, one must seek money to ransom him, otherwise one commits an offense.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are four kinds of matters regarding which a disciple should deliberate with the preceptor: first, giving the Dharma; second, not giving the Dharma..."
One should abide in the first case: when food is provided. One should not abide in the second: when food is not provided. One should abide in the third: when both the Dharma and food are provided.
As for the fourth—when neither the Dharma nor food is provided—one need not consult the teacher; whether by day or by night, one should depart. This applies equally to the *ācārya*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] is also the same; thus its text says: "Regarding the four phrases of 'dwelling in suffering' and 'dwelling in happiness,' there is no difference. Fifth.

The *Baiwen shi* (One Hundred Questions) states that if one’s teacher is not acting unlawfully yet entices another śrāmaṇera away and commits a grave offense (*pārājika*), this constitutes the fourteenth ground for censure.
Regarding the matter of censuring transgressions: whenever a disciple has a fault, they must necessarily be censured according to reason.

Since the purpose of such censure is to bring the transgression to light, the Vinaya states: "If the teacher does not point out the transgression, yet the disciple nonetheless censures him, [the teacher] says: 'I..."
What transgression has been committed such that you rebuke me? The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If a teacher rebukes a disciple who does not accept it, he should inform the monastery administrator (karmadāna) to suspend his food. If the person is violent and wicked, the teacher should depart himself for one night and then return;
there is no fault in remaining. There are four kinds of rebukes by a disciple: first, regarding those of the highest grade of evil, [the teacher says], "Do not stay in this place."
Those of middling-grade evil are told, "Do not enter my room"; those of lower-grade evil are told, "Do not come; I have a place for you";
and those of the lowest-of-the-low grade of evil are told, "Do not perform services for me. They must not be struck with a staff. The *Śīla-sūtra* states:

"A teacher who fails to drive away or punish a disciple is more culpable than a butcher or a *caṇḍāla*. Such butchers do not destroy the True Dharma, nor are they certain to fall [into the lower realms]."
If one keeps wicked disciples within the three evil realms, one will inevitably be reborn in those evil realms.
Furthermore, to maintain a following for the sake of fame and material gain constitutes a person of false views; such a person is a disciple of Māra. As stated in the *Five Hundred Questions*:

"There was a teacher who did not instruct his disciples. Because the disciples broke the precepts, they fell among the nāgas. Later, upon encountering one another, they returned to harm their teacher."
The details are as extensively explained therein.

Regarding the fifteenth method, the formal censure (*tarjanīya-karman*): the general intent of censure is first to measure one's own anger or joy, next to weigh the gravity of the other's transgression, and furthermore, to employ the appropriate words of censure to bring forth the fault and make it known; thus, by relying on the transgression, one causes the offender to submit.
If the initial punishment is too light, the condemnation is grave while the offense is minor; this is merely a judgment based on personal whim and deviates specifically from the established rules.
How can this constitute a path of mutual benefit? You should cease such thoughts before acting. While outwardly manifesting stern authority, you inwardly harbor compassion and salvation.
To issue harsh words and strict commands to stop future transgressions—there is no method for striking people with staves in any of the various sutras or vinayas. By comparison, this is improper.

Seeing that monks and nuns were frequently subjected to flogging and beatings until the pain pierced to the very core of their predecessors, [the author] then cited the analogy of the physician’s three sons from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

This, however, does not fully grasp the teaching; for while those sons all shared the same level of realization as a "son of the Buddha" (*ekaputraka-bhūmi*) and possessed no distinction in their compassionate hearts, they were thus permitted to administer such punishment.
In the present time, however, the flogging and torturing of sentient beings are all carried out with a mind overflowing with the fierce blaze of hatred and malice.

Inflicting pain upon another would surely not fulfill the intention of a compassionate son; therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that for upper-grade offenses there is penal expulsion (*pravāsanīya*), for middle-grade offenses there is subduing (*pratisaṃharaṇīya*), and for lower-grade offenses there is reprimand (*tarjanīya*), yet even these contain no method of flogging with a staff.

The sixteenth *āpatti* of censure (*ākrośana*) is defined in the Vinaya as follows: to censure someone for life; or to censure someone whose anger does not subside even after they have committed an offense at the beginning of the summer retreat and completed the *varṣā*;
or to censure someone who is not present; or to censure someone without pointing out their specific transgression;
or to continue receiving offerings from someone one has censured—all of these are contrary to the Dharma and constitute an offense.

The seventeenth method, the ritual of confession and apology (*kṣamāpanā-vidhi*), states in the Vinaya: "One should have another bhikṣu lead [the offender] toward the presence of the *upādhyāya* or *ācārya* to be disciplined, so that he may quickly accept the confession.
One should observe whether he has been subdued and become gentle, and then know the proper time to accept the confession.
Therefore, the Vinaya says: "One should go before the two masters, fully assume the dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*), join the palms, and say: 'Venerable Sir (or Sister), I now confess.'"
If one regrets [the offense] and vows never to commit it again, yet the preceptor does not grant permission, one should perform repentance three times during the day.

If the preceptor still does not permit it, one should immediately humble oneself, comply, and seek to resolve the transgression. If one humbles oneself without opposition and seeks to resolve the fault, the two masters shall accept [the request];
if they do not accept it, one must be dealt with according to the Dharma.
Chapter Sixteen: The Ritual for the Recitation of the Precepts (*Poṣadha*).

This chapter consists of five major sections: first, the time and season; second, the conditions for assembly; third, the ritual procedure; fourth, miscellaneous practices; and fifth, the abbreviated recitation.
First, regarding the timing, there are five [occasions]: (1) it may be known that the Uposatha may be recited on the fourteenth or fifteenth day;

(2) as for "before or after a meal," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that while the Uposatha may be performed before a meal, one commits an offense by performing the Uposatha at dawn, because later-arriving bhikṣus would not hear the precepts;
(3) the precepts may also be recited during the day and night; (4) as for "increasing or decreasing," this...

In the Vinaya, regarding the section on external boundaries and disputes among bhikṣus: if a bhikṣu comes from outside, the Buddha instructed that the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha) should be adjusted accordingly.
If one knows he will arrive on the fourteenth day, the recitation should be held on the thirteenth; if he arrives on the fifteenth, it should be held on the fourteenth.

If he has already entered the boundary and it is impossible to recite together with him, one should inform the Saṃgha, saying: "The recitation of the precepts cannot be performed today; we shall perform the recitation on the fifteenth."
In this manner, it was increased up to the fifteenth day; yet if [the offender] did not depart, they were forcibly brought together to recite the *Vinaya*.

In the midst of the *Vinaya*, only two instances are clarified and not three are mentioned. Furthermore, in the latter part of this *Vinaya*, it is recorded that the bhikṣus of the country of Kauśāmbī fought for six years without reciting the *Prātimokṣa*.
Also, Ānanda suspected that the bhikṣu Ghoṣila had committed theft, and six *poṣadha* ceremonies passed without [the matter being resolved].

If one has been dissatisfied with the *Sāṃghika* community of fellow practitioners for twenty years and has not recited the *Prātimokṣa*, then by this standard, not reciting the Dharma for many years does not even merit an apology.
The common saying that "the Dharma perishes if it is not recited three times" is erroneous. Regarding the five appropriate and inappropriate times (*kāla-akāla*):

according to this Vinaya, when strife has persisted for a long time and the *Prātimokṣa* could not be recited, the community has now newly attained harmony; thus, it must be recited at an inappropriate time (*akāla*), as is the case in ordinary circumstances.
Because it occurs outside of the [proper] time, it is called "untimely" (*akāla*).
Regarding the second point, the gathering of conditions: the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that the *poṣadha* was held at an improper time, which hindered the practice of the Path;

therefore, the Buddha ordered that it be conducted according to fixed seasons so that everyone would know. The *karmadāna* (Vina) should rise early in the morning and announce to the Saṃgha: "May the Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha listen! Today is the [specific] day of the bright fortnight... or...
On such-and-such a day of the dark fortnight, the community of monks being in harmony, at such-and-such a time and place, announces to the Saṃgha that they shall recite the Prātimokṣa;

this is declared once and is sufficient. Nowadays, monks and nuns treat this recitation lightly, mostly performing it in the darkness of night, which causes later generations to have improper deportment.

Although the texts permit recitation at night, it is better to recite during the day. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that those who distribute the voting sticks do so for the sake of inquiries from lay donors (*dānapati*).

If the monks do not know the number of heads [in the assembly], the Buddha ordered that counting sticks (*śalākā*) be distributed; if they do not know the number of *śrāmaṇeras*, he likewise ordered that counting sticks be distributed.

If someone offers items for the *poṣadha* ceremony, the *śrāmaṇeras* are also permitted to take them. Although they do not reside at the place where the *poṣadha-karman* is performed, because they receive the counting sticks, they also obtain a share.
As the Vinaya states: "Because they receive offerings, the distribution of counting sticks extends to the *śrāmaṇeras* as well. If [the assembly] has not yet...
One who has received the ten precepts may also receive a tally (*śalākā*) because they partake equally in the offerings; thus the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Even those who have not yet received full ordination or the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera are included within the number of the Saṃgha. Regarding the procedure for inviting members by turn, there should be no distinction in principle.

The *Pañcavargika Vinaya* states: "The tally must be at least as short as five fingers and at most as long as a cubit (*hasta*); it must be no thicker than the little finger and no thinner than the smallest [finger]."
One must not shorten the eating sticks.
Regarding the third ritual procedure: this single section is insufficient on its own and must be supplemented by various other schools and human commentaries to refine the Vinaya.
It states: "When the day for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) arrives, the senior monk (*upādhyāya*) should instruct the bhikṣus, śrāmaṇeras, and others to sweep [the assembly hall]."
At the stūpa and the monastic quarters, have the high and low ground leveled and treated with mud; sprinkle the floor with scented water and prepare various incenses and flowers.

Even during the winter months when living flowers are not available, artificial flowers may be used. Within the hall where the precepts are recited, spread mats everywhere, including outside the threshold, so that sandals and shoes may be removed.
When the mallet is struck to assemble the Sangha, novices are not excluded and must enter together with the others.

When receiving voting sticks in the hall, the *Sifen jiejing xu* (Preface to the Four-Part Vinaya) opens the way for śrāmaṇeras to listen. If one follows other schools, those who do not [receive the precepts] are many;

if the śrāmaṇeras and the bhikṣusaṃgha recite the precepts separately, they should each assemble at their respective places when the bell sounds, and there is no need to gather together as described in the lower section on the rules for śrāmaṇeras.
When the saṃgha first enters the hall, they first bare the right shoulder and remove [their upper robes].

One should remove one's shoes, join the palms, and perform prostrations. If one fears that the crowd will be too noisy to allow for individual prostrations, one should simply bow the body and enter from the side.

(Regarding this, many temples in the Shu region have long practiced bowing to the Buddha while seated on couches; however, I have not seen scriptural authority for this and fear it is not in accordance with the Dharma. When a subject bows to a sovereign, how could they do so while remaining on a couch? Even a worldly king does not permit this, so how much less so for the Dharma King?
Tripitaka Master Wuxing of Bopapo stated that even in the Western Regions, there is no such custom.)
He further spoke a verse, saying: "Maintain the precepts with purity like the full moon; let body and speech be bright and stainless.
Being pure, harmonious, and free from conflict, one may then participate in the *poṣadha*. Having spoken thus, each should sit in their respective place.
The junior bhikṣus should rise to prepare hot water and clean towels; various kinds of flowers should also be prepared on three or five trays."
Regarding the five or three copper basins for scented water: nowadays, many use alms bowls to carry the water, but this is not a practice that generates merit.
If the assembly is large, one should have five or three junior monks assist in carrying them; each must bare one shoulder, remove their boots, and maintain proper dignified demeanor.
The *karmadāna* (Venerable of Affairs) shall take the scented water and the bath-water, wash his hands, and then hold the water.
When the *sthavira* (Elder) arrives before the seat, he kneels with his knees apart (*hugui*), and the *karmadāna* (Vina) personally distributes the bathing sticks (*yuchou*).

Nowadays, it is common for the *sthavira* to be sent to distribute the bathing sticks; this is not the correct ritual. At the time of distributing the bathing sticks, each member of the *saṃgha* recites a verse: "The noble *arhat* monks have assembled; the assembly of ordinary beings is in harmony.
With fragrant water, we bathe the pure sticks; through the *poṣadha*, may all sentient beings be delivered. Having finished speaking, he orders a young novice to [distribute them].
When Kāśyapa was about to proceed with the perfumed water, he first offered pure water; as he received the water, he further spoke this verse: "The water of eight virtues purifies all defilements;
Poured over the palms, it removes the stains of the mind. One who upholds the prohibitive precepts without flaw or transgression— May all sentient beings likewise be so.
While correctly performing the bathing with the fragrant decoction, he again spoke this verse: "The fragrant water perfumes and bathes, permeating all..."
The defiled dharma-body is fully endowed with the five parts; Prajñā is perfectly illuminating and complete, while liberation fills all sentient beings.
When the dharma-realm is fused, at the time of receiving the hot water, one may only use it to wash the hands and is not permitted to rinse the mouth. Such occurrences happen frequently nowadays;

therefore, the *weina* (ritual director) should specifically mark this. Once the bath-vouchers have been distributed, he should proceed to stand at the place for striking silence and take up the mallet.

Having washed [the hands], one should hold the counting sticks (*śalākā*) with the left hand and grasp the mallet with the right hand. One should strike gently and slowly; having struck once, one should rest the hand and release the mallet so as not to make a sound, and then chant it. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it simply says: "Listen to the distribution of the *śalākās*," and there is no other method.
