The instruction is to have one person go out and another receive [the guests], and so on, until they have received them and counted them. Having known the number, he proclaims:
"There are so many bhikṣus, so many śrāmaṇeras, and so many renunciants in total. Although based on this text, it is still not complete;
therefore, we supplement the deficiency with human speech. Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen: now the assembly of monks from the ten directions speaks.
If the interior and exterior of the *Kaṭhina* (monastery) are tranquil and free from all obstacles, it is fit for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).

I, [Name], a bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī], for the sake of reciting the precepts, shall distribute voting sticks (*śalākā*). Those of the upper, middle, and lower seats shall each receive the sticks according to the Dharma.

This includes the formal announcement and the entrustment [of the duty]. (This is a regular ritual procedure; one recitation suffices. Furthermore, there are those who announce, "It is fit for the *poṣadha*"; this, however, is a case of confusion and lacks clarity.

Regarding the recitation of the precepts (*Poṣadha*), it is now appropriate to substitute this with the recitation of the *Śīlaskandha* (the Precept Text), as this is logically consistent and free from contradiction. Furthermore, various masters have placed the introduction to the *Śīlaskandha* before the formal recitation;
among the novices (*śrāmaṇera*) present, some say "collective protection" (*shouhu*), some say "guarding the door" (*shouhu*), and others say "protecting the external purity.

However, there is no scriptural authority for these practices. When great *śramaṇas* enter, there is no fault in not reciting them, as the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya) states that the introduction to the precepts is [part of the formal procedure].

If they have already received permission, why must one immediately announce it? At the time of making the formal motion (*jñapti*), the text itself is concise; there is no need for preliminary dispatches.

If one says "announce the protection" (*saṃvara*) because of the distribution of voting sticks (*śalākā*), then for the sake of distributing the voting sticks, one should say "proceed with the protection.

If one does not announce "proceed with the protection," one may not say "collect the protection. Furthermore, if one has novices (*śrāmaṇera*) guarding the door and protecting [the assembly], what then?
It must be made clear that if this proclamation is for the protection of the Great Saṃgha, and the desire (*chanda*) has not yet been announced, how could one be permitted to depart?
Once the bell has been struck once, both the ordinary and the noble follow it; since the assembly is already gathered, why is there a need to proclaim again?

If outside śramaṇas enter, and because the assembly is incomplete due to doubts or omissions, it is necessary to proclaim again—yet if they are not being sought out together, how can they be sent away?

If there is doubt, and the assembly of monks has already gathered without prior suspicion, one should know that empty chanting is merely a hollow talk; who could accept such a transgression of false speech?
When the recitation is finished, the *karmadāna* comes before the *sthavira*, kneels on his right knee, and hands the voting tally (*śalākā*) to the *sthavira*.
The *sthavira* should then kneel on his right knee with palms joined; all the monks likewise follow the ritual procedure of the *sthavira*. The *sthavira*...

When formally taking up the tally-stick (*śalākā*), one should recite this verse: "The tally-stick of the unimpeded liberation of Vajra is difficult to obtain and difficult to encounter, like a golden fruit;
I now receive it with joy upon my head, and all sentient beings shall do likewise. When returning the tally-stick, one should again recite this verse:
"Endowed with purity, I have received this tally-stick; endowed with purity, I now return this tally-stick, firm and steadfast."
Having joyfully renounced [the merit] without omission, one speaks thus to all sentient beings; having finished speaking, one immediately hands it over to another and returns to one's original seat.

In this manner, it is passed on in succession until it reaches the Great Assembly (Mahāsaṃgha). When the Karmadāna arrives, he stands at the place of silence and receives the counting sticks (*śalākā*) from those who hand them over to the Elder (*sthavira*).
The Karmadāna may count them himself, or [the Elder may do so]. This is also the case when *śrāmaṇeras* recite the precepts in a separate location.

The *karmadāna* (Vina) shall go there to take the voting sticks (*śalākā*) for the novices (*śrāmaṇera*). When the novices arrive and sit among the assembly of monks, the *karmadāna* shall go to the place of silence and stand there;
he shall strike for silence and say: "Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen! Next, [the voting sticks] for the novices and female novices (*śrāmaṇerī*) shall be distributed.

Having said this once, he shall go to where the novices and female novices are, distribute them, and having finished the distribution, collect them and hand them over to the presiding elder (*sthavira*) to count.
When the counting of those seated is finished, the *karmadāna* (Venerable Leader) collects them all and returns to the place where silence is maintained.

Standing there, he strikes for silence and proclaims: "Venerable Sisters, listen! At this single residence, for one *poṣadha* ceremony, there are [number] bhikṣus, [number] bhikṣuṇīs, [number] śrāmaṇeras, [number] śrāmaṇerīs, and [number] śikṣamāṇās;
in total, there are [number] persons. Each is pure. This assembly of renunciants is harmonious and shall perform the *poṣadha*. Above, it accords with all Buddhas..."

To repay the four debts of gratitude, for the sake of all sentient beings, each person shall recite once from within the Sūtras a pure and wondrous verse. The assembly of monks joins their palms and simultaneously recites the verse:
"Pure as the full moon, having attained purity through the *poṣadha*, when the actions of body and speech are pure, only then should one perform the *poṣadha*.
(From the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*). Once that *karmadāna* has raised the counting sticks and approached the *sthavira*, he prostrates three times.
Having addressed the senior monk (*sthavira*), one says: "The community of monks is harmonious and requests that the Venerable Sister recite the precepts for the assembly.
If the senior monk wishes to speak himself, he says: "This dharma of the precepts is precisely what I shall recite," and then he proclaims it.
If he is unable, he says: "This recitation of the precepts is properly for [so-and-so]; however, because I am old and weak, my speech is turbid and foul, and I fear..."

After the assembly has been troubled [by the failure to recite], one should invite a person capable of recitation. The *karmadāna* (vinaya-master) should perform another prostration and then rise to go before the second senior monk (*sthavira*).

There, he should follow the same procedure of question and answer as before, without any difference. If the second senior monk is unable to recite, one should directly invite a person capable of recitation;
it is not necessary to proceed further down the ranks. Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Whether it be the senior monk or the next-ranking seat..."

If one is unable to recite it oneself, one may appoint another who is capable to recite it. If such a person has been appointed, one should strike the gong and announce: "Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
The Sangha has appointed the Vinaya Master [Name] to recite the Vinaya for the Sangha in the *brahmanī* voice. The Vinaya Master [Name] ascends the high seat (one announcement).

The Karmadāna [Name], using the *brahmanī* voice, may either announce this after having been discreetly requested, or he may do so without being announced; in all cases, he shall announce it before the Sangha.

Since one must invariably state both names together, the Vinaya text below prescribes that during the Council (saṃgīti), when appointing various Arhats, they were appointed by chanting both names together.

Once the Saṃgha has made the appointment, the Vinaya Master (vinayadhara) should rise and properly assume the dignified demeanor (īryāpatha). Having entered the midst of the Saṃgha and spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), he should perform prostrations toward the four directions to the Saṃgha.
Then, kneeling with his right knee on the ground, he should say: "I, [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so, bow my head in salutation (namas)."

I respectfully address the Sangha: as I have been appointed by the Sangha to recite the Vinaya, I fear there may be errors; I pray that those who join me in recitation will show compassion and grant their instruction.
Having spoken thus, one should perform another prostration and then ascend the seat. When ascending the seat, one must not cross one’s legs;
one must step onto the steps with feet together before shifting them. I have recently observed that monks and nuns frequently act in this manner, and therefore I have distinguished this point.
The marking of the outer ritual space is also called "ascending the steps and traversing the tiers" and "gathering the feet.
The remaining water from the perfumed bath is sprinkled by the *karmadāna* on the left and right; one should leave a vacant space in the center intended for people to pass through.

Fragrant flowers are also scattered so as to be all-pervasive. At the moment of scattering the flowers, each recites this verse: "Scattering flowers creates pure radiance; adorning with precious flowers..."
Spreading canopies and scattering myriad precious flowers throughout the ten directions as an offering to all Tathāgatas (*from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*).

Having spoken thus, the *karmadāna* strikes for silence and directs people to make offerings with Brahma-sounds and hymns of praise. When it comes time for the incense-offering and the recitation of verses, the assembly of monks should join their palms and each recite this verse:
"The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, and the fragrance of liberation—like clouds of radiant light, they pervade the entire world."
"Making offerings to the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, universally perfumed by seeing and hearing them, one realizes tranquil extinction" (from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*).

Having completed the offerings, the *karmadāna* must remain standing and wait until the preceptor has recited up to the point where it says "those who have not yet received full ordination shall come forth.

At that time, the preceptor should temporarily cease the recitation and allow the śrāmaṇeras to come forward. The śrāmaṇeras should fully maintain their dignified deportment as they approach the assembly and act according to the prescribed conduct.

Having performed three prostrations, one kneels with the right knee on the ground and takes the seat of honor. The presiding elder should instruct them, saying: "Command all [śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās]:
'Since your years are not yet sufficient and your practice is not yet complete, you are unfit to enter the number of the saṃgha for the formal ritual (karmavācanā).

You must wait until your years are sufficient and your practice is complete, and after you have received full ordination (upasampadā), you shall then be permitted to participate in the recitation of the precepts.'"
Each person shall return to their original place and recite the precepts quietly and with focused mindfulness, without distraction;
only then may they rise and perform one more prostration before departing in order. If the śrāmaṇeras and others are to recite the precepts separately, this [procedure] is not required.

Once the Precept Master has announced, "Those who have not come, declare your *chanda*," he next announces, "Who has sent the bhikṣuṇī to request instruction? (For the nuns, this question is not asked. If...
The one who receives the entrustment should rise and go into the midst of the Saṃgha; having paid homage, she kneels on her right knee, joins her palms, and says:

"Venerable Sirs, the harmonious Saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs from [Name] Monastery has dispatched the bhikṣuṇī [Name] for half a month to prostrate at the feet of the venerable Saṃgha and to request instruction for the bhikṣuṇīs.
(From the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*) Having spoken thus three times, she kneels long before the Elder, bows her body, and joins her palms.
One should say, "Venerable sir, out of compassion you are able to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; please do not take a seat higher than [ours].
Or one may say, "So-and-so is elderly and lacks virtue; he is unfit for this task; please invite someone more capable.

In this manner, one should proceed through the succession down to those with twenty years of seniority (*vassa*), questioning them thoroughly and not merely asking three or five. This is because those with twenty years of seniority or more are all capable of instructing the bhikṣuṇīs.

Therefore, if there is no one capable, one should return before the presiding elder (upādhyāya) and say: "I have inquired of all those seated below me, and they all decline, saying they are not capable.

The presiding elder should then say: "Venerable sirs, it is not that you are incapable of going; rather, it is solely because you cherish your primary practice (samyak-karman) that you do not accept the invitation.
When the nuns come to visit the preceptor for the precepts the following day, he should say: "There is no instructor among this assembly."
The admonition for the nuns is as follows: "Furthermore, there is no one among the nuns who can preach the Dharma well. Nevertheless, the Elder has issued an instruction to the assembly of nuns:

'You should be diligent and energetic, practicing the Path according to the Dharma; be careful and do not be negligent. (This passage regarding "should be diligent" appears in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, while the subsequent portion appears in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*).

Once this person has returned to their original seat, the Preceptor of the Precepts says: "The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall we perform? The Karmadāna replies: [He states the specific ritual to be performed.]

Regarding the *Karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts (it is incorrect to say nowadays that "reciting the precepts" refers to the *poṣadha* itself): the Preceptor must wait until the *Karmadāna* (Venerable of the Assembly) is seated before making the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

This is because if the announcement is made while he is not yet seated, there will be a discrepancy between those who are seated and those who are standing; would this not constitute the fault of a "separate assembly" (*pṛthaggaṇa*)?

When the recitation of the precepts is finished, at the verse beginning with "May those capable protect the precepts," the *Karmadāna* should strike the bell three times to summon those who have not yet received full ordination.
If someone comes to listen, and if a *śrāmaṇera* has not yet arrived, one should wait for them to arrive before preaching; if no one arrives at all, one should simply finish reciting the precepts.

After the *karmadāna* strikes the gavel three times to inform those outside that it is finished and they may enter, once the recitation of the precepts is complete, one should chant the *Caturvarga-gāthā* introduction as a *bhāṣya*.
This was established by the sages who possess the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) through the creation of prohibitions and incantations, so that others may feel shame and remorse.
This [precept] subsumes all those who lack a sense of shame and remorse; thus the Tathāgata established the prohibitions and recited the *Prātimokṣa* every half-month.

Having explained the benefits of the recitation of the precepts, one bows in homage to all Buddhas. The *Mātṛkā* states: "One must not perform a partial *bhāṣya* (recitation). To perform a partial *bhāṣya* constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

(If one does not understand the preceding Sanskrit sounds, it is also permissible to perform the *bhāṣya* in the local vernacular. Once the Preceptor has descended from his seat and entered among the Saṃgha, he should prostrate in thanks, saying:
The junior [bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so respectfully apologizes to the Saṃgha: "Appointed by the Saṃgha to recite the Vinaya, my three modes of action were not diligent and there were many errors.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me their grace and joy. The members of the Saṃgha should then each recite this verse of self-congratulation:

"The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is the foremost joy; To hear the Dharma and practice it brings the joy of gladness. The great assembly is in harmony, abiding in tranquility and extinction."

"May all sentient beings be swiftly freed from defilement and find peace and happiness. Then, recite the verses from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*: "The appearance of the Buddhas is joy; preaching the True Dharma is also joy;
the harmonious assembly of the great multitude is joy; and gathering together as renunciants is joy. Thereafter, chant the three prostrations and disperse.
Question: If one who practices mixed conduct asks whether it is permissible to depart before the *poṣadha* has been fully recited—having reached only halfway—may they go? Answer:

Since the original intent was for the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to be performed, although this is currently a mere announcement (*jñapti*), this *poṣadha* is nonetheless a matter belonging to the category of formal rituals;

therefore, one must declare their consent (*chanda*) in order to be permitted to leave. If a visiting *bhikṣu* or *bhikṣuṇī* from outside the boundary wishes to hear the recitation of the precepts, they should proceed directly [to the assembly].
One must not go from the place where the *Poṣadha* is being recited to another location, for fear of interrupting the recitation by others.
If the *Nidāna* has not yet been recited and the proclamation of purity (*pārisuddhi*) has not yet been made, incoming monks may enter in order and sit according to their rank.

If the *Śīla-ācārya* (Preceptor of Discipline) sees others arriving, he must immediately cease the recitation; if he does not stop, the visiting preceptor should reprimand him to stop and wait until the sitting is complete.

Following the sequence of the text regarding the place where one resides, one should explain it accordingly. Once the introduction has been recited and the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts) has been proclaimed, all should enter the midst of the Saṃgha.
After performing four prostrations toward the Saṃgha, they should kneel with their right knees on the ground.

One person shall announce the purity (*śuddhi-ārocana*), saying: "Venerable Sisters (or Bhikṣus), may the Saṃgha listen: [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so and others, numbering so many persons, are all pure. Having made this announcement, they should sit down in their respective order.
The Preceptor shall recite according to the sequence; if there are those who are not pure, he shall address each one individually, saying: "Venerable Sisters (or Bhikṣus, or Bhikṣuṇīs), listen!

[Name], having committed such-and-such an offense, has been prevented from participating in the *Poṣadha* and has not yet obtained purification through confession. He/She shall confess according to the Dharma later.
Having said this, he shall continue with the subsequent recitation following the previous formula. Even if many guests arrive or the number of people is large, [he should proceed as follows]...
When the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) is finished, one must have the host recite them again from the beginning; if they do not recite them, they should be dealt with according to the rule.

Therefore, the Vinaya states: "If many [nuns] come, one should explain it again for them. If many nuns from various monasteries come to request instruction and admonition (*ovāda*), one may accept the invitation at will.

One must first list the names of the monasteries and the individual nuns, and then conclude by summarizing the intent of the request. One must not say generically: "The nun so-and-so has been dispatched by such-and-such a monastery."

If the nuns, such as [Name], are unable to understand the text, and if there is no one among the assembly capable of reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, then the procedure for the *poṣadha* shall follow the previous method exactly:
one person shall be appointed directly to preach the Dharma and recite the sūtras, while all other instructions and admonitions shall be omitted, and the assembly shall then disperse.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If one's faculties are dull, if one is ignorant, or if there are obstacles such that one cannot go to another monastery to recite the precepts..."

At the very least, one must recite a single verse, saying: "Commit no evil, practice all that is good, and purify your own mind; this is the teaching of all Buddhas. Only after doing so may the assembly disperse;
it is not permitted to disperse without reciting anything at all. If the full verse cannot be recited, one should say:
"Be careful and do not be negligent," and only then may they disperse. If one remembers [the verse] while on the seat for the recitation of the precepts...
One who has committed an offense must immediately reveal it with a mental recitation, saying: "I, [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so, have committed such-and-such an offense;

I shall perform the confession according to the Dharma once the *poṣadha* recitation is concluded. Having done this, one may then hear the precepts. If there is doubt regarding whether an offense has been committed, one should mentally recite:
"I, [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so, have developed a doubt concerning such-and-such a matter; I shall [resolve it] once the *poṣadha* recitation is concluded."

Regarding the determination [of the procedure]: if one remembers having committed an offense before the precepts have been recited, one should first perform confession and then be permitted to hear the precepts.

The fifth is the abbreviated recitation. This Vinaya contains eight kinds of difficulties, namely: difficulties caused by kings, thieves, water, fire, the sick, non-human beings, evil insects, and so forth;
or difficulties where the great assembly cannot gather, where seats are few, where there are many illnesses, where it rains, or where there is strife during the preaching of the Dharma.
At night, for such reasons as these, it is permitted to give a brief exposition of the meaning.

That is to say, if there is a leader or administrator among the assembly who is well able to govern the community, and whenever it is midsummer or midwinter and he fears that the monks will become exhausted, he should provide a brief recitation of the precepts.

When the assembly has gathered at dawn and the *karmadāna* (Venerable of Affairs) has finished making the formal announcement (*jñapti*), the presiding elder (*upādhyāya*) further announces to the Sangha: "Today is the day for the recitation of the precepts."
"Venerable assembly, I pray that you all gather early so that I may briefly explain [the precepts]; do not use various excuses as a pretext to give rise to weariness or indolence.
If you act in this manner, it will also be a skillful way of governing the assembly, and your minds will be free from anxiety or regret.

The Preceptor of the Uposatha (Śīla-ācārya) should weigh the presence of obstacles and the distance of the location, observing whether the time for proceeding is difficult or not. If the time is distant, he should then recite up to the thirty-ninth or fortieth [offense], and the rest should be omitted.
If one briefly omits [the recitation] due to difficulties such as proximity, old age, illness, or feverish conditions, one should first recite the *Nidāna* (Introduction) and then omit the remainder.
How is it omitted? Having finished reciting the *Nidāna* for the *Poṣadha* and having asked whether there is purity, one should say:

"Venerable Sisters, these four *pārājika* dharmas are constantly heard by the Saṃgha... and so on, up to: "Venerable Sisters, these seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* dharmas are [constantly heard by the Saṃgha]."

From "The Community has often heard" (*saṃgha suti*) onwards, one must explain in detail until the end of the precepts. If a sudden emergency arises, one should simply say, "The Community has often heard.

If even the full introduction cannot be recited, one should say: "On this day of such-and-such month, at the time of the *poṣadha* for the recitation of the precepts, may the members of the Saṃgha each rectify their body, speech, and mind;
be cautious and do not be negligent. (Having finished speaking, they disperse. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that when one wishes to perform a *karma*...

Regarding those monks whose number is unknown, one should perform the rite before the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*; since the recitation is a formal regulation for the Saṃgha, the assembly must not be dispersed.

Next, concerning the rules for individuals: if a single person resides alone, they should go to the hall for the recitation, sweep and sprinkle the area, and prepare the requisites for the *poṣadha* exactly according to the previous procedure.
If visiting [monks—whether *bhikṣus* or *bhikṣuṇīs*] arrive in a group of four or more, [the same applies].
One must then explain it in detail: if there are three or fewer persons, each should address the others, saying: "Venerable Sister (or Venerable Brother), please attend with one mind:
today is the fifteenth day of the month for the Saṃgha’s recitation of the precepts; I, [Name], a bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī), am pure. (Recite this three times.

If there are two persons, they likewise address one another in the same manner. If there is only one person, one should reflect in the mind and speak aloud: "Today is the fifteenth day for the assembly of monks..."

"I, [Name], am pure regarding the recitation of the precepts" (recite three times). If one has committed a *pārājika* offense, one should be expelled and is not permitted to participate in the recitation of the precepts.

If one has committed an offense from *saṃghāvaśeṣa* downward for which there is no person present to whom one may confess, one should go before an image, mentally acknowledge and reveal the transgression, and then say:
"I, the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī] [Name], respectfully inform all Buddhas of the ten directions: now..."

On the day the community of monks recites the precepts, if I have committed a certain offense, I should not participate in the *poṣadha* (one recitation). If I have committed a minor offense, I should not recite the precepts;
rather, having reproached my own mind, I may then proceed with the recitation.

Chapter Seventeen: Observing the Summer Retreat (*Varṣā*). This chapter’s main sections comprise eleven parts:
1. The intent behind the regulations; 2. The explanation of the names; 3. Differences in the timing of the conclusion; 4. The extension of the summer retreat due to intercalary months.

1. Urging the four parties; 2. The five mental recollections; 3. Forgetting [the retreat] and its completion; 4. The seven [factors] and the boundaries; 5. Encountering difficulties and the opening of the summer retreat; 6.
Whether the summer retreat is valid when one leaves the boundary and encounters difficulties; 7. The five benefits of the *kārttika* month and their gains and losses.

First, regarding the explanation of the name through the analysis of its intended meaning: this Vinaya regulation applies across the three seasons, yet its intent lies in compassion for sentient beings.

Furthermore, it specifically concerns the summer months, as there are three faults to be avoided: first, wandering about without purpose hinders the cultivation of the path and one's spiritual practice;

second, harming the lives of living beings is a profound violation of compassion; and third, since such actions are improper, they invite public censure and slander. To prevent these three faults, the regulation of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) was established.
The *Yaśas-āvadāna* states that in the Western Regions, twelve months are combined to form three seasons, namely: spring, summer, and winter.
Therefore, the Vinaya says that for the crown prince, a "three-season palace" was established. From the first month to the end of the fourth month is called the "hot season";
from the fifth month to the end of the eighth month is called the "rainy season. Consequently, in that land, by the time of the fourth month, people frequently pile up firewood and timber.

The *Yi yu yue biqiu anju* (The Rainy-Month Retreat of the Bhikṣu) is specifically for the sake of the constant rains; thus the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* names the summer retreat "the rains" (*varṣā*), while the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* names it "the year" (*saṃvatsara*).
The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* names the summer retreat "the *la*" (*laba*). The remaining terminology can be understood. This term "*la*" (*laba*) signifies "conjunction" (*saṃgha*).
Therefore, the secular ritual says: "*La* means conjunction. The Sage established that bhikṣus should sit in the summer retreat for three months.

Because they settle together according to conditions rather than scattering, the meaning is that they should be combined. Furthermore, an external scripture states: "The *zu* (ancestral) signifies the beginning, while the *la* (winter solstice) signifies the end.
Thus, we know that to refer to the *xia* (summer retreat), one speaks of its beginning; to refer to the *la*, one speaks of its end.

A tradition records that although it rains for four months in the Western Regions, the torrential rains are most severe in the sixth and seventh months; in the fifth and eighth months, the rain is somewhat less.
Because it is subtle, there is the "later" *anvārambhaṇa* (post-retreat) period.

Regarding the difference in the timing of the second formal establishment (*saṃgha-karman*): Question: Since the summer retreat consists of four months, why is only a three-month period formally established?

Answer: There are two intentions for the establishment. First, because the physical forms of those who depend [on others] require material support and nourishment, the three-month period is established while opening the possibility for the later period.

There is one month for providing robes for one's person; secondly, if the binding [of the rainy season retreat] is completed at the end of the fourth month, it applies only up to the sixteenth day of the fourth month, and only then does it constitute a valid completion.
If, due to some circumstance, it cannot be bound then, the teaching would be too restrictive and difficult to practice constantly.
Therefore, the Sage established the rule beginning from the sixteenth day of the fourth month until the fifteenth day of the fifth month.
The reason for opening the first month and continuing the formal observance (*pravarana*) until its conclusion is to compassionately accommodate those of middle and lower capacities.
Although the Vinaya speaks of three types of *vassa*—the early, the middle, and the late—according to the actual wording of the formal resolution (*kammavācā*), there are in fact only two:

that which is resolved on the sixteenth day of the fourth month is the "early" [observance], while from the seventeenth day onwards, up until the sixteenth day of the fifth month, constitutes the [middle] period.
According to this Vinaya, for the Great Bhikṣu-saṃgha, if one does not enter the rains retreat either before or after [the prescribed dates], one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if one does not enter the retreat before [the first day] and fails to enter it by the sixteenth day of the fifth month, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding the third point, the extension or reduction of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) based on an intercalary month: although there is no explicit canonical text [stating] that one must rely on an intercalary month for the *anvārta* (summer retreat), the principle encompasses all schools in determining it by means of the intercalary month.
The Sarvāstivādins state: "If an intercalary month occurs during the summer, one may receive the rain-clothing (*varṣāśāṭī*) for one hundred and twenty days.

Since even the legal provisions for that clothing rely on the intercalary month of the summer, receiving the summer retreat itself should logically follow this same principle as a universal rule. Furthermore, this is consistent with the original intent of the *anvārta*.

The intention was set for a three-month retreat, yet this summer has not yet reached its full term; if one goes beyond the boundary during an intercalary month, does this not violate the original commitment and break the *varṣā*?

The *Mātṛkā* states: "Once the *anupravrājana* (rainy-season retreat) is completed, even if a king establishes an intercalary month, when the days of the retreat are counted as full, one performs the *pravāraṇā* and receives the *kaṭhina* robe.
This implies that the receiving of the robe is not accomplished [if the calculation is incorrect]. Whether one relies on the intercalary month or not—since both texts state this...

When the time for the dual proclamation arrives, one may accept or reject [the invitation] according to circumstances, whether the path is open or obstructed. If one does not rely on the intercalary month, when ninety days are complete, one may perform the *pravāraṇā* and depart.

If one relies on the intercalary month, one should follow both treatises. Question: If one accepts a single day and month that includes an intercalary two-month period, is it permissible to stay outside [the monastery]?
Answer: It is not permissible. The original intent of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is to discipline the three karmas so they do not wander or disperse, while also...

With the intention of benefiting sentient beings and rescuing all things, one has already emerged from the boundary at sunrise; since this is not the formal practice, it is provisionally permitted for a period of one month.

Once that period has passed its limit, if one were to further prolong it, there would be no doubt that one would violate the summer retreat (*varṣā*). If an intercalary month falls in the fourth or sixth month, the duration is fixed at one hundred and twenty days.
If an intercalary month occurs in the fourth month, and the boundary is established on the first day of that intercalary month starting from the sixteenth day of the preceding fourth month:

Furthermore, it abides for four months; if the formal act (*jñapti*) is performed after the second day of an intercalary month, it gradually diminishes because it exceeds the intercalary month and takes up the first day of the fifth month as its actual date.
If the formal act is performed from the first day of the fifth month up to the sixteenth day, it abides for three months.
If there is an intercalary seventh month, [the period begins] from the sixteenth day of the fourth month until the first day of the fifth month.
Those who perform the formal act of confinement (*pravāraṇā*) during the first three months shall remain for four months, because the intercalary month has not yet arrived;
those who perform the confinement from the second day of the fifth month onwards shall all remain for five months, because they enter the intercalary month before the ninety days are complete.
The fourth person, having properly cultivated dignified deportment, should approach a [bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī] and say: "Venerable Sir (or Sister), please attend to me, [bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so.
For the purpose of repairing a dwelling where the roof has leaked during the three-month summer retreat at such-and-such monastery, I shall perform [the *varṣā-śāṭī* ceremony].
(This is to be said three times. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the person before him should reply: "Do not be negligent."

He replied, "I am observing it. He was asked again, "Upon whom do you rely to maintain the Vinaya? He replied, "I rely upon such-and-such a Vinaya master. [The Buddha] told him, "If you have doubts, you should ask.
He replied, "So be it. Therefore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "There was a bhikṣu who did not himself maintain the Vinaya nor rely on one who maintained the Vinaya;
while observing the rains retreat, he developed doubts, yet had no one to ask. ... [The Buddha] said: 'One should observe the rains retreat relying upon a place where there is a Vinaya master.'"

If one’s dwelling is narrow or cramped, it is permitted to stay near a *vinaya-dhara* (master of discipline) for a period of seven days, traveling back and forth to remain at the center while mentally relying on the distant *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat).

If doubts arise, one may go to consult him. According to the subsequent text of this Vinaya, a bhikṣu who does not rely on two masters of the *vinaya* during the summer retreat commits a *pāyattika* offense.

(If one is observing the *varṣā* in a village, among mountains, or under trees, one must immediately change the aforementioned location to a monastery; furthermore, if the dwelling is dilapidated, it must be repaired.)

One should name the retreat according to its preceding basis; for some say they dwell in retreat based on the Emperor’s village, while others say they dwell in retreat based on the Dharma-realm—both of these are erroneous.

Question: Why is it that during the summer retreat (*varṣā*) within a monastery, one is required to attend to the maintenance of the quarters? Answer: The repair and upkeep of the quarters serve to benefit the three periods of time.

What was maintained by those of the past allows for our present enjoyment; what is currently repaired serves as a provision for the future. If one does not maintain them, [the benefit] of the three periods is lost.
For one who does not enter the subsequent *anvārambhaṇa* retreat, from the seventeenth day of the fourth month until the sixteenth day of the fifth month, they should say:
"Venerable Sister (or Elder), please attend to me with a single mind; I, the bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī) [Name], shall observe the three-month summer retreat at this monastery;
because the dwelling is dilapidated, I am here for the purpose of repairing it. (Recite this three times.)

Regarding the fifth [method], the *manasikāra-vassa* (mental dwelling for the rains retreat): one should properly cultivate the deportment, proceed before an image of the Buddha, and after making the aspiration, declare with both mind and speech:
"I, the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so, now rely upon this monastery for the three-month summer rains retreat; because the dwelling is dilapidated, I shall repair it.
(Recite this three times. If relying on the residence of a layperson, or for those observing the later retreat (*paccima-vassa*), it should be done according to the specific circumstances.

Corrected. Regarding the sixth point, "forgetting the completion": the Vinaya states that if one forgets to bring it to mind, yet has come for the sake of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), then the *varṣā* is indeed completed.

(Since it specifies "having come," there is concern that for a resident monk, it might not be completed; however, if a resident monk has made a firm resolve to remain here for the entire summer and suddenly forgets to declare it, this must also be considered as an allowance. This applies if he has come from outside...)
Regarding matters not pertaining to those who have entered the *anvāgama* (the period following the rainy retreat), they are not permitted as in the previous case.
As for the seventh point concerning the boundary (*sīmā*), the Vinaya states: first, one foot enters the boundary; second, both feet enter the boundary;

third, one foot enters the monastery (*ārāma*); fourth, both feet enter the monastery. If the dawn light (*ābhāsvara*) appears while one is thus situated, it is also permitted. It is not stated that those coming from outside would invalidate this.

Eighth, regarding whether a summer retreat (*varṣā*) remains valid when one encounters difficulties: according to this Vinaya, there are two kinds of difficulties, namely the difficulty of life (*jīvita-vighna*) and the difficulty of the holy life (*brahmacarya-vighna*).
First, as for the difficulty of life, it refers to such things as ghosts, spirits, thieves, and the like, or predatory beasts and venomous insects;
or being unable to obtain food, drink, medicine, or attendants at will. If one dwells in such a place, one's life will be cut short. Therefore, the Vinaya says: [text continues].
"If I remain here, it will surely create obstacles for my life"—if the Buddha permits one to go for these reasons, he grants leave. Regarding the two obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacarya*):
if one is enticed and seduced by a woman and fears violating a grave precept, the Buddha also permits one to go.

If one reaches that place and a formal bond (*sāṃghāṭi*) is established, from the very day of departure one must diligently seek a secure place of residence. Even before such a residence is secured, although one may... [the text continues].

If one does not break the *anvārambhaṇa* (rainy-season retreat) after spending the night, it is because there was no intention of disrespect; conversely, if one acts contrary to this, the retreat is not established.
If one has secured a dwelling place and the rules for the summer retreat follow one’s person, one must not leave the boundary without a valid reason, for fear of breaking the summer retreat.

If there are no difficulties at the original location, one likewise may not return, as the retreat has already been formally established. Thus, the preceding and succeeding periods of the rainy-season retreat are seen in this Vinaya.
If there are two kinds of difficulties, one should inform the *dānapati* (donor) and request to move away; whether they grant permission or not, one should depart on one’s own.

Regarding what was explained above, if following other schools (*nikāya*), it is not said that one obtains the summer [residence]; however, here we rely on the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, which states that one obtains the summer [residence].

Therefore, the treatise says: "Moving during the summer does not break the *anvaya* (rainy-season retreat). Question: If, due to circumstances, one goes outside the boundary and spends the night, forgetting to receive the *rātri-vāsa* (overnight stay), is it permissible?
Regarding the summer retreat (*varṣā*), neither the various Vinayas nor the Śāstras contain a definitive textual ruling; however, the *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu* states:

"If one forgets during the summer retreat that they have not received the seven-day pass and goes outside the boundary, upon remembering, they must immediately repent. They may obtain one seat [of merit], but they may not exceed three repentances. If they repent more than three times, the year [of the retreat] is not fulfilled.

(Note: "Repentance" refers to recalling the original state of forgetfulness; one should immediately return. Question: What if, due to circumstances, one goes outside the boundary and suddenly encounters water or land?

The path is severed by various difficulties and obstructions; failing to reach the boundary constitutes the loss of the summer retreat (*varṣa*). No answer is found in any of the sutras or vinayas, nor is there any textual passage that definitively severs [this matter].

Formerly, the masters of the Office of Buddhist Affairs (*Zhaoxuan*), who unified the administration, along with the various Tripiṭaka masters, compared and weighed the right and wrong of the matter and unanimously declared that one does indeed obtain the summer retreat.
Although there is this definitive ruling, if it truly serves a great benefit for the Three Jewels or for oneself, then from the perspective of principle, it may be permitted.

If one opens [the boundary] for the sake of breaking the precepts or performing useless activities, and suddenly encounters difficulties, there is no doubt that the summer retreat (*varṣā*) will be broken, further increasing one’s transgressions.

If one asks whether, having gone outside the boundary, one might encounter circumstances and spend the night, and then, as the dawn light appears, emerge and be able to join the assembly for the summer retreat—the answer is:
if one follows the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) may be used as a substitute; one must ensure that the head, hands, and feet enter within the boundary. If...
Relying on the wall outside, one may not remain during the summer retreat.
Ninth: Having accepted the *saptāha* (seven-day) leave to go outside the boundary, if one encounters difficulties and does not return, does this constitute a valid *varṣa* (rainy-season) residence?

According to this Vinaya, if there are parents, brothers, sisters, or former spouses with whom one has had illicit relations, and there is a favorable condition for generating goodness and extinguishing evil, [one may go].
If you stay with sincere intent until the summer retreat has passed and the obstacles have subsided, you must return immediately; you may not remain and thus break the retreat without doubt.
Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "During the summer, if a monk departs for another region, he must not travel by circuitous routes on the way;
he should go directly to his destination, and once the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is completed there, he must return. Thus, one knows that staying behind certainly constitutes breaking the summer retreat.

Tenth, regarding the gains and losses of the five benefits of *kārttika*: according to this Vinaya, from the sixteenth day of the seventh month until the fifteenth day of the eighth month—after the summer retreat has concluded—is called the *kārttika* month.

The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that its original name is *kāṭhina*, but for the sake of brevity, it is simply called the *kārttika* month. This is translated as the "Month of Merit" (*guṇa-māsa*), because during the summer...

Sitting [in meditation] is laborious; the Kai-cheng era (839–841) established five benefits for the profit and advantage of bhikṣus. What are these five benefits? There are three regarding food and two regarding the three robes:

first, accepting invitations from behind [the assembly]; second, eating separately from the group; third, visiting the homes of others before or after a meal without needing to announce one's departure;
fourth, being permitted to keep extra robes without declaring them as pure (*śuddha*); and fifth, being permitted to remain apart from the three robes.
Regarding the meaning of "keeping [robes overnight]," it is said that for the specific precept concerning extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), one must discuss the matter separately.

If one obtains them on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, they must be formally declared as pure (*śuddhi*) and kept within ten days; this is because the benefits of the "timely" (*kāla-lābha*) and "untimely" (*akāla-lābha*) periods do not overlap.
Even if one obtains them on the fifteenth day of the eighth month—which falls within the "timely" period—they must still be declared as pure within ten days.

Because it would involve retaining [an extra robe] beyond the proper time, if one obtains an extra robe during the designated period, there is no need to perform the *śuddhika* (purification) rite until the tenth day has passed;
this is permitted because it falls within the proper time. However, upon reaching the fifteenth day of the eighth month, one must perform the *śuddhika* rite all at once.

If one fails to do so, then when the dawn light appears on the sixteenth day, one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). The *Samantapāsādikā* states that the fourteenth day of the fourth month is the limit.
One who settles [the robes] on the day [of the *pravāraṇā*] obtains five benefits; after the seventeenth day has passed, one cannot be said to "reward the former and punish the latter.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are five kinds of persons who are not entitled to the *varṣā-cīvara*: first, one who has been suspended (*ukkhepaniya*); second, one who has broken the *varṣā*;

third, one who has abandoned the path (*prahīṇa-mārga*); fourth, one who is dead; and fifth, one who has not made an entrustment (*an-ādeśana*). There are ten faults for one who breaks the *varṣā*. First, it is...
First, one is rebuked by all Buddhas; second, one is censured by devas and worldlings; third, one violates the summer retreat; fourth, one incurs transgression;

fifth, one is not permitted to receive the *kaṭhina* robe; sixth, one is deprived of the five benefits; seventh, one does not receive alms offerings; eighth, one does not receive the robes for the rainy season retreat;
ninth, one's ill repute spreads abroad; and tenth, one will later feel regret upon entering hell.
Chapter Eighteen: On the Acceptance of the Day. This chapter has five main sections:
first, clarifying the correctness or incorrectness of the conditions for the formal act; second, clarifying the method for mental recitation when staying alone;
third, clarifying the method for face-to-face procedures; fourth, clarifying the methods for the community; and fifth, clarifying what constitutes a valid or invalid acceptance of the day.

Regarding the first point concerning the existence of valid reasons [for departing], the *Vinaya* states: "In all cases of receiving a formal authorization (*jīvitāvadhi*), the essential conditions must involve matters that benefit the Triple Gem, major affairs, or invitations from lay patrons;

provided they can produce wholesome states and eliminate unwholesome ones, one is permitted to go. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "For whose sake does one receive the seven-night authorization? The Buddha replied:
"One receives it for the sake of the seven classes of disciples. Provided it can produce wholesome states and eliminate unwholesome ones, one should go, even if sent by another."

If a messenger is not dispatched, both [the donor and the recipient] may accept [the invitation]; however, if one hears of the death [of a relative] while on the road, or if they turn back from their precepts, or enter the assembly of non-Buddhists, or if the eight difficult circumstances (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) arise, in all such cases one should not go.
The meaning is that unless it concerns matters of great benefit or extreme urgency, it is improper to accept [the invitation].

Since the *poṣadha* (observance day) has not been established, to recklessly count it as part of the summer retreat, to be conceited about one's lack of virtue, and to presumptuously accept the offerings of others—[these are grave errors].

Because committing an offense involving five *māṣaka* coins constitutes a grave transgression, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If one has personally completed the summer retreat and accepts offerings, it is a grave offense.

The commentary explains that this refers to cases where there was originally no intention [to deceive], yet one regards oneself as having a sincere heart while accepting the offerings; in such cases, there should be no offense. This is like the case of receiving the precepts without them being successfully conferred, yet believing oneself to have obtained them.
Whenever one hears the *karmavācanā* or later realizes that one's own acceptance of offerings was invalid, one should cease the matter and not continue with it.

How could there be anything that exceeds this? According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one seeks robes, bowls, medicinal herbs, and so forth for one's own sake, all of it constitutes the meaning of "receiving the day" (*āpatti-dina*).

It is said that those who are poor and lack robes or medicine are permitted [to seek them]; however, if one is personally ill and unable to observe the "receiving of the day," they are allowed to go directly without violating the summer retreat (*varṣa*).
Thus, the Vinaya states: "One must not eat at will, nor visit those who are tending to the sick, and so forth."

[The text] opens both [paths] and proceeds directly. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If the road is short, one may also receive the *divasa* (day-period) for the purpose of staying overnight. The commentary explains:

"If, for the sake of livelihood or seeking profit, one falsely pretends to be associated with the noble and eminent to beg for grain, wheat, and so forth; or if one accepts employment to oversee the copying of scriptures, the painting of images, or the construction of Buddha-basins;
or if, due to various invitations, one’s mind lacks sincerity; or if, having received the *divasa* for a single occasion, one subsequently manages affairs for the community [of monks]."
Regarding matters that are either actual events or not yet encountered but merely imagined as future conditions—such useless matters are not to be accepted.
The *Five Hundred Questions* states: "If one who has violated the precepts earns wealth through business and uses it to build a Buddha image, they will still not escape hell;

how much less could they obtain merit? Question: Is it permissible to exchange [requisites] with others? Answer: Yes, for it is permitted to receive them. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One may accept [requisites] for seven days while staying in a village."
If seven nights have not yet elapsed and the task to be performed is not yet finished, one may return to the original location. The Buddha said:

"As long as there are remaining nights, one should announce [the intention] and then depart. The meaning is that this refers to obtaining permission for the remainder of the original matter after having already announced it; it does not mean obtaining permission for a different matter.
If one has received the *jìrì* (extra days) for matters pertaining to the Triple Gem as a whole, they may be used interchangeably, such as when performing tasks for the Buddha.
When the Dharma and the Sangha are obtained for joint use, there is the condition of receiving a day’s leave (*jñapti-dina*).

If there is great benefit, such as privately commissioning scriptures or images, or if one is invited according to the order of the Sangha, or invited by another who has relinquished their own invitation, these all constitute conditions for receiving a day’s leave. However, regarding the specific case of an invitation relinquished by another, one must ask the original host for permission; only then can it be validly established.

Regarding the second method, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If there is someone within the boundary who is capable of waiting for one to come and receive [the formal act] face-to-face, yet one nonetheless performs the mental recitation (*cittānujñā*), it is not accomplished. Therefore, it must be truly without anyone present that one may perform the mental recitation. The text says:
"I, [name], a bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī), now receive the seven-day rule to go outside the boundary for the sake of a certain matter, and shall return."

"I shall enter the rains retreat here" (recite three times). This means that if there is no bhikṣu present, one may go [to another place] after informing a śrāmaṇera or a lay attendant of the circumstances.
"I now accept the seven-day rule; having gone beyond the boundary, I shall return as soon as it is concluded—you should know this.

In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is asked: "Where does one receive the seven-day [permission]? The Buddha said: "Within the boundary. From whom is it received? It is received from the fivefold assembly."
Regarding the third method, the procedure for formal authorization (*sammukhāvinaya*): one approaches a [monk or nun] and says: "Venerable brother/sister, please attend to me.
I, the monk/nun [name], now receive the seven-day leave to go outside the boundary for a certain purpose, returning here to observe the rains retreat. (Recite this three times).

Regarding this mental reflection (*cittavijñapti*) and the formal authorization, the various Vinayas and commentaries mention only the name "receiving" (*pratigraha*), but there is no specific text for the formula of "receiving [something]."
According to tradition, although this is not the word of the Buddha as stated in the *Karmavācanā* (ritual formulas), there is no impediment to its practical application.
This seven-day rule permits only six nights; once the sixth night has passed, one must certainly return by the seventh day.
Regarding the fourth category of communal legal procedures (*saṃghakarma*): the meaning is that the matter must necessarily coincide with the actual date.

It is only on the fifteenth day of the month that one may perform the *karmavācanā*; one must not extend a seven-day period to complete the month, nor may one, having already received the month-long period, further receive a seven-day period so as to total thirty-seven days outside of the [standard] period—none of these constitute a valid reception. Nowadays, many...

Because of this matter, [the preceptor] asks the Saṃgha: "The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall we do? They reply: "We shall perform the *jñapti-karman* for receiving the *saptāha-vidhi* (the seven-day rule).

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let monk so-and-so receive the *saptāha-vidhi* and go outside the boundary on the fifteenth day (or as the case may require, for one month), for the sake of such-and-such a matter, and then return here to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*)."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen to me. Bhikṣu [Name] has received the *saptāha-atireka-vidhi* (the procedure for being away for more than seven days) on the fifteenth day;
he shall go outside the boundary for a certain purpose and return here to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
Which elders of the Saṃgha consent to the Saṃgha granting bhikṣu [Name] the *saptāha-atireka-vidhi* to go outside the boundary on the fifteenth day for a certain purpose and return?"

Regarding the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) herein: since the Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent, and no one objects, the Saṃgha grants the monk [Name] the *saptarātrātikrāntika-vidhi* (the rule for exceeding seven days).
On the fifteenth day, he shall go outside the boundary for a certain purpose and return here to complete the *varṣā*.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. The meaning is that if one observes the *varṣā* based on a specific boundary (*sīmā*).

Within one's own boundary (*sīmā*), it is not permissible to receive the formal authorization (*jñapti*) on the site of the *karmavastu* (the ritual ground), because that is not the place where one’s original intention was directed.

Furthermore, since the two boundaries are distinct, how could they be used interchangeably? If one observes the rains retreat (*varṣā*) within the *karmavastu*, it is likewise impermissible to receive the authorization or to stay overnight together with those in the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*);
there is no doubt that this would constitute a breach of the retreat.
Fifth, regarding those who have obtained the heavy [precepts] but have not received them as such: the questioner asks whether the day of receiving the heavy precepts can be established.

The respondent answers that by examining the meaning of a certain passage, it can be established that the heavy precepts were received. How is this known? The answer is that there are three points: first, citing a factual case to prove the heaviness;

second, citing the underlying principle to prove the heaviness; and third, citing a scriptural text to prove the heaviness. First, concerning the citation of a factual case: the *Wubai wen shi* (Five Hundred Questions) is a work from the Western Regions.
The Tripiṭaka Master Vimalākṣa personally translated this from his own mouth; his virtue surpassed that of past and present, and his fame covered the world.
He was most proficient in the Vinaya Piṭaka, and the excellence of the resulting text serves as a reliable witness. Later, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha also arrived;
he too was a great master from the Western Regions who was extensively learned in both Buddhist and non-Buddhist teachings, thoroughly practiced the Vinaya, and had also personally...

Having examined the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Treatise on Elucidation) and its commentary in their Sanskrit originals, I have obtained both the translation and the text itself; furthermore, I have personally practiced this method.

Now, arriving in the Tang Dynasty, masters such as Tripiṭaka Master Prajñāvarman and Vinaya Master [Śīlabhadra] were both eminent patriarchs from the Western Regions who had traveled through many countries.
I heard only that they had obtained the combined version, but I did not hear of them reciting the single version alone. Master Prajñāvarman said: "Provided that the conditions..."

In accordance with reality, even regarding a single matter, it is permissible to receive the precepts repeatedly; this was the Buddha’s original regulation for various matters, as he feared that reckless conduct would lead to the violation of the summer retreat (*varṣa*).
Since there is now benefit [to be gained], how could we not permit it? This differs from the prohibitions of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), which do not allow for such exceptions.

This practice is currently observed in the Western Regions (India), though those who come from the Middle Kingdom (China) all strictly observe the rule of receiving them only once. These individuals are all close to the state of sagehood (*ārya*).

To claim that this practice is a false act or a deceptive fabrication of the late age, while claiming that borderland people have produced such a strange and erroneous interpretation, is surely unjust.

Second, regarding the citation of scriptural meaning as proof: as previously mentioned, if a donor requests a seven-day period and there is further monastic business to be managed, how could it not be permitted?
If that were so, why does the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* state that one may accept [the invitation] for one seven-night period, but not two?
Regarding the "seven-night limit," it is stated that one may not receive two periods of seven nights for a single matter;

this does not mean that one may not receive them again for different matters. Whether the matters are distinct or the purpose has been fulfilled, one may receive the seven-night limit for each preceding matter as appropriate.
Although received repeatedly, no offense is committed—just as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, where one receives the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts repeatedly before others.
Because they are distinct, one obtains the initial [period] in both cases. Furthermore, if one is earnestly requested by one's parents to remain, one does not break the summer retreat;

since one can comply with their words, how could accepting further days immediately constitute breaking the summer? If you claim that such a request is a difficulty, yet you suppress them and compel them to accept further days, would that then not be a difficulty?
Moreover, during the summer, if one is frequently summoned for official business while traveling, or if it is necessary...

If a person has already completed the formal undertaking (*upasaṃpadā*) for seven days, fifteen days, or one month, how can it be said that they have not completed the undertaking and therefore may not depart?
Since they cannot abandon what they have undertaken, if one says that they may go directly because of difficulties, then I too face difficulties in undertaking it again;
would this not then be impossible? Even going directly is permitted if the days of the undertaking are observed.

If it is even more beneficial, why not permit it? Furthermore, as previously requested for one month, a slight increase was still granted; yet when requesting seven days later, why is a great benefit not permitted?

Moreover, if at the end of the summer retreat only one or two days remain, and there is a matter of great benefit requiring one to go, one should not remain to undergo the formal reception [of the *varṣā*].
If one were to receive further days, it would immediately constitute a breach of the summer retreat. This is precisely the case.

If one sits upright [in meditation], how can one go out on a journey? One asks: "By what means do you know this? [The answer is: "One may also receive the *saptāha* (seven-day) leave for one, two, or three days. The Vinaya states:
"If the time is insufficient, one should immediately receive the *divasa* (day-leave); returning, one is further permitted to receive the seven-day leave.

Thus, it is known that this is permissible. Regarding the third citation as proof, the Vinaya says: "It merely states that the Buddha has not yet permitted me to go on such a matter; it does not say 'the Buddha...'"
It is not permitted for me to go out on such business repeatedly; the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Whether there is an invitation or no invitation, one must go outside the boundary;
all such cases are permitted provided one accepts the seven-day period. From this, it is known that if permission is granted for one type of matter, others of the same class are likewise permitted.

If that is so, why does the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* state that when the Saṃgha is in conflict, one should go to inform a nearby resident monk and immediately proceed to reconcile them? If [the reconciliation] has already...
Regarding the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), one may go away for seven days; if those seven days are exhausted, one should break the *varṣā* and depart. The Sarvāstivādins answer:

"This is because the rule for the thirty-nine-night period had not yet been established. [The opponent asks: "If that is so, why does the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, in the section on the settlement of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), state that when the seven days are exhausted, one should receive the thirty-nine-night period and depart, and when the thirty-nine nights are exhausted, one should break the *varṣā* and depart?"

Answer: Since it has already been established that the period is limited to thirty-nine nights, one may not extend it further; moreover, as the various Vinaya schools differ, how can they be cited as precedent?

For instance, according to the *Dharmaguptaka*, those who depart for the purpose of schism do not break the summer retreat, whereas those who depart without such a reason do not receive the [formal] invitation (*pravāraṇā*).
According to the *Sarvāstivāda*, one is permitted only thirty-nine nights and may not receive [the invitation] again; if one were to receive it, the summer retreat would be broken.

Knowing this is distinct, it is like the five-part division regarding the reception of the seven-day leave (*saptāha-ānatti*). If one asks about a doubt, why is the previous doubt not permitted while the subsequent question is allowed?
The *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu* states: "If one has received the seven-day leave but the period is not yet full and returns, there is no need to receive it again;
once the seven days are complete, one may receive it again. It is also permissible to receive it for a single occasion each day. And so forth.

Regarding the *Saptāha-vinaya-vidhi* (The Code for the Seven-Day Period), it is stated that if there is a matter requiring attention, one first establishes the conditions for the seven-day period, and subsequently re-establishes those conditions.

(The Commentary states: If the matter for which the seven-day period was requested has not been concluded, one does not violate the *anvārohana* (the formal suspension of the rains retreat) by returning; however, this incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
If the matter remains unfinished, one may remain outside for up to six nights; on the seventh day, upon returning, if it is already the eighth day, one must again request the seven-day period.

Having gone outside the boundary to stay overnight, one first receives a seven-day leave for the sake of a teacher’s illness. Upon going outside the boundary, when three nights have passed and the illness has been cured, one must return immediately.
If there is another donor who invites one, one may still use the remaining three nights to stay outside the boundary.

If the matter is still not resolved after those days, one returns to the original location and requests another seven-day leave; this is called "first establishing the conditions for seven days, and subsequently establishing the seven days."
Chapter Nineteen: The Conditions for the Invitation (Pravāraṇā) and the Confession of Faults Raised.

This chapter has two main sections: first, the summary of the eleven points regarding the intent of the regulation and the explanation of its name; second, the conditions for the assembly and their correspondence. Third, the conditions for the gathering of the Saṃgha.

1. Establishing the four criteria for discerning right from wrong; 2. The five qualities required for performing formal acts (*karmavācanā*); 3. The five qualities required for the conduct of the *pravāraṇā*; 4.

The five qualities required for the *pravāraṇā* before the Saṃgha; 5. The nuns coming to request the *pravāraṇā*; 6. The allowance for abbreviated procedures when encountering difficulties; 7. A comprehensive summary of miscellaneous practices.
First, regarding the explanation of the name through the regulation of the mind: During the ninety-day period of practicing the Way, one refines both body and mind;
yet many people are deluded about themselves and fail to recognize their own faults. Therefore, it is appropriate to look up to the pure assembly for their compassionate instruction.

By freely declaring one’s own transgressions, one allows the Sangha to investigate and raise them, thereby manifesting that there is no private concealment within while appearing pure without; hence, it is called *Pravāraṇā* (Self-Indulgence).

Regarding the second section on the conditions for the assembly (*saṃnipāta*), first the time periods are clarified: the Vinaya states that the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the seventh month both permit the *pravāraṇā*;

furthermore, within the rules concerning the robes offered during an emergency (*ātyayika-cīvara*), the sixteenth day also permits the *pravāraṇā*. Thus, these three days are fixed. Next, the persons and the ritual procedure are clarified:

even if one has violated the summer retreat (*varṣā*) and failed to observe the period of residence (*anupravrājana*), although such a person does not obtain the full benefits of the summer retreat, [the *pravāraṇā* may still be performed].

Because the principle of raising a formal charge (*ukkhepaniya-kamma*) is the same, it must necessarily depend upon the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) of the Saṃgha for its administration. The Vinaya states:

"If those who have entered the latter half of the rainy season retreat (*paścima-varṣā*) wish to join those who have completed the former half of the rainy season retreat (*pūrva-varṣā*), they must wait until the days [of the retreat] are fulfilled before they may return."
Regarding the third [section], the *Pratyaya* on the Assembly of the Saṃgha: A minimum of five persons is required before one may formally appoint [an official] to announce the *Pravāraṇā*.

One should strike the wooden mallet to assemble the Saṃgha, and each person should sit upon a mat spread on the ground. This is because the place where a transgression is raised must be free of such [elevations];

if one sits upon a bed, it further fosters arrogance and indolence. The Vinaya contains this regulation; the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that one should perform the *Pravāraṇā* by spreading grass mats on well-mud-plastered ground.

Furthermore, they should bared their right shoulders, place their right knees on the ground, join their palms, and proceed from outside to offer warm water, scatter flowers, chant the counting of ballots, and perform the ritual for reciting the *Prātimokṣa* together;
however, the words for reciting the *Prātimokṣa* are omitted and replaced with the formula for the *Pravāraṇā*.
Even the *śrāmaṇeras* must all assemble, as the purpose of the formal censure is identical [to that of the full assembly], and only after the announcement has been made may they depart.
Fourth, regarding the discernment of whether a person is qualified or not: the Vinaya states that one must possess two sets of five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*).

First, the five virtues for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) are: first, being free from attachment; second, being free from aversion; third, being free from fear; fourth, being free from delusion;

and fifth, knowing whether the *pravāraṇā* has been performed or not. Next, the five virtues for the formal act of accusing (*codanā*) are: first, knowing the proper time and not acting at an improper time; and second, being truthful and not being false.
Third, one benefits others rather than causing them harm; fourth, one is gentle rather than coarse and fierce; fifth, one possesses a compassionate heart rather than harboring anger.

If these virtues are not complete, then when one attempts to perform the *jñapti* (formal motion) at an improper time, there is fear of disturbing the Saṃgha and, conversely, bringing trouble upon oneself.

Regarding the reason for appointing two persons, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) is unclear on this point; however, according to the texts of various schools—namely the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü) and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Moshengqi lü)—both appoint two persons.

"Human beings" refers to two or more individuals, up to a large number of people (because the *saṃgha* is numerous, they take turns performing the duties). The *Sānqián wēiyí jīng* (Sutra on Three Thousand Modes of Deportment) states:
"One must appoint two people to perform the *pravāraṇā* for the *saṃgha*; once it is finished, they face one another to confess their offenses;
one must not wait for others to announce the *pravāraṇā*, because the *saṃgha* has not appointed them. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* state that they are to be appointed.
A virtuous senior monk shall perform [the ritual] (in the present time, it is common to appoint a youth to perform it, which gives rise to unwholesome signs).

Fifth, regarding the formal act (*karmavācanā*) with the addition of the motion: the senior *vinaya*-master shall appoint two individuals from among the assembly who possess the five virtues of both categories;

there is no need to call them to stand, lest it result in a schismatic formal act. As previously stated for the announcement of consent (*chanda*), one says: "Venerable Sisters, may the Saṃgha listen."
(Bhikṣu or Bhikṣuṇī), [Name], I have received your consent for the *pravāraṇā*. You have granted your consent for the *pravāraṇā* regarding the legal matters of the Saṃgha.
(One statement suffices. Now, those conducting the proceedings do not clearly follow the procedure for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) when declaring consent.
Since you have made such a declaration within the dwelling, you may not revise it at the last moment; you must instead obtain the consent for the *pravāraṇā* from the bhikṣus within the dwelling.

If a person holding the *chanda* (consent) should speak erroneously at the time [of the ceremony], they may correct it before their seat. One asks the Saṃgha: "The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall be done? The answer is: "The *pravāraṇā* (self-criticism);
appoint a person by *karmavācanā*. Again, one asks: "Who among the assembly is able to act as the five-virtue (*pañca-guṇa*) *pravāraṇā* officer for the Saṃgha?
If there is one who possesses these virtues, they answer: "I, [Name], am able. "Great Virtuous Sister, let the Saṃgha listen: If the time is right for the Saṃgha..."
Please listen with patience as the Saṃgha appoints [the bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so and so-and-so to act as the recipients of the *prātimokṣa* for the Saṃgha.

This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Great Virtuous Sisters, may the Saṃgha listen: the Saṃgha appoints [the bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so and so-and-so to act as the recipients of the *prātimokṣa* for the Saṃgha.
Which of you elders and sisters approve of the Saṃgha appointing [the bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so and so-and-so to act as the recipients of the *prātimokṣa* for the Saṃgha?
"Since the Sangha has granted permission for [the monk or nun] so-and-so to act as the one who receives the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) on behalf of the Sangha,
and since the Sangha consents by remaining silent— no one having raised an objection— the matter is thus settled and shall be maintained accordingly."

Regarding the sixth procedure for the duties of the five virtuous officers: once the Sangha has appointed them, they immediately rise from their seats, go to the head of the assembly, and prostrate at the feet of the Sangha.
Kneeling on their right knees, if it is in the open air, they should move within arm’s reach and perform a *jñapti* (formal motion) to harmonize the Sangha, saying:

"Venerable Sisters, may the Sangha listen. Today the community of monks performs the *pravāraṇā*. If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha, being patient and attentive, grant its consent to harmonize."
The formal motion for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) is as follows. Next, to clarify the procedure for the *tṛṇaprastāra* (spreading of grass):
the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that one should have grass spread upon the seats for the *pravāraṇā*. The commentary explains that those performing the rite today apply a distinct method:

prior to the *pravāraṇā*, they should seek out soft grass in advance and, according to the number of monks present, cut a separate portion for each and place it before the presiding elder (*upādhyāya*). Once the five virtuous ones (*pañca-guṇa*) have been appointed, these five virtuous ones take [the grass].

Having distributed a blade of grass to each person from the senior-most monk down to the junior-most, the five virtuous ones (pañca-varga) also take a blade of grass and hold it in their own hands until they reach their respective seats;
thereafter, they spread them upon the ground. If the assembly is large, three or five people should assist in the distribution.
Once the distribution is complete, they go before the senior-most monk and announce: "May all the monks each take their seat upon the grass mat."

Baring the right shoulder, kneeling with the right knee on the ground, and joining the palms in accordance with the Dharma, one performs the *pravāraṇā* (self-exhortation). (The Sangha all exhort one another according to the ritual for chanting. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"The Tathāgata sat together with the monks upon grass seats and addressed the bhikṣus: 'Each of you take your place upon the grass seats; I wish to perform the *varṣā-vāsa* (the end of the rains retreat),' and so forth, as extensively described therein."
