Regarding the seventh point, the five virtuous qualities for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) before the Saṃgha:
one person should go before the *sthavira* (senior monk) and sit upon a large seat; another person should go before the junior monks and sit. The Vinaya states:

"If the *sthavira* sees the five virtuous ones approaching, he shall adjust his robes, kneel with his right knee on the ground, bare his right shoulder, and join his palms; all the other monks shall do likewise. The text for the *pravāraṇā* says: "Great..."
(Virtuous Sister), with a single mind, reflect: "The Saṃgha today performs the *pravāraṇā*. I, [Name], a Bhikṣu or Bhikṣuṇī, also perform the *pravāraṇā*.
If there be any offense seen, heard, or suspected, may the Virtuous Elder Sisters out of compassion speak to me; having seen the offense, I shall confess it according to the Dharma.
(Recite three times). After the Elder has spoken, he returns to his original seat. This is the first of the five virtuous ones; this sequence proceeds until the third.
The one sitting before the *sthavira* performs the second set of five duties (*pañcavarga-dharma*) in the same manner as above; thus it proceeds in succession down to the lowest seat.

The *Vinaya* states that for a sick monk, the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) may be conducted according to his own convenience. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the five virtuous ones (*pañca-guṇa*) each go to their own seats and perform the invitation facing one another;
they must not wait until the entire Saṃgha has finished. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that once the assembly of monks has finished speaking...
The five virtuous ones approach the presiding elder and announce: "The Saṃgha has completed the *pravāraṇā* with one mind. Only after this do they pay homage, offer praise, and withdraw.

(In these present times, the age of semblance, the Dharma declines as people become corrupt; thus, when one's own conduct deviates from principle, even if one performs good deeds, they are immediately brought to light, while evil is concealed. If one were to punish such transgressions, disputes over faults would become even deeper. Therefore, the methods for investigating and censuring are omitted here in brief;
those who are able to promote and practice them should consult the detailed original texts.)
Eighth, regarding the arrival of a bhikṣuṇī to request the *pravāraṇā*: if no bhikṣuṇī arrives, perform the *pravāraṇā* according to the usual procedure, which differs from the *poṣadha*.
One must inquire whether a bhikṣuṇī is present; if a bhikṣuṇī has arrived, before the *pravāraṁā*, instruct her to stand in a place where she is within sight but beyond hearing.

Once the Saṃgha has performed the *pravāraṇā* for as long as required, the presiding elder (*sthavira*) should assess the time—whether it is early or late—and determine if the bhikṣuṇī can return. He should then issue the command.
The five virtuous ones said, "Stay for a moment until the nuns' *pravāraṇā* is concluded; we shall then summon the nuns to the midst of the *saṃgha*.

Once they have prostrated at our feet, we will have them declare the three matters—what has been seen, heard, or suspected. After the great assembly had remained silent for a long while, the elder should instruct the nuns, saying:

"The great assembly, from the highest to the lowest, remains entirely silent and says nothing regarding having seen an offense. This is surely because within the community of nuns there is no deficiency or transgression, and without..."
Having attained purity, each of you should diligently practice the Path, being prudent and not negligent.

When the bhikṣuṇīs have returned to the monastery after the *pravāraṇā*, this instruction should be transmitted to the assembly so that all may know it (this method is fully detailed in the lower section on the instructions for bhikṣuṇīs). This is called the method of the daytime *pravāraṇā*.
Nowadays, the *pravāraṇā* is mostly performed on the fourteenth or fifteenth day at night. If the bhikṣuṇīs arrive the following day, the gong should be struck.

When the assembly is gathered, those who do not come must be asked for their consent (*chanda*). Once the great assembly has assembled, the nun comes into the midst of the monks with her usual deportment and requests the three matters;
the rest is the same as the procedure described previously. Question: This is not the method of the Saṃgha; why is it necessary for everyone to assemble or for consent to be requested? Answer:

Because the nuns rely upon the Saṃgha, they must have their offenses formally raised by the Saṃgha. If even a single person is not in harmony, then the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) is not accomplished, just as it is not accomplished for the Saṃgha itself.

Within the *Śikṣamāṇā-śikṣāpada*, there was originally no ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*); nevertheless, it requires that one first announce one's consent (*chanda*) according to circumstances before administering the instruction.

For this reason, according to the principles of the Saṃgha’s Dharma, there is no partiality or distinction; thus, there is no obstacle to applying the rules for the *Pravāraṇā* ceremony of both monks and nuns equally as part of the Saṃgha’s Dharma.

The ninth [section], the brief exposition for those encountering difficulties: If this Vinaya contains the eight calamities or other such circumstances, one may perform a brief *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish), as explained above regarding the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*).
One who possesses the five virtues should first make the following announcement: "Venerable Sisters, may the Saṃgha listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits it, because of these current difficulties, let each member of the Saṃgha perform the *pravāraṇā* with three statements."
Having made this formal announcement (*jñapti*) in this manner, once the assembly of monks has simultaneously faced one another and each has recited it three times, they may depart.

If the danger draws near and they wish to recite it again, even a single recitation requires a formal announcement (*jñapti*). According to this Vinaya, if the danger is urgent, they are also permitted to depart directly.
If the assembly is large and the space is cramped, or if it is damp, hot, windy, or rainy, or if the circumstances of the danger are somewhat distant and not yet imminent, [they may depart].

Regarding such matters as these, they may also be explained briefly; one should cause those possessing the five virtues to recite before the three or five senior monks, while for others, it suffices to recite once and then rise.
Alternatively, if one person receives the *pravāraṇā* from two people, they should stand between them and receive it from both sides;
in all cases, each must be announced individually so that the entire assembly may know and hear it. Therefore, the Vinaya states: "One must not speak in whispers."
Regarding the *pravāraṇā*: nowadays, some may have two sets of five virtuous ones (*pañcavarga*) receive the *pravāraṇā* simultaneously;

this is contrary to the Dharma. Therefore, the Vinaya states: "The *pravāraṇā* is performed simultaneously [but] in a manner that avoids confusion, proceeding one by one starting from the senior monk (*sthavira*).

Having previously clarified the procedure for six persons, the present explanation of the procedure for five persons is intended to distinguish it, lest people practice it indiscriminately. If within the boundary...

The five virtuous ones (pañca-vṛddha) may not seek [individual] desires; they must first perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to appoint one of them. Once that is concluded, another person is appointed.
Two persons may not be appointed simultaneously, because if two were appointed, they would not be included in the count of the Saṃgha.

At the time of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), one of the five virtuous ones sits together with the Saṃgha, while the other five virtuous ones perform the *pravāraṇā* among themselves in turn. When the matter is fully settled, the two groups of five virtuous ones [conclude].
If they face one another and speak as described above, or if there are four or fewer people, or two people using the method of mutual hand-giving, they must assemble within the entire boundary;
they may not receive *chanda* (consent), nor may they appoint the five virtuous ones (*pañca-guṇa*). When four people face one another and one person speaks separately, he says:
"Venerable Sisters, please attend with one mind: today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*. I, [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so, am pure."

(Recite three times. If there are three other persons, it is as previously described. If two persons are facing each other, [the senior] should say: "Venerable Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind:
today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*; I, the Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī named so-and-so, am pure. (Recite three times.

If one person is to perform the rite through mental recitation (*manasikāra*), they should go to the place where the *poṣadha* is held, sweep and sprinkle it, arrange the seats, prepare scented water and voting sticks (*śalākā*), and wait for the visiting Bhikṣus.
If you have come, you should proceed before the image, fully assume the dignified posture (*īryāpatha*), and with mind and speech recite three times:
"Today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*; I, [name], a bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī], am pure."

Tenth, regarding the inclusion of those who have committed miscellaneous offenses: if four or fewer persons have committed *pāyattika* or *prātideśanīya* offenses, regardless of whether they confess them themselves or are formally accused, they must perform confession (*pratideśana*) before the *pravāraṇā*.
If they have committed *dukkaṭa* (or *duṣkṛta*) offenses, they must likewise perform a mental confession (*cittapratideśana*) before the *pravāraṇā*.
If they have committed *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or *sthūlātyaya* offenses, there is no provision for formal disciplinary punishment; they simply join the assembly.

Regarding the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) incurred by remaining [in the assembly] after the announcement has been made, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one should wait until the assembly is complete before performing the formal act (*karman*), and that one must not obstruct the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) of the Saṃgha.

Question: Why is it said in the context of the *pravāraṇā* before the Saṃgha that "if one sees an offense, one may confess it," whereas in the cases of confession before an individual or through mental recitation (*manasikāra*), it is always stated that one is "pure"?

Answer: Because the purpose of the formal act of suspension (*utkṣepa-karman*) within the Saṃgha is fully realized there, it is permissible for one who sees an offense to perform confession. In contrast, the other two methods do not fulfill this specific requirement. Therefore, the former allows for confession upon seeing an offense, while the latter two require one to be already pure.

If one discusses an individual, although there is the formal act of "lifting" (to address faults), because it does not encompass the full governance of the community, one simply speaks of "pure lifting" (pariśuddha-utkṣepa) to respond to the Saṃgha.
If, after an individual or the Saṃgha has completed the *pravāraṇā*, more guests arrive—if they are few, one informs them of the purity;
if many, one should speak again for them. If, after two people have performed the ritual, three more arrive, one should perform the *pravāraṇā* as a formal act of the Saṃgha.

If two people come, it is the same as the method for responding to an inquiry. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one may not observe the rains retreat within this boundary and perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony elsewhere.
According to this *vinaya*, those who entered the first rains retreat perform the *pravāraṇā* and then divide the summer robes;

those who entered the second rains retreat may share in receiving the goods, but must wait until the days are complete before returning to divide the rooms and bedding. This applies likewise to the conclusion of the rains retreat according to this *vinaya*.

Regarding not departing when there is an offense, the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If one does not depart due to a valid reason, there is no offense. If there is no valid reason, even staying outside the boundary for one night and returning is an offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If, after the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one does not depart for one night, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).
However, if one has not set a limit [on the duration], or if one stays at a place where one was not invited, there is no offense."
Chapter Twenty: An Essential Commentary on the *Śīla-sūtra*.

This single chapter is the most essential of all; it serves as the lock and key for restraining body and speech, and as the mirror for discerning what constitutes an offense and what constitutes its observance.

If this were omitted and not recorded, one would fear that practitioners would remain ignorant of what is held and what is transgressed, and their study would yield little practical benefit. Furthermore, if both the text and its meaning are fully elucidated...

This is not a mere transcription of what has been clarified; rather, I have now diligently investigated the various chapters, extracting their essential points and providing word-by-word explanations for difficult passages. As for the remaining portions, the text is sufficiently clear and can be sought out on one's own.

Part One: A Concise Explanation (The actual number of monastic precepts in this Vinaya is two hundred and thirty-one; when including the two *aniyata* [undetermined] rules and the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* [methods for settling disputes], the total is two hundred and fifty).
The First Precept on Sexual Misconduct (Violated by both monks and nuns). It is established as an offense when four conditions are met: first, the proper organ; second, a defiled mind;
third, the application of effort; and fourth, contact with the object. The Vinaya states that humans, non-humans, and animals—these three types—are all objects of violation.
If one originally possesses a lustful mind and engages with the aforementioned objects, it constitutes an offense regardless of whether one is awake or asleep. If [the object] is dead...

If the physical form has not yet decayed, or even if it is partially decayed, as long as one causes the mind of lust to enter the three places—even if only as much as a hair-tip—one commits a grave offense.
The "three places" refers to a woman’s three: the anus, the vagina, and the mouth; for a man, there are two: the anus and the mouth. Question:
Does this precept apply to sexual play? Answer: According to the Vinaya, it constitutes an offense whenever there is the intention of sexual desire.
Because it is a grave offense, the *Vinaya* states: "At one time, there was a bhikṣu who, out of playfulness, placed the male organ of a young boy into his own mouth and toyed with it.

Although he originally had no lustful intent, because he experienced pleasure at the moment of entry, he committed an offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "In the mouth, the act is completed as an offense once it passes the teeth;
for the other two [sexual] passages, the specific dimensions are not considered. This *vinaya* further states: "If, due to enemies, thieves, or others, one is forcibly..."

If one holds the male organ and causes it to enter the three [female] orifices while having no lustful mind oneself, provided that during these three stages—the initial entry, the time of being inside, and the time of exiting—there is not even a single thought of experiencing pleasure, one does not commit a grave offense (*pārājika*). If one experiences pleasure at any one of these times, one commits an offense.
If a *bhikṣu* and a *bhikṣuṇī* instruct each other to engage in sexual intercourse, the one who acts upon the instruction commits the offense. The instructor is also culpable.

If one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense while the preceding person did not instruct them, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*. For the three lower assemblies (*parṣad*), whether they were instructed or not, both the instructor and the perpetrator incur a *duṣkṛta*;
if they persist in the act, they are subject to expulsion (*pravāsanīya*). Next, the non-offenses are explained:

if one is asleep and lacks awareness (this refers to cases where one is coerced by an enemy); if one does not experience pleasure (this refers to cases where an enemy is about to commit the act against another); or if there is no intention for sexual misconduct whatsoever (this refers to having no general defiled mind).

The Second Precept on Stealing (the same offense for both monks and nuns). Six conditions must be fulfilled for the offense to be complete: first, there is an object belonging to another; second, the perception that it belongs to another;

third, the intention to steal; fourth, the object is of significant value; fifth, one initiates the preparatory effort; sixth, the object is moved from its original location—at this point, the offense is committed. Question:

Since "belonging to another" is easily understood, what is meant by "an object not belonging to another"? Answer: The *Sudarsana-vibhasa* states: Suppose a son commits evil deeds and his parents drive him away. Later, the father...
Regarding the death of the owner: an object that has no master is called "ownerless"; using it incurs no offense. The Sarvāstivādins say:

when there is a boundary between two kingdoms, the empty space between the two marked borders is what is called "ownerless. Furthermore, if a kingdom is destroyed and the king has fled, and a subsequent king has not yet assumed control, any object within this area is also called "ownerless.
If one takes and uses such things with the intention [that they are ownerless], in all cases there is no violation. As for... [the text ends here].

In the first category of objects, these are grouped into twelve types: (1) stealing property belonging to the Buddha; (2) stealing property belonging to the Dharma; (3) stealing property belonging to the Sangha; (4) the mutual misappropriation of the Three Jewels;

(5) mutual misappropriation of the substances themselves; (6) mutual misappropriation between images and the Three Jewels; (7) mutual misappropriation of the objects themselves; (8) lending on interest;
(9) providing hospitality for monastics and laypeople; (10) stealing human property; (11) stealing non-human property; (12) stealing livestock.
Regarding sentient beings:

first, one who steals property belonging to the Buddha does not incur an offense [of pārājika] with respect to the Buddha, because the Buddha has no sense of "mine" regarding objects and thus there is no affliction or harm [to him].

One incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), as such property is categorized as being equivalent to that which is not a sentient being. Thus, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is said: "Stealing..."

Regarding the image of a celestial deity, its robes constitute a *sthūlātyaya* offense; the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* further states that if one uses pearls or flower garlands for the purpose of making offerings to a Buddhist temple, one must not take them arbitrarily.
Whether one knows [the prohibition] or not, one commits a *sthūlātyaya*. If there is a guardian, the offense is incurred in relation to that guardian;
if there is no guardian, the offense is incurred in relation to the merit of the donor. Thus says the *Vinaya*.

The *Ya jing* (Ya-sūtra) states: "If one steals banners, canopies, or other items from a stūpa of the Buddha or a stūpa of a śrāvaka, it constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*) with respect to the original donor, because it severs their merit.

The *Shisong lü* (Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya) states: "If one steals property of a Buddhist monastery (*vihāra*) or offerings within a shrine, if there is a guardian, one commits a grave offense based on the value [of the object].
The *Shansheng jing* (Śraddhā-pratilambha-sūtra) also states: "It likewise constitutes a grave offense with respect to the guardian. The *Shisong lü* further addresses theft...
According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, if one steals an image of the Buddha for the purpose of making a pure-hearted offering, thinking, "He was a disciple and I am also a disciple;

thus, there is no offense," there is indeed no offense. However, if it is for the purpose of selling it, even if a bird dies within a stūpa or other items are obtained, they must be used solely for the stūpa;
to use them otherwise constitutes the offense of theft. The *Mātṛkā* states that stealing from the Buddha [is a grave offense].
In the case of bodily relics (*śarīra*), stealing less than five constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense;

stealing five or more constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). Second, regarding the theft of Dharma-objects: since the Dharma is insentient and lacks a self-mind, the offense is determined with respect to the person guarding the object.
Thus, the Vinaya states: "At one time, a bhikṣu stole another's scripture. The Buddha said: 'The words of the Buddha are priceless; [the value] is calculated based on the paper and ink.'"
Because it constitutes a grave offense, we know that this refers to the person who guards [the scripture], not to the Dharma itself. The *Wubai wenda shi* (The Five Hundred Questions) states:
"One must not blow dust or dirt from atop a scripture with one's mouth (the same applies to images). If one burns an old scripture, one incurs a grave offense;

if one does so unknowingly, one commits a light offense. The *Shisong lü* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) states: "If one borrows another’s scripture and refuses to return it, causing the owner to harbor doubts..."

Regarding the offense of *sthūlātyaya* (this occurs when the mind has not yet reached a definitive resolve; if it has reached a definitive resolve, one commits a grave offense): The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that stealing another’s secret formulas constitutes a grave offense. Question:

As previously discussed in the treatise, stealing images or relics for the purpose of making offerings is not an offense. By the same logic, since I also have a virtuous intention for the sake of making offerings to the Dharma, I too should be without fault.

Answer: If one intends to take them for mutual exchange, there is both offense and non-offense. If the intent is merely to steal for one's own use, it is an offense; if the intent is for mutual benefit or for the sake of the Dharma, it is not.
If a person makes a sūtra with a mind focused solely on themselves and does not share it with others, would they not incur a grave offense? It is the same for making an image.
If one wishes to make an image with a mind that extends to both oneself and others, as stated in the treatise, there is no offense; the case of the sūtra is likewise.
Third, regarding the theft of property belonging to the Saṃgha: if there is a guardian or custodian, the offense is determined in relation to that guardian.

If the person who holds charge of the property steals it themselves, according to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, the theft of property belonging to the Saṃgha constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). There are four categories for classifying this property of the Saṃgha:
first, "permanently established permanently" (*nitya-nitya*), which refers to the monastic kitchen, storehouses, temple buildings, communal utensils, gardens, and flowering or fruiting trees.

Regarding monasteries, fields, servants, livestock, and so forth, because their substance pervades the ten directions, they cannot be divided for individual use; they are to be regarded collectively as belonging to the Saṃgha.
As stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "As for the property of the Saṃgha, even if all bhikṣus were to assemble, it may not be divided. This follows the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Second, regarding the permanent endowments of the ten directions, such as the regular food provided for the Saṃgha, these encompass the four quarters and are restricted solely to that location.
If there is a restricted area guarded by a supervisor, and several people together steal or damage property therein, they should incur a light offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one takes food intended for the Sangha back to one's own room, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:

"If one takes property belonging to the Sangha and uses it as if it were one's own, giving it to others, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*" (this is based on the rule regarding stealing Sangha food). If one takes such items with the intent to steal, the offense is determined according to the value of the object (as if it were property belonging to a specific owner).
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* is also the same as the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, and other texts: one who eats monastic food without striking the bell commits the offense of theft.

Furthermore, if one sees food in an empty monastery and steals and eats it, the offense is determined according to its value (as previously stated, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense). Third, regarding "that which is present before one" (*pratyakṣa*):
the gravity of the offense is determined in relation to the original owner. Even if many people share an object but only one person guards it, the offense is determined in relation to that guardian.

Regarding the four offenses involving the forfeiture of property: this refers to cases such as when the light belongings of the five groups of monastics (the *pañca-vargika*) have passed away while present before the assembly.

*Śīlasamuccaya* states: "If one steals the property of a deceased bhikṣu, if the *karman* has not yet been performed, the offense is light with respect to the monks of the ten directions (meaning that if there are fewer than five people, one commits only a *sthūlātyaya*).

If the *karman* has already been performed, it is grave with respect to the monks present (meaning that if the limit of five people is reached, it is grave). If it occurs at the time of death, it depends on the instructions of the deceased."

Regarding those who steal property, the offense is determined according to the agreement with the person to whom it was entrusted. According to this Vinaya, as for the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions—whether belonging to the Saṃgha as a whole, to many individuals, or to a single person—it must not be divided or sold, nor should it be taken into one's own possession; in all such cases, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

When people see this ruling, they may think that stealing property of the Saṃgha does not constitute theft if it is immediately seized back; however, no explicit textual authority has yet been seen to support this, and if it is seized, the offense is established.

Because this rule temporarily obstructs the communal use of the Sangha, the offense is light; however, if it is permanently taken for one's own use, it is as grave as described in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If one steals with the intent to misappropriate a valuable item belonging to the Sangha worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, the offense is grave; if it is worth even one *kārsāpaṇa* or more, it is a *thullaccaya*."

Regarding the fourth point, the mutual appropriation of the Three Jewels: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if the temple administrator (*māmādhi*), who is the master of the monastery, mutually appropriates the property of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, it is said that he does not commit an offense. However, the Buddha declared this to be a *pārājika* offense.

This refers to the current situation where those in charge of affairs for a Buddha image take the provisions of the Saṃgha, or employ the Saṃgha’s donkeys, horses, family members, slaves, and so forth, for the construction and maintenance of the Buddha-dharma.

These cases are all adjudicated according to the Vinaya: if the full five [units] are reached, it constitutes a grave offense regarding precious objects. The *Ratna-mudrā-sūtra* states that the two types of property belonging to the Buddha and the Dharma must not be used interchangeably, because there is no one appointed as a steward for the property of the Buddha and Dharma, and furthermore, there is no one with whom one may consult or report matters; this differs from the property of the Saṃgha, such as permanent endowments (*sthavira*) or property dedicated to the visiting community (*caitya*), which may be mutually requisitioned as needed.
When a monk in charge of affairs requires such items, he must harmonize with the Saṃgha by soliciting their consent (*chanda*) and distributing voting tallies (*śalākā*) to achieve a formal assembly.
If one may use [the property]—specifically, if one uses the property of the Saṃgha to repair a stūpa—one must obtain it according to the Dharma through the harmony of the Saṃgha;
if they are not in harmony, one should exhort the laity to perform the repairs.

If there is even a single coin’s worth of property belonging to a stūpa, because the donor offered it with a sincere heart, all devas and humans should conceive the notion of "Buddha" and the notion of "stūpa" toward that object, even regarding the wind.
If [an object] is blown away or ruined, it may not be traded for jewels as an offering; for regarding the property of a Tathāgata’s stūpa, no one sets a price.

According to this text, if monastic seats are set up within a Buddha hall, or if scriptures and images are placed within a monastic cell, these constitute "mutual use" because the positions of the Three Jewels are distinct.
If these items are merely temporarily installed, there is logically no harm. The *Wubai wenda* (Five Hundred Questions) states: "Originally, they were not..."

In the hall of a Buddha-stūpa where an image is enshrined, it is not an offense for bhikṣus to stay overnight together provided they create a partition, because when the Buddha was alive, he also stayed in the same room as his disciples.

The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*) states that the Buddha permitted the use of servants, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and so forth within monasteries and stūpas, each having its own designated purpose; these must not be used interchangeably. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* likewise maintains this.
Regarding land belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions that is not in harmony: one may not construct a stūpa or plant flowers and fruit trees for the Buddha upon it.

However, if the Saṃgha has already divided and allotted such land, they are permitted to offer it as they wish. If there are flowers in unlimited abundance, they may be used for offerings according to need.

In times of famine and scarcity, if there is no distinction between the gardens and fields of the Triple Gem and no one to consult, the Saṃgha may use them as they wish provided they remain in harmony.
Regarding the disposition of water belonging to a stūpa: if it was produced through the labor of the stūpa, the Saṃgha may use it with a heavy [karmic] consequence;
if the labor was provided by the Saṃgha, one should weigh the amount and not exceed the limit, for exceeding it results in a heavy offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"Flowers from trees within the Saṃgha’s garden are permitted to be taken for making offerings to the Buddha-stūpa. If there are fruits, one should have someone gather them for consumption. Large timber is to be provided for the Saṃgha as rafters."
The Liang dynasty used tree bark, leaves, and so forth; these may be used by monks as well, and they may also be used for the monastery’s cooking pots and utensils. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:

"If one plants trees on land that one has already appropriated, once the wood is obtained, it may be used to repair rooms without needing to inform the Saṃgha. If it is a tree belonging to the Saṃgha, it may be used to repair a stūpa;

having obtained the consent of the Saṃgha, it may be used. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Wood from trees within the precincts should be supplied in proportion to their quantity to provide fuel for the warm bathhouse (*jentāka*)."
When using the kitchen or a separate room for food, one must not take more than what is required.

If there is no fixed limit, one should take as much or as little as necessary, provided it is dry and withered (even though this text exists, one must still measure one's own needs). This Vinaya states that King Bimbisāra offered a garden to the Buddha, who then ordered it given to the Saṃgha;

thus, we know that the Three Jewels may not be used interchangeably. Therefore, one should encourage giving to the Saṃgha; however, if the original donor intended the gift to apply to all Three Jewels, then it may be used accordingly.
If one uses up a portion of the object, there is no offense; however, one must never break this object into three parts, as that would contradict the original intention of the donor.

Furthermore, the karma of stealing property belonging to the Sangha is extremely grave; for by stealing even a single item, one incurs sin in relation to all ordinary beings and sages throughout the ten directions.
Thus, the Flower-Cluster Bodhisattva in the Vaipulya Sūtra said: "Even the five heinous crimes and the four grave offenses I can save from, but stealing from the Sangha I cannot."

Regarding material objects, I do not save for them; furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that the sin of stealing property belonging to the Saṅgha is equal to the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).
The *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi Sūtra* states that using the property of the Saṅgha carries a transgression greater than the sin of killing eighty-four thousand parents.
Moreover, the *Record of Lingyan Temple in Guandong* relates that once there was a visiting bhikṣu who died suddenly and arrived in hell.
It is observed that those who lift stone caskets for Avalokiteśvara to record the removal of offenses, or who take wood from monastic trees to dye cloth for private use, all incur grave offenses.
These calamities arise because they violate the precepts; therefore, practitioners should reflect carefully upon their use of resources.

Fifth, regarding "mutual substitution based on the substance": this refers to cases such as intending to dedicate [an offering] to Śākyamuni but changing it to Amitābha; intending to dedicate it to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* but changing it to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*;
or intending to dedicate it to a monastic dwelling but changing it to food for the Sangha. All such acts violate the original intent of the offering and constitute the offense of mutual substitution.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "If one gives what was permitted for this place to that place, one commits an offense. (Based on this principle, items belonging to the Buddha [or the Sangha]...)

It is permissible to create images of Bodhisattvas and noble monks; because the ranks of master and disciple are distinct, one may fashion them as articles for adornment and offering without fault (provided that one's original intention was not to treat them as ordinary objects, one does not commit an offense). The *Wubai wenshi* (Five Hundred Questions on Matters) states:
"To use Buddhist colors to create the forms of birds and beasts constitutes an offense, except when done before a Buddha for the purpose of making offerings, in which case there is no offense.

The *Sifen lü shanfan buque xingshi chao* (Excerpts from the Vinaya-mātṛkā of the Dharmaguptaka School) states: "If a donor originally gave a garden or fruit trees intended for clothing, medicine, and so forth, and [the recipient] steals them..."

If one diverts food intended for distribution, its value shall be calculated according to the gravity of the offense; if it was intended for a monastery but diverted to make food, one commits a *sthūlātyaya*.
When provisions at a residence are scarce and everyone wishes to disperse so that no one remains to guard them, one may obtain the consent of the Saṃgha to reduce the usage [of the store].
One may also take heavy items such as garden fruits to make food while guarding them; this applies even to the dwellings of the Saṃgha from the four directions.
If a monastic dwelling is destroyed, one may sell coarse materials to repair it. In times of rebellion or chaos, it is permitted to take such items with one;
once the rebels have ceased their activities, they should be returned to their original location. To make offerings to this image is equivalent to making offerings to that image;

[otherwise] one incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that Upāli asked the Buddha: "When a monastic dwelling is destroyed, is it permissible to sell the bedding and other belongings belonging to the Saṃgha?"
Regarding the repair of a dwelling, the Buddha said it is permitted. He was asked again: "If two rooms are in ruins, may one sell one room to repair the other?

The Buddha said it is permitted. The *Mātṛkā* states: "If one takes property belonging to the Saṃgha from these four directions with a mind of theft and transfers it to another monastery, one incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*), because it is returned for the use of the Saṃgha;
thus, one does not commit a grave offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the neighboring temples to the left or right are in ruins..."
Regarding the offering of bedding and requisites (*śayanāsana*) for common use within a single delimited boundary (*sīmā*), the *Pañcaśata-praśna* states:

If a layperson offers food to a monk who has not yet been ordained, he must inform the Sangha before giving it. If he requests food on behalf of the Sangha, he must inform the Sangha and seek their permission to take the Sangha’s food along the road.
If the Sangha does not grant permission, or if he proceeds without informing them, he must repay the value of the food upon his return; otherwise, he commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
When rice is offered to the Saṃgha for a communal meal, once the monks have departed, the host uses it to make offerings to subsequent groups of monks;

if he does not strike the *gandī* bell [to announce this], he commits a grave offense (*pārājika*) upon eating even a single mouthful. Based on the meaning of this text, one must not arbitrarily take monastic food beyond the boundary to eat;

even if there was no initial intention to misappropriate it, one commits a grave offense. Furthermore, even if the bell is struck, one still does not escape the charge of theft, because the location of the food has been definitively assigned. Therefore...

Regarding the passage in the Vinaya concerning those who share material offerings (*lābha*) but recite the precepts separately: it permits the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for harmonizing the Saṃgha.

If one could simply obtain [the benefits] directly, what need would there be to establish a common boundary (*sīmā*)? If one is sent on errands for the Saṃgha and there is no place along the way to beg for food, it is permitted to harmonize with the Saṃgha and carry the food while traveling;

it does not necessarily require the ringing of the bell. This is based on the preceding text from the *Samantapāsādikā* regarding the monastery keeper. If there is a temple, a manor, or a mill, the bell may be rung.

When eating, there is no need to join the community of monks. If a *karmadāna* (officer) acting on behalf of the Saṃgha inspects and leads a *śrāmaṇera* or a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) and livestock to a monastery estate to consume the Saṃgha’s grain and fodder, according to the aforementioned *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

However, if it is for one's own use—whether for the Saṃgha or an individual—and one calculates the value of the livestock, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*). The Vinaya states: "If a country is ravaged and desolate, and there are no people at one's dwelling place..."

If one takes the property of this monastery to another monastery or to another country, and it is later returned to its original location, and someone takes that property back to that original monastery,
they shall be dealt with according to the law if they do not do so.

The sixth point concerns the mutual relationship between the "images" (pratibimba) and the "jewels" (ratna). This refers to the mutual relationship between the Three Jewels as sustenance (*dhāraṇa*) and the Jewel of Principle (*tattva-ratna*).
The Sarvāstivādins ask: "Among the various offerings made to the Three Jewels while the Buddha was in the world, why was one person’s portion always received?

Why, after his parinirvāṇa, is only one specific portion taken? They answer: "While the Buddha was in the world, he utilized them through his physical body (*rūpa-kāya*); therefore, one person [the Buddha] was taken."
Because the merit of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) after its parinirvāṇa surpasses that of the Sangha, one portion is taken.

Furthermore, when the Buddha was in the world, those who spoke of giving "the Jewel of the Buddha" would place [relics] within stūpas of his nails and hair to make offerings to the Dharma-body; for the Dharma-body is eternally present in the world.
If one gives to the Dharma, it is divided into two parts: one part is given to the sūtras, and one part is given to those who recite the sūtras and expound the Dharma. If one gives to the Dharma...

Regarding precious objects, they should be suspended within a stūpa; if one offers precious objects to the Saṃgha of Jewels, they should likewise be placed within the stūpa as an offering to the Saṃgha of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya).
If one says they are offered to the "General Assembly of Monks" (saṃghika-saṃgha), both ordinary and noble ones may receive them, as such a term is not restricted.
Knowing this, when receiving offerings, one must clearly understand what is permissible and what is obstructed, ensuring that funds are not interchanged to cause discord.

Seventh, regarding the mutual [use] of objects belonging to the Buddha: first, these are categorized into four groups. First are the objects for the Buddha’s personal use, such as halls, clothing, beds, and curtains.
These must be enshrined within a stūpa for offerings and may not be diverted for other purposes, as previously stated in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra*.
The *Wubai wenda* (Five Hundred Questions) asks: "May objects belonging to the Buddha be purchased to acquire implements for making offerings? [The answer is that they may not.]

It is permissible to sell silk offered to the Buddha to make robes for the Buddha. Furthermore, if a pillar in a Buddha hall breaks and is replaced, the old pillar may be offered to the Saṃgha, but the Saṃgha must not use it.
According to the Vinaya, items such as garden seats belonging to the Buddha all belong to the stūpa (tā), and therefore they must not be used interchangeably.
Regarding offerings belonging to the image of the Buddha, they may be diverted at will; other uses are as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "Using the property of a Buddhist stūpa..."

The Buddha spoke regarding the matter of "sending out" [property], saying: "It is not permitted to transfer property belonging to the Buddha to another monastery; to do so constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If all the monks have departed, one may inform the Sangha, and if the Sangha permits it, there is no offense in taking it away.

A bhikṣu may use [materials] to create images of the Buddha or scriptures, but he must not take the property [thereby acquired]. If he obtains the family members or livestock of the Buddha’s household, he must not employ them; rather, these three should be used as offerings to the Buddha."

Regarding images and objects, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that although it is permitted to sell flowers offered to the Buddha if they are in great excess, if incense and lamps remain in great excess, they should be sold and the proceeds placed within the "Inexhaustible Treasury" (*akṣaya-nīvi*).
The *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu* states that if there are many banners for the Buddha and one wishes to perform other Buddhist rites with them, this is permissible provided the donor does not object.
Fourth, regarding items offered to the Buddha, according to this Vinaya, such items are used for the worship of Buddha-stūpas.
Regarding those who eat from the food intended for the repair of a stūpa, the *Sudarsana* states that if a bhikṣu is present to offer the rice before the Buddha, that bhikṣu may eat it;
if there is no bhikṣu, even a layperson (*avadātavasana*) attending upon the Buddha may eat it. (The two items belonging to the Dharma and the Saṃgha may be understood by analogy with what preceded.)

Eighth, regarding lending: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that when lending between the two types of property—those belonging to the stūpa and those belonging to the Saṃgha—one must clearly record the transaction with a formal document, noting the time it was lent and the time it is to be returned.
When there is a handover of administrative duties, the details must be read aloud before the Saṃgha and formally proclaimed so as to entrust them to the successor;
one who violates this incurs an offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if an individual lends property belonging to a stūpa or the Saṃgha and subsequently dies, the value must be repaid.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* also permits borrowing items from the Saṃgha to construct a private room. *Sujāta* states that for a sick person, one may borrow items belonging to the Triple Gem provided they are repaid tenfold;
for others who are not ill, it is feared that this would not be permitted.
The ninth [point] concerns the reception of monastics and laypeople. In this Vinaya, when Upāli arrived at a certain residence and was not welcomed, the Buddha said:
"If one knows the Dharma and the Vinaya, wherever they go, they should be received and provided with food and drink.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, because such a person serves as my representative, they must be provided for; the meaning corresponds to that given to those in charge of monastery affairs (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*) in the text below.
Since robes are items present before [the community] from all ten directions, it is known that they are not for the supply of the permanent property of the four directions.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If there are evil robbers, donors, craftsmen, or even kings and ministers who have the power to cause harm or benefit, one should provide them with food and drink.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a layperson enters the monastery and is not given food, and they give rise to resentment, the Buddha said: [He established a rule].

One should give [the food] using a vessel of poor quality; furthermore, if one dislikes the Buddha’s words and gives it using a fine vessel—[this refers to those who see faults in the Sangha, such as high-minded gentlemen who are well-versed in transcendent matters and say that the food is difficult to digest, giving it out of a sense of disdain rather than parsimony]—then for such persons, sending it away in vain causes no harm. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"When providing firewood, fuel, lamps, and so forth for kings and great ministers, it is permitted to use nineteen coins; there is no need to inform the Sangha. If they ask for more, one should inform the Sangha before providing them."

If the person is a wicked thief, it does not matter whether they are many or few; even for a sick child who requests the "Precious Medicine" (saṃghaguruka-bhaiṣajya) of the Saṃgha, one may give it provided they pay two and a half *kārsāpaṇas*.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that if laborers are divided into upper and lower shifts, those of the upper shift are provided with clothing, while those of the lower shift are not permitted to receive long-term provisions;
however, they are supplied with food and clothing. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if a day’s labor is hired from a worker, [the fee must be paid].

If one encounters wind or rain and is unable to complete the work due to these difficulties, the Buddha has ordained that the laborer be compensated according to the amount of work actually performed.
Regarding the tenth category, stealing another's property, there are two initial types; first, regarding damage to the primary owner, there are three cases:
(1) items such as cotton or silk within a chest where there is both a sense of ownership and a guardian; (2) items such as grain in a field where there is a sense of ownership but no guardian.
Beans are a treasure-trove within the ground where there is no sense of "mine" and no one to guard them.
If one steals these three types of objects, one incurs an offense by first harming the primary owner and secondly harming the guardian. Regarding the guardian, there are two cases:

first, those who possess a sense of "mine" and guard the object separately, such as when property that is to be distributed among the Sangha is entrusted to someone to watch over it; second, those who have no sense of "mine."

Regarding the protector who seizes prohibited items from a checkpoint, or when a monk’s lost property is seized by an official, and so forth—if one steals these two types of objects, the offense is determined in relation to the protecting owner. There are seven such cases to distinguish:
first, the protector who prevents loss for the owner, as the *Sudarsana-vibhasa* states: "A bhikṣu acts as a protector for another individual, or even for the Three Jewels."

If wealth is guarded with diligence, secured with firm locks, and stored within the house, yet a rogue bhikṣu should steal it through a hole or from within the building, or take it by force—wherein the guardian is unable to prevent or restrict it—the offense is incurred solely by the original owner; in such a case, the items are not subject to restitution.
However, if the owner guards them with negligence and fails to diligently record and protect them, and they are stolen by a thief, [the responsibility lies with the guardian].

A bhikṣu must necessarily compensate for an object [entrusted to him], because he incurs an offense by failing to protect it for the sake of its owner. Second, regarding the loss of entrusted property:

as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if a bhikṣu accepts another’s entrusted goods while traveling and they are damaged or destroyed on the road—if he damaged or destroyed them with a good intention, he need not compensate;
if he damaged or destroyed them with an evil intention, he must compensate. This applies to borrowed objects regardless of whether they were damaged intentionally or not.

Regarding the meaning of "if one with an evil mind breaks anything, it must be compensated": nowadays, there are many who, out of a good intention to wash or repair the bowls and utensils of others, damage them;
these do not require compensation. One who obtains an object stolen by thieves has two types [of ownership]:
first, when the owner is not present, the thief's intent to steal weakens the owner's protective mind, and thus the taker achieves the status of "owner" through their perception.

Even if one has the intention not to relinquish it, if one later sees the original object and takes it back, one may not seize it; because it has left its original location and belongs to the thief, the principle is established.
If one seizes this object, one incurs a grave offense (*guru-dharma*); thus the Vinaya states: "At one time there was a bhikṣu who seized the property of a robber.

The Buddha said: "This is a *pārājika* offense. Next, regarding seizing what is present before one's face: because the sense of protecting [the property] is strong, one who seizes it by force incurs the offense immediately upon hesitation.

If one’s intention has not yet been fixed on the original owner and the sense of protecting the mind is strong, such that the intent to abandon the original object has not yet ceased, one may take it; therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If a thief seizes an object and flees, and a bhikṣu pursues the thief and recovers the original object, there is no offense.

Furthermore, if he pursues the thief in the dark and the thief hides the object before fleeing, the bhikṣu may immediately take it and bring it back. Moreover, if he is gradually approaching a village while pursuing the thief, he may [recover it] through conciliation."
If one obtains [the property] through intimidation, there is no offense; however, in matters involving death, one should not report it to the authorities.

As for the aforementioned phrases, they all refer to being robbed face-to-face. If one has already formed the thought that the item is lost, regardless of whether the thief’s intent is certain or uncertain, and subsequently retrieves it, this constitutes robbing the thief again.
Regarding the "owner who gives to the thief," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When a thief comes with stolen goods, or..."
If one receives a gift out of kindness, or because another pursues one out of fear, and takes it so as to become its owner, one may take it provided one does not beg for it from a thief.

If another person gives it voluntarily, one may accept it; once accepted, however, it should be dyed with a discolored hue. If there is someone who recognizes it as their own property, it should be returned.
If one purchases a robe from a thief-monk (cora-bhikṣu) and the original owner sees it, one must not simply seize it back; rather, it should be returned [to the original owner].

Regarding the original rule on "fivefold seizure" concerning thieves and their leaders, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If the authorities have not yet arrested [the thief] and have not yet recorded the names of the stolen goods, one may take items deposited with a bhikṣu;
however, if they have already been recorded, one must not take them. If it is said that the items are being offered to a Buddha-stūpa or the Saṃgha, one may take them.
One should carry them out openly and must not conceal them. If asked what these items are, one should answer.

Regarding the statement that "it is not permitted to take property belonging to the Buddha-Dharma," this follows the Sarvāstivāda school. Taking objects prohibited by the state out of the boundary constitutes an offense;
if the person dies, the previous judgment holds that one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), while subsequently violating the royal decree constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a king’s subject is sentenced to death and one steals [the person] with the intent to carry them out, one incurs a grave offense. Apart from these cases, if it is not permitted but there is no death, there is no offense. This is according to the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-putra-sūtra*.

If one claims not to pay the king’s tax but does not steal from the *saṃghika* (monastic) property, and uses a stratagem to exempt oneself from official taxation on a bhikṣu’s goods, one does not incur a grave offense (*pārājika*).
This is because: first, there was no prior agreement; second, it is an unreasonable tax. Our Vinaya states: "A bhikṣu has no obligation to pay taxes, as he differs from laypeople.
If a bhikṣu conceals or misrepresents the property of a layperson for their sake when it comes to official taxation, he incurs a grave offense. (Regarding the present time...)

6. Regarding the case where monks or nuns falsely claim for others vehicles, oxen, people, horses, and so forth: if the value calculated according to the above standard reaches five *kārsāpaṇas*, one incurs a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). 7. Regarding the giving of property by a madman:
the *Mātṛkā* states that if a madman personally offers an object as a gift and does not recognize his parents or relatives, a monk may accept it;
however, if his parents can be identified and he does not give it with his own hand, it must not be accepted. 8. Regarding the guarding of another’s property: [the rule concerning] the owner...
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There was a watchman who gave a robe to a bhikṣu; being uncertain, [the bhikṣu] did not know whether he had become its owner.

The Buddha said: 'One may accept it according to the donor's gift; it is improper to beg for it. The Vinaya further states: 'If a person guarding another's property gives an object to a bhikṣu, the Buddha said:
"This person is indeed the owner; it may be accepted."'"

Eleventh, regarding the theft of non-human property: according to the *Pañcavargika*, if one steals another's covered burial mound, a banner, a parasol, clothing from within a shrine, or any object protected by another, and it is worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*).

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, if one steals the property of a non-Buddhist stūpa or objects used for divine sacrifices, one incurs a grave offense (this is determined as a grave offense based on the presence of a guardian).

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, if one steals the clothing, flower garlands, or other items belonging to a celestial deity image, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* (this is determined as a *sthūlātyaya* based on the nature of the object).

Therefore, the Sarvāstivādins state that taking five *kārsāpaṇas* or more from a non-human being constitutes a grave *sthūlātyaya*, while taking four *kārsāpaṇas* or less constitutes a light *sthūlātyaya*.
According to the *Samantapāsādikā*, there is no offense for taking the property of various ghosts and spirits or objects tied to trees that have no guardian;
this refers to cases where non-humans do not guard them.

Regarding the twelfth case, stealing the property of animals: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that taking what was left over by a tiger constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense because the expectation [of further food] has not been severed;

however, taking what was left over by a lion does not constitute an offense because the expectation has been severed. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that one who takes the remains of food eaten by any bird or beast incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The second [case], the perception that there is an owner, is easy to understand. Next, we shall explain the third: the presence of a thieving mind (*cauryacitta*).

However, even those who actually practice according to this one gate cannot avoid grave offenses. Why is this? Because they do not recognize the characteristics of the precepts (*śīlākāra*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If the temple master or the *māmādika* (steward) uses the property of the Three Jewels for mutual purposes out of good intentions, this is also a thieving mind. This Vinaya says:
I say that because this person is deluded, they commit a *pārājika* offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are six kinds of intent for theft:
taking by means of harshness, taking with contempt, taking under another's name, taking by force, taking what has been entrusted, and taking interest.
Taking interest is light, while the other five are grave. The *Mātṛkā* states that there are three kinds of intent for plundering: namely, seizing by force.
Having taken [an object] with gentle words and having received a gift, to then take back five parts of it is called stealing. There are four kinds of thieving mind:
namely, a deceitful mind, a crooked mind, a hateful mind, and a mind of fear. If one takes another's property with these four types of minds, all are termed stealing.
The Vinaya states that there are ten kinds of thieving mind: namely, a dark mind, a perverse mind, a crooked and distorted mind, a fearful mind, and a constantly [resentful] mind.
Taking another's property with a determined intent to steal; taking through intimidation; taking what has been entrusted; taking upon seeing [the owner];
and taking by relying on [the authority of] others (that is, begging under the pretext of the power of monastics or laypeople).
The fourth heavy offense refers to five *kārsāpaṇas* or the equivalent value of five *kārsāpaṇas*. Among these, they are categorized and grouped into seven degrees of gravity;

when one reaches the full measure of five [units], it constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). The *Mātṛkā* states that taking hundreds or thousands does not constitute a heavy offense, provided it is done repeatedly with a resolved intention to desist, or if one repeatedly takes four *kārsāpaṇas*.
These two cases do not result in the offense of a heavy offense, as explained in the Vinaya regarding objects that cannot be acquired.

Regarding burning, burying, or destroying the color [of property], these are offenses involving many people. As for the gravity of the offense when the value reaches five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, the Vinaya states:

"If many people dispatch one person to steal five *kārsāpaṇas*, or if many people share the theft, or if many people steal together as a single unit, and the value reaches five, it is a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).
If four reach five and constitute a *sthūlātyaya* offense, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: 'Stealing from many people...'"

Regarding "undivided property" (this refers to the light belongings of a deceased person that have not yet been divided): when five thieves each take one coin and the offense is classified as grave, it is as described in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
if five people each contribute one coin and send one person to guard and manage them, if a thief steals with the expectation of [taking from] the guardian, the offense is classified as grave.
When many people together steal six coins and the offense is classified as grave, it is as described in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*: four disciples and their teacher [committing the theft].

If they instruct one another to steal six *kārsāpaṇas* together, each incurs one *pārājika* offense and one *sthūlātyaya*. This means that while the act itself does not constitute a *pārājika*, instructing another results in only one *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the determination of a grave offense (*pārājika*) based on the location, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "It depends on the value of the place, whether noble or base.
That is to say, in this land the value is less than five [units], but in that land it exceeds five; or in this land the value exceeds five, but in that land it is less.

Regarding the reduction of five [units] and the basis for severing [the offense] at its original location, the *Mātṛkā* states: "Kāśyapa, whether the value is high or low—if it is high, reducing it by five constitutes no offense;

if it is low, exceeding five constitutes no offense. The *Sudarśana-vibhāṣā* states: "If one steals with the intent to do so and proclaims, 'This land is certainly mine,' and the owner of the land conceives doubt, one commits a *sthūlātyaya*.
If the owner loses their resolve [regarding ownership], it is grave. If they come to question the Saṃgha and the answerers agree [with the claimant], [it is likewise]."

If all [the monks] are heavy [offenders], and they dispute over a garden or field and the judgment is rendered contrary to principle— even if one employs many verbal sophistries, such as falsely claiming to have completed the summer retreat (*vassa*) or chanting the *Mahāpadesa*—
if the value of the property obtained reaches five *māṣakas*, it is all a heavy offense. The fifth [case],
regarding the application of skillful means, is easy to understand.

Sixth, regarding "lifting from the spot": as the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states, when lifting one tree it is light, but when lifting two trees it is heavy (this refers to measuring and taking another's land), and so on until even the amount of a single hair or a single grain of barley is heavy, because the value of the ground is immeasurable.

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one steals another's ox or horse and has not yet formed the intention that it is acquired, even if all four legs have been lifted, it does not constitute a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* [also notes] the case of empty, quiet places.

In the case of stealing from a fixed location, if one forms the perception that it has been acquired and moves it, the offense becomes grave (*sthūlātyaya*). This is like throwing a staff into the air; there is necessarily the principle that it must fall.
According to this Vinaya, if one steals by concealing another's counting-sticks (*śalākā*), the offense is grave. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"Whether it be moving the pieces in backgammon (*akṣa*) or shifting the stones in chess (*caturaṅga*), these are all grave offenses" (meaning they are grave when involving wagered objects, and a *duṣkṛta* when not). Next, to clarify what constitutes non-offense: this Vinaya states that taking with the perception that it is one's own is non-offensive.
Regarding the perception of refuse, the perception of what is temporarily acquired, and the perception of a friend—all such perceptions do not constitute an offense.
The Vinaya states that the "perception of a friend" must possess seven qualities: first, being able to perform what is difficult to do; second, being able to give what is difficult to give;

third, being able to endure what is difficult to endure; fourth, confiding secret matters to one another; fifth, mutually concealing each other's faults; sixth, not abandoning one another when encountering suffering; and seventh, [the remaining quality].
Not disparaging those who are poor or lowly—those who can practice these seven dharmas are one's true and virtuous friends.
The third precept regarding killing (a violation common to both monks and nuns).
The fourth precept regarding claiming to have attained holiness (a violation common to both monks and nuns).

These two matters concerning the precepts are rarely described; even regarding the conditions for their transgression, they have already been briefly explained above in the section on the characteristics of receiving the precepts.
Second, the concise explanation of the nine [offenses] of the second category.

The First Section on the Loss of Precepts (The Female Faculty): Three conditions must be present for an act to reach completion: first, the intention; second, the movement of the physical organ as the means; third, the emission of the seminal essence.
One commits an offense under this Vinaya except in the case of a dream, which is not an offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: The Buddha told Śāriputra, "A dream is empty, false, and unreal. If a dream were real, there would be no one practicing the holy life within my Dharma."

The *Sudarsana-vimokṣa* explains that there are four kinds of dreams: first, dreams resulting from the disharmony of the four great elements, such as seeing mountains collapse, the earth shaking, or flying through the void at night while asleep; or seeing tigers, wolves, lions, and wicked bandits pursuing one during the day.

Second, dreams based on prior perceptions, such as seeing blue, yellow, red, or white, or men and women during the day, which are then seen again in the middle of the night. Because these two types are unreal, the Sūtra says they are "like a dream and like an illusion."
Third, dreams involving celestial beings and good or evil spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): if it is a celestial being who is a good spiritual friend, they manifest a good dream;
if it is a celestial being who is an evil spiritual friend, they manifest an evil dream. Fourth, dreams of signs from previous lives:

whether these involve merit or transgression from a person's prior existence, if it is merit, a good dream is manifested—such as reciting scriptures or prostrating to the Buddha; if it is transgression, an evil dream is manifested—such as killing or stealing. (Because these two are real, the Sūtra says: "Ordinary people... [text continues]).
People merely grasp at the characteristics of dreams; if one dream is attained, one transgression is extinguished, and so on, as explained in the *Buddhanāma Vaipulya Sūtra*.
The second precept regarding physical contact (*niḥsargika-pācattika*): it is an offense when five conditions are met: (1) a human female; (2) the perception of her as a female;
(3) a defiled mind; (4) physical contact; (5) the act of touching. The Vinaya states that both the bhikṣu and the woman must be unclothed.
If there is physical contact between the bodies, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense: one case when the monk is clothed and the woman is unclothed;
two cases of *sthūlātyaya* when both are clothed; and a *duṣkṛta* offense when both are clothed. The *Daśādhyāya-vinaya* states:

"If a woman is submerged in water and opens her hands for a bhikṣu to grasp, even if lustful intent arises, he should merely grasp one place and not let go until she reaches the shore. Once on the shore, he must not intentionally touch her again."
Regarding the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one crosses water with a lustful mind while touching a woman, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one touches an object with a woman, offers a blessing, holds a vessel while serving food, grasps the head or tail of a rope, or holds a staff, wood, or similar items—all these are improper conduct (*anācāra*).
If done with a lustful mind, it is a *duṣkṛta*. To move an object with a lustful mind is a *sthūlātyaya*. [This applies even at] city gates or on roads.

If one encounters a woman in a narrow passage who insists on blocking the way in her agitation, one should wait until she has passed. If the woman has something she requires, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) give it to her.
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one should place the object on a bed or a table and say, "You may take it yourself.

If one is carrying a heavy load and cannot lift it while there is no *kappiya-kāraka* nearby, the bhikṣu should lift it and place it in a high location so that she may carry it herself. If she asks for [assistance], [he should provide it].
When a woman of upright appearance brings food at mealtime to one who has conceived lustful thoughts, she should set down her bowl on the ground and have another person hand it to him.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a woman pours water for a bhikṣu and the stream does not cease, and the bhikṣu conceives improper thoughts toward the woman, he immediately gives rise to doubt.
The Buddha said: "This is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. (In the present day, there are many women and nuns who personally distribute scented water and bestow [offerings] during the *zhāi*.)

When touching objects such as needles, thread, or vessels while performing the residual practice of burning incense, one should suspend them; all other vessels and such items should be placed on the ground before taking them up for use oneself). Regarding what constitutes no offense, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If one perceives [the object] as being one's mother, daughter, sister, or sibling; or if it is for the sake of warding off cold or heat, or for warmth or coolness;
or if it is due to dangers from water, fire, weapons, deep pits, or predatory beasts, and there is no defiled mind—there is no offense."
The Third Precept on Vulgar Speech with a Woman (Prāyaścittika; for a nun, a *sthūlātyaya* for vulgar speech with a man). This offense is committed when seven conditions are met:
1. A person who is a woman; 2. The perception that she is a woman; 3. A mind possessed by defilement (*rakta-citta*); 4. Vulgar speech; 5. The perception that it is vulgar speech;

6. The completion of the words; 7. The other person understands them. According to this Vinaya, one commits the offense of vulgar speech only when one fully understands the meaning of the words regarding sexual desire.
This is not the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Even if one engages in virtuous deeds, if the mind expresses a lustful intent, it is still a transgression that remains unresolved.

According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, those who naturally prefer coarse speech commit a *sthūlātyaya* offense. This Vinaya explains that for women, practicing the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth does not constitute an offense.

Section Four: Praising One’s Own Body with Vulgar Speech as an Offering to the Precepts (The *Thullaccaya* for a Nun Praising Her Body Before a Man). An offense is incurred when seven conditions are met: 1. There is one person; 2. She is a woman; 3.
There is the perception that she is a woman; 4. She possesses a mind of defilement; 5. She praises her own body by speaking vulgar speech; 6. She has the perception that it is vulgar speech; 7.

Her words are intelligible and the other person understands them—then she commits the offense. In this Vinaya, there are two types of praising one's body: first, praising the physical form (*rūpakāya*).

The second praise for abundance and excellence concerns the profoundity of one's lineage; furthermore, there is praise for one's own person regarding the foremost practice of maintaining the precepts.
One who offers sexual desire as an offering to me is [considered] a remnant.

The fifth precept concerning matchmaking (the same offense applies to both monks and nuns) is established through six conditions: a single person, two individuals—one male and one female—the perception that they are a male and a female.

Third, acting as a matchmaker; fourth, the perception of being a matchmaker; fifth, the completion of the formal proposal; sixth, receiving the words and conveying them back and forth. One immediately commits an offense according to the Vinaya, which states:
"If for even a single thought-moment, or even for a brief instant, one facilitates a union through matchmaking, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"In the process of receiving words and reporting them, there is the messenger who receives the words, and there is the messenger who conveys the words; that messenger is dispatched to deliver the message."
When the messenger returns to report, [the offenses] are all numerous *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The *Vinaya* states: when receiving the words from the man's family, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
when reporting to the woman's family, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; when returning to report to the man's family, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* state: if one does not permit the return report, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if one permits the return report, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If...
If one draws up a written contract stating that she is not his wife, yet has not yet formally repudiated her, the marital rites (*āranya-dharma*) are already severed and they no longer interact.

Regarding those who reconcile such unions, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a master keeps many wives and concubines but does not treat them equitably, leading to strife, and a woman privately seeks out a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu then acts as a mediator for them; or, if husband and wife are not in harmony, he encourages [reconciliation]."

If they bring about a union, it is all *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). If a woman or a girl returns home and a bhikṣu goes to her house and urges her to return early, it is *sthūlātyaya*—this being because he fears the husband might become angry and thus prevent their meeting.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one acts as a male messenger for a female, or as a female messenger for a male, or acts as a long-term messenger, it is *sthūlātyaya*.
According to this Vinaya, the bhikṣus perform a formal act of motion and resolution (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to appoint a person [for such duties].

Acting as a matchmaker for all cases of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, one must inform the Saṃgha; acting as a matchmaker for a lay attendant (*karmadāna*) and providing wedding requisites, one must ask the Saṃgha if it is appropriate—these are all *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one uses property improperly, one commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-mātṛkā* states:
"If one acts as a matchmaker for those who are already pregnant, or acts as a matchmaker for oneself, these are all *sthūlātyaya*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu..."
Even to the extent of seeking out excellent breeds of horses for others to mate, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; for other animals, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Vinaya-ksudraka* states:
"If a bhikṣu releases animals so that they mate with one another, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*"; according to this Vinaya, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding non-offenses, the Vinaya states: "If it is for the sake of one's parents, a faithful donor (*dānapati*), or one who is imprisoned..."
It is not an offense to take a written account of matters concerning the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, or a bhikṣu suffering from a grave illness and present it [to the authorities].

The sixth precept: The rule against constructing an oversized dwelling for the Saṅgha without an owner and without authorization (for Bhikṣuṇīs, this is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). It is established through six conditions: first, there is no owner; second, it is for one’s own sake;
third, one has personally solicited materials; fourth, it exceeds the prescribed dimensions; fifth, it was built without authorization; and sixth, it exceeded the authorized dimensions.
If one intends to build a six-room dwelling, it constitutes an offense against this Vinaya. If one wishes to construct such a room, one must first ascertain that there are no obstacles or hindrances;
only then may one go before the Saṃgha and request the formal authorization (*dharmakarma*). If the person is not to be trusted, the entire Saṃgha should go together to inspect the site.

If the person is trustworthy, the Saṃgha shall grant permission for the construction. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "In a place free from obstacles and hindrances, the ground should be leveled like the surface of a drum; thereafter, one goes before the Saṃgha."
This Vinaya [text] requests that the length be twelve *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha’s hand and the width seven *vitasti*.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one *vitasti* of the Buddha’s hand is two feet; by this calculation, the room in this Vinaya is twenty-four feet long and fourteen feet wide. The *Sudarśana-vinaya* states that these measurements refer to the interior space.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the height of the walls is twelve feet. Whether male or female, whether lay or ordained, all are considered owners of the room.
Regarding the statement "because these have owners, it is difficult to build where there are no owners," this Vinaya refers to tigers, wolves, and ants.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that one must not build even if there is an ant's nest; however, if ants are seen foraging for food, one may build after driving them away.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings and for the sake of the bhikṣus, [prohibited building] at the four crossroads.

Places where many people gather for games, brothels, market stalls, places for grazing livestock, dangerous areas, gardens, fields, community trees, cemeteries, those bordering villages, or near roads, are all considered difficult or obstructed locations.
