This is the fifth precept concerning sleeping for more than three nights with a person who has not received full ordination (*upasampadā*) (an offense common to both monks and nuns). An offense is committed when five conditions are met:

(1) the presence of a person who has not received full ordination, whether male or female; (2) the formation of a private chamber; (3) sharing a bed together; (4) being aware that one is sharing a bed; and (5) exceeding [the limit of] three nights.

Having already committed the *gāthā-vinaya* offense after three nights, if one stays with a *śrāmaṇera* for two nights and stays with a woman on the third night, one incurs two *pārājika* offenses according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
It says: "If one exceeds three nights, the offense is complete. If one has not yet repented and stays again, the offense increases further;
there is no second exemption. Once the repentance is completed, one should stay in a separate room, and thereafter one may stay for two more nights.

This Vinaya states that when there is no further lodging available, by the third night, before the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇa*), one must have a *śrāmaṇera* or a layperson (*avadātavasana*) leave, or leave oneself, so as to protect against the dawn light;
this is permissible even until the fourth night. However, whether one leaves on one's own or sends another away, there is no further allowance for staying.
Therefore, according to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, if there is no place to go by the third night, one should not lie down in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

If one remains seated until the appearance of the dawn light reaches the fourth watch and there is no other place to go, one may be sent away when the dawn is about to break, or one may leave of one's own accord.
(According to this principle, one must certainly depart by the fourth watch; if one remains seated during the first watch, the permission for departure is not established.)

The Sixth [Offense]: Reciting the Precepts Together with One Who Has Not Received Full Ordination (a Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense for both monks and nuns). An offense is committed when five conditions are met: first, it is a teaching spoken by the Buddha;

second, it consists of two words, phrases, or syllables; third, the person has not received full ordination; fourth, one recites in unison with them, phrase by phrase; fifth, once the words have been finished, the offense is incurred.

According to the Sarvāstivāda, if the phrases are the same and the voices are synchronized, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense); if the voices are synchronized but the phrases differ, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

The Seventh Precept: Prohibiting the Disclosure of Another’s Gross Offense to One Who Has Not Received Full Ordination (Applicable equally to monks and nuns). This offense is established through seven conditions: 1. Being a monk or a nun; 2.

Having committed an offense belonging to the first two categories (Pārājika or Saṃghāvaśeṣa); 3. Knowing that one has committed such an offense; 4. There being no monastic legal exemption (*anāpatti*); 5.
Disclosing it to one who has not received full ordination; 6. The words being clearly articulated; 7. The other person understanding the meaning. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If..."
If one is appointed to speak of a certain offense against a specific person, yet speaks of a different offense to another person, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If one is appointed for this bhikṣu, yet speaks to another person, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one is appointed for this person, at this place, in this house, or in this village, yet speaks to another person or at a different location, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Karmavastu* states: "If one speaks to a bhikṣuṇī..."

To speak [of such matters] in the presence of a *śrāmaṇerī* is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a *bhikṣuṇī* speaks to a layperson (*avadātavasana*) regarding even a minor, general transgression of a *bhikṣu*, it is a *thullaccaya*.
This Vinaya specifies five instances where a *thullaccaya* occurs: if one mentions the name, the clan, the physical marks, the robes, or the dwelling place.
To speak of one's own offenses is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Karmaprabheda-śāstra* states: "It would be better to destroy a stūpa or damage an image [than to commit such a disclosure]."

Not to speak of another’s grave offense; if one does speak of it, one destroys the Dharma-body. Whether the preceding bhikṣu has committed an offense or not, [speaking of it] constitutes a *thullaccaya*.

Eighth: To truly claim to have attained the Path and speak of it to one who has not received full ordination. (This precept is an offense common to both monks and nuns. This matter of the precept is rare, and thus it is treated briefly.

Not mentioned [in the preceding]. The ninth precept concerning teaching the Dharma to women for more than five or six words (The *niḥsargika-pācattika* for a nun teaching the Dharma to a man). It is established as an offense when six conditions are present:

first, it is a human woman; second, she is known [to be such]; third, she has not requested [it]; fourth, there is no wise layman present; fifth, the words are articulated; sixth, [the speech is completed].
If one speaks more than five or six words, one commits this offense. For those who do not request an explanation, it is permitted to speak up to five or six words;
however, if requested by another, one may speak according to the extent of the meaning. "Five words" refers to: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all non-self.
"Six words" refers to: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all impermanent. To add even one further phrase constitutes an offense; therefore, [the Sangha]...
Having spoken these six phrases, one says, "May you quickly bring an end to suffering. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states:
"With the exception of a man of intelligence"—meaning one who understands human sentiments and the meaning of speech—who may serve as a witness;

there is no offense. If one speaks for the sake of a young girl or a barren woman, it is all *duṣkṛta*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Whether blind or deaf, they are also called 'non-persons' (*amanuṣya*). If...

"One blind and one deaf—these two constitute a single person. If she is asleep, it is likewise called 'no person. If one speaks for her mother, daughter, or sister, one also commits the *pañcāpatti* (fivefold offense).
It is said: 'From now on, I permit you to speak the Dharma for a bhikṣu by means of a skillful method so that the woman may hear it.
Once you have finished speaking five or six words to a woman, you should say: "Sister, the Dharma is correctly equal [for both of us]."'"
In this case, it is not an offense if one rises from the seat and departs, and returns later to speak because there is a specific reason.
It is also not an offense if, having finished speaking five or six words to one woman, one speaks further for another woman, and continues in this manner for an unlimited number of women.
Furthermore, it is not an offense if one is reciting a sutra oneself and a woman comes to listen, and she asks about the essential meaning, which one then explains to her.
Regarding the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*: if a woman asks about matters within the *Dīrgha-āgama*, one may answer according to her questions until the entire *Āgama* is exhausted.
If the sound remains continuous and uninterrupted, it constitutes a single *pārājika*. If it is broken, each phrase constitutes a *pārājika*.
However, if a single line of scripture and its commentary together form six phrases, there is no offense.
The Tenth Precept on Digging the Earth (a violation common to both monks and nuns). A violation occurs when five conditions are met: first, it is native soil; second, one perceives it as native soil;

third, one digs it oneself or causes another to dig it; fourth, when causing another to dig, one does not utter the "purification speech" (*jñapti-vākya*); and fifth, the soil is damaged even as much as the leg of a mosquito. The Vinaya states:
"Provided that one instructs another to dig without uttering the purification speech, it constitutes a violation regardless of whether the person is present."
To dig in the presence [of a living being] also constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If one rolls stones on a path, leaps, bounds, runs back and forth across the ground with the intent to cause the earth to break, or even throws objects with the intent to cause damage such that they injure [beings] as small as the legs of a mosquito, it is all a *thullaccaya* offense.
Even if one intends only to injure level ground, it is still a *thullaccaya*. This extends to dragging wood or driving oxen and horses [over such ground]."
When entering or exiting, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, if one wishes to level the ground, doing so entirely constitutes an offense against the earth-clods.

If one person cannot lift it and another breaks it, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense); if it is heavier than that, there is no offense. If one throws an object onto the ground without the intent to cause injury, there is no offense.

If one drives a nail into the wall of a room and thereby damages the labor already performed, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline). This applies when [the damage] was already present.
The *Konglun* states that one does not commit an offense if, by one’s own means, one digs many times but stops after each instance;
for every instance where one stops in the middle, it is a *pāyattika*. If one causes another person to dig, for every instance where the other person digs, it is a *pāyattika*.
The *Sengqi* says that if there is sand or stone in the ground, one does not commit an offense. The *Shanjian* says that if a wild fire approaches the monastery...
For the sake of protecting one's dwelling, a bhikṣu may clear away grass or dig into the earth to cut off a fire; if a fire burns his hand, he may throw it onto the ground without offense.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, digging into the earth where the ground is covered is not explicitly forbidden; this rule should be applied by analogy to permit such use.
The Eleventh Precept on Destroying Living Seeds (a violation common to both monks and nuns). The Vinaya states that there are five kinds of living seeds:
root, branch, joint, *valaja*, and seed. The commentary explains that among roots, those that do not require joints to grow are "root-seeds," such as the radish root and others.
Those that require joints to grow from within the root are called "*valaja* seeds" (or "joint-seeds"), such as sugarcane, bamboo, and reeds.
Those that grow from branches without relying on nodes are "branch-propagated seeds," such as willows and camellias.

Those that grow from branches by relying on nodes are called "node-propagated seeds," such as coriander and dock. "Seed-propagated seeds" refers to seeds that produce further seeds, such as rice, wheat, and beans.
These five names are established based on the distinctions between their origins and their final forms.
Next, the clarification of purification (*parikarman*) also has five kinds, namely: [purification by] fire, knife, wound, bird, and breaking so that it is no longer capable of germinating;

these are explained in detail below. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Regarding seeds from roots and stems, one purifies them by cutting them with a knife. Regarding seeds from joints (*parvan*), one purifies them either by cutting them with a knife or by removing the nodes and eyes.

Regarding seeds from the heart (*mūla-bīja*), such as coriander (*śatapuṣpā*) and *lābu*, one should purify them by softening them through pounding. Regarding seeds from fruits (*phala-bīja*), [one purifies them by... " [The text continues with further details on the methods of purification.]
Regarding "seeds" (bīja), such as rice, wheat, and the like, they should be cleaned by removing the husks; if they are to be purified by fire, this applies to all five types.

Regarding "pitted seeds" (phalabīja), such as dates and apricots, these should be cleaned by scratching them open so that the pit can be removed before eating. Regarding "fire-purified" (agniparimārjita) fruits, those with pits must be eaten together with the pit.
Regarding "skin-encased seeds" (tvagbīja), such as pippali and jambu, all of these must be purified by fire. This applies to all fruits.
When ripe, they fall of their own accord; if they touch wood or stone and become damaged like the feet of a mosquito, they are considered pure and the seeds may be removed for consumption.
Regarding grains wrapped in husks, such as those of the *yā-lǐu* (a type of willow), walnuts, pomegranates, and the like, these all require purification by fire.

Regarding seeds wrapped in chaff, such as those of *xiāng-dì-mù* (sandalwood), sesame, and *rěn* (sesame oil plant), if they are seedless, they should be purified by softening them with a mallet; if they have seeds, they must be purified by fire. As for seeds in pods, [the same applies].
Regarding "encased seeds," such as soybeans and the like: while the seed has not yet formed, it should be purified by softening and crushing; once the seed has formed, it should be purified by fire.

Regarding *māmadi* (grain storage), if the granary has not been purified, one fears that young bhikṣus who do not know the Dharma might handle it improperly; therefore, one should have a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) purify it.

Even if, at a later time, one constantly says "thresh it away" [to avoid handling it oneself], there is no offense. Other similar cases should be understood accordingly. If one uses five types of raw seeds...
If one throws [an object] into a pond, a well, water, excrement, urine, or among refuse, it is a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline).

If it dies, it is a *pāyattika*. If one walks among grass with the intent to kill, it is a *vinayātikrama*; if it is injured even as much as the leg of a mosquito, it is a *pāyattika*. Standing, sitting, or lying down [with such intent] is likewise.
If moss grows on a stone or mold forms on a cake or wine, these must be supervised by a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*); otherwise, one commits an offense. If [the sun]...
When drying [the water], one may remove the duckweed floating on the surface by hand-picking it away; however, where cattle or horses have passed, one may take it away to clear the water for use.
If there is no such path, one should seize a clod of earth or a stone and throw it upward toward the Brahma-heaven, saying: "Go up to the Brahma-heaven!
When it falls back down, one may then use the water at the spot where it was cleared. To overturn the duckweed in the water is a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.

If one throws [an object] onto the bank, one commits a *thullaccaya* offense. When entering the water to wash, if aquatic plants or weeds cling to the body, one should rinse them off by submerging oneself in the water so they fall away.

If one cuts down a *chao-jun* (a morning mushroom), it is a *vinayātikrama* offense. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If one requires flowers or fruit, one may personally grasp the branch and have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) take what is below;
it is also permissible to embrace the *kappiya-kāraka* while taking it. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Regarding all grasses and trees, if..."
If there is something one needs, one should say to the *kappiya-kāraka* (the person authorized to handle things): "You know this. If they do not understand, one should say again: "Look at this.
If they still do not understand, one should say again: "I need this. The Vinaya states that if one does not say "look at this" or "know this," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The same applies to damaging the ground. There is no offense for [clearing] a path covered with living grass, or for opening a path by cutting branches or knocking down leaves, provided it is not done intentionally.

Twelfth Precept on Annoying the Saṃgha with Irrelevant Speech (The same offense applies to both monks and nuns). An offense is committed when five conditions are met: first, engaging in frivolous speech through body or mouth; second, persisting in such behavior without ceasing;

third, performing the *jñapti* motion to censure and restrain the individual; fourth, being formally summoned and questioned by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma; and fifth, further violating the instruction.

One immediately incurs an offense for which the precept has not yet been established; since the physical and verbal karma of the previous life was frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*) and there was no yet-ordained Sangha to disobey, one merely incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
After the precept has been established, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* for verbal frivolous speech, termed "engaging in heterodox debate," and for physical frivolous speech, termed "causing provocation.
Although the two subsequent offenses equally violate a single established rule, they are combined and do not constitute separate divisions, according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Although these may be truthful words, they are called frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*) because they are untimely;

or, even if timely, they are so because they accord with decline and affliction and lack benefit; or, even if beneficial, they are so because the words lack a fundamental basis, the logic is disordered, and they are spoken in a way that disturbs the mind—all such cases are termed frivolous speech.

The Thirteenth Precept on Reviling the Monastic Officer (Applicable equally to monks and nuns). It is established through six conditions: 1. A monastic officer has been appointed by formal ritual (*karmavācanā*);
2. One knows that this person was appointed by the Saṃgha; 3. One manages affairs according to the Dharma, free from attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion;
4. One utters words of reviling or abuse; 5. The verbal expression is complete; 6. The other person hears and understands it—either hearing it without seeing, or seeing it without hearing.

It is not heard that both [parties] commit the *pañcāpatti* (fivefold offense). It says: "If the Saṃgha appoints someone without performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), and others speak such slanderous words, for every word it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
According to the *Vinayakṣudraka-vibhaṅga*, reviling another or conveying the reviling of another to them is in all cases a *duṣkṛta*.

The Fourteenth Precept on Spreading Monastic Bedding in an Open Area (a violation common to both monks and nuns). A violation occurs when six conditions are met: first, it is a bed belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions;

second, one knows this; third, it is an open area; fourth, one spreads it oneself or causes another to spread it; fifth, upon departing, one neither picks it up oneself nor instructs another to pick it up;
sixth, as soon as one passes through the gate, the offense is committed. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "There was a bhikṣu who saw monastic bedding spread out..."
If one does not spread bedding oneself nor cause another to spread it on an open space, and fails to lift it up after sitting or lying down thereon, it is a *pāyattika*. The Buddha said:
"It is also a *pāyattika* if one goes to a *bhikṣuṇī* monastery and, having spread out the bedding of the *bhikṣuṇī* saṃgha, fails to lift it up;
or if at a layperson's house during a gathering, having borrowed bedding, a *bhikṣu* fails to lift it up after finishing his meal; or if a steward has left the monastic bedding out in the sun."
If one is at the edge [of the bed], or in meditation, or asleep, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mahāsāṃghika* says:

"If an image is placed upon a monastic bed and a bhikṣu prostrates and touches it with his hand but does not lift it up, it is also a *sthūlātyaya*. If many people prostrate and all touch it with their hands, it belongs to the last person.
According to this Vinaya, one commits an offense as soon as one leaves the door.
The Fifteenth Precept on Not Putting Away Monastic Bedding Spread in a Secluded Place (a shared offense for both monks and nuns). An offense is established when six conditions are met:

first, it is monastic property; second, one knows it is monastic property; third, it is spread in a secluded place; fourth, it is used for one’s own benefit; fifth, one neither puts it away oneself nor instructs another to put it away;
and sixth, one either leaves the boundary or remains for more than three nights, at which point the offense is incurred.
The Sixteenth Precept on Forcibly Spreading Out a Monk’s Bedding to Annoy Another (a violation common to both monks and nuns). Five conditions must be met for the offense to be established: 1.
One has previously borrowed a dwelling place and already settled there; 2. One knows that another person is already residing there; 3. One intends to cause annoyance and disturbance to that person;

4. One forcibly spreads out bedding within that space; 5. One sits or lies down upon it. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one opens or closes a door for the purpose of annoying another, it constitutes an offense.

Opening a locked door or window, locking a door or window, extinguishing a fire, lighting a fire, lighting a lamp, chanting incantations, reciting scriptures, or preaching the Dharma—each of these actions, when done against the wishes of another, constitutes a *pāyattika*.
The seventeenth precept:

Expelling another from a monastic cell. (Expelling someone from a cell during spring or winter is an offense for both monks and nuns; during summer, it is a *pāyattika* for a nun and a *duṣkṛta* for a monk. Complete.

The four conditions for the offense of [expelling] one [monk] from the quarters of the Saṃgha of the Four Directions are: (1) it is during the spring or winter; (2) he has already settled and established himself there;
(3) one intends to disturb his mind; and (4) one drags him out of the room. Regarding this, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

when dragging another bhikṣu, if he is leaning against a pillar, grasping a door, or resting against a wall, if he leaves even one of these positions, it constitutes a *thullaccaya*. If one rebukes him verbally, it is likewise an offense as soon as he leaves his position in accordance with the words spoken.

*Tikūnilan* (this *lan* is pronounced lightly): according to this Vinaya, for the four assemblies, it is auspicious [to follow] the *Daśādhyāya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. If one is fond of snoring while sleeping, one should rise and practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*);
if one cannot practice walking meditation, one should rise and go to a secluded place; one must not disturb others.

The Eighteenth Precept on Sitting on a Ladder-Legged Bed in a Multi-Story Building (a violation common to both monks and nuns). It is established as an offense through four conditions: first, it must be a multi-story building;
second, the roof must be thin; third, it must be a ladder-legged bed; and fourth, one sits or lies down with the body relaxed—thereby committing the offense.

The Nineteenth Precept on Using Water Containing Living Beings (a shared offense for monks and nuns). An offense is committed when four conditions are met: first, there is water containing living beings;

second, one knows that there are living beings in it; third, one does not employ a straining method; and fourth, one uses the water as intended. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the living beings are too minute, one should make a triple-layered strainer.
If there are still living beings present, one should construct a separate well. Even after careful inspection, if there are still living beings, one should [proceed accordingly]."

If one leaves the dwelling place after using water containing insects, there is one *pācittiya* offense for each act of pouring with a single method; according to the number of breaths, there is a *pācittiya* for every inhalation and exhalation.

If one causes another to pour, there is one *pācittiya* for each utterance. If one causes another to pour rapidly, there is a *pācittiya* for every word. Regarding the pouring on living beings, it is impermanent:
either what was previously present is now absent, or what was previously absent is now present. Therefore, one must be mindful day by day.
If one sees that there are no insects, one may use it.
Regarding the twentieth precept on inspecting the roof for three days (a violation common to both monks and nuns): this matter is rare, so it will be briefly mentioned without further elaboration.
The Twenty-first Precept: Not Sending a Monk to Instruct Nuns (Not Applicable to Nuns). The offense is established through five conditions: 1.

The Buddha has already permitted the teaching of the Dharma and established the eight *gurudharmas* as a regulation; 2. The formal procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for appointing a monk has already been enacted; 3. One goes to assemble the community of nuns without having been appointed by the Saṃgha;
4. One teaches the Dharma and the eight *gurudharmas*; 5. Upon the completion of the teaching, the offense is incurred. If this is in a nunnery, [the rule applies] according to this Vinaya.
If one enters a separate room within the monastery to preach the Dharma for nuns, even if it is past sunset, it is considered auspicious because the harm is slight.
This is the twenty-second precept concerning the monk who has been appointed to preach the Dharma for nuns until sunset (this does not apply to nuns).
This matter is rare and thus not described in detail; however, the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* states that if one goes to a nunnery, a village, or a monastery near a village, one must announce [one's arrival].

In cases such as visiting the families of robe-donors and so forth, one does not commit an offense; however, if one commits an offense outside the village according to this Vinaya, it is not an offense if one goes to a nunnery for the sake of a great assembly to preach the Dharma in a general manner, rather than by appointment from the Saṃgha.
The Twenty-third Precept: Reviling the Teacher (No offense for a nun). This precept concerns a rare matter and is therefore not discussed in detail. The Twenty-fourth Precept:

Giving Robes to a Nun Who Is Not a Relative (For a nun giving robes to a monk who is not a relative, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense). It is established as an offense through five conditions: first, she is a bhikṣuṇī; second, the recipient is not a relative;
third, she perceives the recipient as not being a relative; fourth, she gives the robe with a sincere heart; fifth, excluding cases of exchange.

The *Yì* (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra) states that if one does not commit an offense against the first five [categories], one incurs an offense upon receiving [the robe]; this Vinaya does not inquire as to the size of the robe, but rather classifies it as a *thullaccaya* (提).

The *Sārvastivāda* school says that giving robes to the three groups of *bhikṣuṇīs* constitutes a *thullaccaya*. (There is no such text in this Vinaya; according to their own inclination, they follow the rule regarding the washing of robes, where the two groups [of nuns] seem to incur a lighter offense.)

The Twenty-fifth Precept: Making Garments for a Nun Who Is Not a Relative (A Nun Making Garments for a Monk Who Is Not a Relative is a *duṣkṛta*). An offense is incurred when four conditions are met: first, the individual is a bhikṣuṇī; second, the recipient is not a relative;
third, she personally delivers the cloth and dispatches a bhikṣu to make it; fourth, the offense is committed as soon as the work is done.
According to this Vinaya, every cut made with the knife, as well as every stitch made with the needle, constitutes a *thullaccaya*.

The Twenty-sixth Precept: Sitting with a Bhikṣuṇī in a Secluded or Exposed Place. (If a Bhikṣuṇī sits with a Saṃgha member, it is a *duṣkṛta*. It is established as an offense through four conditions: 1. It is a Bhikṣuṇī; 2.

One sits together with a member of the three [lower] groups of the *paṇḍaka* or the fivefold [Saṃgha]; 3. Regarding sitting together with the three groups of the *paṇḍaka*, both [the male and female] commit a *sthūlātyaya*; 4.

The conditions for the offense in secluded or exposed places are clarified by the precept itself, as the *śikṣāpada* text specifically mentions "secluded"; thus, one knows that both commit the offense. 5. There is no third person present; 6. They sit together.
Violating this precept involves two types of offenses—those committed through seeing or hearing—in secluded places. If one is blind but not deaf, or standing rather than sitting, it is auspicious.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if the distance in a secluded place is one *zhang*, it is a *thullaccaya*; at one and a half *zhang*, it is a *dukkaṭa*; at two *zhang*, there is no offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Sitting together with a nun in a secluded, empty place; or a nun inviting a bhikṣu for a meal; or a nun sitting together with a bhikṣu."
When a nun comes to serve food, as she departs after serving, for each and every time, the bhikṣu should rise and say, "I wish to rise;
do not let her suspect that I am acting unlawfully. If the nun departs [after he has risen], there is no offense.

The Twenty-seventh Precept: Traveling with a Bhikṣuṇī by Appointment. (The Bhikṣuṇī’s appointment to travel with the Saṃgha is auspicious. An offense is incurred when five conditions are met: first, she is a bhikṣuṇī; second, there is verbal agreement to travel together;
third, there is no valid reason [for the journey]; fourth, they travel along the same path; and fifth, they cross a boundary, at which point the offense is committed.

The Vinaya states that there is no offense if: there was no prior agreement; they are traveling with a large group; there is a place of suspected danger or fear; or they are going to a place where they will find safety.
The twenty-eighth precept: Regarding the rule against traveling on dangerous paths while carrying a nun’s robe, and the rule against agreeing with a nun to ride in the same boat.

(If a nun agrees with a monk to ride in a boat, it is an offense. This offense is established through six conditions: 1. It is a nun; 2. It involves one of the three assemblies (monks, nuns, or both);

according to the *Upāliparipṛcchā*, all three assemblies commit the offense together; 3. There is a mutual agreement; 4. They ride in the same boat; 5. Excluding cases where they are in different boats.
It is not an offense for a boat to commit the four acts, provided it is moving up or down with the current; nor is it an offense to cross directly, or if the boatman loses control of the vessel.

There are five circumstances where there is no offense: (1) when there is no cause or condition, such as when there are many laypeople on board; (2) when there is a reason for fear; (3) when one is made to stay out of earshot of others; (4) when one is within earshot of others;
(5) according to the *Pāṇḍulohitaka-vastu*, if one enters a boat with both feet, it constitutes an offense immediately.
The Twenty-ninth Precept: Eating Food Praised by a Nun (A nun praising the virtues of a bhikṣu while eating food is an offense). An offense is committed when four conditions are met:
first, it is food praised for its virtues by one of the three groups of nuns; second, one knows this; third, one receives and accepts it; fourth, with every swallow, an offense is incurred.

The Vinaya states that "praising" refers to [a nun] praising [the donor] as being an āraṇyaka, a piṇḍapātika, or even one who wears the three robes, and so forth, regarding the food obtained from morning until midday.
At every swallow, one should eliminate [the fault of] consuming food, clothing for the body, oil for lamps, and so forth; even in cases of illness, it is not permitted. There is no offense if:
one does not know that the donor previously had such an intention; if there was a thought of teaching and converting when there was none; if the nun acted on her own initiative;
or if the donor ordered the nun to manage the affairs and she ate without intentionally having taught or converted anyone. There is no offense in these cases.

The thirtieth precept: Agreeing with a woman to travel together on the same road (*ni-saha-puruṣa-gamana-śikṣāpada*). Regarding the conditions for this precept, it is identical to the rule concerning traveling with a nun, with the sole exception that it concerns a laywoman instead.

Section Thirty-one: Receiving More Than One Meal at a Single Place from a Non-Relative (A Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense for both monks and nuns). Five conditions must be met to constitute this offense: first, receiving more than one meal from a non-relative; second, knowing [the donor is a non-relative];
third, being without the condition of illness and so forth; fourth, receiving the food beyond the limit; fifth, consuming the food, at which point the offense is committed.
The Vinaya provides an exemption for those who are ill, meaning that if the illness worsens after leaving the village, there is no offense. This also applies if the water or land routes are cut off.
There is no offense if one receives food equally [as prescribed].

The thirty-second precept on eating in succession (*paryuṣitabhojana-śikṣāpada*) (a shared offense for monks and nuns). It is an offense when five conditions are met: first, one has previously accepted an invitation for the five types of staple foods (*bhojaniya*), regardless of whether the host is a monastic or a layperson, or whether they are a relative or a non-relative;
second, the food is sufficient to satisfy one's hunger; third, there is no valid reason or cause [for the offense].

The conditions refer to illness and so forth. There are four [factors]: receiving a formal meal at a different location; and committing an offense with every swallow (because one turns away from a previous invitation to go to a subsequent house, it is called "successive eating").
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu arrives at a donor's house and says, 'Upādhyāya, today I shall eat at my home,' this is designated as a place of eating.
The bhikṣu should reflect: 'The food is not yet cooked; I shall go to that house. He must first make a formal announcement."
If one departs without informing [the host] and arrives at that place, one incurs two *pāyattika* offenses: first, for not informing the household where one was invited;
second, for turning away from the place of invitation. According to this Vinaya, there are two kinds of food: first, *bhojaniya* (soft food), which refers to the five types of main meals:
1. rice, 2. parched grain flour (*maṇḍa*), 3. boiled rice, 4. fish, and 5. meat; second, *khajjaka* (hard food), which refers to...

There are five types of food resembling [actual] sustenance: first, roots; second, stalks; third, leaves; fourth, ground food (referring to rice, wheat, barley, and so forth); and fifth, fruit porridge.

Regarding the latter, there is no offense if the porridge as it first emerges from the cauldron does not form characters when drawn upon; however, if it forms characters, it constitutes a *thullaccaya* (offense of wrong-doing).

According to this Vinaya, there are five benefits in giving porridge: first, it removes hunger; second, it removes thirst; third, it digests residual food; fourth, it regulates the functioning of the large and small intestines; and fifth, it eliminates ailments caused by wind (*vāta*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are ten benefits to be gained from the offering of gruel: namely, the upholding of pure precepts; being honored and respected by others;

timely provision through the gift of gruel; the tenfold benefit and advantage for the practitioner; the enhancement of physical complexion, strength, longevity, and happiness; eloquence in speech; the clearing away of undigested food and wind-disorders;

and the elimination of hunger and thirst. These are called excellent medicines as taught by the Buddha. Those who wish to be born among humans or devas and to enjoy long-lasting happiness should [partake in this].
Regarding the offering of gruel to the Saṃgha, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states that if one accepts an invitation for a meal from the previous house, there are three cases:
(1) If the previous house offers only food and the subsequent house offers both food and clothing, it is permitted to go [to the latter] and there is no offense;

(2) If the previous house offers only food and the subsequent house offers only clothing, having gone to the subsequent house to receive the clothing and then returning to the previous house to eat, there is no offense. If...
If one does not go to the previous host and furthermore fails to eat for the entire day, it is solely because of violating one's commitment; thus, one commits three minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*).

If one was invited by the previous host to a single-meal meal and then invited by the subsequent host also to a single-meal meal, but turns away from the former, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that on festival days, frequent invitations do not constitute an offense.
This rule—that one does not commit an offense except in cases of illness—refers to those who are unable to eat a sufficient amount in a single sitting.
The Thirty-third Precept on Eating Apart from the Assembly (a violation common to both monks and nuns). It is an offense when seven conditions are met: first, there is a donor;

second, there is an invitation by the Saṃgha in order or a separate invitation or separate begging; third, it concerns the five kinds of formal food within the proper time; fourth, the eating place constitutes a formal assembly;

fifth, one knows that virtuous bhikṣus within the boundary have not gathered; sixth, there is no [allowable] cause or condition; and seventh, for every swallow, one commits a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). This rule does not exist in this Vinaya.

The question is asked: "Do both monastics and laypeople become donors? *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "It is required that four people be invited separately; once they have all accepted [the invitation], they constitute a *saṃgha*.

Thus, one person sits down, covers his bowl, and does not eat, while he waits for the other three to finish eating; only after they have finished does the one person eat last. This does not constitute an offense.
Therefore, it is known that when all accept, they constitute a *saṃgha*. This Vinaya states: 'If two or three people eat at will, there are four pure attendants (*karmadāna*)."*

The above should be divided into two groups and enter the meal in alternation. (If the monks outside the gate and those inside the house are separated by more than sixty-three paces, it is not termed a "separate assembly," as they belong to different natural boundaries.

According to the *Bā-śāstra*, if a donor makes a long-term invitation with a limit set by day, first inviting people according to their preference so that each is fixed in their place, then on the first day of the meal, everyone gathers together; or, if there was no prior separate invitation.
If there is absolutely no one to prevent it, this great merit cannot be obstructed; one should strike the *gandī* bell.

Once the Saṃgha has assembled, the monk who exhorts [the donors], whether he be a lay donor (*dānapati*) or otherwise, should stand in a high place and cry out at the top of his voice: "Those with sixty years of seniority, enter!
Whether they be many or few, let even a single person enter, and that shall constitute purity. Those who have been previously invited should each stay in one place; if there are none...
If there are no monks of sixty or fifty years' seniority to enter, then even if only one *śrāmaṇera* is called by name to enter, it is pure.
If there are none at all, it is likewise pure. If [the names] were not called on the first day, they should be called every day according to the procedure of the first day.
If they were called on the first day, then for subsequent times, whether someone is obstructed or not, there is no fault; however, if this is not done...

Regarding these two types of food: if at the time of a meal there is even one bhikṣu within the boundary who does not eat together with the group, the entire saṃgha incurs the offense of a separate assembly (pṛthaggaṇa).
Even if there are no bhikṣus within the boundary, if there is still an obstruction to eating or the food is impure;
or if during a ninety-day invitation or a long-term invitation, as at the first day, it is announced that the ninety days have concluded, yet the donor continues to provide [food].
Regarding the fortnightly offering (*pakkhika-pūjā*), one should recite the *dharmadeśanā* as previously established for the sake of purity; it is not necessary to recite it again.

However, at the conclusion of the ninety-day period, the bedding and furniture of the monastic quarters (*vihāra-śayanāsana*) must be recited for every day. If they are not recited daily, they are not pure.

If there are two locations within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) where the Sangha resides, and on a single day there is alms-food from a donor (*dānapati-bhojana*) at both locations, there is no place for the *poṣadha*.
If one passes by a place where the *poṣadha* is not being held and does not invite it there, or if one does not send even a single portion of food to a single person,
this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for the Saṃgha. If a donor makes a special invitation to four or more monks from the regular sequence of the Saṃgha to enter the *poṣadha* boundary to eat,
or brings food into the boundary to specially invite monks, one monk from the regular sequence of the Saṃgha at the place where the *poṣadha* is to be held should be invited.
If a person sends a portion of food that is not [properly] prepared in this manner, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
It is the same if there are two or three places [where food is sent]. One need not take [food] from one’s own place by passing it around.

If a person has been invited and a portion of food has already been sent, and another monk arrives from a different location, if one obstructs him or does not give even a single portion of food, it is a *thullaccaya*. If not... [the sentence is incomplete in the source].
In such cases, when three people or fewer eat in separate places at different times, there is no fault.
If one has previously intended to invite a member of the Sangha but forgot to do so, and a portion of food has already been set out for the head of the assembly, it should be sent to that monk.
If the distance is great, one should take this food and distribute it in order. If there is no monk within the boundary of the village, [one may proceed accordingly].

In two separate locations within the same boundary (*sīmā*), if two donors each invite four or more monks, the *gandī* (wooden gong) must be struck at both places. One monk from each group should mutually invite the other, and one portion of food should be mutually sent.

If other bhikṣus arrive later, they must likewise follow this sequential procedure. Although the original monks were invited first and the guests later, it is not permitted for the guests to enter [the first group's space];

otherwise, it constitutes a separate invitation (*pṛthag-bhakta*). Conversely, if there was originally no sequence of monks but one subsequently becomes established, it is the opposite of the preceding case.

This refers to the offense of "separate invitations and separate begging," where even those who are of one mind and in harmony all commit the offense because it does not require the formal delimitation of a boundary (*sīmā*) to constitute the offense.
Thus, the Vinaya states that Devadatta took his own five followers to beg for alms from house to house; therefore, we know this constitutes an offense.

Even if they were all gathered together, as long as they do not act in concert with the Saṃgha, they still commit the offense. As the *Karmavibhaṅga-śāstra* states: "Four people [who] separately invite [food] while among the Saṃgha [commit an offense]."

If one sits in order alongside others to receive food but does not share the same meal as the Saṃgha, it constitutes an offense in all cases (based on this principle, the single instance of "sitting in the Saṃgha's order" applies only when they are not assembled;

regarding the offense of eating separately from those who beg for alms, whether they are assembled or not, it is a *pāyattika*). According to the *Kṣudraka-vastu*, three types of bhikṣus—those with deranged minds, those who have been expelled, and those outside the boundary—are not counted within the Saṃgha;

although four such individuals are present, they do not constitute a separate assembly (*nānā-saṃgha*). Thus we know that while these [three] are exempted, according to this Vinaya, there are seven conditions under which one commits no offense. All other cases are offenses.

The sixth point is that it is not essential to discuss whether one is currently afflicted by illness; rather, "not committing an offense" refers to cases where, at the very least, one stumbles upon the heel and thus does not commit an offense.
The *Sāriputrābhidharma-vinaya-śāstra* (Shanjian lü piposha) states that this refers to when sand or dirt enters [the wound] such that one is unable to walk.
The thirty-fourth precept: Taking back the provisions for a bride or a merchant’s journey beyond three bowlfuls (a shared offense for both monks and nuns).
This precept is rarely encountered and is thus described only briefly.

The Thirty-fifth Precept: The Prohibition Against Eating After Having Sufficient Food (For a nun, eating five types of solid food after having already finished her meal constitutes a *pācittiya*). This offense is incurred when five conditions are met: first, the food is sufficient;

second, one knows the characteristics of sufficiency regarding the object; third, one abandons the formal posture; fourth, there is no valid reason (namely, being ill or having further food, in which cases there is no offense); and fifth, one eats again, at which point the offense is committed.

The Thirty-sixth Precept on Exhorting Another to Eat Until Satiated (Naiḥsargika-pāyattika): It is an offense when five conditions are met: first, another person has finished eating; second, they are already satisfied;

third, one speaks and forcefully exhorts them; fourth, the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (remaining-food) ritual has not been performed; and fifth, the other person consumes the food. At that point, the offense is incurred.

The Thirty-Seventh Precept: Abstaining from Eating at Improper Times (Violated by both Monks and Nuns). A violation occurs when four conditions are met: first, it is an improper time; second, one perceives it as an improper time;

third, one consumes food that is fit for the proper time; and fourth, there is a swallow for every swallow. The Vinaya states that "proper time" refers to the period from the appearance of the morning light until midday;
according to this rule, it is the same for all four continents. The Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya states that even during the longest days, the daytime...
Eighteen *muhūrtas* constitute a night, and twelve constitute the longest period of night; eighteen constitute a day, and twelve constitute the shortest.

The extension and contraction of these intervals can be understood accordingly. The *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra* states that King Bimbisāra asked the Buddha, "For what reason do the bhikṣus eat only at midday?
The Buddha replied, "The devas eat in the early morning; the Buddhas of the three periods of time eat at midday."

Western beasts eat at dusk; ghosts and spirits eat at nightfall. The Buddha prohibited eating after midday in order to sever the causes of the six realms of existence and to cause practitioners to be equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If food has been vomited but has not yet passed the throat, swallowing it again constitutes no offense; if it has passed the throat, it is a *thullaccaya*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* records that when Anuruddha’s disciple was ill and took emetic medicine after midday, he became distressed. The Buddha said: [the rule applies to those who have eaten].

Even when rice gruel was squeezed from a juice-sack made of rice, wild millet, bamboo shoots, or bamboo leaves, the patient did not recover. The Buddha permitted [the gruel] to be given in a secluded place.
(As the various schools differ on this point, they should not be used interchangeably; one should follow what is most urgent and appropriate.)

The Thirty-eighth Precept on Eating Leftover Food from the Previous Night (a violation common to both monks and nuns). A violation occurs when three conditions are met: first, it is leftover food from the previous night; second, one knows it to be so;

third, one swallows it—thereby committing the offense. According to this Vinaya, if one receives food today, stores it within the boundary, and keeps it until the next day to cook and eat oneself, for every swallow one incurs seven offenses:
namely, three *thullaccaya* and four *dukkaṭa*. These are: first, eating what has not been formally received (*appaṭiggahita*); second, eating what is not permissible (*akappiya*)... [and so forth].

The thirty-ninth precept on the refusal of food (*pratigraha-śīla*)—[involving] the three remaining overnight [foods] (these three are *tiṭṭha*), the four cooked indoors, the five kept indoors overnight, cooking by oneself, and impure contact (these four are *kappa*).
This applies equally to monks and nuns (*bhikṣu-bhikṣuṇī-sādhāraṇa-āpatti*). Within this, there is a sixfold analysis: first, the intent behind the regulation of receiving food;
second, the person who receives; third, the object of the food to be received; fourth, the food to be received; fifth, the method of receiving food; and sixth, [the exceptions].

Regarding the forfeiture of the *pratigraha* (receiving) rule, first, concerning the meaning of receiving food: the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that before the Buddha had established the rule for receiving food, monks would eat at the homes of their acquaintances without having received it.
Laypeople rebuked them, saying, "We do not rejoice in seeing these evil men wearing robes of cut and dyed color who eat without having received food;
this is called 'taking what is not given' (*adattādāna*). This is also recorded in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
For five reasons, one [precept] is established: first, to eliminate the causes and conditions for theft; second, to serve as a witness; third, to stop slander;
fourth, to fulfill the virtues of few desires and contentment; and fifth, to give rise to faith and respect in others, as well as to allow non-Buddhists to obtain benefit.
Second, as for the one who can receive [the precepts], they must be a bhikṣu. As the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* says: "The one who can..."

Regarding the recipient: a bhikṣu who possesses the precepts abides in his own nature (*svabhāva*). (The Commentary states: Because he has committed no transgressions at the time of receiving the full ordination, it is said that he "abides in his own nature.

If one who has broken the precepts, one who has been expelled, or one subject to the thirteen difficulties (*trayodaśa-ānantarya*) receives food and gives it to another bhikṣu, the act of receiving is not accomplished, as they do not abide in their own nature. Regarding the third point, the object of the food received, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says:
Regarding the acceptance of food from celestial beings, those in the wilderness, or spirits (yakṣas), the Buddha said: "It is permitted to accept [food] from a monkey offering honey and the like.
The *Sudarsana* states that gods, humans, spirits, animals, and flying birds all constitute valid recipients of food.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that for the purpose of providing a witness, non-humans, animals, and ignorant children are all excluded.

Regarding the formation of the ritual acceptance (*pratigraha*): according to this textual passage, in the first three cases and the fifth part, when an animal or a hungry ghost accepts [the gift], it constitutes a valid acceptance only if they understand human speech.

Fourth, regarding the distinction between the formation and non-formation of acceptance based on the food received: the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Vinayavibhāṣā*) states that for medicinal substances of large quantity, acceptance is not required;

this applies to both the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Samantapāsādikā*. This present *vinaya* (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*) further exempts water and tooth-sticks from the requirement of acceptance.

The *Jianyun* (Record of Observations) states: "If coarse dust falls into the bowl, it may be removed and one may eat without offense. If fine dust falls, it cannot be removed; one should have another person hand over the food.
If food is passed to a neighbor and some falls into one's own bowl, it constitutes acceptance (*pratigraha*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

'If dust is blown by the wind, or if dust comes from a cow shaking its body as it runs, or even from birds or women walking while trailing their garments on the ground [and falls into the bowl, it does not constitute an offense]. '""*
If dust comes and settles upon the bowl, all such dust does not defile the grass used as a base for the food; thus, the grass leaves are considered accepted.
However, if the dust defiles both the grass and the food, everything must be received again. The only exception is when an animal shakes its body;
if one receives the food with the intention [that it is clean], it is said to be "accepted. All other instances where there is no such intention to receive must be received again from another.
If, while walking with parched grain, some of it spills from the container and falls into one’s bowl, if one receives it with the intention [of eating], it is called "received";
if one receives it without such intention, it is not called "received. The same applies to other food. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"It is permitted to carry food while walking so that others do not see it; when eating, one should go out of the path, take a handful, and eat it without formally receiving it. (5.2)

Regarding the method of receiving [food]: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that for those who receive by mental intention (*manasikāra*), because there are people from border regions, those with wrong views, or evil bhikṣus, one does not accept food and gives it to others;
at that time, one should mark the ground with signs and, when covering the bowl with leaves to place the food inside, one should say:

"I receive, I receive," whereby the reception is accomplished. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says that this is also the case for people in pure lands. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* mentions the burning of horse stables.
If a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) hurriedly places food on the ground and says, "Take this and eat," the monk with eye disease may press down on grass to receive the food.

(In the present day, many monks and nuns press down on the ground to receive food; how is this any different from being blind? The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When [the food] is lowered, one perceives it; when it falls into the bowl, one does not perceive it;

when it first descends, one perceives it; when it falls, one does not perceive it. These two cases constitute valid reception (*pratigraha*), yet because they do not conform to proper decorum (*airyāpatha*), one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When the bhikṣu Rāma arrives at a shop while begging for alms, if someone gives him parched grain (*piṣṭaka*) using a measuring bucket that is tied to other buckets with ropes and chains, he should be told to untie them so they are separated;
if they cannot be untied, he should instruct [the donor] to pour it onto leaves and hand it over.
If the bottle of clarified butter or oil is placed on the ground with its rope attached, he should tell [the donor] to lift it by the rope and hand it over, or hang the food above the well.
If a bhikṣu is at the bottom of a well and says from the top, "Receive, receive! Do not let grass or wood grow in the middle," it constitutes a valid reception.
If a bhikṣu on the roof of a house tells a layperson (upāsaka) to place food in a vessel using a long pole or a rope with a hook, and says, "Place it here!

while pointing to the top of the hook, and says, "Receive, receive," it also constitutes a valid reception. If a layperson hangs fruit from a tree and lowers it down, it is the same; as is the case with a cow.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu who has received food intends to travel a long distance and there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), he may borrow an ox and place his provisions for food in a bag.
He makes one knot for each meal and ties them until the time of eating. If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one person pulls the cord while another receives it;
if he says, "I receive," the act of receiving is validly accomplished. If the provisions are exhausted before reaching the destination, he should wash the bag clean again.
It was also according to the previous rule: A bhikṣu begged for sugarcane from a layperson, but the person refused to give it to the bhikṣu, saying, "Take it yourself to eat.
The bhikṣu then tied the sugarcane securely with a rope and placed it upon the head of an ox, saying, "Know that this is a living being;
if there is a fire nearby, drive the ox past the fire so as not to burn it. One person supported the head while another untied the rope.
When one says, "I accept," the acceptance is accomplished; the same applies to the rest. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

When food is being served, if a lay attendant touches a bhikṣu’s hand, if it is not done lightly, the acceptance is accomplished; if it is done lightly, touching the bhikṣu’s hand, one should not accept.
When pouring ghee or oil into a bowl without interruption, the Buddha said: "This is a downward flow, not an upward flow; it accomplishes the acceptance. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

When a pure person (śuklavāsas) brings fruits or vegetables, one should instruct them to place them down from a distance. If a fruit falls onto the grass and moves away immediately, it is not considered "received" (*pratigṛhīta*);

if it stops for even a brief moment, it is considered received. (When walking among grass and trees to maintain purity, one should walk a considerable distance; nowadays people stop at the very edge and walk only a short distance, which does not accord with the intent of physical purity.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that if one throws [the food] from afar and it rolls across the ground until it falls into the hand of a bhikṣu, it constitutes acceptance. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states this regarding large assemblies.
It is difficult to find a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle impure items), so a bhikṣu may accept and use [impure things] himself.

If the iron spear or cauldron is hot and cannot be accepted, one should place two pieces of wood crosswise on the ground; the bhikṣu steps upon them and says, "I accept. In this way, the acceptance is valid.

Furthermore, according to the latter part of this Vinaya, if one intends to accept oil but mistakenly accepts ghee, the acceptance is not valid. Acceptance is only valid when the mind and the object correspond. (6)

Regarding the loss of the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) of food, the *Vyākaraṇa-śāstra* (Treatise on Exposition) states there are seven kinds of loss of the dharma: 1. Loss through the intentional abandonment:
If a person, having no further use for this food, intentionally abandons it by giving it to another, they lose the acceptance. 2. Loss through being forcibly seized by another:

If someone other than oneself—specifically one of the same class (meaning not one of the five groups of renunciants, hence "not of the same class")—forcibly seizes it because it belongs to them, one loses [the acceptance]. 3. Loss through transformation...

The first is the loss through improper action (*kṛta-vipatti*), which refers to employing supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) inappropriately. The second is the loss through transformation of nature (*vikāra-vipatti*), such as changing from male to female.

The third is the loss through abandonment of the precepts (*śīla-tyāga*). The fourth is the loss through death (*jīvita-tyāga*). The fifth is the loss through the extinction of the True Dharma (*saddharma-vināśa*). Regarding this Vinaya, there are three types of loss:

first, spontaneous loss (*svarasa-nirhāra-vipatti*), meaning that once one has received and attained the right to eat [the alms], when that time has passed, it is called spontaneous loss. Second, loss due to contact with adverse conditions (*pratyaya-sparśa-vipatti*).

"Loss" refers to the loss [of the status of being "received"] through contact with a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person). Third, there is the loss through the transformation of the raw into the cooked. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"Once one has received fresh ginger, if it sprouts, the status of having received it is not lost. After it has been purified by fire, the place where it has sprouted must be purified again;

however, that which has not sprouted may be eaten. Salt that has turned into water may be eaten. The *Vinaya* states: "If food is not given to one, and one takes it for oneself and places it in the mouth and swallows it..."

If one swallows [food] at an improper time beyond the seven-day limit, it is also a *pāyattika*. To eat without having received [the food] for as long as one lives, except under special circumstances, is a *duṣkṛta*.

The fortieth precept: The prohibition against requesting fine food (*bhakṣya*). (For a nun, it is a *duṣkṛta*. One commits this offense when four conditions are met: first, it is fine food (referring to milk, curd, fish, meat, and so forth);

second, one is not ill (meaning one is capable of eating a single sitting-meal to satiety); third, one does so for one's own sake; and fourth, one swallows it, at which point the offense is incurred. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one must not accept [such food] from a butcher.
One may not beg for meat from a butcher’s house, nor for milk or curd from a dairy, nor for silk from a silkworm-raising household. The *Wubai wen shi* (Five Hundred Questions on Matters) states:
"To demand fine food when not ill constitutes a grave offense."
The Forty-first Precept: Regarding Giving Food to Renunciant Non-Buddhists (For a *bhikṣuṇī*, giving food and clothing to lay non-Buddhists is a *sthūlātyaya*).

An offense is committed when five conditions are met: first, the recipient is a renunciant non-Buddhist; second, one knows them to be such; third, it is food; fourth, one gives it with one's own hand rather than placing it on the ground or having someone else give it;
and fifth, the recipient accepts it, at which point the offense is incurred. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a non-Buddhist comes to beg, one should give from one's own portion."
One should not set aside a portion for oneself and then give it to others; nor should one give monastic food to beggars, birds, cats, or the like.

One should measure the amount of one's own food, take a portion from within that amount to give, and must not take more than one's share to bestow upon others. The *Sengqi lü* (Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya) states:

"If one's parents, brothers, sisters, or those who have gone forth among non-Buddhists come, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) give to them; if there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, [one may give directly]."

Thus, if you eat, you may eat; if you do not eat, it is as you wish. According to the Sarvāstivāda, there is no offense in giving to one who holds the view of non-existence (*avīkṣika*).
However, if the Saṃgha gives [to such a person], it must not be given with one's own hands; otherwise, it is a transgression.
The forty-second precept: Not informing [a fellow monk] before going to another household prior to or after a meal to which one has been invited (an offense common to both monks and nuns).

An offense is committed when five conditions are met: 1. One has previously accepted an invitation; 2. It is either before or after a meal; 3. One does not inform [a fellow monk]; 4. One goes to another household; 5.
Upon entering the gate, the offense is incurred. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Before eating" means the time prior to having eaten; "after eating" means after having finished the meal.

Although the day has already dawned, it is designated as "after the meal" (provided it is still before mid-afternoon). If a bhikṣu seeking alms arrives at the house of a donor (*dānapati*), and the host says, "Today we have invited various bhikṣus to eat here;
I pray that you, Master, will accept my invitation," and having accepted according to these words, the bhikṣu thinks, "Who is able to receive this heavy gift?
When he wishes to depart, he should inform [the host] before leaving; if he does not inform them, he incurs an offense.
Regarding the *pācittiya* offense: there were two bhikṣus who had each separately accepted an invitation from a single household.
The first bhikṣu said to the second bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, let us go together today to the house of the donor for a meal.
If the second bhikṣu departs without having informed [the host], he incurs a *pācittiya*. If the second bhikṣu invites the first bhikṣu, the principle is the same.

It is said that if one person accepts an invitation and there is no one else to inform, one should inform the host's family or a *śuddhaka* (pure person) so that they know and do not disturb the host when he comes to inquire about the location.
One must also inform [the host] regarding a regular place of invitation. There is no offense in the following cases: if one is seriously ill;
if one informs [the host] before departing; during the month of *kārttika*; during the time for the distribution of robes (*cīvara*); or if there is no one available to inform.

No offense is committed [in these cases]. The forty-third precept: Regarding sitting insistently in a household where there are treasures (the same offense for both monks and nuns). This matter is rare and thus not described here. The forty-fourth precept:
Sitting in private with a laywoman (for a nun sitting in private with a layman, it is a *pāyattika*). An offense is committed when four conditions are met; the first is as follows:

If a laywoman sits in two secluded places (dvivivikta), in three ways where no third person is present, or in a place where one cannot reach the door with an outstretched hand, she commits a *pācittiya* offense according to the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*.
If she sits facing a closed door where there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, it is a *thullaccaya*; if she sits facing an open door and there is a *kappiya-kāraka* outside, it is a *dukkaṭa*;

if there is a *kappiya-kāraka* inside, there is no offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the mother, sister, or *kappiya-kārakas* are asleep, deluded, insane, or mentally disturbed [there is no offense]."
An infant is neither a human nor an animal; although it is a human, it is also called "solitary.
If a *pācittiya* offense occurs while sitting for an entire day between a monk and a woman, and one rises from this position repeatedly, each instance constitutes a *pācittiya*.

If a lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) comes and goes without interruption during work—such as when there are passersby on the road toward the gate for the duration of a meal—and a lay attendant on the upper or lower floor sees them from afar, [the rule applies].
None of these constitute an offense against this Vinaya. Those who do not commit an offense include: if one extends one’s hand to the door while sitting;

if one causes a bhikṣu seeking alms to see two bhikṣus acting as companions; if there is a recognizable person nearby; or if there are circumstances of difficulty and so forth—none of these constitute an offense.

This concludes the forty-fifth precept regarding sitting in the open with a laywoman (for a nun sitting in the open with a layman, it is a *pāyattika*). An offense is committed when four conditions are met: first, [the presence of a laywoman]; second, [sitting together]; third, [in the open]; fourth, [without a valid reason]. One commits the offense when these are complete.
If one sits with a laywoman in two circumstances—namely, in an exposed place, in the absence of a third person, and within arm’s reach—one commits an offense. The *Śāriputra Vinaya* states:

"If one sits with a woman in an open space, for every time one rises and then sits again, one incurs as many *thullaccaya* offenses as there were instances. If they sit at a distance of half a *vyāma*, it is a *thullaccaya*;
if at a distance of one and a half *vyāmas*, it is a *dukkaṭa*; if more than two *vyāmas*, there is no offense."
The Forty-sixth Precept on Expelling [a Monk] from the Village Without Providing Food (a violation common to both monks and nuns). It is an offense when five conditions are fulfilled:
first, one is a bhikṣu; second, food has been previously promised; third, one does not provide the food; fourth, one expels him with a malicious intent;
and fifth, he departs beyond the range of sight or hearing—this constitutes an offense.
The forty-seventh precept on accepting an invitation for medicine for more than four months (a shared offense for monks and nuns). This precept concerns a rare matter and is not described here.

The forty-eighth precept on viewing military arrays (a shared offense for monks and nuns). One commits this offense when four conditions are met: first, it is a military array; second, one intentionally goes to view it;
third, there is no legitimate reason [for going]; and fourth, upon seeing it, the offense is incurred. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one enters a village or city..."

If one encounters an army on the road and does not form the intention [to look], there is no offense. If one forms the intention and raises or lowers the head to peer and seek to see, it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If an army sets out for battle to defeat enemies, and because there is the cause of death therein, one observes impermanence, there is no offense.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that passing through the road is not an offense; however, if one stands still and looks to the left or right, it is an offense.
It is permissible to violate the rules of decorum [for a specific reason].
The forty-ninth precept concerning staying for more than three nights in an army due to a particular cause (a violation common to both monks and nuns).

The fiftieth precept: Staying for two nights among an army due to a specific cause and going to observe the arraying of troops and their engagement in battle (this offense applies equally to monks and nuns).
These two precepts involve matters that are rare, so they are not described in detail.
The Fifty-first Precept on Abstaining from Alcohol (a violation common to both monks and nuns). A violation occurs when three conditions are met: first, it is alcohol;

second, there is no cause such as a serious illness; and third, one drinks it, at which point the offense is committed. Although the substance of this rule is alcohol, if it does not possess the color, fragrance, or taste of alcohol, it should not be drunk.
Conversely, if the substance is not alcohol itself but possesses the color, fragrance, and taste of alcohol, it may be drunk. If one drinks [the former], [an offense is incurred].
If one drinks sweet-flavored liquor, sour-flavored liquor, or eats yeast, dregs, and so forth, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.
From this day forward, those who take me as their teacher must not even put the tip of a blade of grass into liquor and place it in their mouth.
If other medicines fail to cure an ailment and liquor is used as medicine, there is no offense. According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, this is the rule.

This precept is extremely grave; it can bring about the four pārājika offenses, with the sole exception of causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and it can also destroy all other precepts as well as other evils.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one splashes or sprinkles water and land upon one another, it is a *pācittiya*; if both are in the water, it is a *thullaccaya*. The Fifty-third Precept on Tapping or Prodding Others (a shared offense for monks and nuns). An offense is committed when four conditions are met: first, one is a bhikṣu; second, one has the intention to cause annoyance;

third, one uses the ten fingers of the hand or foot; fourth, upon making contact, the offense is incurred. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, pointing at a bhikṣu with a finger is also a *pāyattika*;

pointing with five fingers incurs five *pāyattikas*, and even designating someone by name to be sent away incurs a *pāyattika*. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if one strikes [another], it is likewise an offense.
If one tickles a *śrāmaṇera* or an animal, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense according to this Vinaya; if one uses any other object to tickle them, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if it was not done intentionally, or if one awakens someone who is sleeping.
The Fifty-fourth Precept on Not Accepting Admonition (a shared offense for monks and nuns). An offense is committed when five conditions are met: first, one intends to perform an improper act;

second, another person offers a formal admonition in accordance with the Dharma; third, one knows that what one is doing is improper while knowing that the other person’s admonition is correct; fourth, one rejects the admonition and does not accept it;

and fifth, one acts according to that [rejection], thereby committing a fundamental offense of violating the admonition. Although the offense is established by the mere utterance of words, it is classified as a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

Refusing to accept admonition does not constitute an offense at the moment; rather, it constitutes a *pāyattika* (thullaccaya) offense once the act has been committed and the meaning of having defied the admonition is established.

This precept is most essential for restraining those who would violate the rules. Fearing that there might be transgressions resulting from such actions, one should not assemble the entire Saṃgha to offer admonition for every single case;
instead, one person should go everywhere to offer admonition, and if [the offender] defies it, they incur a *pāyattika*.

The Fifty-fifth Precept on Terrifying Bhikṣus (a shared offense for monks and nuns). Five conditions must be fulfilled for the offense to be established: first, one is a bhikṣu; second, one intends to terrify the other;
third, one points out various matters involving the six sense objects, one by one; fourth, one manifests these signs through speech;
fifth, the offense is incurred as soon as the other sees or hears them, regardless of whether the other person actually becomes frightened or not.
The Fifty-sixth Precept on Bathing During the Waning Half of the Month (a shared offense for monks and nuns). An offense is incurred when five conditions are met:
(1) one has previously bathed; (2) less than half a month has elapsed; (3) there is no valid cause or reason; (4) one bathes again; and (5) one washes more than half the body.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the period from the completion of the fifteenth day until the next full moon is termed "half a month. According to this Vinaya, there are six circumstances under which no offense is incurred.
1. The time of heat refers to the forty-five days following spring and the first month of summer; 2. The time of illness refers to when, at the very least, the body becomes foul-smelling; 3.
The time of work refers to when, at the very least, one sweeps the ground in front of one's house; 4. The time of wind refers to when, at the very least, there is a single whirlwind; 5.
The time of rain refers to when, at the very least, a single drop of rain falls upon the body; 6. The time of travel refers to when, at the very least...
If one travels back and forth for half a *yojana*, the gates are all opened and there is no offense. Regarding bathing together with laypeople in a communal bathhouse, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
