Regarding the three types of burning without a cause—grass, wood, and having flames—the fourth is "burning," which constitutes an offense according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

It states: "If one makes a wheel by spinning fire, or if there is grass or wood within the fire and a bhikṣu stirs or gathers it, all such acts constitute a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). If one burns seeds that have the potential for life, there are two offenses: first, destroying living beings; second, burning fire.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if the flame reaches a height of four finger-widths, it is a *pācittiya* (offense requiring expiation); this is the rule of this [Mūlasarvāstivāda] Vinaya. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is a *pācittiya* when the flame is high enough to reach four fingers. This is the rule of this [Mūlasarvāstivāda] Vinaya.

If one requires fire for an illness and thus causes one’s own body to ignite, or instructs another to ignite it, there is no offense (this should apply to death; if on earth or stone, there is no offense). The fifty-eighth precept:

Stealing another’s robes or bowl (the offense applies equally to monks and nuns). An offense is committed when three conditions are met: first, the person is a bhikṣu and the items are his robes or bowl;
second, one intends to alarm or disturb him; third, one takes and hides them. The Vinaya states that there is no offense if [the items] are in an open space.

Fearing that wind or rain might cause [the items] to be soaked or ruined, one may lift them up; however, if the owner is by nature negligent and leaves their clothing and belongings in disarray, one may store them away as a form of admonition, provided this does not constitute an offense.
This is the fifty-ninth precept concerning the light use of truly pure gifts (suddhika-dāna) without consulting the owner; it is an offense for both monks and nuns. This matter is rarely encountered.

Not explained. Wearing the three white robes (the *tricīvara*): Precept No. 60 (a shared offense for monks and nuns). An offense is committed when four conditions are met: first, they are the three robes; second, they are one’s own property;
third, they are not stained or damaged; fourth, the act of wearing them constitutes the offense. (For nuns, the same applies to the *nivāsana* and the shoulder-covering robe.)

Therefore, the sixty-first precept against taking the life of an animal (a violation common to both monks and nuns) is established through five conditions: first, it must be an animal; second, one must know it is an animal;
third, one must have a conscious intention; fourth, one must employ the means; and fifth, the act of taking its life constitutes the offense.

The Sixty-second Precept on Drinking Water Containing Insects (a violation common to both monks and nuns). Five conditions must be met for the offense to be established: first, water containing insects; second, the perception that it contains insects;

third, not employing a strainer; fourth, drinking or using it; fifth, the act of swallowing, which constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. (If the life of the insect is severed, it falls under the preceding precept;

however, because the intent is to strictly protect the lives of sentient beings, two separate precepts are established. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Once a bhikṣu has received full ordination, he must maintain a water-strainer and a ritual water-pitcher in accordance with the Dharma; if he lacks these," [he commits an offense].

If one uses a corner of the *kāṣāya* as a filter and no companion among the group possesses one, the entire assembly incurs an offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that traveling twenty *li* without carrying a water-strainer constitutes an offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If you have filtered water and wish to examine it, have someone look at it until they can see fine patterns on the palm of their hand.

While examining it, if it takes as long as an elephant carrying a bamboo cart to turn around, you should know that there are no [living beings] and it may be used. If it is to be given away, [it must be filtered]."
When the host invites a bhikṣu to eat, he should ask whether the water has been strained. If it has not, he should strain it himself, or have a trustworthy person instruct them to strain it;
however, he must not entrust this to one who is untrustworthy, nor should he say, "Do not kill or harm the insects.
He should place the water in a vessel and return it to its source. If the source is far away and there is a pond nearby where the water will not spoil for seven days, he may place the insects there.
If one knows that there are insects in water, one must not lend a vessel or a rope to another person.
If there are insects in the water of a pond or pool, one must not shout out, "There are insects in this water. If someone asks, one should reply, "Venerable sir, look for yourself.
If one knows that a companion or fellow disciple is present, one should say to them, "There are insects in this; you should strain the water before using it."

The sixty-third precept on causing doubt and distress to others (a violation common to both monks and nuns): This precept is not discussed here as it is rare. The sixty-fourth precept on concealing another’s grave offense (a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
for a nun, concealing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is the same as for a monk, while concealing a *pārājika* incurs a heavy offense): It is established through six conditions: first, the person is a bhikṣu;

second, he has committed an offense belonging to the first two categories (*pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*); third, one knows he has committed it; fourth, one forms the intention to conceal it; fifth, one does not disclose it.

The Six Classics clarify that as soon as one reveals [the offense], it constitutes an *āpatti*. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If hundreds of thousands of people together conceal the offense of a single person, all incur the *thullaccaya* offense.

(The sub-commentary on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one speaks toward a single person, it stops there. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the offender is fierce and evil and one fears there will be trouble, one should reflect:
'That person's own conduct has its own karmic retribution; it is like a fire—one should only save oneself, for who knows [the consequences]? "
Regarding other matters in this Vinaya: if one speaks after a light meal, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); likewise until midnight.

If one knows it is after midnight and intends to speak but has not yet spoken when the characteristic marks appear, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). For concealing other offenses, one’s own offense, or another person’s offense, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

Section Sixty-Five: Bestowing Full Ordination on Those Under Twenty Years of Age (A Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense shared by both monks and nuns). The offense is committed when four conditions are met: first, the person is under twenty-two years of age;
second, one knows they are under twenty-two; third, one bestows full ordination upon them; and fourth, the three *karmavācanās* are completed, at which point the offense is incurred.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, those sixty years of age or older may not receive the full precepts; even if a preceptor forcibly confers them, it is invalid.
Because those who are unable to endure the path of ascetic practice have dull and weak minds and faculties, it is permitted for them to become *śrāmaṇeras*.
However, those under seven years of age are not allowed to be ordained, nor may those under twenty receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

This is because such individuals are fickle and unstable, incapable of enduring hardships such as cold and heat; if they were to receive the Great Precepts, many people would criticize them, whereas if they remain *śrāmaṇeras*, no one does.
The *Mātṛkā-vinaya* states: "For those whose age is not yet full, it is permitted to count the years spent in the womb; if still not full, it is permitted to count intercalary months;
if still not full, it is permitted to count the fourteen-day *poṣadha* observances. If [the age] is still not full, the Buddha said:

'One who has truly attained the fruit of Arhatship—this is the supreme reception of full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). Although they have not yet reached twenty years of age, they obtain the precepts and there is no offense. (The commentary says: If previously..."

If one does not know that the offense has been received, but harbors doubt, it is only then that [the offense] is opened; one may not preemptively know the number of times the precepts have been received, for if one does so, the ordination is not accomplished as it violates the teaching).

Regarding the sixty-sixth rule: "If one knows that a dispute has already been settled, yet initiates it again, [the offense is incurred]. (This applies equally to monks and nuns). This rule is not described here because it is rare.

The sixty-seventh precept: Agreeing to Travel with a Thief (a violation common to both monks and nuns). An offense is committed when six conditions are met: first, there is a thief; second, one knows [he is a thief];
third, there is a mutual agreement; fourth, they travel along the same path; fifth, they do not remain within range of sight or hearing; sixth, upon crossing a boundary, the offense is complete.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this constitutes traveling with a person who owes one a debt.
The sixty-eighth precept: Speaking that desire does not obstruct the Path in violation of the three-fold admonition of the Saṃgha (a shared offense for monks and nuns).
The sixty-ninth precept: Engaging in common business and speech with a person who has been formally charged with holding wrong views (a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for nuns).
The Seventieth Precept on Expelling a Śrāmaṇera (Niggaṇṭha): These three precepts are rarely encountered and thus are not discussed here.
The Seventy-first Precept on Refusing Encouragement to Study (a violation common to both Bhikṣus and Bhikṣuṇīs): Five conditions must be met for this offense to be established:

1. One has the intention to cease learning; 2. As before, one is properly encouraged to study; 3. One knows that what one is doing is improper and that the other person is offering admonition; 4. One acts [upon that refusal].

The seventy-second offense: disparaging the *vinaya* precepts (a transgression common to both monks and nuns). This offense is established when five conditions are met: first, it concerns the *vinaya*; second, it occurs while a monk is reciting the precepts; third, one forms the intention to suppress the Dharma so that it does not endure for long; fourth, one utters words of disparagement; and fifth, [the words are understood]. Upon the completion of these five factors, the offense is incurred. The meaning of "not accepting the exhortation" is that the offense is committed as soon as the five words are finished. The offense is established when these five conditions are present. The phrase "

If one speaks with full comprehension, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one rebukes before the *Poṣadha* has been recited, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one rebukes during the recitation, it is a *pāyattika*; if one rebukes after the recitation is finished, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
According to the *Pañcavargīya*, if one forms the intention to cause others to distance themselves from the *vinaya*, and then fails to recite or study it while disparaging it, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one forms the intention to disparage the *Prātimokṣa* so that it may not endure for long, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. According to this *vinaya*, if one disparages the *Abhidharma*...
The Abhidharma and Sūtras, etc., are auspicious.

The seventy-third precept on not listening attentively (the same offense for both monks and nuns). An offense is committed when four conditions are met: first, at the time of the extensive recitation of the precepts;
second, sitting within the assembly; third, forming the intention not to listen; fourth, the recitation of the five categories of offenses; fifth, the recitation of one *pārājika* offense.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: From the introductory section (*nidāna*) through to the auspicious conclusion (*pātimokkha-piṭaka*), for each individual precept within the interval, every [violation] is not permitted;

one incurs only a *thullaccaya*. This *thullaccaya* cannot be confessed before an individual; it must be confessed before an assembly of those who uphold the precepts with dignity and are worthy of reverence.
That person should reprimand them, saying: "You have lost a source of wholesome benefit, for you did not show respect during the fortnightly recitation of the *pātimokkha*."

The seventy-fourth precept on disparaging the Sangha after having participated in a formal act (*karmavācanā*) and being appointed as an administrator, which involves failing to listen with a focused mind or failing to attend with an attentive ear;
having been reproached, one commits a *thullaccaya* offense and must confess. (This offense is common to both monks and nuns. It is established by four conditions:

first, there is a gift of property before the assembled Sangha; second, one has participated in the formal act and been appointed as an administrator; third, one acts arbitrarily [without authorization]; fourth, [one subsequently] disparages the Sangha.

If one subsequently regrets [the act] and slanders the Saṃgha, saying that it possesses attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion—these four statements constitute a *pārājika* offense according to the Vinaya.

Generally, if the Saṃgha is in harmony, whether or not a formal *karmavācanā* has been performed, if one rebukes those who are being disciplined, or those who are virtuous elders, or those who are impoverished, after they have already been reconciled, it is a *thullaccaya*.
If one rebukes them from outside [the community], it is a *dukkaṭa*.

The seventy-fifth precept: Leaving while the Sangha is deliberating on a matter without having granted one’s consent (the offense is the same for both monks and nuns). It is established as an offense when five conditions are met: first, it is a formal matter of the Sangha; second, one knows it is a formal matter;
third, one has not granted one’s consent (*chanda*); fourth, one rises and departs abruptly; and fifth, one steps with both feet across the threshold.

Regarding this Vinaya rule, if one leaves without granting consent during a deliberation on one of the four matters [of the Parajika], it is a *Thullaccaya*; for other matters, leaving without granting consent is a *Dukkata*. Four.
The offense of disputing without cessation because one has tolerated a schism in the Saṃgha is grave.

The seventy-sixth rule: Regretting after having granted consent (*chanda*). (This offense is common to both monks and nuns. It is an offense when four conditions are fulfilled: first, a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed according to the Dharma;

second, consent is granted according to the Dharma; third, one suddenly contradicts this by saying it was not valid; fourth, the offense is incurred as soon as these words are finished. (Sarvāstivāda).

In most cases, if one has already reached an agreement regarding a matter other than a formal monastic act (*saṃgha-karman*), it is an offense of wrongdoing (*duṣkṛta*) to later regret that agreement.

However, if the Saṃgha performs an illegal formal act (*adharma-karman*) and one is unable to turn it back at the time, there is no offense if one remains silent and does not criticize it, even if one speaks of its impropriety later.

The Seventy-Seventh Precept on Eavesdropping on the Four Disputes (a violation common to both monks and nuns). The "four disputes" refer to disputes regarding speech, disputes regarding seeking, disputes regarding offenses, and disputes regarding matters.

Because this precept is rarely encountered, its full set of conditions is not detailed here. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one hears that others harbor enmity and intend to kill or harm one another;
or hears that bandits have arrived; or knows that unrighteous bhikṣus have devised evil schemes to steal monastic property—the person in charge who hears this must [act immediately]."

He addressed the Saṃgha, saying: "Each of you must remain vigilant. If I hear an evil sound, and if the Teacher comes secretly at dusk to inspect the various rooms, and hears disciples speaking either Dharma or non-Dharma, he must not immediately praise or reproach them face-to-face.
Only when he returns at a later time may he then offer words of commendation or censure. This is the rule, whether two people are conversing in a dark place or walking along a path."
When conversing with someone in front of them, one should snap one's fingers or cough; failure to do so incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

The seventy-eighth precept on striking a bhikṣu with a mind of anger (the same offense applies to both monks and nuns). An offense is committed when four conditions are met: first, being a bhikṣu; second, giving rise to a mind of anger;
third, forming the intention to strike; and fourth, actually striking him. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, even using a handful of sand or beans constitutes an offense.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if many bhikṣus follow each individual *tīrthika*, harboring anger and lustful intent, and strike a woman, their sin is grave—equivalent to shedding the blood of ten trillion Buddhas. Why is this?
Because [the bhikṣu] is able to show people and devas the way out of the evil realms and even toward Nirvāṇa. Thus says the *Mahāsāṃghika*.
If an animal enters a monastery and strikes or tramples upon an image, a fruit tree, or other objects, one may use a staff, wood, stones, the ground, or other means to frighten it away;
however, one must not strike at or threaten the animal.
The Seventy-ninth Precept on Fist-fighting (Applicable equally to monks and nuns). The necessary conditions can be understood from the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*.
If one raises one’s hand or a weapon toward many bhikṣus, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each individual.

The Eightieth Precept: Groundless Slander (Saṃghāvaśeṣa for Nuns). The requisite conditions are the same as those for the four grave offenses; the only difference is that this offense is minor. The Eighty-first Precept:
Intruding into the Royal Palace (An offense common to both monks and nuns). This precept concerns rare matters and need not be explained in detail. The Eighty-second Precept:

Taking Lost or Cast-off Valuables (An offense common to both monks and nuns). One commits this offense when five conditions are met: first, it must be a valuable object. It applies generally to all such items.
1. Both oneself and others; 2. along with various ornaments; 3. places that are not dwellings or lodgings; 4.
taking by stealth without intent to return it to the original owner; 5. the offense is committed the moment one seizes it.

Regarding "lost treasures" mentioned in this Vinaya, these refer to gold, silver, pearls, amber, musaragalva, agate, lapis lazuli, shells, jade, and wrought or unwrought precious metals. Regarding "ornaments," these refer to copper.

Using iron, lead, tin, or white brass to create ornaments constitutes an offense according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*. This is based on the *Vinayottaragrantha*, which takes the incidental discovery of treasure as the causal origin (*nidāna*).
It states that the actual offense occurs simply by taking hold of such treasure (differing from the interpretation of the older commentaries).

According to this Vinaya, if these items are ornaments for the worship of stūpas or monasteries and are kept securely for safekeeping, there is no offense (this should be understood as an allowance made for cases where no *viśuddha-puruṣa* [pure person] is available). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If it is for the purpose of worshipping an image..."
If there are vessels coated with gold or silver, one should have a *karmadāna* (attendant) hold them; if they should fall to the ground, one should assist in picking them up.
In places where there is no gold or silver, if they are entirely coated [with lacquer], one should grasp them by wrapping one's hands around them. Once grasped, they must not be let go.

If one sees discarded clothing or belongings, one should announce it so that others may know of it. If there is no owner, one should hang it in a high and conspicuous place so that people may see it. If someone...
If someone says, "This is my property," one should ask, "Where did you lose this property? If the answer is consistent, it should be returned.
If there is no one who recognizes it, it should be kept for three months. If it is found within the grounds of a stūpa, it shall be used for the stūpa;

if found within the grounds of the Saṃgha, it shall be used for the Saṃgha of the four quarters. If it is an object of high value, such as necklaces, gold, or silver, it must not be displayed openly when being proclaimed.
The Bhikṣu who has obtained the jewel should examine it carefully and repeatedly to observe its characteristics before lifting it up.

When it is brought back for identification, if it corresponds [to the description], he should give it to the assembly of many people rather than in a private place. Furthermore, he should instruct them to receive the Three Refuges, saying:
"The Buddha did not establish a regulation regarding this; you must look at it yourself. If no one comes to claim it, let it remain until [the appointed time]."

For three years, one should use it as before within the boundary of that precinct. If, while repairing an old stūpa, one uncovers a treasure trove by digging the ground, and if the *karmadāna* (lay attendant) is not to be trusted, one must inform the king.
If the *karmadāna* is trustworthy, one may set it aside until the three years have elapsed;
then it should be used for the construction of the stūpa. If the king becomes aware of this and asks the bhikṣu, "Did you find a treasure trove here? he should reply, "I did."
Once it has already been used for this stūpa, the king says: "Since it has already been made, these merits belong to me; return them to me.
If the king says, "Do you not know that the treasures within the earth belong to me? Why have you exhausted them? Return them to me!
the bhikṣu should at that time return the property of the stūpa. If the stūpa has no property, he should beg for it on behalf of the stūpa and return it.
The King asked, "According to the Buddha’s Vinaya, how should a bhikṣu act? He replied, "If one finds objects on the grounds of a stūpa, they should be used for the stūpa;
the same applies to the grounds of the Saṃgha. The King said, "There is no offense for using such items for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha.

The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states that even holy persons such as Anāthapiṇḍada took possession of hidden treasures; therefore, one knows there is no offense, especially when the items are obtained spontaneously.
Regarding objects, they are not termed "stolen. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If one enters a village and finds abandoned items, one must not take them.

If someone takes them and gives them to a bhikṣu, he may accept them; they are then the property of that donor. If clothes are blown into a village by the wind, one must not take them with the thought that they are "rag-robe" (pāṃśukūla) material.
However, if they are found on a deserted road where no people are present, one may take them. If there is treasure upon the clothes, one should step on it with one's foot [to remove it].

If one leaves clothes out in the open and they are seen by a messenger who follows them to their dwelling, and only then discovers they contain valuables, these should be entrusted to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) to serve as the price for robes and medicine, with a value fixed at five *paṇas*.

If a monk has set aside such clothes and does not come to reclaim them after twelve years, the community of monks shall assemble to appraise them and use the proceeds for the sake of the Saṃgha of the four directions.
If the original owner later returns and the Saṃgha offers to repay him with its own property, he should not accept it. If he does not accept, it is well.
The Eighty-third Precept on Entering a Village at an Improper Time (a shared offense for monks and nuns). An offense is committed when five conditions are met: first, it is not the proper time;

second, there is no prior announcement or invitation; third, one has not informed another monk; fourth, one is heading toward a layperson’s house; and fifth, upon entering the gate, the offense is incurred. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If one comes from a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) after announcing to a monk that one is entering a village, and then returns to the hermitage..."
If one has already made the prior announcement and then re-enters a village, it is an offense of expiation (*pāyattika*).

If one enters a village from a monastery within the village, and having left that village, returns to the original monastery and then re-enters the village, it is an offense of expiation for entering with the same prior announcement.

It is likewise an offense of expiation to enter without making the announcement when within the same boundary (*sīmā*) as virtuous bhikṣus. This applies whether one enters a dwelling place, an aranya, or a location near a village.

Regarding the offense of entering a village without informing the monastery: the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that if one informs the community as a whole before entering the village, there is no offense regardless of where one subsequently goes.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if two people residing in an *araṇya* (forest hermitage) both go out together, they should inform each other in turn.
If one person goes first and the other follows later, and there is no one else to inform, one should form this thought: "If..."
If, while on the road, one sees a bhikṣu at a village nunnery, one must announce one's presence before entering.

If the road passes through a village and there is a stūpa or a deva-shrine within that village, one should pass straight through by following the path. If one turns left or right onto a side path, it is a *thullaccaya* offense;

the meaning is that if one turns onto a side path and enters another village boundary without having announced one's presence, one commits an offense. Furthermore, [this applies] when circumambulating.

Regarding the time of entering a village: if one originally informs [the others] but then loses track of them and subsequently enters the village, it constitutes an offense against the *Saṃghāṭi-vinaya*.
It states: "If many people are traveling on a road and wish to enter a village, they should inform one another in succession before entering.

Once they have reached their lodging and wish to go outside again to gather firewood, grass, or wood—if they exit by the same path as before, there is no offense; if they exit by a different path, there is [an offense]."

Regarding the "white" (śukla) *pāyattika*, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "All laypeople's residences are termed 'villages' (*grāma*). Based on this wording, one must also announce [one's arrival] at the quarters and courtyards of the monastery attendants (*karmadāna*) within the monastery."

The Eighty-fourth Precept on Making Beds Exceeding the Prescribed Measure (a violation common to both monks and nuns). Five conditions must be met for the offense to be established: first, it is a bed; second, it is a monastic bed or has already been designated as such;

third, it exceeds the prescribed measure; fourth, one makes it oneself or causes another to make it; fifth, upon its completion, the offense is incurred. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, even making a monastic bed [exceeding the measure] constitutes an offense (whereas a secular bed does not).

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is likewise. There is no offense if the original intention was to cut down [an existing bed]. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one may exceed [the limit] if one obtains [the materials].
When measuring a bed, if one intends to cut it down for fear that the donor might see it and be displeased, one should bury the legs; even if one uses cut wood to support the legs, it is an offense.
If one sits on the same bed all day, every time one stands up and then sits back down, for each instance of standing up, it is a *vyatikrama* (transgression) against another's bed.

In a house of merit (*puṇya-śālā*), there is no offense regarding high beds. Furthermore, if one does not cut [the legs] and fails to repent, it is a *vyatikrama*. According to this Vinaya, the height of the feet should be like that of the Tathāgata.

Regarding "eight fingers," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one finger is two *cun*; thus, [the measurement] is one foot and six *cun* in length (as for the discussion of height, depth, width, and breadth, these may be determined according to one's discretion).
The eighty-fifth precept concerning the prohibition against stuffing a bed with *tūla* cotton (this offense applies equally to monks and nuns).
The Eighty-sixth Precept on Making Needle Cases from Bone, Tooth, or Horn (a violation common to both monks and nuns). Since these two precepts are rare, they are not explained here.

The Eighty-seventh Precept on Oversized Sitting Mats (an offense for nuns only). One commits this offense when five conditions are met: first, making a sitting mat; second, it being of excessive size;
third, making it for oneself; fourth, making it personally or having someone else make it; fifth, the offense is incurred as soon as it is completed. This is according to the Vinaya-mūla-saṃvara.
The *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) is two *vitasti* (handspans) of the Buddha in length and one and a half *vitasti* in width; both length and width may be increased by an additional half *vitasti*.

It is five parts of one *vitasti* of the Buddha [in width], which is two feet (calculated as four parts), making a total length of five feet and a width of four feet for the seat-furniture (*āsandikā*). Exceeding these measurements constitutes an offense; likewise, exceeding them in either dimension is an offense.

Apart from this, the method for its construction and acceptance is as explained above in the chapter on accepting robes. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one wishes to repent, one should cut off the excess beyond the prescribed measurement and perform the repentance according to the Dharma.

Regarding the remainder [of the cloth], one should perform the *śuddhika* (purification) rite; if ten days have already passed, it is considered "extra clothing" (*atireka-cīvara*) and must be relinquished.
This concludes the eighty-eighth precept concerning the oversized cloth for covering sores (*vrana-praticchādana-cīvara*), [a *pācittiya* offense for a *bhikṣuṇī*].
Precept 89: Regarding the robe for bathing when it exceeds the prescribed measure (a violation common to both monks and nuns). Precept 90:
Regarding making a Buddha-robe when it is equal in measure [to the standard robe] (an offense of *dukkaṭa* for nuns). These three precepts are not explained here because they are rare.
The Fourth Section: A Concise Explanation, Part Two. The First Precept:
Receiving Food with One’s Own Hand from a Non-Relative Laywoman (A Nun Taking a Bhikṣu’s Food is a Duṣkṛta). This offense is committed when five conditions are met:

first, it is at a lay residence; second, the nun is not a relative; third, one is not ill or otherwise exempted by circumstances; fourth, one receives the food with one’s own hand; and fifth, one swallows it.
If one violates this rule, whether the food is proper or improper, one commits an offense; however, there is no offense in any of the following cases:

if one has an illness, if one places the food on the ground to give it, if one causes another person to give it, if one gives it within a monastery, if one gives it at a nunnery, or if one gives it outside the village.

The Second Precept on Receiving Food from a Layperson through the Biased Instruction of a Bhikṣuṇī (A Bhikṣuṇī Receiving Food from a Bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense). The offense is incurred through four conditions: 1. Being in the house of a layperson (*avadātavasana*). 2.

Receiving biased instruction by skipping one's turn (*vyatikrama*). 3. The assembly remaining silent and not rebuking the act. 4. Swallowing the food, at which point the offense is committed. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"The first seat-holder (*agra-upasthāyaka*) should rebuke those who do not heed the words; this applies even to those who have newly received the precepts."
One who is thus addressed may also receive the *saṃghāṭī* robe; if one is scolded three times yet does not stop eating, there is no offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If monks in two separate locations sit separately and eat separately, they must also inquire [of each other] and give instructions; until this is done, one must not eat. It is the same for those sitting behind.
There is no offense if one says: 'Sister, please stop for a moment; we must wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating. Or...
If a donor instructs a *bhikṣuṇī* to distribute [the food] and she does not give it out of partiality, there is no offense.
The third precept regarding receiving food from a family of practitioners (*śikṣamāṇā-śikṣāpada*) (a *pāyantika* for a *bhikṣuṇī*).
The fourth precept regarding sitting down to eat in a forest hermitage (*araṇya-śikṣāpada*) (a *pāyantika* for a *bhikṣuṇī*). These two precepts are not explained here because they are rare.
The fifth section, the one hundred precepts of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*), is easy to understand both in text and meaning, so there is no need for further explanation.

As for the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), their text and meaning are vast and extensive, and their underlying intent is difficult to clarify; furthermore, since instances of their violation are somewhat rare, they are omitted here without further description.
Essentials of the Vinaya, Middle Volume,
Part Two: Chapter Twenty-one on the Monastic Director Governing the Assembly.

This chapter has five major sections: first, the rise and decline of the Teaching; second, the qualifications for those who oversee monastic affairs; third, the application and suspension of the Teaching;
fourth, the commonality and particularity of the Sangha’s food; and fifth, the regulations for entering the assembly and wearing the robes.

First, regarding the rise and decline of the teaching: To serve as a model for a monastic community and to govern its members, one must have virtue fully cultivated within and a majestic spirit strictly observed without.
One should master a single school of the Vinaya teachings while simultaneously investigating the ancient precedents; one must not shrink from toil and hardship, nor seek fame and reputation.

This causes monks from distant regions and different schools to feel joy in having a place to turn their hearts, and it inspires those practicing within the boundaries to exert their spirits and advance in their practice.
In governing the multitude, what task would one not undertake? Therefore, the Vinaya states: "That which is not prescribed shall not be prescribed;

that which is prescribed shall be put into practice. In this way, gradually, the Dharma is made to endure for a long time. If a rule deviates from common sense, lacks regulation, and instead resembles vulgar custom, how can it serve to rectify the multitude?
One should rather withdraw privately and rest, employing a compassionate heart. Thus, the Vinaya states: "To prescribe that which is not prescribed is [a transgression of] that which is prescribed."
Thus, by severing [the lineage] in this manner, one causes the Dharma to perish gradually and swiftly.

Second, regarding the qualifications for the *karmadāna* (officer in charge of affairs): here, we shall provide a general summary of all necessary virtues; one must certainly be able to manage and measure matters accordingly.
If one violates these rules, then when raising objections, one will not know the proper time, disputes will arise from such matters, and evil dharmas will be difficult to extinguish.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "Do not repeatedly expose the faults of others, for fear that you will destroy the True Dharma.

If one fails to possess these virtues and yet pardons offenses without administering discipline, the True Dharma will likewise perish. This Vinaya stipulates that a person who exposes the faults of others must possess five virtues:

first, knowing the proper time and not doing so at an improper time; second, being truthful and not being false; third, acting for the benefit of others and not for their detriment; fourth... [text truncated]
Being gentle rather than harsh; possessing the five kinds of loving-kindness rather than malice—one who can resolve matters for others should be endowed with five virtues:
first, purity in maintaining the precepts; second, great learning; third, extensive recitation of the two sections of the Vinaya;

fourth, the ability to question and answer, as well as to provide instruction and reprimand according to the Dharma and to carry out formal acts of suspension (pravāsanīya-karman) so that [the offender] may attain the five [benefits]; and fifth, skillfully extinguishing disputes and adjudicating legal cases.

Regarding the duties of one who adjudicates the affairs of others, they must possess five qualities: first, being well-acquainted with what constitutes an offense; second, being well-acquainted with what does not constitute an offense; third, being well-acquainted with... [the text continues]. Furthermore, when performing one's own duties, one should reflect upon five points: first, observing whether the matter before one is factual; second, observing whether it is appropriate for the present time;
third, observing whether the Sangha has become defiled by impurities; fourth, observing whether there will be benefit; and fifth, observing whether one has obtained virtuous companions.

When adjudicating the affairs of others, one must likewise possess these five qualities. First, being well-acquainted with what constitutes an offense; second, being well-acquainted with what does not constitute an offense; third, being well-acquainted with... [the text continues].

One who well understands the four light [offenses] and the five heavy [offenses], who possesses decisiveness and freedom from doubt, and who abides in the *vinaya* and the *vinayamātṛkā*, is a person capable of admonishing others.
There are five qualities that such a person need not possess: first, a lack of shame and remorse; second, a lack of extensive learning; third, constantly seeking out the faults of others;
fourth, delighting in strife and contention; fifth, wishing to abandon the Jewel of the Path. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "I permit two..."
There are two types of persons who may serve as administrators (karmadāna): first, an Arhat; second, a person who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna. Why is this so?

Because other bhikṣus whose precepts are incomplete and whose minds are not impartial are unfit to serve as administrators. Furthermore, there are two other types of persons who are fit for monastic affairs:
first, those who can purely uphold the precepts and recognize the retribution of karma; second, those who fear the future world.

Regarding offenses, there are those who possess a sense of shame (*hrī*), a sense of dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), and a mind of remorse (*kaukṛtya*). Such persons have no wounds or sores within themselves and also protect others.
If one lacks these virtues and, following merely one's own common sentiments, hastily adjudicates another, one instead incurs self-reproach;

how then could one rectify the community? Therefore, the Vinaya states: "I say that such a person is foolish; thus they commit a *pārājika* offense," meaning they are unacquainted with the net of the teachings.
Since it is difficult to rectify the grave offenses committed in secret, this is truly a great warning; one should carefully examine the sacred teachings and reflect upon oneself as a person.

Third, regarding the success or failure of upholding the teachings, there are two parts: first, a general clarification of the differences between transformation (*hua*) and regulation (*zhi*); second, clarifying the attainment of the teachings.
Regarding the first point concerning the differences in transformational regulations, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:

"If, in future ages, there are kings of the four castes who, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, would rather sacrifice their own bodies and lives to protect a single bhikṣu who abides according to the Dharma than protect immeasurable wicked bhikṣus, such a king shall, upon casting off his body, be reborn in a Pure Land; whereas if he follows the wicked, that king’s [retribution] shall be immeasurable."
In this world, if human kings and others do not govern, they will cause the Three Jewels to be severed and deprive sentient beings of their eyes;
even if one has cultivated precepts, generosity, and kindness for immeasurable eons, these will be lost. Furthermore, those bhikṣus who have committed transgressions must also be disciplined:
for one or two months they should be subjected to harsh tasks, or not spoken to, nor allowed to sit or dwell together with others, or they should be expelled.
In kingdoms, or even in as many as four kingdoms where the Buddha-dharma exists, one should discipline such evil bhikṣus so that virtuous bhikṣus may dwell in peace and receive the Dharma;
thus, the Buddha-dharma will endure for a long time without perishing. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that because this violates royal regulations, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "If a virtuous bhikṣu is left unrebuked, you should know that such a person is no longer within the Buddha-dharma."
If one can drive away and punish those who are internal enemies, such a person is my disciple, a true Śrāvaka. The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states:
"World-Honored One, you should subdue those who ought to be subdued and receive those who ought to be received. Why is this?
Because through subduing and receiving, the True Dharma is enabled to abide for a long time; devas and humans become abundant, and the evil realms are diminished."
Regarding those who are unable to follow the turning of the Wheel of Dharma set in motion by the Tathāgata, the *Daśacakra Sūtra* states:

"If there are sentient beings of dull faculties who wish to arouse roots of goodness but are indolent, lacking wisdom, losing right mindfulness, and being attached to their dwellings and the four requisites of support,
and who are far removed from virtuous friends— such beings should be instructed and exhorted to manage monastic affairs and serve the Buddha."
The Dharma-teacher (upādhyāya) and the Preceptor (ācārya) are those who establish and manage the meritorious sites. Next, regarding the gains and losses in teaching:

when discussing the monastic community, among those currently occupying positions—whether of the ordinary rank or otherwise—who can claim to be free from transgressions? Since one inevitably encounters conditions that lead to offenses, one ought to rely on the *pien-chu* (the *Prakaraṇa-grantha*) to administer disciplinary measures in accordance with the teachings.
Yet, what I have recently observed is that monks and nuns do not rely on the holy teachings, but instead establish illegal regulations and openly practice them.
In matters of reward and punishment, they may drink alcohol and beat one another, compelling the loser to forfeit property. At the time, they collectively agree to violate established regulations;
yet later, they themselves contravene them by concealing the items and refusing to return them. Because of this debt of property, they consequently commit grave offenses.

Although they know it is contrary to the Dharma, they establish such rules because they have collectively agreed to them. How can this not demonstrate that through regulations contrary to the Dharma, the True Dharma is rendered unable to prevail?

It may be that such errors or minor transgressions lead to harsh punishment and expulsion, yet when one seeks repentance, it is not accepted; as years and months pass, the offenses become even deeper.

One may thus retreat from the Way and fall into worldly ways, perhaps causing various bhikṣus to harvest grain and wheat, clear away grasses and trees, engage in planting and plowing, or practice medicine through acupuncture and moxibustion to treat illnesses according to secular prescriptions, all while greedily seeking worldly profit.

If one enriches oneself by personally operating a shop or stall to sell goods for profit, openly gathering for wine and meat, or following worldly customs by establishing regulations for matchmaking and engaging in improper conduct for pure practitioners (brahmacārin), one commits a grave offense. If one consents to or cohabits with such illegal regulations, they are not to be followed.
If the leaders of the community have the power to forbid such violations but do not, individuals should act on their own behalf.
Regarding the method for one's own liberation, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If an illegal regulation is being enacted, one should reprove it and cause it to cease.

If they do not listen, one should explain what is according to the Dharma, and having finished speaking, may rise and depart. If there is someone of authority within the assembly who reproves [the rule] but does not permit one to leave, one should say to those nearby:
'This is an illegal regulation; I cannot endure it. It is to be established for three persons and must not exceed four."

Fearing that the matter of either becoming a monk or causing a schism in the Saṃgha might arise, this Vinaya text does not, in its subsequent sections, permit one to accuse a monk on behalf of the Saṃgha.

One must instead speak to a person who is in agreement; if such a person cannot be found, one should state that one sees [the fault] but does not wish to [accuse], so as to remain in accord with a protective mind (*ārakṣacitta*).
What is this protective mind? It should be expressed as follows: "That person has acted unrighteously and will receive their own karmic retribution; what concern is it of mine?"
My concern is like this: when a fire breaks out and burns a house, one should only focus on saving oneself; how can one attend to other matters?

Regarding the five parts [of the *pañcavastuka*], if one has previously given consent (*chanda*) but later regrets it within the context of the precepts, there is no offense if one remains silent and does not criticize when an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is being performed, provided one cannot turn it back.
Furthermore, regarding the precept against not giving consent, there is an opening for non-offense in the following case: if one performs what is non-... (the text is incomplete).
Question: If one rises and departs during a formal legal act (*dharmakarma*) without having granted consent (*chanda*), is there no offense? Answer: There is no offense.
This is because at that time, those within the boundary (*sīmā*) acted together in harmony; although he was subsequently penalized for failing to obtain [consent], he did not commit an offense.

There is no hindrance to performing an illegal act (*adharmakarma*), yet if it is a transgression against the rules, the Sangha may command him to perform an intensive confession (*uttaraguru-pratikramaṇa*).

Those who merely see the shadow of the Path dare not refuse or disobey it; yet those of inferior capacity reject the assembly and refuse to comply, acting without shame or remorse and committing offenses without ceasing.
Were it not for disciplinary punishment, by what means could they be brought to rest? It is like a slow donkey that must be struck with a painful whip.
When one intends to discipline and expel such a person, there are nine methods according to the Vinaya. What are these nine? First, censure (*tarjanīya*); second...
1. Expulsion; 2. The three types of dependence; 3. The four prohibitions against entering the homes of laypeople; 4. Not acknowledging one's offense; 5. Not repenting for one's offense; 6.
Declaring one's consent (*chanda*) while not obstructing the Path; 7. Punishment for verbal abuse; 8. Silent expulsion. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Just as the Brahma-heaven punishes those of the Form Realm—where silence is considered pleasure—by making them speak, whereas in the Desire Realm, silence is considered distress, these disciplinary rules were established in opposition to worldly sentiments."
Together we shall not speak of it. Since the Great Sage passed into seclusion in the West and the True Teaching flowed to the East, many years have elapsed;

as the Dharma and its images have declined toward their end, those who violate the disciplinary codes have suddenly nearly exhausted them. These nine dharmas all involve *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures), yet they are omitted here for brevity;

one should refer to the original texts for their preservation. If one hears these teachings, one may instead be subjected to humiliation and defilement of the pure mind, as people rely entirely upon their own power and influence.

Those who harm the pure person harbor increasingly evil intentions that are truly difficult to subdue; this causes the Great Teaching to cease its function and its remaining traditions to fall into corruption.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "To institute what is not prescribed and to cause the precepts to be destroyed leads to the swift extinction of the Dharma."

Fourth, regarding the commonality and specific restrictions of the Sangha’s food: The human body is a great affliction; thus, one must rely on physical sustenance to survive. Wearing black robes is a shared practice, and there is no partiality or restriction;
the ten directions all follow this principle without contradiction. There is neither host nor guest—this is what is always appropriate.

Within these [monasteries], food and drink are shared by both the ordinary and the holy. When the wooden mallet sounds, they assemble from afar and near to eat together. This is the current practice in various monasteries.
Repeatedly cutting off the food of the Sangha to satisfy one's own palate while neglecting other beings, such a person’s disposition is narrow and their intent is unequal;
they wound the feelings of the entire community and block the path of the Sangha throughout the ten directions. To transmit such errors to later generations is a profound failure;

the evil karma of stinginess and greed in eating alone is even more excessive. Thus, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states that the Buddha told Kāśyapa: "The bhikṣu who manages monastic affairs frequently receives..."

If a monk is stingy with the property of the Sangha, hoarding it or failing to provide for it at the proper time, or if he gives it away haphazardly—whether giving to some and not to others—a *karmic-causing* (*akusala-mūla*) bhikṣu who acts as an administrator shall, because of this, be reborn among the foul and loathsome hungry ghosts (*preta*), where he will constantly eat balls of excrement.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "An administrator bhikṣu would rather eat his own flesh than ever use the property of the Triple Gem. Furthermore, the sutra says:
It is said that a single thought of evil can open the gates of the five unwholesome paths: first, one evil can burn away one's roots of goodness;

second, from evil arises further evil; third, one is rebuked by the sages; fourth, one falls away from the fruits of the Path; and fifth, after death, one enters the evil realms. The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states:
"One should practice the Path with a single mind, following the practice of the Dharma, and not dwell on the necessities of food and clothing."
Even if one were to offer a single portion from within the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft between the eyebrows) of the Tathāgata to all monastic disciples of the final age, it could not be exhausted;
this refers to the five portions. It is said that the assembly of monks of the ten directions has their own allotted food which arrives at the appointed time;

there is no need to summon laypeople (*avadātavasana*). Furthermore, those who are capable of impartiality may also be given food—meaning that while those who can cause benefit or harm are permitted [to receive it], others should be prohibited from doing so. (*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*).
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) come, it is not an offense for the community of monks (*saṃgha*) to give them food;

however, one must not give it with one's own hand, because non-Buddhists constantly watch for the faults of bhikṣus. Therefore, it is permitted to give it to them. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* further states:

"Regarding the communal food (*saṃghika-bhakta*), four signs should be made—such as striking the gong (*ghanṭā*)—as already explained above, so that everyone within the boundary (*sīmā*) may hear and know of it. Thus, there are four [signs]."

Signs must necessarily have fixed limits and may not be confused; if there is no certainty, the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*) is not established. One who lacks the four signs is termed a "thief of the Saṃgha.
If one establishes the four signs, whether [the assembly] comes or does not come, there is no offense. Even if one establishes the signs, if there is an obstruction, it is still an offense.

(According to this principle, one should establish the signs to ensure certainty and prevent confusion. If one replaces the bells and chimes, they should first be struck to assemble the monks, announce the matter so that they know, and only then may the exchange be made. If...
Within a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), there may be two or three monasteries that share the same *poṣadha* and mealtime;
when the bell is struck, no one shall obstruct anyone else, for they are pure and without fault. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:

"If five Dharma masters reside in a single monastery or village, they should strike the gavel to assemble the monks and distribute [offerings] in succession without stinginess or begrudging others' shortcomings; this is called dwelling according to the Dharma and performing great merit."

If a monk of boundless virtue violates the precepts, yet five others remain pure and uphold the Buddha-dharma according to the Dharma out of compassion for all sentient beings, their merit is incalculable.
In the latter part of this Vinaya, it states that when a visiting bhikṣu first arrives, he should first inform the Sangha of the established rules and procedures.
The *Sāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (Shanxian lun) further says: "If one arrives at an empty monastery and sees fruit on a tree, one should strike the *gandī*."
If there are no [attendants], one must clap the hands at least three times before taking food; otherwise, one commits the offense of stealing food and drink. It is the same for other cases.
If visiting bhikṣus arrive and the resident bhikṣus are unwilling to strike the *kṣaṅ* (gong), the visiting bhikṣus should strike it themselves; in this case, there is no offense.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, at any place where the Saṃgha eats, there should be a fixed limit based on the number of people present, calculated according to the portion of food allotted to the Saṃgha.

Regarding the second category, the pure locations, there are four different types: first, where the fences or walls are incomplete. This Vinaya states: "Half-fenced," "mostly unfenced," and "entirely unfenced.

if a donor or a supervising bhikṣu, while constructing a monastery for the Saṃgha, designates it in this manner, saying, "This place shall be made pure for the Saṃgha."

This refers to the layout of a monastery (ārāma), where monks reside within its perimeter. Regarding the offense of storing cooked food overnight, it applies regardless of how long one has resided there;

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the bhikṣus wish to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to designate one room, one corner, half a room, half a corner, the central courtyard, or the entire interior of a ward as a pure ground, all such requests are permitted.

Within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), one must point toward the place where the boundary is established from afar and may not sit in the center.

(If it is a peripheral room, a quiet place, a heated chamber, or a dining hall, one may proclaim the boundary according to the specific location; it need not be restricted to a single spot, nor must the name of the person making the proclamation be included in the formal motion.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) has not finished washing vegetables on impure ground when the dawn appears, there is no offense.
In this Vinaya, it is said that if a bhikṣu brings food seeking pure ground and the dawn appears before he finds it, there is no offense.
Regarding "cooking within the four watches": if one is within the boundary and originally cooks for others rather than for oneself exclusively, and gives it to another, [there is no offense].
There are others who wash their hands before receiving food.

Regarding the seventh section on determining the permissibility or prohibition of offenses, there are two parts. First, concerning the four types of medicine—namely, *kālika* (timely), *yāmika* (non-timely), *saptāhika* (seven-day), and *yāvajjīvika* (lifetime)—if it is *kālika* medicine, it must necessarily have been cooked overnight; because its utility is great and it is required for regular consumption, it must be taken [at the proper time].

Regarding the remaining three medicines, those not subject to the rules for "adding" (adhika-dharma): first, as for simultaneous medicine (*sāmayikī-bhaiṣajya*), if one adds the noble Dharma for the sake of a medical condition, there are both general and specific applications.
As for non-simultaneous medicine (*akālika-bhaiṣajya*), it may be consumed after midday provided the dawn-sign (*aruṇodaya*) has not yet appeared;

if the dawn-sign appears, its status as "mouth-legal" (*mukha-dharma*) is lost, and it becomes "leftover," "tainted by overnight storage," or "untouchable," thus giving rise to the category of non-timely medicine. As for seven-day medicine (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*), it is prepared... [text ends].

Regarding the *dharmakathika* [rules], it is permitted within a purified kitchen (*antaḥśuddha-maṇḍapa*) that there be no fault of "residual overnight storage" (*saṃnihita-doṣa*) or "improper handling" (*parāmṛṣṭa-doṛṣa*).

On the morning of the eighth day, one should arise and prepare [the medicine]; as for the offenses mentioned below, they apply throughout one's life. As for medicines taken for life, these must necessarily be cooked from dead seeds and lack the characteristics of living seeds. The Vinaya permits "overnight storage within," "cooking within," and "self-cooking.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the offense of "self-cooking ginger broth" is incurred when there are still living parts present. (Based on this, only three offenses are permitted for seven days.)

[One] should not stay overnight [with them]. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that honey-syrup may be kept overnight and drunk by a sick person; this must be an allowance due to difficult circumstances.
In this Vinaya, the keeping of ghee and oil overnight is permitted for use as nasal drops and the like, whereas other impure medicines do not permit such an application.

Next, regarding the presence or absence of the four transgressions—namely, "storing within" (*antar-upasthāpana*), "cooking within," "cooking for oneself," and "impurity through contact"—the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are three types of persons who may eat together.

"Overnight-staying" (*antara-vāsa*) refers to senior *bhikṣus*, the Saṃgha, trainee novices (*śrāmaṇera*), and so forth; it also includes four or three *bhikṣuṇīs* according to the aforementioned rules, as well as *śikṣamāṇās*.

According to this Vinaya, a *śikṣamāṇā* may eat with a senior *bhikṣuṇī* after [the meal], but she may not stay overnight with her. (This may be an allowance made because there were no *śrāmaṇerīs* present.

"Overnight-staying" means that once a pure area (*pariśuddha-sthāna*) has been demarcated, eating together within the monastery grounds (*vihāra*) constitutes this offense. (In none of these cases is it said to be "pure.")

Regarding the bhikṣus on the ground: "cooked within" refers to having formally established a *kappiya-bhūmi* (pure ground), and then cooking inside the monastery; "cooked by oneself" refers to a *mahābhikṣu* cooking for himself.

As for the three types of persons mentioned above, one should not eat [food prepared by them]. Regarding "badly handled": if one takes fruit oneself and gives it to a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), and then receives it back to eat, this is "badly handled.

(If one is uncertain whether it has been relinquished to another and then receives it back, it is likewise "badly handled. The *Sarvāstivāda* school says that there is [a fault] regarding eating food that was stored overnight.

If one has received food in three ways, formed the thought that it is one's own, and kept it overnight—whether together with others or not—one commits a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) for the night;

if one eats it, one commits a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). (This is because it is "leftover overnight"; this is also the same in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*). If one takes up food with one's own hand, it is called "improper taking"; if one forms the thought that it is one's own and keeps it overnight, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Regarding the faults of "eating together with others" and "storing overnight," these four faults are now discussed in relation to persons, time, place, and food.

First, concerning "storing overnight within" (*antar-śaya*) in terms of place: this does not apply to other objects, nor to the two types of purified places (*pariśuddha-sthāna*), nor to the formal act of notification (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) or that which is within the boundary (*sīmā*);
it applies to all. In terms of time, it requires the passage of the dawn (*aruṇodaya*). In terms of persons, it refers exclusively to *bhikṣus*.
People know that there is an offense regarding the violation of the rules concerning pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*). When questioned, it was not clear whether the sun had risen;

a dog brought food, and the wind blew fruit down. The Buddha said: "If one does not know [the situation], there is no offense. For nuns, four cases apply, all as described above, regarding eating on pure ground. If an object has left the ground, there is an offense in all such cases.
If it has not left the ground, there is no offense for those who have not yet grown legs (i.e., young children); once they have grown legs, there is an offense.

The *Zu-feng-shuang* (Foot-meets-Frost) and other such texts all concern the karmic limitations (*śīla-pratyaya*) that correspond to the four medicines. Generally speaking, as discussed above, those medicines boiled internally must be prepared in a purified location and sealed off.
Regarding the time, they apply throughout day and night; regarding the persons, they apply to all seven classes of the Saṃgha; and regarding the food, they apply to both raw and cooked items.

Among the four medicines, only the one taken for life (*yāvajjīvika*) is permitted to be boiled within the boundary (*sīmā*); the remaining three are not allowed. Thus it is stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
Because Ānanda warmed the Buddha’s rice near the gate of the Jetavana, it is known that one may not cook within the boundary (*sīmā*).
Regarding the "three types of self-cooking": in terms of location, it applies to both pure and impure grounds; in terms of time, it applies to both day and night;

in terms of persons, it is restricted to three monks and four nuns. Regarding the discussion on the arising of food, the Buddha permitted re-cooking, so there is no offense. Among the four medicinal substances, this is added.
Regarding the rule that [medicines] may be kept for as long as one lives, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If raw food has been purified by fire, it may be cooked. How is it purified?

By touching it once with fire (this applies by analogy to rice, vegetables, and so forth). Regarding cold food being reheated, the *Pañcaśata-praśna* states: "If a bhikṣu obtains those purified medicines, he may prepare them himself;
the four 'evil touches' are permissible. As for the location, it is permissible whether on pure or impure ground; as for the time, it is permissible at any time of day."

Regarding those who approach others at evening, there are several types of *bhikṣu* (great monks): First, that which was originally not received but grasped directly is called "defiled contact" (*duṣṭa-sparśa*).

Second, that which is connected by oily grease is called "defiled contact" (such as when a bowl, utensil, towel, or cloth is stained with food grease and impure). Third, that which is lost through spontaneous lapse is called "defiled contact.

(Regarding the four medicines, if the general non-addition method is applied, they all lose their status after noon; if the four addition methods are applied, the three medicines each lose their status according to their respective limits, while those for life-long use do not lose their status. Fourth...

To lose the state of "receiving" (prātimokṣa-saṃvara) due to encountering circumstances is called an "unwholesome contact" (*akuśala-sparśa*), such as when a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) touches or moves a vessel.

Fifth, to lose the state of "receiving" through a firm resolve to renounce it is called an "unwholesome contact," such as when one has already accepted food with the resolve not to eat it later, yet subsequently eats without having received it again, thereby incurring a *thullaccaya* offense.

Regarding *sāmaṇeras* and lay attendants, there is merely the "contact of grease" (meaning that after grasping a bhikṣu’s bowl, one eats until grease remains on the hands, and then grasps a monastic vessel without washing them). Furthermore, for the *bhikṣusaṃgha*, there are four types of cases where an "unwholesome contact" does not occur: first, ... [text truncated] ... of one.

Receiving by grasping does not constitute an improper touch (as when food is placed in a vessel used by laypeople and a bhikṣu receives it with upturned hands; although both the monastic and the layperson hold the food, it does not constitute an improper touch. Losing the formal acceptance due to circumstances does not constitute an improper touch (as when a lay attendant touches the food and the bhikṣu loses the formal acceptance, he washes his hands and receives it again;

It does not constitute an unwholesome touch; furthermore, three phrases summarize the preceding text: first, there is a touch that is not unwholesome. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If a precept-observing bhikṣu mistakenly touches monastic food," and this Vinaya [states]: "If one forgets to receive fruit while carrying it, upon seeing a *kappiya-kāraka*, one should place it on the ground, wash one's hands, and receive it again.
Second, there are two cases of unwholesomeness that do not constitute a touch. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts intentionally..."
Regarding "touching" (spraṣṭavya): according to this Vinaya, because the bhikṣus harbored mutual resentment, they touched the pure food of others, thereby rendering it impure.
The Buddha said: "That which is not touched is pure; that which is touched is impure—a duṣkṛta offense. Thirdly, regarding both touching and being defiled, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If a precept-observing bhikṣu touches [food] out of negligence, it is called impure. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one grasps fruit from a tree and examines whether it is ripe..."
The ripe [fruit] is also called "unwholesome contact" (*akuśala-sparśa*). Regarding food, this applies to both raw and ripe varieties.

As for the eighth case regarding fruit that falls onto one another: this Vinaya states that if food items are placed upon a tree and all are severed from the root—if the roots of the tree are in impure ground while the branches and leaves cover pure ground, and the fruit falls onto pure ground—or if it is blown there by the wind.

If birds or beasts fall due to rain, provided no one touches them and they fall by chance, even if they pass through the "bright phase" (the period after dawn), they do not constitute "overnight storage" (*antarāvasita*), provided they are fruits that have reached full growth.
If fruits or vegetables from an impure ground have not yet reached full growth and sprout repeatedly as they are moved about, there is no "overnight storage";
they may be taken at any time and brought into a pure kitchen. However, if the fruits or vegetables have already detached from their original source...

Regarding the location, according to the *Sūtra* and the comparison with the *Bhikṣu-vinaya*, if a bhikṣu knows [the fruit has been stored overnight], he must not eat it. (The above follows the general meaning; the specific details of the Vinaya text are not yet clear.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the root of a tree is situated on pure or impure ground, and a bhikṣu is likewise on pure or impure ground, and fruit falls therein without being caused by the bhikṣu, and has remained overnight, it may be eaten.
However, if one sees that the fruit has fallen on impure ground, one must have it purified."
If people gather [fruit] and leave it overnight, one may eat it provided one does not know whether it was placed in a pure or impure location;
however, if one knows it is on impure ground, it must not be eaten. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a tree stands on both pure and impure ground, the fruit follows the status of the ground;

at whatever time it is gathered, it is considered pure. If fruit falls from a tree on pure or impure ground onto impure ground, it should be brought into the clean kitchen immediately. If not... [text ends].
If melons or gourds grow on pure ground, they should be harvested at the proper time and brought into a clean room; the same rules apply to transporting grain, rice, beans, and so forth.
If a bhikṣu is unaware that he is on impure ground, the act is valid; if he knows it is impure, it is invalid.
This is largely consistent with the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* regarding what is known and what is unknown.

Regarding the ninth point, the relaxation of eight matters during times of scarcity: this Vinaya permits these because, when grain and rice were extremely expensive and people suffered from famine such that almsfood was difficult to obtain, even if one received a small amount of food, it might be taken away by thieves.
Out of compassion, the Buddha permitted the following: eating and sleeping together within the boundary; cooking within the boundary;
cooking for oneself; taking food for oneself; both monastic and lay food; and both aquatic and terrestrial fruits—none of which required the ritual of *atireka-kappa* (the "leftover" procedure).

If the Dharma were to establish fixed offenses, one would have to permit eight types of offenses, namely: eating what was stored overnight (*antarāpaṇa*), cooking within the monastery (*antargrāma-pākya*), cooking for oneself (*svayaṃpākya*), food touched by an impure person (*duṣṭasparśana*), food not received through formal invitation (*anadhiṣṭhita*), eating after having finished a meal (*atipariṇata*), and the three *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses regarding food kept overnight. Furthermore, the meaning of the four *pratideśanīya* offenses includes the destruction of living beings, such as water and land fruits;

if one eats them without having formally accepted them (*anadhiṣṭhita*), how could they be considered pure? The Vinaya states: "If at that time the world returns to a state of worthlessness, and one relies on these permitted foods," the Buddha said: [and so forth].

Although one previously rejoiced in oneself, one now causes the Saṃgha to rejoice; because of these few days [of service], it receives the name "joy.

Regarding the four methods for treating *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that some call it "calling one back into the assembly," while others call it "uprooting the root of the offense. According to the *Vinaya*, it is called *āpattivyūḍhi*.
It is said that through the arising of pure precepts, one attains pure liberation; this skillful maintenance and undertaking is called *āpattipariśuddhi* (purification of offenses).

The first section is divided into five parts: 1. Confession with concealment versus confession without concealment; 2. The duration of days for concealment; 3. The methods of general and specific confession;
4. The formal application of the *karmavācanā*; 5. The forfeiture of various practices and all wholesome dharmas (*śukladharma*).

First, regarding what constitutes concealment (*paticchādana*) and what does not: the Vinaya states that concealment is established when there is recollection, absence of doubt, and recognition; the opposite of this does not constitute concealment.

Furthermore, even if one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it does not constitute concealment if one has renounced the path, become a *śrāmaṇera*, is mentally deranged, insane, or has been formally accused (*tri-udghāta*).

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Even if one lives together with thieves, is subject to expulsion, is living separately, or is among those who are mute, deaf, or from border regions [it does not constitute concealment]."
If a bhikṣuṇī, or even a śrāmaṇerī or upāsikā, dwells together with such a person, it does not constitute concealment;

yet, if she fails to confess toward him, it likewise does not fulfill the five factors [of confession]. It is said: "If, in this land, there are many who recognize [the offense] as grave and one does not wish for them to know, it is not called 'concealment';
however, if one conceals it from that person, it constitutes concealment. Furthermore, if one conceals it from one's upādhyāya or ācārya..."
All those who fear human censure do not achieve concealment; for others, concealment is achieved. The *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* states:
"If one forgets, it also does not constitute concealment" (having first instructed them to repent for the *duṣkṛta* offense of concealment, one then grants the formal act of concealment).

Regarding the second case, concerning the length of days of concealment: although one may remember the number of offenses committed under this Vinaya, if one does not remember the specific count but only knows the length of the days of concealment, one is to be disciplined based on the total number of days.

If the number of days is not remembered, one is to be disciplined from the time of becoming pure (that is, from the time of receiving the precepts prior to the commission of the offense). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If the number of months and days is not remembered, it should be reckoned from the time of receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*)."

Regarding the essentials of the treatment: if one has requested purification (*pārivāsika*) after five or ten years of concealment, one is not permitted to recite the *dhāraṇī* (formula for purification) because the full measure of time since the request for purification is already known. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one does not remember the nights, one should ask:
'Did you commit an offense during a year or more? If they say no, one asks again: 'Did you commit an offense during one, two, or three years? [The response] follows according to their silence."
However, the "place" (處) refers to the governance by the Dharma (the term *sui* [year] is still a name for the summer retreat).

Third, regarding the general and specific confessions (*zongbie chan*), the Vinaya states that whether one knows the number or not, whether there has been concealment or not, whether it is a single offense or multiple types, these are all collectively confessed through the *karmavācanā*. Furthermore, there may be a bhikṣu who has committed numerous *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, or...
Regarding the concealment [of an offense] for one day up to ten days, the Buddha has generally prescribed that one perform the ten-day confession (*daśāha-pratikarma*).

Regarding the four correct applications of the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), this is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the deportment of the person performing the confession; second, the actual application of the ritual procedure. First, regarding the clarification of deportment:
one first removes the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*), puts on the five-strip robe (*pañcaka*), and bares the right shoulder. The Hu... [text continues].

Kneeling with palms joined, bowing his body and lowering his head, he wept with grief amidst the assembly of monks. He lamented to himself, "This transgression of mine was on the verge of leading me to the place of death;

it is only by relying on the World-Honored One’s compassionate instruction regarding the methods of repentance that I have been saved. Having thus reproached himself in various ways, he prostrated toward the four directions before the assembly of monks.

Then, kneeling with palms joined before the *karmadāna* (the master of ritual), while being instructed by an attendant, he requested [absolution]. Although there are many types of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension from the community),...

For now, let us follow the procedure for those who have committed offenses out of a desire for pleasure; other remaining categories may be understood from the formal list. The formal request for absolution is as follows:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed the following three *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses—namely, intentional emission, touching a woman, and coarse speech—each of which I do not recall the number of times (if the number is recalled, state "I recall"). I have concealed them for one hundred nights (the duration may be adjusted according to the time elapsed)."

"I now request from the community of monks the *parivāsa* (probation) of one hundred nights by means of a formal act (*karmavācanā*). May the Sangha, out of compassion, grant me the *parivāsa* of one hundred nights.
(Recite three times. The presiding elder asks the Sangha: "The Sangha is now in harmony; what shall it perform? [The respondent] answers:

"The formal act of concealment (*parivāsa-karman*). "Venerable Sangha, listen! This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed the offense of intentional emission [of semen] and the coarse offense of touching a woman."
