I do not recall the number of times I committed each of the three *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses involving harsh speech, nor do I recall the number of nights I concealed them.

Now I beg the Saṃgha for the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of concealing [the offense] for one hundred nights. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the venerable Saṃgha listen and grant its consent:

the Saṃgha now grants the monk [Name], who has committed intentional emission of semen, the formal act of concealing [the offense] for one hundred nights. This is the motion (*jñapti*). Great Virtues, may the Saṃgha listen: the monk [Name] has committed intentional emission of semen.
I do not recall the number of times I committed the three *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses of touching women, using harsh speech, and concealing them for one hundred nights;
I now request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of concealment for one hundred nights. May the Saṃgha now grant the monk [Name] the formal act of concealment for one hundred nights.
Which elders consent to the Saṃgha granting the monk [Name] the formal act of concealment for one hundred nights?

"Whoever approves, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak. (Thus it is said three times. The Sangha has approved and granted the *karmavācanā* for the concealment of [the offense] for one hundred nights to the monk so-and-so.
Since the Sangha has approved by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

Fifth, regarding the method for revoking the formal motion (*jñapti*) concerning mixed conduct: the meaning is that after the *karmavācanā* has been performed, one declares, "This *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is the sacred teaching;
it is a true medicine. Keep this in mind. To revoke thirty-five matters is the method of subduing (*nigraha-dharma*); do not allow any transgression.
To diligently serve the assembly and respectfully honor pure bhikṣus is the method of disciplining (*vinaya-dharma*). One.

First, the eight matters such as the formal announcement of compliance (*anuvartana*) constitute the method of disclosure (*āviṣkaraṇa*). One should proclaim [the offense] with a sense of shame and remorse, deeply reproaching oneself, and announce it according to the Dharma without omission;
one who violates this loses the night’s rest. Having thus shown the words to be used, on the day the Saṃgha assembles, one should immediately announce it to the Saṃgha, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, the bhikṣu so-and-so, have committed the intentional emission [of semen] and touched a woman."
I do not recall the number of times I committed the three *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses of harsh speech.

Having concealed them for one hundred nights, I have requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of concealment for one hundred nights. The Saṃgha has already granted me, the bhikṣu [Name], the formal act of concealment for one hundred nights.
From this day forth, I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall practice the concealment; I inform the venerable Saṃgha so that they may know my conduct.
[The procedure for] concealing [an offense] (recited three times as above). The Vinaya states: One should visit pure bhikṣus at the three times of day;

whatever is to be done must be performed according to the Dharma and must not be contravened. On the day of the Poṣadha, one should sweep and sprinkle the Poṣadha hall and provide all necessary provisions.
Even if one is staying in a small room and a visiting bhikṣu arrives and asks to be sent out, one should reply: "Venerable Sir, you may not."
Because the two persons are staying together, they may not go out. If monastic robes or requisites are offered according to the distribution, one should take them in order of seniority.
When sitting, one should sit below the *mahābhikṣus* and above the *śrāmaṇeras*.

One must not walk for meditation (*caṅkrama*) together with a pure (*pariśuddha*) bhikṣu, nor share the same mat or plank; one must create a partition before being permitted to sit, even when receiving offerings.
For pure bhikṣus, it is no different from the method for a preceptor as described previously. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"At the very least, four pure bhikṣus may perform the *parivāsa* (probation). One undergoing *parivāsa* must not sit on the same bed, nor stay in a secluded place, because visiting bhikṣus might not see him.
The *Samantapāsādikā* states: "If someone invites one who is undergoing *parivāsa*..."
Alternatively, if one has received the precepts from another and obtained the authorization to suspend the practice of a formal act (*dharmakṛtya*), one may resume it upon returning;
if there are many bhikṣus in the monastery and it is difficult to inform them, one may suspend the practice during the day and resume it once the dawn has not yet appeared.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that even for the six-night rite, one may obtain authorization to suspend it for twenty-five nights. The Vinaya further states: "If the great assembly..."
If it is difficult to assemble [the community] and one does not wish to go, and if that person is weak and possesses much shame, they should go to a pure bhikṣu and say:
"Venerable Upādhyāya, today I relinquish the instruction; I shall not perform it. (This is accomplished by saying this once.
If one later wishes to perform it, one should again go to the pure bhikṣu and say: "I now act according to the instruction. (This is accomplished by saying this once.)
One shall then obtain the fivefold [purification]. If one does not relinquish the practice of the *parivāsa* (probation), upon exiting the boundary and seeing a bhikṣu, one should declare in general:

"I, the bhikṣu so-and-so, having completed so many days of the *parivāsa*, have so many days remaining; may the Venerable One bear this in mind. If it is not so, one must relinquish the practice of the *parivāsa*.
Upon seeing a bhikṣu, there is no need for such a declaration; one should go to another place and request the Saṃgha there to perform the practice anew.

In this Vinaya, those who have performed repentance may perform acts for one another, such as bowing, welcoming, and seeing off; they may also receive the eight services, including prostrations and announcements from śrāmaṇeras and upāsakas.
Regarding the rules for losing the night (*rātriparihāṇa*): first, going to another monastery without informing [the resident monks];
second, not informing [them] when visiting bhikṣus arrive; third, not informing [them] when leaving the boundary for a necessary purpose; fourth, walking slowly within the monastery.

1. Not informing [the Sangha] of the five types of illness; 2. not sending a messenger to inform [them]; 3. two or three people staying together in one room; 4. residing where no bhikṣus are present; 5.
not announcing [the assembly] during the fortnightly *poṣadha* ceremony—regarding these eight matters above, if even one rule is omitted, one loses the status for that night.
Once obtained, it is not lost; if not yet obtained, it is not established. Although the formal wording of the announcement according to the Vinaya is incomplete, the meaning is supplemented here.
When performing this, one should maintain proper dignified demeanor and go before a pure bhikṣu, declaring: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed numerous offenses of intentional emission, touching women, and coarse speech—each constituting a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense—and have concealed them for a hundred nights.
I now request from the community of monks the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of concealment for those hundred nights."
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], have already been granted the *parivāsa* (probation) for concealment for a period of one hundred nights; I have already practiced it for [X] days, and [Y] days remain.
I inform the Venerable Ones that I am practicing the *parivāsa*. (Recite this three times. The Saṃgha need not assemble for this;

this is the procedure for a single person to disclose their offense. There is no separate rite for a group of monks. The above text for the announcement (*jñapti*) is the method for addressing a single Bhikṣu. If...
When many visiting monks arrive, they should be gathered together in one place and the following announcement (*jñapti*) should be made: "Venerable sirs, listen with one mind... and so forth;
the subsequent phrase says, "I announce to the great assembly of venerable sirs so that they may know. The remaining procedures are the same as above.

If a venerable person of superior standing arrives, one should wait until they have entered the room before making the announcement. On the day of the *poṣadha* ceremony, the announcement is made: "Venerable Sangha, listen... and so forth.
The formal announcement (*jñapti*) to inform the venerable Saṃgha is as described above in the Vinaya:

"If one walks slowly within the monastery grounds without making an announcement, and if the person ahead moves quickly and exits the boundary while one intends to announce it, then even though the announcement was not made, the requirement is not lost and there is no offense.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When a visiting bhikṣu runs toward the boundary, he should proceed according to the Dharma and must not run after him; they should remain together within their own territory."
Regarding those undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) for six nights who fall ill: one should send a messenger to inform the Saṃgha, saying: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen.

The bhikṣu [Name], a person undergoing *parivāsa*, has committed such-and-such an offense; being ill, he is unable to come to inform the Saṃgha. (This is to be stated three times. The other rules for persons under probation may be understood accordingly.
Regarding this practice, the virtuous elders of various regions have deliberated and commented that since the Buddha's teaching spread to the East, those who conceal their offenses...

All say that the days [of penance] are not fixed; various masters each establish their own principles, mutually adding points of agreement and difference. Now, taking the prevailing view, the Great Master says:

"Among all the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings, this method of repentance (sāṃghāṭī-dharma) is the most extreme in weighing the toil and subduing the body and mind, and it is exceedingly grave in its compassion.
When one examines this labor, what fault could there be in reducing the number of days? Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one does not perform the *parivāsa* (probation), and so forth..."
The Buddha stated that even one who has committed an offense can still achieve purification; this principle may also be applied here by using that case as an analogy for this one.
However, when performing the ritual, I fear the procedure might not accord with the Dharma. If performing the *karmavācanā*, one should say:

"I, the bhikṣu [Name], having already completed the days of concealment, now request *mānatva* from the community of monks," and so forth. It is unnecessary to say "completed" (*kṛta*), and the remaining procedures are the same as those for requesting it below.
Six nights prior [to the completion of the probation], the senior monk (*upādhyāya*) shall inform the Saṃgha, saying:

"This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has already practiced *parivāsa* for several days and has undergone great hardship; he has now offered his apologies to the Saṃgha. May the Saṃgha now release him from the remaining days?
When the Saṃgha replies, "Very well," they shall then grant him the six-night rite (*ṣaḍrātra-dharma*). If the days of concealment were few and the actual practice was complete, this is not required.
Having finished speaking, he formally requests the *mānatva* penance, saying: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed three *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses—namely, intentional emission of semen, physical contact with a woman, and lewd speech—each of which I cannot recall the number of times I committed;

I concealed them for one hundred nights. Having already requested from the community of monks the *karma* for concealing them for one hundred nights, the Saṃgha has granted me the concealment for one hundred nights."
[The Karmavācanā: "I, the bhikṣu [Name], having already completed the days of concealment, now request from the Saṃgha the six-night *mānatva*.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the six-night *mānatva*. (Recite this three times. The Elder asks the Saṃgha:
"The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall it perform? [They] answer: "The *karmavācanā* for the six-night *mānatva*. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed the three saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses of intentional emission, touching a woman, and coarse speech, each of which he does not recall the number of times;
having concealed them for one hundred nights, he has requested from the community of monks the *karmavācanā* for concealment for one hundred nights.
The community has already granted this bhikṣu, so-and-so, the *karmavācanā* for concealment for one hundred nights. This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has already performed the concealment.
Today, [Name], from the community of monks, requests a six-night *mānatva*.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant it, may the Saṃgha now grant this monk, [Name], a six-night *mānatva*. This is the motion (*jñapti*). Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
This monk, [Name], has committed three *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses: intentional emission of semen, touching a woman, and lewd speech; each of these was committed without concealment.
Having remembered and concealed [the offense] for one hundred nights, he has requested from the Saṃgha the *parivāsa* (probation) for one hundred nights.
The Saṃgha has already granted the *parivāsa* for one hundred nights to the bhikṣu [Name].
This bhikṣu [Name], having already completed the days of probation, now requests from the Saṃgha the six-night *mānatva* (penance). The Saṃgha now grants the six-night *mānatva* to the bhikṣu [Name].
"Whichever elders among you approve of granting the *mānatva* penance for six nights to the monk [Name], remain silent;

whoever does not approve, speak. (Thus it is said three times. Since the Saṃgha has approved and remains silent, it is understood that the Saṃgha has granted the *mānatva* penance for six nights to the monk [Name].
Having received this formal act (*karmavācanā*), he shall immediately [remain] within the Saṃgha."

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed the three saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses of intentional emission, touching a woman, and coarse speech, each of which I cannot recall the number of times;
having concealed them for one hundred nights, I have requested from the community of monks the *parivāsa* (probation) of one hundred nights.
The Saṃgha has already granted me the *parivāsa* of one hundred nights. I, the bhikṣu [Name]...
Having already completed the days of concealment, I now request from the Sangha the six-night *mānatva*. The Sangha has granted me the six-night *mānatva*.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], from this day forth shall practice the *mānatva*; I inform the Venerable Sangha so that they may know I am practicing the *mānatva*.
(Recite three times. If one has already practiced for one night up to six nights, it should be said as follows:
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], having already completed one night, have five nights remaining in the presence of the venerable Saṃgha; I inform you of this.
The remaining procedures are the same as above. If visiting Bhikṣus arrive, change "the venerable Saṃgha" to "the venerable ones," etc. If there are many people, one should say:
"Venerable sirs, for the sake of those performing the *mānatva* penance, the procedure for concealing [the offense] is to be carried out collectively."

The rule is that one must always remain overnight within the Saṃgha; each day one must inform the Saṃgha so they may know of this distinct dwelling, ensuring one does not become separated from the Saṃgha.
This does not mean merely being in the same location as the Saṃgha. Regarding the two aforementioned rules: if one conceals [the offense], it is treated according to the former rule;

if one does not conceal it, it is treated according to the latter rule; in both cases, one is cleared of the offense. If one commits a grave offense against either of these two rules, both rules are violated, and in both instances, the penalty is severe.
The method for treating this today is rare in practice, so it is omitted here.
Next, the legal rules for the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*) state: "It should be performed within an assembly of twenty pure bhikṣus;
if even one person is missing, it is not accomplished and is considered illegal. Venerable Saṃgha, please listen: I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed the offense of intentional emission of semen.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], having committed three saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses—namely, touching a woman, using coarse language, and [the third offense]—each of which I do not recall the number of times, and having concealed them for one hundred nights, have already requested from the Saṃgha the *parivāsa* (probation) of one hundred nights;
the Saṃgha has already granted me the *parivāsa* of one hundred nights. Having completed the days of probation, I now request from the Saṃgha the six-night *mānatva*.
"I, bhikṣu [Name], having already been granted six nights of *mānatva*, have completed the practice of the six nights of *mānatva*.
I now request from the Saṃgha the *karmavācanā* for the removal of offense. May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the *karmavācanā* for the removal of offense.
(Recite three times. The Elder asks the Saṃgha: "The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what is it that you are performing? They reply: "The *karmavācanā* for the removal of offense, O Venerable One."

The Saṃgha has heard that this bhikṣu, so-and-so, committed three saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses—namely, intentional emission, touching a woman, and coarse speech—each of which he does not recall the number of times he committed;
having concealed them for one hundred nights, he has requested from the community of monks the *parivāsa* (probation) of one hundred nights.
The Saṃgha has already granted the *parivāsa* of one hundred nights to the bhikṣu so-and-so. This bhikṣu so-and-so has [completed it].

Having completed the period of concealment, this bhikṣu [Name] has requested from the Saṃgha the six-night *mānatva* penance; the Saṃgha has already granted the six-night *mānatva* to the bhikṣu [Name].
This bhikṣu [Name], having completed the six-night *mānatva*, now requests from the Saṃgha the *karmavācanā* for rehabilitation (*āpattivyutthāna*).
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant the bhikṣu [Name] the *karmavācanā* for rehabilitation.
The formal motion for the *naiḥsargika-karman* (act of deliverance from offense) is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen.

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed the offenses of intentional emission, touching a woman, and coarse speech—each a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense—countless times, and he concealed them for one hundred nights.
He has already requested from the community of monks the *parivāsa* (probation) of one hundred nights; the Saṃgha has now granted the bhikṣu so-and-so the probation of one hundred nights."
The night-ritual (rātrī-karman) for this bhikṣu so-and-so has been performed; he has already completed the days of concealment and has requested from the Saṃgha the six-night *mānatva*.
The Saṃgha has already granted the six-night *mānatva* to this bhikṣu so-and-so.
This bhikṣu so-and-so, having completed the practice of the six-night *mānatva*, now requests from the Saṃgha the *vyutthāna-karman* (the rite of restoration). Who [among you]...?
"Venerable sirs, if you approve of the *karman* for the rehabilitation from offense (*āpatti-vyutthāna*) for the monk so-and-so, remain silent;
whoever does not approve, speak. (Thus it is said three times. The Sangha has approved the *karman* for the rehabilitation from offense for the monk so-and-so.
Because the Sangha has approved by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. Having performed the *karman*, the presiding elder exhorts him, saying: "Good son, listen now."
In the age of the Semblance Dharma, repentance is extremely difficult; having committed such a transgression, one stands on the brink of death.
Nowadays, even the names of such wicked bhikṣus are no longer welcomed, let alone being permitted to hear your confession. From this day forward, do not commit such offenses again.

Even if you wish to repent, the necessary conditions will be difficult to fulfill. Thus, through various exhortations suited to the occasion, the Sangha shall ensure that such things are not repeated in the future.
There is indeed this admonition.

Regarding the third [section], the method for repenting *sthūlātyaya* offenses, it is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the differences in the methods of repentance; second, the actual application of the sacred teachings.
Within the first part, there are further two sections. First, concerning the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the first two categories of offenses, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says:
If a grave offense arises from the first category (pārājika), this constitutes a proximate preparatory act (*upakrama*);
that is, when the physical or verbal action has been initiated but not yet fully accomplished, one must confess before the entire Saṃgha.

If a light offense arises from the first category or a grave offense arises from the second category (saṃghāvaśeṣa), one should perform repentance before a group of four [monks or nuns] outside the boundary (*sīmā*). If a light offense arises from a saṃghāvaśeṣa, one should perform repentance before a single [monk or nun].

The *Mahāsāṃghika* *Pāyattika* Dharma, section two: Regarding those that are inherently *sthūlātyaya* and not merely preparatory offenses, the Vinaya states that "keeping" refers to using human hair and shaving the hair from three places—namely, the anus, the urethra, and the armpits—which constitutes three; wearing the robes of non-Buddhists; pouring [liquids] into the lower part of the body;
walking naked; keeping stone bowls; eating raw meat and blood, and so forth. These must all be confessed before one person; they constitute a violation of the *karmavācanā*.
Polishing a monk’s bowl; stealing three *kārsāpaṇas* together with a woman; touching her while one is clothed and the other is unclothed; acting as an agent for another;

the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses regarding the boundaries of a small assembly; and the four persons outside the boundary performing confession—all such cases where one steals four *kārsāpaṇas* or more within the boundary and performs confession before a large assembly—are classified as *sthūlātyaya*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that offenses such as tearing or breaking robes and bowls out of anger, or destroying a stupa, are all *sthūlātyaya* when committed against a single individual.

Regarding the confession of persons who have committed offenses under the first two sections of this Vinaya, as well as those who instruct others to commit *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses), these are all offenses of ultimate completion;

their relative gravity is distinguished in the same manner as above. If one personally engages in the various preliminary expedients (*pūrvaprayoga*) toward an object, one must likewise perform both types of repentance according to the gravity of the offense.
When requesting the formal rite of confession, one must necessarily describe its gravity, its origin from a specific section, and so forth.
The *Saṃghāvaśeṣa-vibhaṅga* states: "If one knows [the offense] and does not conceal it, it is said that one commits a *sthūlātyaya*.

The *Mātṛkā* states: 'If one causes another to fall into a state of transgression, one commits a *sthūlātyaya*. The *Vinaya* states: 'If one instructs another and they complete [the act], it is a *sthūlātyaya*;

if they do not complete it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is subsumed under the ultimate [offense] and should be confessed before a small assembly. Second, regarding the actual performance of the ritual (*vidhi*):"

This is divided into three parts: the assembly, the small group, and the individual. First, regarding the method for the assembly, the Sarvāstivādins state that regardless of whether the offense is light or heavy, one must first perform three formal requests (*jñapti*) in accordance with the Saṃgha, and only thereafter request a master of confession to receive it.

The master of confession performs a single motion (*jñapti*), after which the offender confesses three times before the individual [master], following the procedure for *pāyattika* offenses. Now, these three types [of methods] are based on the *Daśabhāṇavāra*.

Recite: Regarding the first category, for a heavy offense committed through preparatory effort (*prayoga*) or for stealing four *kārsāpaṇa* coins, one must confess before an assembly of at least five monks within the boundary (*sīmā*).
This is because the confessor, having made a formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize with the Saṃgha, does not count as part of the quorum.
Within this, there are seven distinct points: first, having struck the gavel to assemble the monks, one prepares the proper dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*) and proceeds into the midst of the Saṃgha.
Having prostrated toward the four directions to the Saṃgha, one next requests confession, saying: "Venerable Sisters (or Brothers), may the Saṃgha listen.

I, [name], a bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī), have committed a grave sthūlātyaya offense involving the preliminary stages of sexual misconduct, the number of which I do not recall [if the number is known, state 'I recall it'].
I now request confession from the Saṃgha; may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me, [name], a bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī), the opportunity for confession. (Recite this three times. Second.
Approaching the presiding master of the confession, kneel with the right knee on the ground and request, saying: "Virtuous Sister (or Elder Brother), please attend to me with one mind.

I, the bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī) [Name], now request the Virtuous Sister (or Elder Brother) to act as my presiding master for the confession of a *sthūlātyaya* offense. May the Virtuous Sister (or Elder Brother) graciously grant me the status of presiding master for the confession of this *sthūlātyaya* offense, out of compassion.
(Recite this three times. Third, the presiding master makes a formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize the Saṃgha, saying: "The Saṃgha is now in harmony."

What is the procedure? The answer is: the formal motion for receiving the confession of a grave offense, a *sthūlātyaya*, by means of a single announcement (*jñapti*). "Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen.
This Bhikṣu (or Bhikṣuṇī), [Name], has committed a grave *sthūlātyaya* involving the preliminary act of sexual misconduct. He (or she) now requests the Sangha for confession.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha, out of compassion, grant its consent that I, [Name] Bhikṣu (or Bhikṣuṇī), receive the confession of [Name] Bhikṣu (or Bhikṣuṇī)."
The declaration is as follows. Fourth, for the confession of the root of the offense, the presiding master says:

"Venerable one, since you are a *bhikṣu* (or *bhikṣuṇī*) who upholds the Buddha’s pure precepts, yet now you have violated them—how can you be called a human being? The Buddha established these prohibitive precepts so that one would rather die than transgress them;
they are like a rope of grass used to protect a goose. Venerable elder, since you have broken the pure precepts, you are destined for hell."
To receive the offerings of the faithful in vain is like wrapping one's body in glowing iron; to receive food and drink in vain is like swallowing a ball of glowing iron.
Their coming and going is like that of a hunter: internally ruined and rotten, yet externally appearing complete and pure.

They impudently partake of the offerings of the pure assembly and expect the respect of others as teachers, yet they possess no shame or remorse—none could surpass such people. Thus, by these skillful means, you should instruct those of noble station according to the occasion.
Regarding the ritual for abandoning offenses through the Five Clarities: "Venerable Sister, please attend to me with one mind.

I, the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so, have committed a grave *sthūlātyaya* offense involving the preparatory stage of sexual misconduct. I now confess and repent before the Venerable Sister; I dare not conceal it.
Through confession there is peace and happiness, but without confession there is no peace. Remembering my transgression, I disclose it; knowing it, I dare not conceal it. May it be so."
"Venerable Sister (or Venerable Brother), remember my pure body of precepts and my fulfillment of the pure *poṣadha*. (Recite this three times.

The sixth [section on] the formal act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) for establishing discipline states that one should question the [monk or nun] previously mentioned, saying: "Do you recognize this offense? If they reply, "I recognize it," one should say:

"Although it is easy to transgress, repentance is extremely difficult. You must reproach your own heart and give rise to a sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*), even to the point that your body withers away and your life ends."
At the conclusion of the shift, do not violate [the precepts]. Seventh, regarding the formal vow and commitment, he replied: "I shall faithfully uphold them and dare not violate them again.

Second, as for the confession of a small group (*kṣudrasaṃgha*), the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If four persons receive the confession of another, there is no sense of 'informing the Saṃgha with a single motion' (*jñapti*);
one may only orally inquire of those nearby. Now, following the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this refers to a small group within the context of extinguishing disputes.
This refers to groups of two or three people; even if there are four, there is no procedure for a *śuddhaka-śveta* (single announcement), as it remains identical to the ritual for a small assembly.
Within this, there are six steps: first, requesting the master of confession (*kṣamāpaka*) as before; second, the one receiving the confession asks those nearby, "Venerable sirs (or sisters), listen:
I shall receive the confession of [the name of] such-and-such a bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī)," to which they reply, "Listen"; third, the explanation is given.

The general preliminaries are the same as before. To clearly explain the formula for relinquishing [the offense], one says: "Venerable Sister (or Venerable Brother), please attend to me with a single mind.

I, the bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī) [Name], have committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense [such as touching a woman’s body or clothing; for a bhikṣuṇī, it refers to stealing three *kārsāpaṇas* or more]. I do not remember the number [of times I have committed it]—[if the number is known, state 'I remember' according to the frequency].

Now I openly confess and repent before the Venerable Sister (or Venerable Brother)," and so forth, as in the previous cases. Fifth is the reprimand; sixth is the proclamation of the root of the offense.

The preceding parts are all the same as previously explained. Regarding the third section, the method for confessing before a single person, there are five parts: first, requesting the confession master;
second, stating the root of the offense—these two are the same as the previous [sections]; third, the formal text for relinquishing the offense: "Venerable Sister, please attend to me.
I, the bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī) [Name], having committed the offense of *sthūlātyaya* by tearing apart my three robes out of a mind of anger, now [confess] before the Venerable One."

(Regarding the Venerable Sister: The confession (*pratikarman*) and so forth are as previously stated; the four types of censure (*codanā*) and the five formal agreements (*samādāna*) are likewise explained as before.

Fourth, regarding the method for repenting *pāyattika* offenses: since the thirty matters concerning forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) are extensive and detailed, explaining them here might cause the student weariness;
therefore, they are set aside for the subsequent chapter so that those seeking [instruction] may easily understand them. Within this section, there are two parts.

Before confessing the root offense (*mūlāpatti*), one must first confess the *tirokuṭika* (concealment) *duṣkṛta* (as explained in detail below). For now, let us set forth the method for confessing the root offense.
First, invite a pure [monk or nun] to serve as the presiding master of confession (*pratideśanā-ācārya*). One should say: "Venerable Sir" (or "Sister"), please attend to me with a single mind.
I, [the monk or nun] so-and-so, now request Venerable Sir (or Sister) to act as my presiding master for the confession of a *pāyattika* offense. May Venerable Sir (or Sister) act for me..."

"Out of compassion, please act as the presiding master for the *pāyattika* confession" (recite three times). The one receiving the confession should say: "How could the physical vessel of such-and-such a person be pure?
This is not a favorable condition for practice. Since you, Elder, have violated the Buddha's precepts, you must repent before the Buddha.
It is like falling to the ground; one must rely upon the very ground to rise again. Therefore, you should give rise to a heart of profound sincerity."
I request all Buddhas of the ten directions to simultaneously provide their empowerment as witnesses for me, and to further explain that offerings and sustenance are difficult to digest.
If a practitioner says, "What kind of characteristics do my transgressions have? How could I conceal them? and wishes to perform repentance, they must fully disclose them.

For those who harbor doubts or lack understanding, these matters shall later be resolved. The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Sūtra on Good Observation*) states: "If, while alive, one has reviled another person..."
One who enters *nirvāṇa* while having reviled others should seek repentance; one should perform confession at the site of *nirvāṇa*.
Having confessed, the gate to the heavenly realms shall not be closed. The words of formal confession are as follows: "Venerable Sister (or Elder Brother), please attend to me with single-mindedness.

I, [Name], a *bhikṣu* (or *bhikṣuṇī*), have committed intentional false speech and slanderous speech, each of which I do not recall the number of times [if the number is recalled, state it according to the frequency of the offenses]. Now, before you..."
"Venerable Sister, I confess and reveal [my offense]; I do not dare to conceal it. Through confession there is peace and happiness; through non-confession there is no peace and happiness.
Remembering my transgression, I reveal it and, knowing it, do not dare to conceal it. May the Venerable Sister bear in mind that my body of pure precepts is complete and that my *poṣadha* is pure.
(Recite this three times. Having finished the confession, one asks: "Do you recognize this offense? The respondent says: [Yes].

The preceptor further said, "From this day forward, do not commit such offenses again, such as [the transgressions of] 'protecting the goose' or 'tying with grass. [The disciple] replied, "I shall receive and uphold these instructions.
Fifth, regarding the method for confessing the *pāyattika* (提舍尼) offenses, there are six parts within it: first, one must confess the *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅) offense of concealment.

Second, the request for the master of confession: "Venerable Sister (or Elder Sister), please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I now request the Venerable Sister to act as the master of confession for the *pāyattika* offenses.
May the Venerable Sister graciously act as my master of confession for the *pāyattika* offenses out of compassion.
(Recite this three times. Third, the confession of evil karma is as before. Fourth, the formal recitation of the text: "Venerable Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind."

(Bhikṣu or Bhikṣuṇī), [Name], when not ill, having accepted food with one's own hands from a non-relative female layperson at a layperson’s house, did not remember the count; now remembering, one says one remembers. [The nun] says: "When not ill, you begged ghee, oil, and so forth from a householder;
you did not remember the count; now remembering, you say you remember. "Venerable Sister, I have committed a censurable act which ought not to be done.

I now repent before the Venerable Sister and shall not conceal it. Through repentance there is peace and happiness; without repentance there is no peace and happiness. I acknowledge this transgression."

I confess this openly and do not dare to conceal it. May the Venerable Sister remember that my body of pure precepts is complete and that I have fulfilled the pure *poṣadha* (one recitation suffices).
The fifth [section], self-reproach, and the sixth, the formal vow, are both explained as before.
Regarding the sixth, the confession of *duṣkṛta* (transgressions): according to this Vinaya, there are two types; first, those committed intentionally, which constitute a fundamental *duṣkṛta*.
Rāma again committed two *duṣkṛta* offenses of improper conduct (*anācāra*): one committed intentionally and one committed unintentionally.

Although there are these two textual accounts, the method for performing two separate confessions has not yet been distinguished. Now, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, if committed intentionally, one should confess before a single person;
if committed through error, one should perform a confession of self-reproach within one's own mind. The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states that for minor offenses...
For those whose sense of self-reproach is heavy, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) is likewise [applicable]. This is clear and evident, manifest even on the public road.
Recently, many masters have frequently cited this Vinaya text; furthermore, there are minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*) for which one does not confess before another person.

Relying solely on this single passage, they have all followed suit in making a general judgment, yet I fear this may not penetrate the great principle and results in a lapse regarding the Dharma. For the Vinaya, based on the minor offenses, [prescribes confession] before another person.
Not confessing before another person refers to an offense committed through negligence; discussing confession before a single person refers to an offense committed intentionally.

For instance, if the offenses of various categories are concealed and not disclosed—not out of doubt or ignorance—this concealment is even more grave; how could it be considered light as a mere error?

Next, to clarify the minor offenses of preliminary effort (*prayoga*) belonging to the various categories: for example, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct, it is when one gives rise to the intention and desires to move the body or speech, yet...

Regarding those offenses for which no preparatory effort has yet been undertaken—ranging from infractions concerning physical form up to *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing)—if one gives rise to the intention to make the body uneven or to wear the three robes improperly, then regardless of whether the offense is light or heavy, one must confess before another person.

This is because the arising of an unwholesome intention to move the body or speech is subsumed under "intentional action" (*sañcicca-kamma*). As for those *dukkaṭa* offenses that stand alone, such as the hundred rules of the *Sekhiya* (Trainings), they are treated in the same manner.

Regarding cases where the offense does not arise after the various chapters [of the Vinaya], there are likewise both intentional and unintentional offenses. Therefore, for one who acts intentionally, one must confess before others;
for one who acts unintentionally, one is to take responsibility within one's own mind. Now, first, regarding the intentional offender, there are two parts:

first, one should repent of the *tshig-ira* (duṣkṛta) of concealment, and subsequently repent of the fundamental *tshig-ira*. One must not, because the names are identical, combine them with the fundamental offense and repent of them together.
The *Pudgalavastu* states: "If one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceals it intentionally, one should be instructed to perform a confession for a *duṣkṛta* offense;

once this has been done, the *paryuṣitaparivāsa* (concealment) *karma* is to be granted. The same applies to offenses from *pāyattika* down to *durbhāṣita*. Now, based on this text, I shall first explain the procedure regarding the precept against sexual misconduct;
the procedures for concealing other categories of offenses may be understood by analogy. One should fully observe the dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*) and, with a sincere mind, speak these words:"
I, [name], a bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī), respectfully inform the Buddhas of the ten directions: I have intentionally committed a pārājika offense against the precept of sexual misconduct;

regarding the preparatory acts (*pūrvakarma*) prior to the actual movement of the body, I do not recall the number of *duṣkṛta* offenses (one should state the number according to how many there were, even if it is in the hundreds of millions).

I recognize these as offenses and now intentionally conceal them, thereby committing *duṣkṛta* offenses for which I do not recall the number; furthermore, I commit *duṣkṛta* offenses by successively concealing each preceding one.
I do not recall the specific number [of transgressions], but I now, before the Buddhas of the ten directions, openly confess and repent, not daring to conceal them.
Through confession there is peace and happiness; without confession there is no peace and happiness. Recalling my offenses, I disclose them and, knowing them, do not dare to conceal them.
May the Buddhas of the ten directions bear in mind that my body of pure precepts is complete and that my *poṣadha* is pure. (One recitation suffices.)
Next, before repenting for the root offenses, first invite one [bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī] to serve as the presiding master of repentance. “Venerable Sister, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī] named so-and-so, now invite the Venerable Sister to serve as my presiding master for the repentance of *duṣkṛta* offenses.

May the Venerable Sister graciously act as my presiding master for the repentance of *duṣkṛta* offenses out of compassion. (One need only say this once. “Venerable Sister, please attend to me with a single mind.”
I, [Name], a bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī), have intentionally committed a violation of the precept against sexual misconduct;

although the preparatory acts did not proceed to physical contact, I do not recall the number of *duṣkṛta* offenses (if they are recalled, say "recalled"). I now confess and repent before the Venerable Sister, not daring to conceal them.

Through confession there is peace and happiness; without confession there is no peace and happiness. Remembering my transgression, I disclose it and, knowing it, do not dare to conceal it. May there be merit.

"Venerable Sister (or Elder Sister), please remember that my body of pure precepts is complete and my *poṣadha* is pure (attained by a single recitation). Second, explaining those who act erroneously:

this refers to when the mind is not bound in mindfulness and, encountering conditions, non-virtue arises externally, such as dressing robes unevenly, sitting or rising improperly, laughing, joking, or speaking falsely; all these arise because of a lack of collected mindfulness.

Regarding all transgressions, one should first confess them; if they were concealed, one should later repent for that concealment. Although there are differences regarding whether the root offense was committed earlier or later, in all cases one must reproach one's own mind.
For other offenses not fully enumerated here, the application may be understood by analogy.

If a crime has been committed and the dawn has not yet appeared, whether the offender knows of it or suspects it, and if the time for the recitation of the *Poṣadha* draws near and they have not yet confessed, they should go before a pure person—either a *bhikṣu* or a *bhikṣuṇī*—and first disclose it.

One who remembers [the offense] says: "Venerable Sister (or Elder Brother), please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī) [Name], have committed an offense and have not yet repented it.
I now disclose it to you, Venerable Sister (or Elder Brother). Hereafter, I shall repent according to the Dharma. (This requires only one recitation to be effective.

Even if the disclosure has been completed, should one subsequently conceal it again, it constitutes a further concealment (*paryuṣita*), just as in the previous case of disclosure. Regarding offenses of doubtful nature, one should go to a single bhikṣu and say:
Venerable Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so, have developed a doubt regarding a certain matter and have not yet been able to confess it.
I now disclose this to you, Venerable Sister; when a time free from doubt arises later, I shall perform the confession according to the Dharma (one recitation suffices).
Chapter Twenty-four: On Restoring Purity after an Offense of Forfeiture (Naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
This chapter has two main sections: first, a general explanation of the distinctions in the rules for forfeiture; second, an explanation of what constitutes a valid or invalid object of forfeiture.

Within the section on distinctions, there are two divisions: those for monks and those for nuns. For monks, the two types of precious materials—wool and silk—are excluded from forfeiture; for nuns, the two types of precious materials—those kept and those traded—are excluded.

(These are distinguished in the treatise because the procedures for relinquishing them differ when performed solely by oneself or in relation specifically to laypeople. Regarding the objects [of relinquishment], there are two categories: self and other. First, regarding the single precept of wool: it is relinquished by oneself alone. Second, regarding the remaining twenty-nine precepts: they are relinquished in relation to others.

Regarding the relationship with others, there are two categories: monastics and laypeople. Two precepts concerning the acquisition and trade of the two types of precious items are relinquished in relation to laypeople;

the remaining twenty-seven precepts are relinquished in relation to the Sangha. Regarding the relationship with the Sangha, there are two categories: general and specific. The begging of a bowl is [an example of] the specific category.

The essential basis of the precepts is to reside within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) of the Saṃgha; the remaining twenty-six categories of precepts apply universally to both types of persons—those belonging to the Saṃgha and those who are individuals.
Second, regarding the substance of the requisites, there are three types: first, robes; second, medicines; and third, the Triple Gem. When taking robes as the object of focus, there is...
I. The Dharma for the Saṃgha; II. The Dharma for Many Individuals; III. The Dharma for a Single Individual. Regarding the [Dharma] for the Saṃgha, there are four:
I. Relinquishing Property; II. Relinquishing Offenses; III. Returning Robes; IV. Miscellaneous Clarifications. Furthermore, relinquishing property has four aspects: A.

Whether relinquishment of property is required or not; B. Whether it is accomplished or not when forgetting or seeing the original object; C. Cultivating the deportment of relinquishment; D. The formal declaration of relinquishment.
Now, first, regarding the first section within [this treatise], concerning the forfeiture of what has been kept in excess (*ātyaya-naiḥsargika*):

with the exception of the eight types of impure wealth, all other items that must be formally dedicated (*paryavadāpana*)—regardless of whether they are light or heavy—must be brought forward for forfeiture.

For example, if a *bhikṣuṇī* possesses sixteen vessels in excess and fails to dedicate them, she is subject to a formal offense; how then could this not be considered a "heavy" offense? This applies even if the excessive wealth has not yet been formally dedicated.

This applies except in cases where a debt has not yet been received, or where an item has been entrusted by another, or where one has purchased another's property but the price has already been settled and the item has not yet been received—in all such cases, there is no need to demand it.
If it was previously received and is now being kept with another, this must be demanded and relinquished.

If it has already entered one’s own hands, with the exception of communal property that has not yet been divided, it should be relinquished to the Triple Gem; otherwise, it definitely belongs to another person.
Incense cloths, desks, tables, windows, doors, curtains, screens, bed hangings, pillows, mats, and the like must not be discarded.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Samantapāsādikā* state that items such as beds, mattresses, rugs, bolsters, woolen carpets, clothing, canopies, and so forth all belong to the category of "room-objects" (*vihāra-vastu*) and need not be formally purified through the rite of *viśuddhi*.

However, for items such as handkerchiefs and alms-bowl bags, if they are not used for wearing on the body, there is no offense regarding keeping them in excess; yet if they are worn on the body, such as sandals, [the rules differ].

Footwear and sandals that are not included among one's robes need not be collected and relinquished; however, other personal requisites—whether woolen blankets or covers—must all be collected and relinquished.
Regarding the three robes, if one leaves them overnight regardless of their quantity and commits an offense of relinquishment, each is specifically named individually in the text.
Next, concerning the relinquishment through sale, this refers to using one's own hand to [sell] items to a layperson.

Whether purchasing clothing, food, or any other requisites—ranging from robes, bowls, and water flasks to sandals and shoes—one does not inquire as to their quality, quantity, lightness, or heaviness.

Although this may not constitute the offense of "keeping in excess" (*atireka*), there is nothing that does not involve one personally adjudicating the price through dispute, whether by raising or lowering it by even a single coin;
thus, all such buying and selling constitutes the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). Therefore, the Vinaya states: "Various kinds of buying and selling constitute *naiḥsargika*."
Since the *Śīlavibhaṅga* (Pāyattika) does not permit this ruling, it follows that fields, houses, slaves, servants, vehicles, and draft animals must likewise be forfeited.

For these, one should merely perform a *duṣkṛta* confession; there is no need for formal forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*), because their nature is that of heavy objects which cannot be carried about while practicing the Path.
The principle states: if one’s means of livelihood are excessive, they should be distributed elsewhere.

If one discards the offenses associated with various locations separately, yet performs a collective confession for them all at a single location, then after the confession is complete, it is permissible to return the robes to those respective locations in sequence.

Regarding the second case: if, after having discarded the robes, one sees an original item that was forgotten and thinks, "Is this not [mine]?"—that is to say, once the robes have been discarded or returned, but before the *pariśuddhi* (purification/declaration of purity) has been performed, if one suddenly sees an original object that had not been discarded and immediately conceives the thought that it belongs to oneself, it then becomes [one's own] again.
If the relinquishing of all stained items is not accomplished, one must further perform the act of relinquishment (*pratyāśraya*).

If one has already relinquished them and performed the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*), yet later sees that the previously relinquished items were forgotten, the prior relinquishment remains valid and the purity is not lost. Regarding the items forgotten later, one must relinquish them separately according to the prescribed form.

If the robes have already been relinquished but have not yet been returned to their owner, and one then sees the original forgotten items, one must relinquish them separately; these, together with the robes relinquished earlier, shall be returned to the owner as a whole.

The *Tong shuo jing yi* (Meaning of the Common Declaration of Purity) states: "Since one knows that it is not easy to recover property once forgotten, at the very moment of relinquishing the property, one should give rise to this thought:
'Whatever items are currently assembled, I now relinquish them all; as for those not yet assembled, I shall certainly relinquish them to the Triple Gem or to other individuals.

Having thus completed the relinquishment, even if one sees the original forgotten object, regardless of whether it is early or late, the previous relinquishment remains valid. If one relinquishes [the property], [it is accomplished].

If, after returning the robe, one has not yet performed the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification), and upon seeing the original object one forgets it, only then giving rise to the thought of relinquishment, this does not constitute [the offense].

This is because the intention of defilement arose first, and the mind of relinquishment arose later. Therefore, regarding surplus property, once the relinquishment is completed, if one subsequently sees that surplus property again, there is the sense of "defiled attachment" (*saṃrakta*).
If, however, one sees the original forgotten object and it is property for trade, there is no sense of "defiled attachment"; this applies if it is indeed property for trade.
When the forfeiture and restoration are completed, if one sees the original object but forgets it, and the surplus property exceeds ten days, this falls under the category of "defiled by association.
One should then treat it as a forfeiture for surplus property; once the offense for trading the property has been confessed and the forfeiture is complete, it remains the same as surplus property.
Third, regarding the practice of the ritual of relinquishment (*śikṣāpada-vinaya*): the meaning is that one brings the items to be relinquished into the midst of the assembly;
having performed the fourfold prostrations to the Sangha as prescribed for the ritual of deportment, one kneels on the right knee near the clothing or objects and holds them in one's hands.

The fourth section clearly sets forth the formula for relinquishment, stating: "Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! I, the Bhikṣu [or Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so, have intentionally kept a surplus of [numerous] articles for more than ten days without declaring them as pure;
this constitutes an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. I have stayed overnight separated from my three robes [specifying whether they are the three robes or five robes];

this constitutes an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. I have obtained wealth through trade; this constitutes an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. I have requested clothing from a householder who is not a relative."

[Having committed] several instances of the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* [offenses]—[specifying the offense, such as "misappropriating the property of the Saṃgha," etc., according to what was committed]—I now relinquish these articles to the Saṃgha. (One recitation suffices.
In the second part, the relinquishment of the offense (*āpatti-pratyaya*), there are seven distinct points: 1. Requesting confession before the Saṃgha; 2. Entreating the master of confession; 3.

The master of confession performing a formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize the Saṃgha; 4. Explaining the root of the offense so that they may recognize its gravity; 5. Formally declaring the offense.
This is called the sixth [step], reproaching [the offender] to induce shame; the seventh is making a solemn vow and formal commitment. First, regarding the request for confession before the Saṃgha:

the [Bhikṣu or Bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so comes into the midst of the Saṃgha, fully assuming the proper dignified demeanor, and speaks as follows: "Venerable Sisters (or Brothers) of the Saṃgha, please listen.

I, the Bhikṣu (or Bhikṣuṇī) so-and-so, intentionally kept [a certain number of] long-term surplus items exceeding ten days without declaring them pure (*paryāpanna*). I have committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). Having stayed apart from my three robes for [one] night... (according to the three cases...)

Regarding robes: if one possesses more or fewer than the five robes [required], one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; if one acquires wealth through trade, one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for however much is obtained.

Once these items have been relinquished to the Saṃgha, one commits a fundamental *pāyattika* offense for each. If one does not remember the number, [the rule states] "if one remembers the number"—meaning one remembers the three robes or the five robes—one must calculate them accordingly.

Furthermore, if one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense regarding the relinquished wealth and then uses it up or destroys it, one also commits a fundamental *pāyattika* offense; this applies even if one does not remember [the specific details].

[Recite the count: "I remember... I remember. If the property is currently present, this [procedure] is not required; according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one borrows a robe and accepts it for use, even if separated from it overnight, one need only confess the offense—the robe itself does not need to be relinquished.
Now, one requests confession from the Saṃgha, saying: "May the Saṃgha listen to me. I, the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī], so-and-so, request confession out of compassion" (recite three times).
Having finished speaking, the presiding elder (upādhyāya) informs the Saṃgha, saying: "I have accepted his confession. Second, the one requesting confession [should address] the master of confession.
One must invite a pure [bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī] who has not committed the four pārājikas, the eight [pārājika-like offenses], or the thirteen *anantarāya* obstacles;

one who has previously committed offenses of the lower four categories (*catur-apatti*) must have already repented them before being permitted to accept another’s invitation. Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"One who has committed an offense may not accept another’s confession, nor may they resolve the offense for one who has committed an offense; furthermore, they may not even say..."

Because the offenses are not identical, within the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when bandits intended to kill two bhikṣus and feared they might die while still bearing their transgressions, the Buddha permitted those whose offenses were not identical to perform confession.

What constitutes "not being identical"? For example, if there are two people who have committed offenses—one having destroyed living seeds and the other having used water containing insects—and such a life-threatening danger arises, the Buddha permitted them to confess. This is not the case at present.

The principle is difficult to grasp and I fear it will not clarify the text of the formal invitation; although the ritual rules do not explicitly describe this matter, its meaning must be established so that the procedure may be complete.
When the time for the invitation arrives, [a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī] says: "Venerable Sister (or Great Virtue), please attend to me with one mind.

I, the bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī) named so-and-so, now invite you, Venerable Sister (or Great Virtue), to act as the presiding master for the confession of a *pāyattika* offense. May the Venerable Sister (or Great Virtue) act for me as the presiding master for the *pāyattika*..."

"O Master of the *pāyattika* confession, out of compassion for me... (recite three times). Regarding the third point, when the one receiving the confession has not yet received an answer, should they not first harmonize with the Saṃgha?
One should say: "The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall it perform? The answer is: "The formal motion (*jñapti*) for receiving the confession.
If one knows that [the offender] should sit and return the robe, one should respond: "Perform the formal motion for receiving the confession and the *karmavācanā* for returning the robe. Great!

(Virtuous Sister), may the Saṃgha listen: [The name of] the bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī [so-and-so] has intentionally kept [a certain number of] surplus articles for more than ten days without declaring them as pure, thereby committing an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;

[he/she] has stayed overnight separated from the three robes [or five robes, as the case may be], thereby committing an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; [he/she] has obtained wealth through trade, thereby committing an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
These articles have now been relinquished to the Saṃgha; herein each has committed a fundamental *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding offenses that cannot be remembered by number (if they can be remembered, one should state them according to their quantity): furthermore, if one has committed the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) by using up or destroying the cloth or wealth [subject to forfeiture] oneself, this also constitutes a root *pāyattika* offense that cannot be remembered by number (if it can be remembered, one need not say "the wealth remains").
Now, I beg the Saṃgha for confession. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant me [the bhikṣu/bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so leave to confess. Thus I inform you.

Fourth, the one who accepts the confession shall explain the retribution for sinful offenses, saying: "Venerable Sister, since you are a disciple of the Buddha, having gone forth from home in reliance upon the Buddha and practicing the pure precepts of the Buddha, why do you now willfully violate them?
What name can such a person bear? The Buddha established the prohibitive precepts so that one would rather die than transgress them;
even when robes and bowls are kept with the person, surplus robes must be declared as 'pure' (*śuddhaka*). Now, by contravening the holy teachings, you are called a breaker of the precepts."

If people lack a sense of shame and accept the faithful offerings of others, eating the food given by others is like having molten copper poured into their mouths, and wearing the robes given by others is like being clad in sheets of hot iron.

Upon death, they enter hell, where in their hunger they swallow glowing iron balls and in their thirst they drink boiling bronze liquid, undergoing various sufferings for immeasurable years. Thereafter, they are reborn as insects, constantly dwelling in latrines.
Because you consumed impure food, you may be reborn among the hairless owls or the featherless birds, or born in a land of the naked where one is perpetually without clothing;

because you have stayed overnight separated from the three robes, you undergo such great suffering. (Venerable Sister), you should now give rise to great shame and remorse, and personally seek mercy and repent before the Buddha and the Sangha.
Within the fifth section, the "Correct Repentance for Sins," there are two major parts; first, the repentance.
Regarding the fundamental offense of concealing a transgression and subsequent regret: within the initial period of concealment, there are nine grades of *duṣkṛta*.
First, having committed the fundamental offense, one forms the intention to conceal it and fails to disclose it; this constitutes one *duṣkṛta*.
When the first watch of the night has passed and the dawn light appears, one commits another *duṣkṛta*. From the second watch onwards, through many nights, one commits yet another [instance].
Regarding the offenses of "successive concealment" (*anuvartana-paticchādana*): these three offenses arise following the original root offense.

Second, if one commits the offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) regarding a robe and, without having yet performed confession, immediately wears it, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for every instance of wearing it;

this constitutes one category of *dukkaṭa*. Furthermore, having passed the first night, if one continues to conceal the offense during the second night and thereafter, this is termed "successive concealment."
Having concealed these two [offenses], and subsequently wearing an impure robe out of attachment, a third offense arises.

These fundamental offenses, along with the concealments and so forth, remain unconfessed when the *Prātimokṣa* is recited; during the three inquiries at nine locations, failing to inform the Saṃgha constitutes the single category of *duṣkṛta* for silent lying.
Furthermore, on the first night, one commits the offense of concealment, and on the second night, one commits the offense of concealment once again.
That which has already passed is called "successive transmission"; these two categories arise after silent lying. Now, these nine categories are collectively termed *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the number of transgressions, they are immeasurable and boundless; they are all included within the confession (*pratideśanā*).

One should say, "I do not recall the number," and so forth, following this procedure for the confession of the first seven groups (*nikāya*) of offenses. Alternatively, if there is no concealment (*praticchādana*), then this [formula] is not required.
Although the nine grades mentioned above are all designated as *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), there are two distinct ways of committing and repenting offenses within their respective stages:
first, when one commits the root offense first and the secondary branches arise later; and second, when one first repents the secondary branches and later repents the root.

This chapter is thus; however, this is not necessarily the case for other sections. The Vinaya contains established texts on this matter, which are not merely human compositions. This concludes the present section.
Next, I shall clarify the sequence of the confession (*pratideśanā*). Within this, there are three parts. First, one should first perform a self-reproach of the mind;

subsequently, regarding the six categories of *dukkaṭa* offenses arising from concealment, one should properly assume the dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*) and, proceeding before an image of the Buddha, bare the right shoulder, join the palms, and speak as follows:
"I, [monk or nun] so-and-so, intentionally possessed many extra robes exceeding ten [days]."

If one fails to perform the *poṣadha* (confession of purity), one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (the specific number of items committed is recorded herein). If one knowingly conceals this offense intentionally, one commits a *duṣkṛta*. If one does not remember the number [of days] but has concealed it for a night, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

If one does not remember the number [of nights], one incurs a *duṣkṛta* for each successive night of concealment. If one wears or uses an impure robe that ought to be relinquished, one commits a *duṣkṛta*. One incurs a *duṣkṛta* by merely stating [the offense once]. If one conceals it for successive nights, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* for each night.
If one does not remember the number [of nights], one incurs a *duṣkṛta*. If one wears or uses an impure robe that ought to be relinquished, one commits a *duṣkṛta*.

If one does not recall the number of nights spent concealing [an offense], it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); if one does not recall the number [of nights] as they pass, it is a *duṣkṛta* for each night of concealment.

If one does not recall the number of times one has committed the *duṣkṛta* of lying by remaining silent during the three formal inquiries at the *Poṣadha* ceremony of the Saṃgha, and then conceals it for a number of nights, it is a *duṣkṛta* for each successive night of concealment.
I do not recall the number of *duṣkṛta* offenses; I now confess and repent them before the Buddha, not daring to conceal them.
Through confession there is peace and happiness; without confession there is no peace and happiness. Recalling my transgressions, I disclose them; knowing them, I dare not conceal them.
May all Buddhas bear witness that my body of precepts is complete and pure, and that I have performed the *poṣadha*. (One recitation suffices. Second, [addressed] to one [monk].
A bhikṣuṇī should first repent before [another] bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī for the three grades of grave *duṣkṛta* offenses committed since birth.

She must maintain proper decorum and first request one pure bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī to serve as the presiding master for the repentance of the *duṣkṛta*. The text for this request is as previously explained in the section on the confession of the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses:
"Venerable Sister, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī named so-and-so, have intentionally kept many extra robes beyond the permitted limit..."

If ten days pass without performing the *poṣadha* (confession of purity), one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense [the specific gravity of which is to be recorded here according to the number of transgressions]. If one recognizes a fault and conceals it for a night, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense;

if the number is not remembered [if remembered, state "remembered"], one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Furthermore, if one wears and uses an impure robe that should be relinquished, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense;

if the number is not remembered, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. During the *saṃgha-poṣadha*, if one remains silent through the nine locations and three inquiries, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of false speech by silence.
I do not recall the specific number of my offenses; I now confess them openly before the Venerable Sister and dare not conceal them.
Through confession there is peace and happiness; through non-confession there is no peace or happiness. Remembering my transgressions, I confess them and, knowing them, dare not conceal them.
May the Venerable Sister bear in mind that my body of pure precepts is complete and that my *poṣadha* is pure. (This is accomplished by a single recitation. The one receiving the confession says:

Reproaching yourself, you should give rise to a mind of weary detachment and reply: "I shall receive and uphold [this precept]. Fearing that it might cause weariness to the Sangha, I shall not abandon my robe until the time [for its relinquishment];
having first performed repentance in another place, I shall subsequently directly confess the *thullaccaya* offense—this is the most essential point.

Third, regarding the repentance for the fundamental offenses (*mūlāpatti*): "Venerable Sister (or Venerable Brother), please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī) [Name], have intentionally kept [a certain number of] extra robes beyond the permitted limit."

If one keeps a robe for more than ten days without performing the *pāriśuddhi* (declaration of purity), one commits an offense of forfeiture and expiation (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If one sleeps apart from the three robes [or five robes, as the case may be], one commits an offense of forfeiture and expiation.

If one sells [robes] and acquires wealth [in whatever quantity], one commits an offense of forfeiture and expiation. Having already forfeited these articles to the Saṃgha, one commits a fundamental *pāyattika* offense for each;
if the number is not remembered, [one says] "I remember" and declares it according to the number of offenses. Furthermore, one commits an offense of forfeiture regarding the robe.
If wealth has already been used up and exhausted, one also commits a *pāyattika* offense of the root category (*mūla-pāyattika*) for failing to keep count [of the items].

(Regarding "failing to keep count": if the substance of the wealth is currently present, this [offense] is not required. Now, I confess and repent before the Venerable Sister; I dare not conceal it. Through confession there is peace and happiness;
without confession there is no peace and happiness. Recalling the transgression, I confess it; knowing it, I dare not conceal it. May the Venerable One...
(Virtuous Sister), remember my pure body of precepts and the fulfillment of the pure *poṣadha* (three times). Sixth, the words of censure: "Do you recognize this offense?
He replies, "I recognize it. Again he says: "Reproach yourself; give rise to a mind of weary detachment, such that even if your body withers and your life ends, you shall not commit it again.
Seventh, the formal commitment: He replies, "I shall receive and uphold [this] upon my head."
Now that it has already passed, I dare not transgress again.

Third, regarding the method for returning robes (*cīvara*), there are two parts: first, distinguishing between what is permissible and what is not; second, performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).

If one possesses an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) for more than one month, an extra bowl (*atireka-pātra*) for more than seven days, medicinal requisites beyond the permitted period, or an urgent gift robe (*ātyayika-cīvara*) beyond the time limit, and if a nun keeps such items for ten days, [the following applies].
Regarding these six articles, all six precepts are violated by the fault of hoarding them out of greed; they must be returned after one night has passed.

This is because the purpose is to sever the continuity of the attachment. If the intention to keep them is not severed, according to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, even if many days have elapsed, it is feared that the offense will not be cleared.

As for the two types of "separation from robes" (*cīvara-vipravāsa*) and other matters such as selling items or misappropriating property belonging to the Saṃgha, one must sit in penance (*prāyaścitta*) to restore them.

If, as if returning after a night has passed, there are circumstances such as a long journey that make it difficult for the assembly to gather, one should perform a *kṣepa-karman* (transference rite) on the spot and entrust [the robe] to a *kalyāṇamitra* (a monk or nun). Once that person has received the robe, they should deliver it in a private place.

Now, to clarify the *karman* for staying overnight apart from one's robe while returning directly, it is said: "Venerable Sisters, may the Saṃgha listen. [Monk/Nun], so-and-so, intentionally stays apart..."

Overnight Separation from Robes: An Offense Requiring Forfeiture (the name of the robe—whether it be one of the three robes or five robes—is to be stated accordingly). This robe has already been forfeited to the Saṃgha.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, now return this robe to [the monk or nun] named so-and-so. Thus is the formal motion (*jñapti*). O Virtuous Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
[The monk or nun] named so-and-so has committed an offense of forfeiture due to overnight separation from his/her robe. This robe has already been forfeited to the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha now...

"Returning this robe to [the name of] the bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī [so-and-so]: Whichever elders or sisters of the Saṃgha consent to returning this robe to the bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī [so-and-so], let them remain silent;
whoever does not consent, let them speak. The Saṃgha has finished returning this robe to the bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī [so-and-so].
Because the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld. If one keeps an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*) and so forth overnight..."
If the return [of the items] is permitted, one should wait until the next day to assemble the Saṃgha as described above to perform the *karmavācanā* for the return.

If the *karmavācanā* is performed on the same seat through a successive transfer, it should be said: "Venerable Sisters (or Brothers), may the Saṃgha listen: The Bhikṣu (or Bhikṣuṇī) So-and-so has intentionally kept several extra robes beyond ten days without performing the *viśuddhi* (purification/declaration).
This constitutes an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. These articles have already been relinquished to the Saṃgha. If...

The Saṃgha, the time having arrived, let the Saṃgha listen with patience. The Saṃgha now takes these robes and articles and gives them to [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so, who shall return them to [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so. This motion is thus made: "Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen.

[Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so has kept many extra robes for more than ten days without declaring them as pure (apariśuddha), thereby committing an offense of forfeiture and transgression (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). These robes..."

The items have already been relinquished to the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha now holds these robes and articles to give them to [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so, who shall then return them to [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so.

Those of you, Venerable Elders and Sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha holding these robes and articles to give them to [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so, who shall then return them to [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so, remain silent.

Whoever does not approve, let them speak; the Saṃgha has approved and the Saṃgha bestows these robes and articles upon [the monk or nun] so-and-so, who shall return them to [the monk or nun] so-and-so. Since the Saṃgha approves by silence, this matter is thus upheld.
The fourth section, a miscellaneous clarification and analysis: If a robe has been relinquished but is retained and not returned, one incurs only a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).

However, if it is subsequently sold for use and never returned, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*) based on the value of the money. Thus, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "The offense is a true relinquishment, while the robe itself is a provisional relinquishment. Question:
If one first confesses the root offense but later regrets it and conceals it, is this permissible? Answer: It is not permissible; therefore, the *Vinaya-mātṛkā* states as follows.
It is said that if one has concealed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and the *mānatva* penance was not performed according to the Dharma, the offense cannot be cleared.
If one performs a *jñapti* (formal motion) alone to relinquish the confession, it requires at least five persons; only then is it valid.

This is because, in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) is included within the category of the "five-person Saṃgha," as the presiding confessor is excluded from the count when the formal motion is being deliberated.

Second, regarding the method for relinquishing medicine: since the forfeiture offense (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) concerning seven-day medicine is rare and the *Vinaya* texts describe it in detail as being largely the same as the relinquishment of robes, one may apply that procedure by analogy.
Furthermore, the relinquishment applies to three types of persons: the Saṃgha, oneself, and a pure person.
