Third, regarding the clarification on the forfeiture of money and treasures: one should take the current stored money and treasures and relinquish them to a pure person (*śuci-pudgala*), saying, "This is mine which I ought not to possess;

you should know this. One must confess the offense before the Saṃgha. When requesting the confession, the presiding monk asks, "Have you already relinquished all the stored money and treasures to a pure person?
If he replies, "I have already relinquished them," [the procedure continues]; if he says, "I have not relinquished them," [it is not permitted].

Having taught the relinquishment according to the Dharma, one then performs the confession of the offense together with the others as before. Second, regarding the relinquishment before two or three people, there are three parts:
first, the relinquishment of material goods, which has four sub-sections: (1) determining what must and what need not be relinquished;

(2) whether the act is completed if one forgets or sees the original object; (3) the ritual deportment for the relinquishment—these three gates are all explained as before; (4) the words of relinquishment.

"Recite 'Venerable Sisters, please attend to me with one mind' (the latter phrase of the formula). Conclude by saying: 'I now relinquish [this offense] to the two or three Venerable Sisters for the purpose of purification.

Apart from this, it is the same as before. Second, regarding the relinquishment of offenses (*āpatti-pratideśanā*), there are six parts; because this is directed toward individuals, there is no formal request (*yācanā*).

First, the invitation to the presiding master (*karmavācaka*) is the same as before. Second, the single formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize the Saṃgha is transformed into a question to those standing nearby, who should then ask."
A bystander says: "Two or three virtuous sisters (de-si), listen as I receive the confession of [the bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so. The bystander should respond: "Very well.
This is from the section on resolving disputes in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, specifically the passage concerning the person who asks for instruction.

Third is the explanation of the gravity of the offense; fourth is the formal declaration of relinquishing the offense; fifth is the censure and remedial treatment; sixth is the making of a solemn vow.

Regarding these four gates, all are explained as before. Third, concerning the returning of robes: because this involves a specific individual, two or three people must properly consult together on the spot;
tomorrow, they shall distribute them according to circumstances. Third, regarding the case of one person, there are three parts:
first, the relinquishing of the material object should be stated as: "Venerable Sister (or Brother), please attend to me with one mind... [and so forth], concluding the sentence with "I relinquish."

Regarding the second [case], "the abandonment of offenses with one person" (dvitīya-prāyaścitta), since there is but one person, there is no requirement for the formal inquiry of the boundary (sīmā-vinaya);

the rest is the same as before. Regarding the third, "the returning of robes," since there is but one person, there is no need for collective consultation; the principle is that one may give them according to one's own discretion.
It is said that if this method for individuals can be used for confession, then for offenses to be confessed involving four persons or fewer, there is no requirement for formal inquiry.

Regarding the ritual for establishing the *dharmadhātu* boundary and the natural boundary: even if no monks are present, one may perform these rites. However, if there are five or more people capable of performing the rite, it must be conducted as a communal legal act (*saṃghakarma*).
It is not permissible to perform it in the presence of only a single person; even within a natural boundary, one must formally demarcate the boundary to conduct the communal legal act.
When performing the formal renunciation (*pratyādeśana*) through correct confession, one person always serves as the object of the rite; therefore, the remaining four constitute the Saṃgha.

Receiving Invitations and Announcing Assemblies.
This chapter’s main sections consist of eleven items: 1. the method for requesting and receiving the assembly; 2. the method for notifying the assembly; 3. the method for arriving at the residence;
4. the method for taking one's seat; 5. the method for purifying the food; 6. the method for offering incense and reciting prayers of merit;

7. the ritual protocol for receiving the food; 8. the method for clearing away the meal; 9. the method for giving the *dakṣiṇā* (alms-offering); 10. the method for dispersing from the seats and returning home.

First, regarding the invitation to receive the assembly, this Vinaya recognizes two types of invitations: first, the sequential invitation (*saṃgha-krama*), and second, the individual invitation (*pṛthag-nimantraṇā*).
Although the Vinaya permits the individual invitation, many sūtras and śāstras prohibit it; thus, sūtras such as the *Brahmajāla* and the *Benevolent Kings* both condemn it.
As the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Sudarśana-sūtra* state: "Even if one were to individually invite the Buddha and five hundred arhats..."

Therefore, it cannot be called "inviting the Sangha as a field of merit" [if one invites only a few]. However, if one can invite even a single semblance of an extremely wicked bhikṣu from within the Sangha, one still obtains immeasurable karmic fruit.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* state: "It is like drinking seawater; one thereby drinks all its tributary streams.
Regarding the sequential invitation of monks (*saṃgha-krama*), the *Pañcavargika Vinaya* states: "It is solely for the sake of liberation that one leaves the household life."
One who has attained this may take part in the succession of the Saṃgha, with the sole exception of those who have violated the precepts. The *Wubai wen shi* (Five Hundred Questions) states:
"If one receives property on behalf of the Buddha, it is improper for a bhikṣu to eat it. One must never enter the door of a tavern. If there is another gate, one may enter.
If invited to a gathering of bhikṣus, one should observe the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*). On that day, if no alcohol is being sold, one may go to a slaughterhouse."

The same applies to the families of one's children. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When attending a gathering at a layperson’s house, one should borrow bedding from the Saṃgha. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If someone comes to invite a bhikṣu for a meal the following day, one must not give a definitive answer by saying 'I will certainly go. Instead, one should say: 'If there are no obstructing circumstances, I shall inform you.
If there is an invitation to the Saṃgha, one should ask for the names [of the host], whether they are guests or long-time residents, and the location of their residence."

One must not go there abruptly; first, one should inform someone. If a person on monthly duty, a garden-keeper, or a *śrāmaṇera* goes ahead to inquire, they may inadvertently reprimand or disturb the *bhikṣus*, or cause difficulties that might lead to the Sangha losing its meal.
Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "In order to know of the invitation, a *karmadāna* must be appointed.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-saṃgraha* translates this as "Protector of the Monastery" (*sī-rù*), while its original Sanskrit term is said to mean "one who pleases the assembly" (*saṃgha-rañjaka*).

*Yunpola* (雲婆羅) means "succession" (*anupūrva*). The *Five Hundred Questions* states: "If one has accepted a private invitation and sends another person in their stead, it is permissible provided the host has no grievance;
if the host objects, it is an offense of falling (*pāyattika*). The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
'If the invited person goes with the Sangha but enters first without informing [the host], it is an offense of falling. If the host prepares food tomorrow, [the monk] should go there today.'"
If one falls [into an offense], it is not a transgression provided the host calls [one back]. If, after the meal, the host does not detain one and one leaves of one's own accord, it is a *pācittiya*.
If a person managing the affairs of the monastery arrives after the monks, it is a *pācittiya*. If one departs before the food has been offered as a gift (*dakṣiṇā*), it is a *pācittiya*.

Regarding others traveling privately and directly reporting [their arrival] to their fellow students, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Although a *śrāmaṇera* has not yet received full ordination, they are included within the number of *bhikṣus*."
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Even those who have not yet received the ten precepts may accept an invitation. The *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* states:
"If one is traveling on the road, one should form the thought: 'I shall eat at that monastery. If one eats at another location, it is an offense requiring confession (*pāyattika*).

If one encounters monks who have accepted an invitation and goes along with them, there is no offense. The *Sarvāstivāda Daśabhāṇavāra Vinaya* states: "If a donor invites the Saṃgha for a meal, the Saṃgha..."
Next, if one speaks falsely, saying "I should go," when one has not yet arrived, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one obtains food, its value is calculated;

the gravity of the offense is determined by the principle that if there is a sequence for the *saṃgha*, to enter privately and appropriate it for oneself, or to divert it to relatives and friends, the sin is the same as the preceding case.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Eating food that comes unsolicited constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense. The *Pi-nai-ye jing* (Vinaya-sūtra) states: "Due to famine, [the Buddha] permitted invitations for only one or two people."
Therefore, if many people go to disturb the host who is giving alms, it constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense; however, there is no offense if it is for the sake of making robes for a sick monk.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu may obtain canopies and various offering utensils for a lay household’s assembly, provided he does not lift them together with a woman.
The *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu* states: "One need only strike the *ghanṭā* (wooden gong) to receive food offerings; it is not necessary to ask."
Regarding "invited" and "not invited": why is the *ghanṭā* struck? It is originally for the purpose of assembling the Saṃgha.

As for the second [category], the "invitation by request," this Vinaya states: if one wishes to accept an invitation, one should go and stay at the place where the Saṃgha regularly takes its small and large meals.
When the donor announces that the time has arrived, the Elder (*sthavira*) should go first, proceeding like a flock of geese.

When departing, the bhikṣus should walk behind with their right shoulders bared. If there are matters concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, or a sick bhikṣu, they should inform the senior monk (upādhyāya or sthavira) and proceed ahead.
If there should be dangers to life or to one's spiritual life (brahmacarya) along the way, whether they are questioned or not, they are permitted to depart.
If the senior monk is walking on the road, one should wait for him at the place where one must relieve oneself before proceeding as usual.
Go forward.

Regarding the third point, concerning those who have been invited to a meal, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When you arrive at the place of the meal, you should remain silent and single-minded, maintaining pure deportment to inspire a sense of goodness in others;
you should enter slowly and sit down slowly, contemplating that this food is difficult to seek and difficult to prepare."
It is said that when arriving at the house of the host for a meal invitation, if the seats for the Buddha and the noble Sangha have not yet been prepared, the assembly of monks must not sit down.
One should first arrange the various scriptures and images in a high and prominent location, ensuring they are extremely pure. Thereafter, one should set out the seats for the noble Sangha;

the ritual for this consists of five fascicles, which were translated during the Liang dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master from China [Guṇabhadra] in response to Emperor Wu’s request. The text is extensive and will not be recorded here.

The present record follows the *Pinvilou Jing* (Piṇḍola Sūtra), which states: "One should invite [the Elder] in advance and prepare a seat in a secluded and quiet place using many soft, light materials.
When I come, there shall be signs at the place where I sit. Nowadays, monks and nuns are mostly arrogant;

they treat this dharma with contempt and insult the sacred ritual, thereby especially violating the Buddha’s teachings. Since they themselves lack reverence, they cause laypeople to lose their respect as well—this is the third point.
Regarding the origins of the *Ratnagupta-dharmaparyāya*, from this point onward, the present Elder has further excerpted from the Sūtras and Vinaya to supplement the preceding text.

Although the sequence of the text is not chronological, it does not deviate from the underlying principle. When arranging the seats for the Noble Saṃgha, they must be sufficient to accommodate a single person;

furthermore, one should instruct the donor to prepare these seats according to the Sūtras, ensuring that they are overnight-prepared and that they are cleaner and more excellent than the seats for the ordinary monks.
Furthermore, one must not prick flowers or scatter them upon it, nor may one paint or gild it with copper or tin to make it resemble a Buddha.
The height of its seat must not exceed sixteen inches; otherwise, it is no different from an ordinary seat.

One must also not use the bowls or basins belonging to the monastic community to hold food; these may only be used to offer to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). If one uses a begging bowl, it is permissible for all [types of offerings].

Furthermore, as for the fact that the transformation body and the retribution body do not contradict the underlying principle: this is because the retribution body of Piṇḍola still exists within the category of those who uphold the precepts, being no different from ordinary monks.
How could one possibly touch the pure vessels of the Saṃgha and thereby violate the holy teachings?

Any money belonging to the noble Saṃgha should be returned to the noble Saṃgha for their use; if there is any surplus, it should be used to make seats for the noble Saṃgha or to fashion vessels for their alms bowls.
Utensils such as spoons, chopping knives, and hand-towels may also be used for offerings such as lighting lamps in the shrine hall;
however, one must not fashion images of the Holy Sangha and place them at the head of the seat. If the Sambhogakāya (the Reward Body) were to come in person, how could one push it aside to sit?

Furthermore, one must not take the property of the Holy Sangha to fashion images of Ānanda, Kāśyapa, or others, because these items belong specifically to those individuals and must not be used interchangeably.
Therefore, the Vinaya states that what is permitted in this instance may not be used in another.
Fourth, regarding sitting on seats: this Vinaya records that Prince Bodhi invited the Buddha to walk upon cloth spread over the steps;
the World-Honored One did not accept it and had it removed for the sake of future bhikṣus. Furthermore, [the Buddha] went...
In the dining hall, one should not sit in confusion or in a jumbled crowd; rather, one should sit according to seniority.

Once the *upādhyāya* (senior monk) has sat down, one should observe the middle and junior monks to ensure they do not act improperly or fail to properly cover their bodies. If there is anyone who does so, one should snap one's fingers to alert them, or send someone to speak to them, ensuring they sit well and according to the Dharma.
This applies equally when the middle and junior monks have already sat down, as it does for those above and below them; this is the rule for the Saṃgha.

It is simply stated that "sitting with the body poorly covered" refers to wearing thin, coarse clothing such that the limbs and body are exposed, as when a *mahallaka* (an elderly or unsteady person) sits improperly (*aniyata*).
If a nun sits improperly, one must not speak to her, fearing she may feel shame; rather, one should employ skillful means to have her take up some object.
If a courtesan intentionally acts in this way, one should rise and withdraw. This rule applies up until the time of being invited to a layperson's home.
Once they have finished inquiring of one another regarding their seniority in age, they shall sit down.

If it is feared that the time for the meal is passing, the eight *bhikṣuṇīs* who are of the highest rank may sit in order, while the others sit according to their place; (the *saṃgha* should follow this practice). The *Wubai wenshi* (Five Hundred Questions on Monastic Affairs) states:
"If one sits together with one's teacher and there is no other place available, one may still not share the same bowl for food. The *Śrāmaṇera-vidhi-sūtra* states: "If one [sits] together..."
When sitting for a meal with one's teacher, one should remain six feet away from the teacher; this is because the Vinaya states that one should not sit behind them.
When going to the meal, one need not cause the other bhikṣus to rise; nor need they rise if one has not yet arrived. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If there is something laughable, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should say: 'How can you show your teeth like this within the Noble Vinaya?'"

If one laughs with bared teeth, one should endure it; by cultivating the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, as well as the thought of death, one should gradually restrain oneself even if laughter cannot be stopped immediately by covering the mouth with a corner of one’s robe.

As for bodily instability, one should move the hands and feet, even to the point of breaking off blades of grass, until one gradually achieves self-mastery. The underlying meaning is that when entering a house of mourning, one must strictly refrain from loud laughter and jesting.
To engage in frivolous talk regarding worldly affairs and thereby incur the reproach of the laity, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If one is invited to a place outside [the monastery] and there is a visiting bhikṣu who cannot enter, one should ask the host for permission to let him in. If he does not permit it, one should say: 'Give me my share of the food; we shall eat together.
If he still does not permit it, one should personally inform the community of the monastery that there is food available and go there instead. Then...

When performing the *sarvabuddha* (universal) recitation, one should gather all the bhikṣus outside the gate in one place; call one person in, and even those who have not yet assembled must also be called in.
Although the *gandī* gong may be struck, one must ultimately ensure that no one is excluded, for only then is the assembly pure.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "The World-Honored One always sits in the midst of the assembly, with the bhikṣus on his left and on his right."

Lay devotee. Regarding the fifth point on pure food, the Elder of this *vinaya* should ask: "Are the fruits and vegetables pure? If it is said they are not yet [prepared], he should instruct them to make them pure. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"The Elder should know who is inspecting the rooms and who is ill; he should instruct that food be given to them. If it is a donor...

If there is someone who is particularly fond [of the recipient], one should say to them: "The Dharma of Long Life should be bestowed; it must not be withheld. If it is already late in the day, one should first take [the offering] and dismiss them so they may depart.

Regarding the sixth [item], the incense-offering and prayer for blessings (*gandha-pūjā-praṇidhāna*): according to this Vinaya, the Buddha performed the prayer for blessings only after he had accepted the parched grain meal (*maṇḍaka*) from the merchants.
In the *Yi Changzhezijing* (The Sutra of the Householder’s Son), it is stated that before the meal, one should perform the ritual of incantation and aspiration (*dhāraṇī-pūrvaka-praṇidhāna*).

The Dharma Master Dao’an, who possessed profound virtue in this land, arranged this method so that it may also be practiced before meals in accordance with the text; there is no error in principle in doing so.

However, when visiting a host’s home, if the patron does not request that you recite the scriptures, you must not recite them from your own initiative. To do so would likely fall under the category of "wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*). Therefore, one should only recite if specifically requested.
The *Ekottarika-āgama* states that when someone prepares an offering, they hold a censer and announce, "The time has come. The Buddha said, "Incense is the messenger of the Buddha;
therefore, it is required. The *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu* and the *Tri-sahasra-vidhi* state that one must not stand while receiving incense.

This was because a bhikṣu received incense from a woman and her hand touched his, causing him to desire to abandon the path (*pravrajyā*). The Buddha said, "If one receives [incense] while standing, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense."
Regarding the chanting (*bhāṣa*) performed when distributing incense, although the specific scriptural passage is not seen, many sūtras and vinayas mention the *bhāṣa* of monks.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that chanting is permitted because the gods hear it and their hearts rejoice. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"The elder should know that for what has been offered by others, he should provide a timely prayer of blessing (*pariṇāmanā*); if he cannot, the next seat should speak; and if he also cannot," [the following should be done].
If there is no one from the highest-ranking seat down to the lowest who is present, all incur an offense. The *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* records that the Buddha said:

"O Bhikṣus, when preaching the Dharma or offering prayers of benediction, you must understand the appropriateness of the occasion. You should know the proper time and the improper time for sorrow, grief, joy, and pleasure;
you must not speak recklessly. (In the present age, those who preach on matters of desire abound in flowery melodies and eloquent rhetoric, yet their mouths produce much empty talk.)"
Seventh, regarding those who receive food and practice giving: if one wishes to receive food, one should first weigh the superiority or inferiority of one's own virtuous conduct before accepting it;
one must not be self-important, for such pride leads to downfall through the act of giving. The *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra* states: "The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

'Consider this single grain of rice—it is produced through a hundredfold labor. It represents the portion of one’s wife and children; yet for the sake of seeking merit, one gives it away. How can this be [right]? "
Regarding the abandonment [of food], the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "Whenever one receives food, one should give rise to a sense of revulsion; it is not for the sake of preserving one's life.
Furthermore, if one receives the faithful offerings of others but does not employ them according to the Dharma, one will enter the three miserable realms and undergo great, heavy suffering.

If one were not to undergo this retribution for suffering, then upon consuming another’s faithful offering, one’s belly would burst open and one’s clothes would fall from the body—unless, of course, the donor had no such karmic debt."
Furthermore, both the giver and the recipient of the gift fall under the influence of giving. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom) states:

"Food is for the sake of practicing the Path, not for the benefit of the body; it is no different from feeding a horse or a pig. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (The Minor Matters of the Vinaya) states:

"When receiving food, one should form a mental reflection at every mouthful; when receiving clothing, one should form a mental reflection at every stitch; when entering a room, one should form a mental reflection at every step. This applies to those of dull faculties."
Regarding the initial attainment of food, clothing, and shelter, the general principle is to form a single thought-moment:

when first about to eat, one should first offer [the food] to the Triple Gem and the sentient beings of the six realms; thereafter, with every mouthful, one should maintain the intention of embracing the Three Refuges.
When setting down the first spoonful of rice, one vows to sever all evil completely; when entering upon the second spoonful, one vows to cultivate all [virtues].
When Śubhamati enters the third [meal period] of the pickled vegetables, he vows that the merit produced by his actions shall be dedicated to all beings so that they may together attain Buddhahood.
If one is unable to perform this mental recitation for every mouthful, one should follow the previous treatise and make a single collective recitation before eating.
The *Āryā-Mahāprajāpatī-sūtra* states that sentient beings eat food the size of a fingernail; the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says it is because of the wilderness.

Having conferred upon the ghost the precept of non-killing, he said to the ghost: "I shall now command my śrāvaka disciples that wherever the Buddha-dharma exists, they must all provide you with food.
If there is any dwelling place where one cannot give, that person is a partisan of the celestial Māras and not my disciple.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If giving to beggars, crows, dogs, and the like, one should measure it according to one's own portion."

Regarding the practice of giving less than one’s share so as not to take what is beyond one’s portion, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that when a spirit or deity receives a single mouthful of food from a human, they produce a reward ten million times greater.
This Vinaya text mentions the establishment of shrines for spirits within monasteries;

tradition holds that in the Central Kingdom (China), Buddhist temples provide shrines for spirits, shrines for the *gārāma-deva*, and shrines for Piṇḍola, all of which are attended by the monastic community at both meal times.
Regarding the food remaining after offerings at the three places, the *Madhyama Āgama* states:

"If a deceased person has offered gifts for a sacrifice, whether they have entered the realm of hungry ghosts or have attained another destination, they will receive [the merit]; it does not fail to reach them because each possesses food for their own livelihood.
Even if the kinsmen have not entered that realm, by merely making the offering, the donor himself obtains the blessing, and this continues until the donor passes away."

Among the six realms of existence, the merit of giving constantly follows one because of the observance of the precepts; however, as a human being, one must necessarily rely on other merits to support the retribution [of this life].

According to this Vinaya, if a bhikṣu eats as soon as he receives food, he incurs the reproach of the laity. The Buddha therefore commanded that one should announce "equally obtained" (*sādhika*) before eating, after which the Sangha may eat.

In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one waits for the announcement of "equally obtained" offerings before eating. If the time [for the meal] is about to pass, one may eat as soon as it is served without fault.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "From now on, the *sthavira* shall wait until the announcement has been made and the sound of 'equal offering' (*samagra-bhukti*) is heard, after which the entire Saṃgha may eat together.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "In a place where nuns are invited, if one eats at will before the announcement, there is an offense of *pāyattika* for every mouthful; minor offenses (*dukkaṭa*) increase for those below [the rank]. The *Ekottarika-āgama* and *Madhyama-āgama* state:
"When kings provide offerings, they personally distribute the food, and commoners do the same. This Vinaya [text] states: "If both divisions of the Saṃgha are invited, first give [to the monks]."
If a bhikṣu fears that the time will pass, he may receive food all at once. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, at the time of eating, one should protect the right hand;
the left hand should be used to receive the vessel. One must not hold the bowl too deep to the lips, nor should one touch the rim with the forehead or nose.
When the meal is finished, a small amount should be left in the mouth, and the water used for rinsing should be poured away. Next, [the food] should be given to the junior monks (*śrāmaṇera*).

If one sprinkles water upon food that has been scattered or disordered during a meal out of fear that it might cause laypeople to lose faith, there is no offense. Regarding spitting water, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"When food adheres to the hand, one must not shake it off; one should instead discard it and pick it up. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not make smacking sounds while eating.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One must not eat with the nose wrinkled."
Regarding "the eighth, having finished eating": the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the elder (upādhyāya) should eat slowly and not finish quickly;

he should remain and watch the juniors so as not to let them eat in a disorderly manner or fail to eat their fill. He should keep a mutual watch over them until they have waited for the distribution of water and the performance of the *svastyayana* (blessing), after which he may finally stop.
It is also said that when a layperson has finished feeding the Sangha, the remaining food materials are left behind.

The *Li-yu-bi-she Za-ahan* (Sūtra on the Mixed Contents of the Li and Biṣa) states that after the Buddha and the bhikṣus have finished eating at a layperson’s home, they each rinse their mouths and wash their bowls;
only then does the Buddha preach the Dharma to the laypeople.
Regarding the ninth, *dakṣiṇā*: The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that giving clothing and other items after a meal is called *dakṣiṇā*.

According to this Vinaya, because the donor departed silently after the meal was finished, doubt arose; the Buddha therefore ordered the elder to recite a great *dakṣiṇā*, even if it were only a single verse, saying:
"If one gives for the sake of benefit, one will surely obtain that benefit; if one gives for the sake of happiness, one will surely obtain it later."
Regarding the Elder Kalyāṇa: if he is able to speak but does not do so, or if he does not accept [the invitation] when it is offered, he incurs an offense.
When the great *dakṣiṇā* (gift) is being announced, the four senior elders must wait together; the others may depart. The *Sāhasrika-vaipulya-vinaya-sūtra* states:
"One must not preach the Dharma to others before having eaten. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that there are four ways of preaching the Dharma after a meal.

First, it is to eliminate the consumption of offerings from the faithful; second, it is to repay their kindness; third, it is to cause them to give rise to a joyful mind so that their roots of goodness may be perfected;
fourth, it is because laypeople should practice the giving of material wealth while renunciants should practice the giving of the Dharma.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that when listening to or explaining the meaning of the teachings, one must synthesize the various texts. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that the bhikṣus requested permission to [accept] those who have broken the precepts.
Those with wrong views and those with impaired faculties chanted and preached the Dharma; because of this, these evil people gained influence and were able to insult the Sangha. The Buddha said:
"I request that a Dharma Master who possesses the full set of sense-faculties preach the *Mātṛkā*.
It says: "If there is no one capable of chanting, they should be appointed in succession. If there are none at all, each should recite a single verse; those who are capable need not [recite more]."
If one commits a *sthūlātyaya*, it is not permissible to recite even half a verse of the *gāthā*; this Vinaya prescribes that one should recite the verse: "Commit no evil; practice all that is good;
purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas. The *Ekottarika-āgama* explains: "Committing no evil" means being fully endowed with the precepts of the body and maintaining pure conduct.

"Practicing all that is good" means having a pure mind. "Purifying one's own mind" means eliminating false views and delusions; this is the teaching of all Buddhas. To remove the conceptions of ignorance and confusion is the precept.

Because the intentional mind is purified, there is no perversion; because there is no perversion, deluded perceptions are extinguished. Regarding the tenth point, the dispersal and return to one's seat:
the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that when returning to the monastery, eight senior monks (upādhyāyas) wait for the others while the rest proceed ahead.

The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states that after the Buddha and the bhikṣus have finished eating, they all enter their meditation chambers to practice dhyāna; at the hour of *pradoṣa* (the late afternoon), they arise from meditation.
And he preached the Dharma. Chapter Twenty-Six:
The Arrival of Monastics and Laypeople at the Temple.
This chapter has four main sections: first, the method for bhikṣus entering a temple; second, the method for the four dignified demeanors; third, [the method for] laypeople...
The Four Methods for Entering a Monastery and the Method of Taking Leave and Bowing.

First, regarding the method for a bhikṣu entering a monastery: according to this Vinaya, when a visiting bhikṣu enters a monastery, he should ascertain the location of the Buddha’s stūpa and whether the elders and others have reached the gate.
He should open it; if he is unable to do so, he should strike gently so that those inside may hear him. If they still do not...

When the visitor reaches the wall and climbs over it, the resident bhikṣu hears that a guest has arrived and goes outside to welcome him. He takes the guest's robes and bowl and places them in the heated chamber (*jantāghara*).

He then asks again about the place for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) and provides water vessels and other requisites. The guest asks the resident bhikṣu, "Do I have a share of a room for my years of seniority?
If the resident replies, "Yes," he should then ask whether anyone else is currently living there. If no one is there, [he may take up residence].
One should ask whether there are bedding, robes, offerings, utensils, rooms, or garments; if there are none, one should take them to the room.

Having received them, one should again ask: "Where are the places for the large and small excretions, the clean and impure areas, the stūpas of the Buddha, the stūpas of the śrāvakas, and the rooms of the first through the fourth senior monks? One must ask each of these individually; if one does not ask, [there is an offense].

The host instructs each [guest] one by one, as stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "If the dwelling is cramped and you do not know one another, it is permitted to sit together on the same bed, but you must not sleep there.

According to this Vinaya, once the guest has received the room and questioned the host, he should first pay homage to the Buddha stūpa, next pay homage to the Śrāvaka stūpa, and thereafter pay homage to the first elder, and so on down to the fourth elder; he should do so with his right shoulder bared.
Taking off one's leather sandals, placing the right knee on the ground, and grasping [the feet of] both [the senior monks], one speaks thus: "Venerable Sir, I pay homage.
Inside the room of the fourth senior monk, one should contemplate and pay homage according to the order of seats, clearly indicating each of the room-owners.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one sees the senior monk when approaching, one should pay homage; if he is difficult to see or too far away, then one stops. This Vinaya [text] specifies that visiting monks pay homage to the senior monks.
One should ask: "Where is the place for the community's formal meal (*mahābhojana*), the light meal (*laghubhojana*), the night assembly, and the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*)?

The resident monks (*paurāṇa-bhikṣu*) should answer as they are asked. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The resident monks should inform the visiting monks of all the regulations of the monastic community.
If the visiting companions have already departed, one must not inform them, saying that they could not keep pace with the group; rather, one should say it is possible [to catch up]."
If one pauses briefly, there should still be a companion; if someone must go on urgent business, they should be provided with provisions and entrusted to their traveling companion.

The *Sānqiānwēiyí* (Three Thousand Rules of Dignified Conduct) states: "When a newly arrived bhikṣu arrives, he should be granted ten things: first, one should avoid giving him a room [without consideration];

second, one should provide what he requires; third, one should inquire after his welfare morning and evening; fourth, one should speak to him of local customs; fifth, one should teach him how to avoid taboos."
1. Six words for requesting [food] when arriving; 2. Seven words for the monastic community’s instructions; 3. Eight words stating that one should speak of the matter and that it may be eaten;
4. Nine words regarding prohibitions by local officials; 5. Ten words indicating the location of thieves and bandits.

Regarding the second point, the four modes of deportment (*catur-īryāpatha*), the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one's four modes of deportment are not in accordance with the Dharma, one does not act as a great light for the world.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When walking, one should look straight ahead; when turning back, one should turn the entire body. The *Madhyama Āgama* states:
"At dawn, one should beg while guarding and restraining the sense faculties; having finished begging for food, one should put away the robes and bowl, and wash one's hands."
Having placed the *niṣīdana* upon his shoulder, he should go to a secluded place;
after walking or sitting in meditation during the first watch of the night, having purified the mind of hindrances, he should enter his room at the time of the middle watch intending to lie down.
He should spread a four-layered *uttarāsaṅga* on the bed, fold the *saṃghāṭī* to serve as a pillow, and lie down on his right side with his head facing east.

Facing the image of the Buddha, one should place the feet one upon the other and clearly visualize the signs (*nimitta*). Then, at the time of late night, one should rise quickly according to the method of the first watch of the night.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The head should face the clothing rack and toward the preceptor or senior bhikṣu. During the first watch, one contemplates one's own karma;
until the middle watch, one lies on the right side with the lower legs stacked, the mouth closed, the tongue pressed against the upper palate, and the right hand used as a pillow."

Extending the left hand upward along the body, one does not abandon mindfulness, wisdom, and contemplation, giving rise to the thought that all devas, humans, nāgas, and ghosts are conditions for practicing the Way as a renunciant;
toward them, whether hidden or manifest, one must not lightly allow any contact.

Even while dwelling in a dark room, one should always exhort oneself; there is even this admonition in common worldly proverbs and established sayings. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The lamp is light."

One must not sleep during the midday period. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If one has more than ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*) and there is a Dharma matter that will certainly be beneficial, even if the teacher does not permit it, there is no fault in going on one's own.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When traveling, first lower the heel and then lower the toes.
When intending to stay overnight along the road, one should send two junior bhikṣus ahead to seek out a lodging place and obtain food for the morning and evening."

When eating, one should announce [one's departure]; when entering a village at an improper time, having returned, one should report it; and one should inform others in turn before entering. The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Whether entering or exiting, coming or going, one should be composed and single-minded; lifting the foot and setting it down, one observes the ground as one walks.
This is to avoid distracted thoughts and to protect sentient beings; such is the mark of a non-regressive Bodhisattva. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not act like a dromedary."
One should sit in the *paryaṅka* (full lotus) posture; if this is impossible, one should extend one leg alternately. The *Ekottarika-āgama* states:

"I now permit bhikṣus to first lean against a seat with their hands and then sit upon it; this is my teaching. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Unless one is ill, one must not sleep during the day.

If one is prone to drowsiness, one should rise and practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). The *Sammohavinodanī* states: "When about to sleep, one should first engage in the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*)."

In each and every thought-moment within this [practice], the *Sānmiàowēiyí* (Three Thousand Dignified Postures) states: "One must not sit in a squatting posture before a senior elder (*upādhyāya*), nor may one sit alongside the three teachers.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When listening to the Dharma, if a senior elder approaches, one should not rise;
if a junior rises, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. However, if one rises out of respect for one's own *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, it is not a *duṣkṛta* offense to rise."
Furthermore, when listening to the Dharma, one must not sit on the same bed as a śrāmaṇera;

a śrāmaṇera may sit on the same bed as a layperson (*avadātavasana*), and a *mahābhikṣu* who has completed three summer retreats may likewise sit on the same bed. The *Sānqiānwēiyí* (Three Thousand Rules of Deportment) states that when about to ascend the bed, one should observe seven rules:
first, one should slowly withdraw and squat down; second, one must not crawl up; third, one must not [allow] the bed to... [be damaged].
1. One should not make a loud noise. 2. One should not make a sound by vigorously sweeping the bed. 3. One should not blow loudly or sigh with great force while contemplating worldly affairs.

4. One should not lie down in a pack like a dog. 5. When rising, one should do so at the proper time; if the mind wanders and is unsettled, one should examine the root cause of its arising. As the *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
"If a bhikṣu is greedily attached to sleep, he neglects the three types of wholesome action (*trikarma*) and no longer practices the Path. The Vajrapāṇi spirits will rebuke him."

Rebuking the Buddha, he said: "One who consumes the faithful offerings of others should not be indolent. During two periods of the night, one should practice seated meditation, recite the sūtras, and perform walking meditation;

during the remaining period, one should rest at one's own leisure. This is called the 'method of reclining. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one should lie down according to the manner of the lion king and must not sleep until sunrise.
One should rise during the latter part of the night and sit upright to contemplate one's own deeds."

Third, regarding men and women entering the monastery: following the ancient custom of Jetavana, whenever the people of the Western Regions reach the gate of the monastery, they adjust their robes and perform one prostration;
upon entering the gate, they again perform one prostration. They proceed straight ahead with composure, without looking left or right.
Having first arrived before the Buddha, they perform three prostrations, then circumambulate him three times, chant three verses of praise (*bhāṣya*), and complete the worship of the Buddha.

Upon arriving at the door of the monks' quarters, one should perform one prostration and then enter. Having seen the *upādhyāya*, one proceeds in order down to the lowest-ranking monk, performing one prostration to each.

If one witnesses matters of right or wrong, one must not criticize or rebuke them; for if one speaks with disdain or reproach, one loses one's own merit and this is not the conduct of entering a monastery.
Furthermore, when first entering the monastery, how could one act by turning one's back on the Sangha to pursue individuality?
The *Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of Leaving Home* states: "Now, those who enter a monastery must first cast aside weapons, staves, and miscellaneous items before entering.
To 'cast aside weapons and staves' means to abandon anger toward the assembly of monks. To 'cast aside miscellaneous items' means to abandon the mind of begging from the assembly of monks.

Having first removed these two faults, one may then enter the monastery. One should proceed in accordance with the Buddha and must not walk in the opposite direction; this is established as the rule."

When obstructed, circumambulate to the left while constantly imagining that the Buddha is at your right; whenever entering or exiting, turn your face toward the Buddha and pay homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Constantly contemplate that their essence is one and the same: that which realizes the Dharma to fulfillment is called the Buddha;
the path realized by him is called the Dharma; and those who study the Buddha’s path are called the Sangha. Thus, they are of one essence without distinction. Lower your head and look at the ground.
One must not look upward; if one sees insects on the ground, do not mistakenly harm or kill them. Do not spit on the monastic grounds. One should chant and offer praises.
If one must personally clear away grass or soil, one may do so. If there is a reason to stay overnight in the monastery, one must not lie upon the monastic beds or mats;
one should instead borrow one's own items for this purpose. Furthermore, one must not sleep within the robes of a śramaṇa, nor engage in flirtatious speech or laughter.
When discussing matters of the Dharma, a śramaṇa must not go to sleep before others have done so, in order to eliminate arrogance.

Furthermore, one must not sit upon the beds or mats of the Saṃgha out of a desire to treat the Saṃgha with contempt; for even among the laity, it is not permitted for a person of low status to ascend the seat of a noble official, let alone presume to sit alongside a world-transcending eminent monk.
Thus, a sutra says: "To share a bed with the Saṃgha is to cause half of one's body to wither away."
Furthermore, when dawn arrives, one should rise before the śramaṇas. All conduct regarding entering a temple serves as a condition for laypeople to enter the Path;
establishing a temple creates the cause for opening a Pure Land, and providing for and nourishing the Sangha constitutes the byway of liberation.
The ritual for a faithful woman entering a temple is the same as before, with the sole exception that she must not assume the physical appearance or occupy the seat of a man.

Speaking with laughter, smearing the face with cosmetics and painting the eyebrows with artificial pigments, engaging in unrighteous flirtation and mutual dalliance, and using hands to push or support others—one must instead restrain the mind, maintain a dignified appearance, follow the instructions of others, and in due order hold incense and offer worship with single-minded devotion.
One must repent and reproach oneself, for being born as a woman always results in perpetual obstacles; thus, there is no cause for practicing or honoring this wondrous Dharma.
One must not act independently, but should accomplish all through others; how bitter this is! One should feel deep shame and remorse.
If one sees a śrāmaṇera performing prostrations like a senior monk, one must not fail to show respect because his rank is low. Such a person is junior to the senior monks but is honored by the laity;
regarding matters such as these, one should exert every effort to practice accordingly.

Regarding the fourth method, the ritual of taking leave: when one has finished the tasks at hand and departs from the temple gate, one should perform prostrations according to the Dharma—three prostrations before the Buddha, one prostration at the gate, and one prostration outside the gate. If the number of monks is small, each should bow once in succession;

if they are numerous, they should bow three times collectively. Generally, when those with defiled, worldly bodies enter the temple and tread upon the pure ground of the Vajra Dharma-realm, [this ritual must be observed].

If one has frequently deviated from ritual propriety, one must atone for those transgressions when departing; according to the amount of offerings made, it is shown that [the departure] was not in vain.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: Paying Homage to the Sacred Image.
This chapter contains six topical sections: 1. Reverencing the Honored Ones; 2. Determining the Honored Ones; 3. Paying Homage; 4. Attending to Parents;
5. Medical Treatment; 6. Funerary Rites.
Regarding the first, Reverencing the Honored Ones, this Vinaya states: "If a bhikṣu reverences the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, and the Precepts, the True Dharma will not..."

If one lacks reverence, one will quickly perish according to the Dharma. The *Āgama* Sūtras state that those who harbor no heart of respect for the Buddha are constantly reborn among dragons and snakes;
having come from such states in the past, they remain disrespectful and drowsy even now.

The *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* records that after the World-Honored One had personally erected the stupa of Kāśyapa Buddha and completed its various adornments, he did so out of respect for the Buddhas of the past.
The *Zizuoli Zengyi Jing* (Sūtra on Increasing Merit through Self-Made Prostrations) states that the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There are five merits from serving the Buddha:
first, physical beauty, because one gives rise to a heart of joy upon seeing the Buddha’s image;

second, a beautiful voice, because by beholding the image, one spontaneously utters the name ‘Namo Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’; third, abundant wealth and rewards, because of making offerings of flowers and lamps."
Fourth, being born into the family of a householder, his mind remains free from attachment upon seeing one's form;
fifth, at the end of life, he is reborn in the heavens—this is the constant law of all Buddhas, and one should train accordingly. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The Buddhas do not regard the birth-body as the object of veneration; if one sees the Dharma-body, this is called making an offering. A verse in this Vinaya says: "He who respects the elders..."
If a person can protect the Dharma, they will attain renown in the present life and be reborn in the good realms in the future. The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states:
"In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, he saw that all people without exception bowed down, humbled themselves, and paid him homage with reverence.

By virtue of this karmic retribution, since his attainment of Buddhahood, whenever he walks through mountains and forests, humans and animals alike bow down and prostrate themselves with their heads at his feet."

In the second section of the *Viniścaya-mātṛkā-śāstra*, it is stated that those of lower standing address elders as "Venerable" (*bhadanta*), while elders address those of lower standing as "Life of Wisdom" (*āyuṣmat*).

Furthermore, those from one year of summer retreat (*varṣa*) up to nine years of summer retreat are called junior monks (*navaka*); those from ten years up to nineteen years of summer retreat are called middle-ranking monks (*madhyama*);
those from twenty years up to forty-nine years of summer retreat are called senior monks (*sthavira*); and those who have reached fifty years of summer retreat or more are [called Great Elders].

All śramaṇas are respected by kings; these are the venerable elders (sthavira). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, a bhikṣu who has no seniority may sit together with one of three years' seniority, up to one of seven years' seniority sitting together with one of ten years' seniority.

Regarding beds: three people may sit on a bed; two people may sit on a bench. A bed that is one and a half cubits longer than a bench allows those of three years' seniority to sit upon it. If the beds are of equal length, those of three years' seniority may share them.
If it is a large assembly and there are few seats, one may connect them together and tie them so they do not move, provided that one may sit together [on them].
If a square mat is three cubits long, four people may sit together on it; if it is shorter than that, they may not. If one spreads out mats on the ground and sits together, there is no offense.
According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, when long benches are joined together, one must simply ensure that the clothing, the mats, and the [individual] spaces are distinct.
If the seats are separated by a gap in the middle such that they are distinct from one another, it is permissible to sit with a woman;

according to the *Mātṛkā-vinaya*, it is permissible to sit on ground coverings with those who have not yet received full ordination. In this Vinaya, śrāmaṇeras shall be ranked according to their year of birth;
if their years of birth are equal, they shall be ranked according to their year of renunciation.

The third term for salutation is *namas* (meaning "deliver me" in its sense; the *Vinayamātṛkā* calls it "reverence," and the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* states that *praṇāma* is translated here as "obeisance").
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are three ways of paying homage:

first, prostration with the mouth; second, bending the knee so that the head does not touch the ground; and third, touching the head to the ground—this is considered the highest. The *Upadhāraṇī-sūtra* states:
When the five limbs reach the ground, one performs a prostration; the *Āgama* Sūtras state that the two elbows, the two knees, and the crown of the head are called "wheels" (*cakra*).

It is also said that this refers to casting the body down with its five parts. This Vinaya states that once a guest has entered the monastery, they should first pay homage to the Buddha stupa, next pay homage to the stupa of the Śrāvakas, and then pay homage to the foremost elder, followed by the second, third, and fourth elders; in doing so, one should bared the right shoulder.
Removing one's leather sandals, placing the right knee on the ground, and bowing with both feet, one speaks thus: "Venerable Sir, I pay homage. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If there are many people, one may simply pay individual homage to the teacher and perform a collective prostration to the others before departing.

The *Sānwei yi* (Three Thousand Dignified Manners) states: "There are five points for circumambulating a stupa: first, lowering the head to gaze upon the Buddha; second, not treading upon insects; third, not looking left or right; fourth, [not...]"
Spitting on the ground; not speaking with others; furthermore, one should contemplate the kindness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

Regarding the *Wubai wen shi* (Five Hundred Questions), it states that a disciple may pay homage at the grave of their teacher to repay their kindness (by this standard, one may also pay homage to a corpse before it has been buried).
According to this Vinaya, a junior śrāmaṇerī should pay homage to a senior śrāmaṇerī, a śrāmaṇerī to a śikṣamāṇā, bhikṣuṇī, bhikṣu, and the Tathāgata.
Regarding the stūpa, one proceeds in this manner, circling from bottom to top until reaching the Great Bhikṣu, who may then pay homage to the Tathāgata and the stūpa.
In the *Five Hundred Questions*, it says: "If a bhikṣu circumambulates the stūpa and female followers accompany him, there is no offense provided there are no upāsakas present.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "When paying homage to the Buddha-Dharma, one circumambulates the Buddha three times, performs prostrations in the four directions, and then departs; this is appropriate."
With the ten fingers and palms joined above his head, he walked backward until he could no longer see the Tathāgata; he prostrated once more, turned back around, and departed.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that one should not perform prostrations within a stūpa. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that before a Buddha-stūpa or a Śrāvaka-stūpa, neither oneself nor others should perform prostrations.
The *Pañcaśata-praśna* states that if a bhikṣu performs prostrations before a Buddha-stūpa, he commits a *pāyattika* offense.

Gñi says: "When performing prostrations at a stūpa, reciting sūtras, copying sūtras, or receiving sūtras, one must not prostrate in the dark (this refers to cases where there is another object of veneration).

Furthermore, when making mud images, washing clothes, bathing, or washing one's hands and feet; when wearing only a single robe; or when walking quickly—one should not prostrate. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"One may not prostrate while sleeping, sewing robes, amidst the great assembly, while traveling on a road, or when ill. This rule is found in this Vinaya.

There are four types of persons whom one should not pay homage to: first, all laypeople and women; second, those who received the precepts earlier should not pay homage to those who received them later;

third, those who have committed a pārājika offense (an extreme transgression), those subject to the thirteen grounds for disqualification, those who have been formally censured, those who have been expelled, and those who should be expelled;
fourth, all those who speak in an unrighteous manner. Furthermore, there are ten kinds of improper conduct that do not conform to dignified decorum.

One should pay homage when [the recipient] is performing major or minor acts, such as being naked, having shaved their head, preaching the Dharma, chewing a tooth-stick, rinsing the mouth, drinking water, eating, or consuming fruit.
The *Sāhasrika-īryāpatha* states that one must not perform prostrations while seated.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states that one must not enter a stūpa wearing leather shoes or *puḍraka* sandals; if the people of that land wear them, they all give rise to arrogance.
Because of the mind, one does not permit wearing [footwear] in places where it is cold and snowy; however, one permits wearing *upānaha* (sandals/boots). The *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu* states:

"Clean and pure boots and shoes may be worn when performing prostrations to the Saṃgha. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When receiving prostrations from others, one must not be like a mute sheep that does not speak; one should inquire after their well-being, asking:
'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you at ease? Are you not weary or distressed by the journey? It says "not together" because [the recipient] does not respond.

The words of the Elder may also be cited; the *Hui-ming Bao-liang Jing* (*Ratnarāśi Sūtra*) states that a precept-breaking bhikṣu who receives the respectful salutations of a precept-observing person incurs eight offenses of contempt: first, becoming foolish and deluded; second, being mute; third, having an ugly countenance;
fourth, having a distorted face such that those who see it laugh in derision; fifth, successively receiving the female body and becoming impoverished.

Seventh, they shall be servants and slaves, their six sense-faculties emaciated and their lifespan cut short; eighth, they shall not be respected by others and will constantly have an evil reputation;

ninth, they shall not encounter even a single Buddha’s era—such is the retribution for these breakers of the precepts, until there is not even a place on the great earth where they can spit or discharge phlegm.
Fourth, regarding serving one’s parents: The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that Piṅgala’s parents were impoverished, so he supported them with food and clothing.

The Buddha said: "If a person were to carry their father on the right shoulder and their mother on the left shoulder for a hundred years, even while discharging excrement and urine upon them and providing them with the most rare and precious garments in the world, they still could not repay even a moment’s debt of gratitude. From this day forward..."
It is permitted for a bhikṣu to provide for his parents with all his heart; otherwise, he incurs a grave offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one's parents do not have faith in the Triple Gem, one should manage their affairs sparingly. If they have faith, one may provide for them freely so that they lack nothing.
If the parents are impoverished, one should bring them to the monastery. If it is the mother who is being washed, one must not touch her; however, one may personally give food to the father."
This is no different from the rules for śrāmaṇeras; all [of these] obtain the *Vinayamātṛkā*.

If one's parents are in poverty and suffering, one should first bestow upon them the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Ten Wholesome Paths, and only then provide them with material gifts. If they are not poor, although they have received the precepts, it is not appropriate to give [them such gifts].
The *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* says: "The girl Maitrī was poor, yet she alone supported her elderly mother and attained [the fruits] in this very life."
Regarding the karmic retribution for a parrot’s filial care of its blind parents and the conditions for attaining Buddhahood, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"The merit and fruit of filially obeying and making offerings to one's parents is equal to the merit of a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
It further states: "If one instructs two people to perform wholesome deeds, there is no way to repay their kindness; these two are one's parents. Therefore, O Bhikṣus...
One should always be filial and support one’s parents without missing the proper seasons; thus should you train.

Fifth, regarding medical treatment: according to this Vinaya, if an elderly or sick bhikṣu is unable to walk, he is permitted to use a handcart, a sedan chair, or a vehicle—excluding female oxen, grass horses, and the like.
For bhikṣuṇīs, it excludes bulls, stallions, and so forth. (The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: [text continues].
If one acts as a physician, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; however, if one compiles medicines for the five groups of renunciants, it is permissible.
Furthermore, if one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or parents are ill while in the monastery, the disciple may also compile medicine for them.

Moreover, if one's parents—who may be poor or lowly—are supported by a *śrāmaṇera* (pure attendant) within the monastery, or if it concerns brothers, sisters, uncles, paternal aunts, maternal uncles, or maternal aunts, one is likewise permitted to compile medicine for them.
If medicine has no owner, one may borrow it; if it is not returned, do not demand it back. This applies even down to the seventh generation. The *Wubai wenshi* (Five Hundred Questions) states:
"If a practitioner of the Way acts as a physician with a compassionate heart, he may take items for his own use.

If another person forcibly gives them to him as a meritorious act, he should accept them. However, if one is ill, one must not ingest [medicines] involving breath or spittle, as these are the same as the practices of external paths. (5)

It is divided [into categories such as] knowing the sequence of assemblies and so forth. One must not excel at calligraphy, nor neglect one's studies; one is forbidden from practicing divination or physiognomy, or inquiring of others regarding good or bad fortune.

According to this Vinaya, one must not practice fortune-telling, recite incantations, or prescribe medical treatments to cure illnesses, because such matters may involve falsehoods that lead to the slander of virtuous people.
However, it permits the study and recitation of books and the study of worldly treatises for the purpose of subduing non-Buddhists.

A newly ordained bhikṣu who learns the methods for incantations may also learn incantations for worms in the abdomen, for treating indigestion, or for subduing poisons and the like, provided it is for self-protection and not for the sake of making a living; such learning of incantations and medical treatments is permissible.

For those suffering from vomiting, one may take hair, burn it, grind it into a powder, mix it with water, strain it, and administer it. For those suffering from fever, one may use *candana* (sandalwood).
If sandalwood paste or aloeswood has been used to treat a wound from poison or gangrene and has already fallen to the ground, one should mix it with water, strain it, and consume it;
if it has not yet fallen to the ground, one should catch it in a vessel, mix it with water, strain it, and consume it—there is no need for a formal ritual of acceptance (*pratigraha*).

Mud from the field must also be mixed with water before being accepted and consumed. One should place five parts of *agaru* (sandalwood) within one’s clothing to ward off insects. When reciting mantras, one must not eat salt.

The *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] permits the method of divine incantations for those who cannot sleep on their beds; it is natural that monks may develop boils and abscesses, for which one should grind wheat and apply it as an ointment.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that impure fats and salt may be consumed; this Vinaya permits the use of impure ghee for nasal irrigation.

The *Mahāsāṃghika*, *Daśabhāṇavāra*, and *Pañcavargika* [Vinayas] state that if there is no other treatment available, it is permitted for a sick bhikṣu to consume [medicinal herbs]; they allow him to stay by himself for seven days.
One must not lie upon the monastic beds or bedding within the quarters; one must not go to the places for defecation and urination, nor to the lecture hall.
Furthermore, one must not accept invitations or meals from the community of monks, nor approach the Buddha to prostrate. One may instead perform prostrations from a distance while remaining downwind.
Once the seven days are complete, one must bathe and fumigate one's robes before being permitted to join the assembly. If one uses incense to apply to a sore, it must first be offered as an oblation.
After attending to the Buddha, one should then anoint the body and go to a secluded place, following the same procedure as before.
Regarding the sixth point, the conclusion of the funeral rites: this Vinaya states that if a layperson comes to the monastery while ill, one should employ skillful means to send them away;

however, if they praise the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one should assist them according to one's ability. If they die, one should carry the body oneself for the sake of maintaining the purity of the *saṃghārāma*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that a bhikṣu must not call [laypeople] by their personal names, such as "Uncle," "Aunt," "Brother," or "Sister," and this applies even to mourning for the deceased;

he may only refer to them as *upāsaka* or *upāsikā*. The *Ekottarika-āgama* of this Vinaya states that when members of the four castes enter the Buddha-dharma, they are all equally called "seedlings of the Śākya" and must not rely on their secular surnames. The *Samantapāsādikā* states:
One must not address a maidservant as "Elder Sister" (dàzì); rather, one should refer to her as a "maiden" (bì). The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"When Māyā passed away, the Buddha personally assisted Rāhula in supporting one corner of the bier, and together they escorted King Śuddhodana to his nirvāṇa; the Buddha himself also lifted [the other corner].

Based on this, when the parents of a bhikṣu fall ill or die, it is permissible to carry them, lift them, and perform their burial; however, one must not change one's robes to white. Therefore, the *Māyā Sūtra* states that one thousand three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...
When the robes of the bhikṣus turn white and no longer take dye within a hundred years, you should know that the Dharma will perish before long.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: Receiving the Three Refuges for Those Who Have Turned Away from the Right Path.
This chapter has six main sections: first, explaining the purpose of its composition; second, the timing for receiving and generating the precepts; third, the method of repentance.

There are six sections: first, the general and specific; second, the sequence of priority; third, the five pairs; fourth, the distinctions regarding the destinies; fifth, the gradual and sudden; and sixth, gain and loss.
Regarding the first, the clarification of the meaning of the Three Refuges, the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states that there are five kinds of Three Refuges:

first, the Three Refuges for turning away from heterodoxy; second, the Three Refuges for the Five Precepts; third, the Three Refuges for the Eight Precepts; fourth, the Three Refuges for the Ten Precepts; and fifth, the Three Refuges for the Full Ordination.

Regarding the four types of the Three Refuges discussed below, they will be explained individually in subsequent chapters. For now, we shall clarify the first: the Three Refuges for Renouncing Evil. Question:
What is the intention behind taking refuge? Answer: One takes the Triple Gem as the object of refuge, desiring that they provide protection and prevent one from being oppressed.
It is like a person who has committed an offense against a king and flees to another country; the king of that land says to him, "I grant you fearlessness."
"Do not leave my realm; do not disobey my instructions, and I shall surely protect you. It is the same for sentient beings who are bound by Māra and subject to the faults of birth and death:
if they turn toward the Triple Gem and do not disobey the Buddha's teachings, there is nothing Māra can do about them.

When asked why they receive these three refuges that overturn heterodoxy, the answer is: because they have long believed in heterodox views and were deeply attached to non-virtuous objects, they now suddenly develop [faith].
Because one has properly taken refuge, it is called "turning away from heterodoxy. Thus, the *Consecration Sūtra* (*Guanding jing*) states:

"At that time, a heterodox practitioner, a Brahmin with the head of a deer, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in greeting, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and said:

'I have long heard the name of Gautama, whose fame resounds far and wide. I now wish to abandon heterodox studies and receive the Three Refuges along with the Dharma of the Five Precepts. The Buddha said: 'Excellent.'"
"Excellent! O Brahmin, since you are able to set aside other paths and take refuge in me, you should repent for the sins of birth and death;
your merit shall be immeasurable and beyond description. The Brahmin replied, "Yes," and having accepted the instruction, he immediately purified his body and speech, further saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me the Dharma-precepts, which I shall observe throughout my life, never daring to violate or neglect them."
At that time, having conferred [the precepts] upon him, the Buddha addressed the brahmin, saying:

"Once you have single-mindedly received the Three Refuges, I shall, for your sake and for the sake of the people of the ten directions, command the various spirits sent by Śakra Devendra to protect such men as you.
There are thirty-six classes of spirit-kings among these benevolent deities; in total, there are ten trillion of them, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The ghosts and spirits take them as their retinue, alternating shifts in the unseen realm to protect men.

For those among such people who uphold the five precepts, there are twenty-five benevolent deities who constantly guard the person, remaining by their side and atop the gates and doors of their dwellings to ensure that all matters are auspicious. Furthermore, each of these aforementioned deities has its own name.
One should keep these precepts as one carries a sash of sacred scriptures; being able to eliminate all evils and unwholesome states, one must never draw near them.
If one violates them, virtuous deities will abandon them, and they shall suffer endless misfortune.

Regarding the second point, the timing for receiving the precepts, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The person receiving the precepts should maintain dignified deportment and approach a renunciant.
The Preceptor first expounds the Dharma to open and settle their mind, and then administers the precepts as follows:
'I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, take refuge in the Saṃgha' (recited three times). I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, take refuge..."

Having completed the refuge in the Buddha, having completed the refuge in the Dharma, having completed the refuge in the Saṃgha (recited three times). Having completed the first three refuges, one immediately generates wholesome dharmas.
Having completed the final three, there is only that which belongs to oneself—namely, the non-informative [karma] (*avijñapti*) of body and speech. The Sarvāstivādins say:

"If one receives the precepts with a mind of profound sincerity, there is both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative karma; if one receives them with a mind of disrespect, there is only its informative aspect" (informative and non-informative refer here to the performed and the unperformed).
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "If a woman who is pregnant fears that the fetus may be endangered, she should first receive the Three Refuges;
then the child will not suffer harm, and once born, it will be endowed with a perfect body and mind, protected by benevolent deities. Question:

When one takes refuge in the Buddha, does this mean taking refuge in only a single Buddha, or in all Buddhas of the three periods of time? Answer: Because they share the same Dharma-body, one must necessarily take refuge in all of them collectively.
Regarding the taking of refuge: although it specifically refers to Śākyamuni as the object when the words are spoken, in principle the refuge must also extend to the other two—Dharma and Saṅgha;
this principle likewise applies.
Third, as for the method of repenting transgressions: the karma one has created must, in principle, be repented and cleansed so that one's conduct becomes pure and stainless.
Regarding the purpose of returning to the original purity, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "First one receives the Three Refuges, and only thereafter does one perform repentance.
Various masters explain this by saying that because these are the Three Refuges for turning away from heterodoxy, one receives them first and repents later.

However, concerning the Five Precepts, the Eight Precepts, and the Three Refuges, the *Madhyama Āgama* clearly prescribes that one must first repent and only then receive them. [The text] addresses the practitioner, stating that [suffering] has been without beginning.
Since beginningless time, ignorance has been so dense and heavy that one has been unable to perceive the Buddha-nature;

because it is not seen, one constantly breaks the precepts and violates the requisites before the Buddha, committing every kind of evil without exception, acting with extreme lack of shame or remorse.

Now, wishing to repent and eliminate these faults, how could one afford to be negligent? It is like a great tree whose roots and sprouts have flourished; if one does not apply effort, [it will continue to grow].
How can one eliminate and sever [karmic retribution]? The *Guhya-karma-vipāka-prabheda-sūtra* states:

"If a person commits a grave offense, having committed it, they should deeply reproach themselves with a sincere mind, repent, and never do it again; thus they can uproot the fundamental karma. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"To disclose all evils—to disclose all evils committed from the very limits of saṃsāra until reaching the place of no-arrival—such are the causes and conditions."
I cannot describe it in full; when the time comes, you should provide instruction and fill in this section. From here on below, the actual method of repentance (*pratikramana*) is clearly explained.

Before one wishes to repent, one should first respectfully invite the Triple Gem to serve as a virtuous condition, relying upon these supreme objects so that [the transgressions] may be proven to be extinguishable.
(The following two verses were composed by another person. I take refuge in all Buddhas of the ten directions; I prostrate to the boundless ocean of pure awakening.

I pay homage with my body, speech, and pure mind, bowing my head in prostration to the holy ones who have attained the Way and its fruits—those who abide in the stage of cherishing all beings as an only son, who dwell in the wondrous Dharma, inconceivable *tathatā*, and the naturally pure *garbha*.
(From the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*). Disciple [Name], together with all sentient beings of the *dharmadhātu*, makes this vow:
I openly confess all sinful karma committed since beginningless time: such as killing one's sovereign or parents, or true persons and arhats;
engaging in warfare and military expeditions, or slaughtering with blades and weapons; hunting birds and beasts, or netting and trapping insects and fish;
or inflicting unjust punishments as a wicked king, including the harming, injuring, or killing of any sentient being, from those with conscious natures down to the most minute crawling creatures.
Furthermore, they prey upon one another like fierce beasts and birds of prey; they steal the property of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as the wealth and treasures of others;

serving as officials or colleagues, they take bribes and accept illicit gains; they commit sexual misconduct outside their own households without distinguishing between kin and stranger, showing no restraint toward monks or nuns;
they give rise to arbitrary likes and dislikes and harbor groundless jealousy; or they practice deceit and falsehood to delude and mislead others.
When rulers and parents do not know or see something, one falsely claims to know it or see it; relying upon ghosts and spirits, one deceives the common world.

Or, through slander, flattery, and double-tongued speech, one incites strife between two parties. One takes the evil words of this person to report to that person, and holds the malicious talk of that person to repeat to this person.
Thus, one obstructs the relationship between ruler and minister and sows discord between father and son, destroying all forms of harmony. Or...
Their speech is coarse and harsh; they disparage others, revile them at will, and indulge in verbal abuse.
