Sometimes they do not speak with integrity, engaging instead in frivolous chatter (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). They describe good as evil, the fragrant as foul, the long as short, and the white as black.

Uttering such fallacious and deceitful words, they mock and toy with others. Furthermore, their minds are set on craving flavors, and they seek after them without restraint. Their nature is thus characterized.
They are bound by much ill-will and anger, or they fail to recognize correct principles, being deluded by false views;

they slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, asserting that there is no cause and effect, and do not believe in practicing virtue to receive the joys of humans and devas, nor do they believe that committing evil leads to the sufferings of hell.
Some claim this body is obtained without cause, while others claim that the future is non-existent and that cause and effect do not exist, thereby destroying stūpas and monasteries.
They burn the scriptures and melt down or scrape images of the Buddha to extract gold and copper; they defile the monasteries and transgress the prohibitions and precepts;
they drink alcohol, eat meat, and consume the five pungent herbs; being ignorant and holding false views, there is no evil they do not commit.
Regarding all these ten kinds of evil karma thus described—whether committed by oneself, taught to others, or witnessed with rejoicing—they have certainly existed since time immemorial.
Through the causes and conditions of sin, one can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts;
or, if born among humans, to have short lifespans, much illness, and to constantly dwell in lowly and base positions as well as poverty; to share wealth with others yet lack autonomy;
to have an unfaithful wife, or for two wives to contend with one another; to be frequently slandered and deceived by others; and to have all one's kinsmen...
They belong to the corrupt and destructive; they do not encounter pleasant speech but constantly hear evil sounds. Whatever they proclaim is always accompanied by strife and litigation.
Though they feign the utterance of true words, people do not believe or accept them. Their spoken expressions are neither clear nor correct.

Greedy for wealth and never satisfied, they fail to obtain what they seek and are constantly on the lookout for the faults of others. They associate with unwholesome friends who together cause them mutual distress.

Those born into families that harm living beings and hold wrong views constantly harbor a mind of flattery and crookedness; since beginningless time, the ten unwholesome karmas have arisen from afflictions and false views.
Now, by the power of the Buddha-nature and right view, they openly confess and repent, whereby all are eliminated and extinguished.
It is like casting a bright pearl into turbid water: by the majestic power of the pearl, the water immediately becomes clear. Thus it is with the Buddha.

The majestic power of this nature is likewise such that when cast into the turbid waters of the afflictions of sentient beings—including the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes—it immediately becomes clear and pure.

I, disciple [Name], and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, from this present body until the attainment of Buddhahood, vow never again to commit such transgressions. We take refuge in and pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem, and we repent.
Having completed [the ritual], next, through the merit of this rite of confession, one should make this vow:
"In a future age, may I and other believers behold the Buddha of Infinite Life with his body of boundless merit.
Having beheld that Buddha, may we obtain the stainless eye and attain unexcelled bodhi. (This vow is from the *Ratnagotravibhāga*.)
Regarding the fourth point, the sequence of the three refuges (triśaraṇa) in their collective and individual aspects, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that there are two ways of receiving them:

first, the individual reception, wherein one says, "I take refuge in the Buddha," and having completed the refuge in the Buddha, one does the same for the Dharma and the Sangha; second, the collective reception, which is as previously mentioned.
Furthermore, regarding the ten precepts (*daśa-śīla*), there are also two types: one says, "I undertake the precept of non-killing," and "I undertake the precept of non-killing."
"Ultimately, even unto my acceptance of non-false view," and so forth—this is called "receiving individually. As for "receiving collectively," it is as explained in the Three Refuges.
This refers to the ten wholesome actions, which are called the ten precepts (*daśa-śīla*). If the teacher says, "I take refuge in the Buddha," the disciple replies, "Yes.
To speak correctly, one says, "I take refuge in the Buddha. If the teacher says "Buddha," the disciple says "Buddha. If the teacher and... [text truncated]

If both the disciple’s words and the teacher’s instructions are incorrect, the Three Refuges are not established. For instance, if the teacher instructs, "Take refuge in the Buddha," and the disciple replies with "Yes" (*er*), or if the disciple fails to speak at all, or if they repeat the teacher’s words incompletely, or if they do not state their own name, and so forth—in all such cases, the reception [of the precepts] is not accomplished.
This is also the case if the sounds of the speech differ, such as when people from two different countries, like those from China and India, do not understand each other's language.
One should instruct them regarding the characteristics [of the precepts]. First, one teaches non-killing, saying: "If one points a blade at another person, such an act is not permitted;
can you maintain this? The disciple replies, "I can. This also constitutes the reception of the precepts. The Sarvāstivādins say:

"When receiving the Three Refuges, if one mentions the Dharma first and the Buddha last, the Three Refuges are not validly established, because the sequence of the Three Jewels is fixed by their respective status. If one is ignorant...
If one speaks out of sequence due to ignorance and a lack of understanding, one incurs no offense and the three refuges are successfully established;
however, if one speaks erroneously while possessing knowledge and understanding, one incurs an offense and the three refuges are not established.

Regarding the fifth analysis, the distinction of destinies (*gati*): the Sarvāstivādins maintain that the three refuges are accessible across all five destinies, with the exception of those in the heavy hells;
however, outside of these, in mountain ranges, under trees, in open fields, on seashores, and even in the light hells, one may successfully receive the precepts.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Question: Do sentient beings in other destinies obtain the discipline of the precepts? Answer: The Sūtra says..."
Since various dragons are also able to receive the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*), we know that they can obtain the "Good Vision" (*Sudarśana*).

Regarding the principle that dragon deities and others can receive the Three Refuges and Five Precepts, it is said that because dragons and other animals lack cognitive understanding due to their karmic retribution, they do not truly accomplish the reception [of the precepts].

Although it is stated in the sūtras that they can receive the Eightfold Fasting Precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), this merely increases their merit; they do not actually attain the state of being "fasting. This is as explained in this Vinaya.

Regarding dragons who obtain the Three Refuges, they are like merchant brothers and others who merely obtain the "refuge for turning away from heterodoxy" (*pāṣaṇḍa-pratyāgamana-śaraṇagamana*) but lack its precepts.

Although within the Vinaya it is stated that one must receive the Three Refuges only when the recipient understands human speech and recognizes its meaning so that the reception of the precepts is thereby accomplished,
those outside this category— such as the ignorant, pigs, sheep, snails, and clams— do not generate the refuge.
Regarding the sixth point, the gains and losses of the gradual versus the sudden approach: Question: Is it possible to receive the Three Refuges both suddenly and gradually?
Answer: According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, it is not permitted. Question: If that is so, why are there lay followers (*upāsaka*) who receive them in one word or two words?

Answer: This refers to cases where the precepts were established before and after; such instances are not permitted. Question: Is it possible to receive each of the three refuges from one, two, or three people respectively? Answer: It is not permitted.
If one does not respond, one may not ask; if one receives the Three Refuges for one year or half a year without responding, the reception is accomplished according to the number of days.
Chapter Twenty-nine: Receiving the Five Precepts.

This major section of the chapter has five parts: first, distinguishing between right and wrong persons; second, the method of receiving [the precepts]; third, gradual versus sudden reception; fourth, the length of the days of reception;
and fifth, the characteristics of upholding the precepts.

First, regarding the exclusion of those who are non-human or non-virtuous, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states that those who have committed heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), those who live as thieves (*caura-vāsa*), or those who have defiled a bhikṣuṇī are not permitted to become bhikṣus.

Although such individuals may obtain the wholesome discipline (*kuśala-saṃvara*) if they become lay followers (*avadātavasana*), their practice of generosity, loving-kindness, and other virtues is not obstructed; however, they possess only mundane precepts (*laukika-śīla*), as these persons are defiled by evil karma.
Furthermore, because it obstructs the Noble Path, one is not permitted to leave the household life. The *Sūtra of Good Birth* states: "One who wishes to receive the precepts shall be asked:
'Have you abandoned your parents, teachers, or those who were ill? Have you not committed murder? Have you not forsaken those who have resolved for Bodhicitta?
Are you not a thief? Have you not stolen the property of the present Saṃgha? Have you not committed unrighteous acts toward a bhikṣuṇī? [And so forth...]"
"Did you commit any unrighteous acts with your mother, daughter, or sister? Are you not a person of dual sexual organs? Have you not intentionally uttered false speech before the great assembly?
Have you not become a wicked person through double-tongued speech? Have you not committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*)?
Have you not violated the grave precepts among the eight precepts? He replied, "I have not. Then, [the teacher] extensively expounded the Dharma for him, specifically this precept.
It is extremely difficult to act as the foundation for the precepts of a śrāmaṇera, a mahābhikṣu, or a bodhisattva, up to and including the attainment of bodhi.
It should be explained that those who receive these benefits will gain merit, whereas those who disparage them will suffer the retribution of the three evil realms without doubt.

After questioning them on the characteristics of the five precepts, if they all say they can uphold them, and after six months of providing offerings to one who is wise regarding the monastic life, it is known that they may be instructed.
Having received the precepts from the harmonious Sangha, one attains the body of a good son; being thus pure, one is a fit vessel for the Way.
The *Dazhidu lun* states that there are five kinds of precepts, beginning with the abstention from killing and ending with the abstention from drinking alcohol.

If one receives one precept, it is called "one part"; if one receives two or three precepts, it is called "a small portion"; if one receives four precepts, it is called "a large portion"; and [receiving all] five precepts is called "the full portion."
This is called the "complete portion" of the five [precepts] for abandoning sexual misconduct. Regarding those who abandon sexual misconduct:
after receiving the five precepts, they further make a vow before the preceptor, saying, "From this day forth, I, [husband or wife], shall no longer engage in sexual conduct.

This is called the five precepts. Now, within these portions, which portion do you wish to receive? Speak according to your inclination. At that time, the wise one shall confer the precepts in accordance with their words.

Regarding the second method of receiving [the precepts] and the timing for the arising of the *śīla*: the practitioner approaches a member of one of the five groups of renunciants and fully maintains the dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
As stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma;

I take refuge in the Saṃgha" (recited three times). "I, [Name], have finished taking refuge in the Buddha; I have finished taking refuge in the Dharma; I have finished taking refuge in the Saṃgha" (recited three times). I...
The Buddha Śākyamuni and the upāsikās bear witness to me: I, [Name], from this day forth for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Preceptor.

One should say: "Listen, you upāsikā! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—who knows men and sees men—has proclaimed these five precepts for upāsikās. Thus, you must [observe them] for as long as life lasts."
"Venerable sir, what are the five [precepts] to be observed for as long as life lasts? Not killing living beings is a precept for an upāsaka (or upāsikā).

In this regard, for as long as life lasts, one should not intentionally kill living beings. If one is able to do so, one should say 'I can' (though the term *nō* is used, it is changed to *nōzu* to mean 'to be able,' without error).
For as long as life lasts, not stealing is a precept for an upāsaka (or upāsikā). In this regard, for as long as life lasts, one should not steal."
If one is able to undertake this matter, one should say: "I can, for as long as life lasts, refrain from sexual misconduct; this is a precept of an upāsaka (or upāsikā).
Within this, for as long as life lasts, one must not engage in sexual misconduct. If one is able to undertake this matter, one should say:

"I can, for as long as life lasts, refrain from false speech; this is a precept of an upāsaka (or upāsikā). Within this, for as long as life lasts, one must not engage in false speech. If one is able to undertake this matter, one should say: "I can..."
For as long as life lasts, one should not drink alcohol; this is a precept for an upāsaka or upāsikā.
Regarding this matter of not drinking alcohol for as long as life lasts, if you are able [to observe it], you should say "I am able. Having thus declared your commitment, you should further say:

"I shall uphold these five precepts of an upāsaka or upāsikā for as long as life lasts, and I shall reverently serve the Triple Gem, diligently cultivate merit, and seek the Buddha-way both far and near."
Regarding the witnesses, the human and celestial years, and the six fast days (*upoṣadha*) of the three long months: if one is able to observe them, these must all be performed.
If one receives only a single precept, the word "five" (*pañca*) should be removed from the text, and it should simply say: "I, as an *upāsaka* (or *upāsikā*), undertake the precept of non-killing.
The remainder of the text is as before. Next, to clarify the timing for the arising of the precepts: this refers to the third recitation of the preceding three refuges.
Immediately after the five precepts are conferred, the three fetters are directly entrusted [to the recipient]; therefore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* asks:
"If one does not receive the three refuges, can one obtain the five precepts? It answers: "One cannot; one must first receive the three refuges before the precepts can be obtained.
The same applies to the eight and ten precepts.

Regarding the third point, the attainment of the precepts through gradual or sudden reception: The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* asks, "Some say that when the five precepts are received in their entirety, how is this matter to be understood?

It answers: "Whether one receives them in small measure or in full, one obtains the restraint of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*); however, because the essential requirement consists of five, they are called 'five'.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and *Upāsakaśīla-sūtra* both state: "From one part up to the full amount," and so forth. The *Ekottarika Āgama* says: [The same].
Question: Is it also possible to receive [the precepts] one by one or two by two? Since they can be received gradually, may one receive one precept from each of five teachers?
Answer: Yes, it is possible. As stated in the *Dharmatrāta-śāstra* (付法藏), Bakula received the single precept of non-killing and obtained the retribution of immortality fivefold.
Question: Once the five precepts have been received, is it possible to receive them again? Answer: According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it is possible to receive them again.
Because this precept was established, at the end of this Vinaya, Queen Mallikā received it from the Buddha for a second and third time.

Regarding the length of the period for the fourth reception, if one asks whether it is permissible to receive it in installments over a limit of five or thirty days, the answer is that according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, one may also receive it for many days until the very end of one's life;
thus, in the *Carma-vastu* (Leather Chapter) of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is said to be either by day or...
Receiving the five precepts and so forth at night also yields a small amount of merit.

Regarding the fifth characteristic of upholding the precepts, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) asks: "Among the five precepts, how many are actual precepts (*bhūta-śīla*)? The answer is: "The first four are actual precepts;
the last one is a prohibitory precept (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). The reason they are grouped together is that it is the root of negligence (*pramāda*), capable of leading to transgressions."

Regarding the four precepts: during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was an upāsaka who, because he drank alcohol, committed adultery with another’s wife, stole another’s chicken, and killed another person.

When others came to question him, he replied that he had not done these things; thus, he committed the offense of lying. Furthermore, he was able to cause a schism in the Sangha and received the retribution of insanity, losing all his wholesome karma.
In the later sections of this Vinaya, it states that there are ten faults in drinking alcohol, as recorded in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that there are thirty-five faults associated with drinking alcohol. The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* says:
"If a person drinks alcohol, it opens the door to unwholesome states, for it obstructs meditative concentration and other wholesome dharmas.
Because there are so many such faults, it is prohibited along with [the other precepts]. This applies equally whether one has received the precept against killing or even all [the other precepts]."

One must not harm any sentient being, whether stationary or moving. Just as the well water in a layperson's house often contains many tiny insects, one must strain it and inspect it before returning it to its source.
If one intends to move about, one must also carry a strainer with oneself.
Furthermore, for one who has undertaken the precept against stealing, one must not take even a single blade of grass or a single grain of rice; thus says the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The *Śāstra* says: When Gavāmpati tested whether a single grain of rice was cooked or raw, he failed to return it to its original owner and thus violated the path of karma;
for five hundred lifetimes he was reborn as an ox, and even after attaining arhatship, he still continued to chew his cud.

Regarding the observance of non-celibacy (*kāmamithyācāra*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that, with the exception of one's own wife, all other men, women, female ghosts, male ghosts, and spirits [are forbidden].
Among animals, those capable of engaging in sexual intercourse all practice what is considered deviant conduct;

although one does not commit an offense with one's own wife, one must nevertheless avoid improper places—meaning non-vaginal orifices—and even when union is permitted, one must exercise restraint once conception has occurred, for fear of harming the fetus.

Furthermore, during the first three years after childbirth, one must remain cautious and avoid intimacy to prevent the depletion of breast milk; this restriction applies unless there is a separate wet nurse present.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* limits [the definition] as follows: "One's own wife in an improper place" refers to the mouth and the anus;
furthermore, all women protected by fathers, brothers, sons, or those who have left the household life for the sake of the Dharma, are also called sexual misconduct.
If a woman without a master comes before the public of her own accord to become one's wife in accordance with the Dharma, there is no offense. The *Tiwei jing* states: "As for age..."

During the six fasting days (*ṣaḍ-upavāsa*) of the three long months, the three luminaries (the moon, the sun, and fire), and the eight *rājā* days—namely, the equinoxes and solstices of spring, summer, autumn, and winter—one must observe prohibitions on these eight seasonal festivals.

Furthermore, for one who has received the precept against false speech, it suffices that the mind be sincere; regardless of whether the object of the statement is true or false, [the precept is maintained].
Question: According to the *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa* (Dazhidu lun), why does the lay follower (*upāsaka*) lack the threefold restraint regarding verbal discipline and pure livelihood?
Answer: Laypeople living at home enjoy worldly pleasures while simultaneously cultivating merit; they are unable to practice the entirety of the precepts.
Therefore, the Buddha required them to observe only the five precepts. Furthermore, among the actions of speech, false speech is the most grave, as it is committed through deliberate deception.
Regarding other afflictions, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally, if one speaks only false speech, the three matters are already subsumed;

if one speaks truthful speech, all four types of right speech are likewise fully subsumed. Because truth is the greatest among all virtues, the *Sūtra on the Arising of Goodness* states that even when speaking falsely, it also subsumes the meanings of frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech. According to this Vinaya, if one drinks alcohol, even...
One must not place grass into one’s mouth; the remaining prohibitions are the same as those mentioned previously.

The Sarvāstivādins state that while lay followers (*upāsaka*) who observe the five precepts are permitted to engage in trade, they must not perform five types of business: first, one must not sell livestock;

however, if one possesses them, one may sell them directly, but must not give them to butchers. Second, one must not sell bows, swords, arrows, or spears; even if one possesses them, [one must not sell them].

1. One must not sell [silk] directly to those who practice slaughter; however, it is permitted to sell it directly to those who do not. 2. One must not make the business of selling alcohol one's profession; however, if one already possesses it, it is permitted to sell it directly. 3.

One must not make the business of pressing oil one's profession, because there are insects within foreign hemp; violating this constitutes an offense, whereas there is no offense if there are no insects. 4.
One must not use the five primary colors for dyeing, because many insects are killed in the process; for example, as in the land of Qin, where indigo is dyed.

Furthermore, many insects are killed when entering places of the five major colors. The *Susheng jing* (Sutra on Good Birth) states that those who have received the precepts should not frequent five types of locations:
the houses of butchers, prostitutes, taverns, kings, and *caṇḍālas*. There are five kinds of actions one should not perform:
selling poison, brewing [alcohol], tanning leather, gambling with dice, and playing chess or *liubo*; as well as singing, dancing, and performing as entertainers—none of these should be done.
One should not associate with such persons even if one has attained [the precepts].
Chapter Thirty: Receiving the Eight Precepts.
This chapter has seven main sections: 1. Explaining the name and defining the scope; 2. The amount of merit obtained by the recipient; 3. Receiving...

One should establish one's resolve by considering seven points: first, the method of receiving the eight precepts; second, the method of receiving the four [precepts]; third, the limits of the fifth [precept] regarding relinquishment; fourth, the differentiation of the characteristics of the precepts;
fifth, the discernment of the levels of the Great and Small Vehicles;

sixth, [the explanation of the benefits]; and seventh, [the explanation of the transgressions]. Regarding the first, the explanation of the names: it is asked, with what intention are the various sūtras and śāstras called the "Eight Precepts and Fasting" (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), or alternatively, the "Eight Barriers" (*aṣṭa-śīla*)?

The one who observes the fast (*upavāsa*) answers that the first eight [precepts] are for closing off the eight evils so that various transgressions do not arise; "not eating at improper times" is the fast itself.

"Fasting" (*zhāi*) means to prohibit the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) so as not to be defiled by the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). Because it cuts off all evils and fully cultivates all virtues, it is called "fasting.
Furthermore, the essence of the fast and the precepts is one, though their names differ; if one seeks the definition through the names, the meaning may be somewhat limited.

Regarding the distinction between the fast (*upavāsa*) and the precepts (*śīla*): "fast" is defined by the practice of not eating after midday, while "precept" has the meaning of preventing transgressions and ceasing evil.

The Sarvāstivādins maintain that there are eight items which constitute the precepts and the ninth which constitutes the fast; thus, because the fast and precepts are counted together, there are nine.

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, these nine items are combined into eight, for the treatise states: "These precepts are divided into eight parts; the first four are the parts of the precepts."
Because it is free from the nature of evil, the first [precept] is called the "portion of non-negligence," and the subsequent three are called the "portions of cultivation.
Other masters state that abstaining from eating at improper times is designated as the "eight precepts" (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*), while the remaining eight constitute the "portions" of these [eight].
If one maintains this view, it contradicts the Sūtra; for the Sūtra states that abstaining from eating at improper times [is itself one of the eight].

The *Ekottarika Āgama*, in its eighth section, states: "Not eating at improper times constitutes the eighth [precept]. The *Zhai fa jing* (Sūtra on the Method of Fasting) combines the performance of music and dance with the application of perfumes and flowers to the body as the sixth [precept].

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* refer to these as the eight branches of the *aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-śīla*. The [text] combines the sixth [precept], the application of flower-oils, with singing and dancing as the seventh;
the eighth is not sitting on high beds, and the eighth is not eating at improper times. The *Abhidharmakośa* and *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* call these the eight precept-branches (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*).
It is not that abstaining from eating at improper times is not part of the fast; rather, it is both the fast itself and a constituent limb (*aṅga*) of the fast.

Although the noble ones' judgments differ—varying between eight and nine limbs when analyzed—the present interpretation, when inferred through its underlying meaning, maintains that according to the Vinaya there should be nine.

Thus, within the ten precepts for *śrāmaṇeras*, this Vinaya divides "singing and dancing" and "unguents and perfumes" into two separate items. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* likewise divides the eight into nine, subsequently clarifying the objects (*viṣaya*) to which they correspond.

Regarding the term *sarvadharmāḥ* (all phenomena): since one who undertakes the fast (*upavāsa*) receives it from among the five groups of renunciants, we know that it cannot be received in the presence of a layperson.
The meaning is that if no one is present, one may perform the full ritual deportment before an image of the Buddha and utter these words:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha," and so forth; thus, the undertaking is successfully accomplished. As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*: "There are some people... [who hold this view].
As for the statement that this precept must be received from another, how can this be considered fixed?
If no person is present, one may simply recite it mentally and verbally, even saying, "I observe the eight precepts," and it is still attained.
Regarding the second point, the extent of the merit gained by receiving [the precepts], the *Cai-fa jing* (Sūtra on the Method of Observing the Fast) states:

"For example, were the sixteen great kingdoms of the world filled with immeasurable treasures beyond description, they would not equal the merit of observing the Buddha’s fasting method for a single day;
compared to that merit, those sixteen kingdoms would be like a single bean. The *Madhyama Āgama* states: "The learned noble disciple maintains..."
When observing the eightfold precepts, if one recollects the names of the Tathāgata’s ten titles, all evil thoughts and unwholesome states will be extinguished and goodness will arise.
A sutra states: "For those who receive the eight precepts, with the exception of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), all other evils shall be eliminated.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "Between the five precepts and the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*), which is superior? It answers: "Because there are specific causes and conditions, both precepts are [efficacious]."
Those who observe only the five precepts do so for their entire lives, whereas those who observe the eight precepts do so for a single day.
Thus, the former have many occasions for practice but few precepts, while the latter have few occasions for practice but many precepts.

If one lacks the great resolve, then even if they maintain the precepts for a lifetime, it is not equal to a person with great resolve observing them for a single day. It is like a weakling serving as a general; though he may lead an army...

Throughout one's entire life, one may ultimately achieve neither fame nor merit, whereas if a hero exerts themselves, chaos is immediately settled; the merit and fame of a single day’s achievement covers the whole world.
The eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*) are likewise compared to the other precepts. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: Question:
For laypeople living at home, do these five precepts alone suffice, or are there further dharmas? Answer: There is the "one-day precept," which is observed on the six days of the *poṣadha*.
The merit is immeasurable; if one observes these precepts from the first day until the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, the resulting blessings are greatest.
Furthermore, it was asked: "For what reason does one receive the eight precepts on the six fasting days (ṣaḍ-upoṣadha) to cultivate merit? The answer is:

"On these days, ghosts and spirits pursue people, seeking to snatch away their lives, causing illness, calamity, and misfortune that bring ill omen to humans. Therefore, at the beginning of the kalpa, the sages taught [this practice]."

People observe the fast and cultivate goodness to create merit in order to avoid calamity and decline; at that time, the method of fasting did not involve receiving the eight precepts, but simply taking one day of not eating as the fast.
Later, when the Buddha appeared in the world, he first taught that for one day and one night one should receive and uphold the eight precepts like all Buddhas and refrain from eating after midday.
This merit leads people to the bliss of Nirvana. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-kośa* states:

In the *Caturmahārājakāyika-sūtra*, the Buddha taught that on the six monthly fast days (*upoṣadha*), the messengers, the crown princes, and the Four Great Kings descend in person to observe sentient beings.
If there are none who practice giving, uphold the precepts, or show filial piety toward their parents, the messengers ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to inform Śakra Devendra;
the hearts of all the gods are then displeased. However, if many do practice giving, uphold the precepts, and show filial piety toward their parents, [the gods rejoice].
The hearts of all the celestial lords, including Śakra, were filled with joy. At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra spoke these verses:
"Those who for six days, during the month of the *śuklapakṣa*, maintain the pure precepts—when such persons reach the end of their lives, their merit will surely be like mine.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Śakra Devendra, how can one speak falsely? If one maintains even a single day’s fast, the merit and blessings thereof [are immense]."
The retribution will surely be as I have described; this is my truthful teaching. Wherever these precepts are upheld, malevolent spirits will keep their distance and one’s dwelling will be secure.
Therefore, by observing the fast and receiving the precepts on the six days of purification, one shall obtain an increase in merit.
Third, regarding the essential requirement of establishing one's resolve: the Sarvāstivādins maintain that if a person wishing to receive the eight precepts first indulges in female beauty,
performs music, craves food and drink, or engages in various forms of play and laughter— acting with such deliberate negligence of heart— and only afterwards receives the precepts,
they do not obtain the precepts regardless of whether it is before or after midday, provided there was no fundamental intention [to observe them].

If one has been negligent in various ways after receiving the precepts, but subsequently encounters a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and receives the precepts again, it is valid regardless of whether it is before, during, or after noon;
in all such cases, the reception of the precepts is successfully accomplished. The *Shansheng jing* (Sūtra on the Birth of Goodness) states:

"If persons of noble status habitually and diligently commit evil deeds, and wish to receive the fast (*upoṣadha*), they must first issue a proclamation throughout their domain that on the day of the fast no evil acts shall be committed. Only through such purity can the fast be attained. If...
It is not that [the precepts] are not established because of the existence of evil vows (*duḥśīla*); for the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"If one receives the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), one must first repent of prior transgressions and only then receive the precepts. This clearly explains repentance;
the criteria for the person, the manner of generating the precepts, and the timing are all the same as what was explained previously regarding the three refuges and the five precepts.
Regarding the fourth method of receiving [the precepts]: the person receiving the precepts should properly maintain their deportment and approach a renunciant to receive them.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "I, [Name], now for one day and one night take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.
As a pure-practice upāsaka (for a woman, say 'upāsikā'), [this is said three times]. "I, [Name], having completed taking refuge in the Buddha..."
Having completed the refuge in the Dharma and having completed the refuge in the Saṃgha, one becomes a *śīlavat* upāsaka (or upāsikā) for one day and one night. (Recite three times.
Having received the precepts, one should next be instructed in the characteristics of the precepts:

"Just as all Buddhas have throughout their lives refrained from taking life, so shall I, [Name], refrain from taking life for one day and one night; it is likewise. Just as all Buddhas have throughout their lives refrained from stealing..."
Just as the Buddhas did not steal for as long as they lived, so too shall I, [Name], not steal for one day and one night;
just as the Buddhas did not engage in sexual misconduct for as long as they lived, so too shall I, [Name], not engage in sexual misconduct for one day and one night;

just as the Buddhas did not speak falsely for as long as they lived, so too shall I, [Name], not speak falsely for one day and one night; just as the Buddhas did not... for as long as they lived... [so too shall I, Name, likewise refrain].
Just as the Buddhas did not drink alcohol for the rest of their lives, so shall I, [Name], refrain from drinking alcohol for one day and one night; it is likewise.
Just as the Buddhas did not sit upon high or large beds for the rest of their lives, so shall I, [Name], refrain from sitting upon high or large beds for one day and one night;
it is likewise. Just as the Buddhas did not wear perfumes, flowers, or garlands, nor anoint their bodies with fragrant oils, nor adorn themselves for the rest of their lives... so shall I likewise.

Just as the Buddhas, for the rest of their lives, do not wear perfumed garments, nor use incense, flowers, or necklaces, nor anoint their bodies with fragrant oils, nor wear perfumed clothes— I, [Name],

likewise for one day and one night, shall not wear perfumed garments, nor use incense, flowers, or necklaces, nor anoint my body with fragrant oils, nor wear perfumed clothes. Just as the Buddhas, for the rest of their lives, do not personally sing, dance, or perform music,
nor go to watch or listen to such performances— I, [Name], likewise for one day and one night, shall not personally sing, dance, or perform music, nor...
Going to observe and listen is also like this: just as all Buddhas throughout their lives do not eat past midday, so too shall I, [Name], for one day and one night, not eat past midday.
Likewise, I, [Name], receive and practice the eight precepts, following the training of the Buddhas;
this is called the *poṣadha*. May I, by virtue of this merit held for one day and one night, not fall into the three evil realms or the eight difficult conditions, nor...
Seeking the bliss of the world of the Wheel-Turning Kings and Brahmā Kings, one vows to eliminate all afflictions and attain *sarvajñā* (all-encompassing wisdom) to achieve the Buddha-way.
(*Poṣadha* means "dwelling together" in the language of Qin. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "Today is the day of the fast.
Summon the upāsakas to bathe thoroughly, put on clean robes, and receive the *poṣadha* dharma. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If there is no one present..."
It is sufficient to merely think in one's mind and say with one's mouth, "I take refuge in the Triple Gem and I observe the eight precepts," and one will thereby obtain them.
Regarding the fifth point, the division of receiving and relinquishing the fast, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"If one first forms the intention to receive [the fast] on the day of the fast, one obtains it even after having finished eating. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* states: "When receiving the eight precepts, one should say: 'For one day and one night.'"

Regarding the prohibitions such as not killing, one should ensure that the verbal commitments are maintained without interruption and not allowed to become confused with the lifelong precepts. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: Question:
Regarding these eightfold fasts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), must they be received in their entirety, or is it possible to receive them partially?

Answer: One may receive as many as one is able to maintain according to one's capacity; whether it be one [precept], such as not killing or not stealing, one may receive them as one wishes. Some say that this dharma...
Question: How is it that one receives these matters for one day and one night? Answer:

One may receive them according to the duration, whether for one day and one night, half a day or half a night, or for a fortnight, a month, and so forth. Regarding the meaning of receiving [the precepts] for one month, one should say:
"I receive the eightfold fast (upavāsa) for one month. The limit of days is determined by the duration of the reception. As for women receiving the precepts, they do not need to expose themselves.
The section on the shoulders is the same as before. Next, to explain the method for relinquishing the precepts:

the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that if, after having received the fast (*upavāsa*), one encounters adverse conditions and is pressured to relinquish the precepts, it is not necessary to do so before the fivefold assembly; it is sufficient to encounter a single person, and the purpose is thereby fulfilled.
The commentary says: "If one possesses a defiled mind and intends to violate the precepts, would it not be better to relinquish them beforehand?"
The repentance for receiving [the precepts] is also obtained; the five precepts and ten precepts are the same in this regard.

Regarding the sixth point, the differentiation of the characteristics of the precepts: the first five precepts are explained as before, while the latter three precepts shall now be further distinguished.
As for "abstaining from ornaments," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "One abstains from non-original ornaments. Why is this so?
If one uses ornaments habitually without becoming excessively intoxicated or deranged, it is said that there are teachers in the world who perversely practice evil discipline,
claiming that when women receive the precepts they must not sleep in the same room as men, nor may they drink milk or stay with small children, fearing the breaking of the precepts; furthermore,
they do not permit sitting or lying on beds eight feet long, requiring them instead to sleep on mats spread upon the ground.
Such various kinds of false practices are all inconsistent with the holy teachings and instead incur the offense of ignorance and lack of study.
For instance, such acts as sleeping in the same room as a man result merely in the impurity of one's precepts; they are not termed "breaking the precepts.
Therefore, the Sarvāstivādins say: "If one has already received the eight precepts, yet whips sentient beings, or says, 'I shall whip you tomorrow,' [this constitutes a violation]."
To cause one's precepts to be impure does not constitute a breach of the precepts. The *Āgama* Sūtras state that regarding "high, wide, and large beds":
a footstool with legs sixteen inches long is not "high"; four feet in width is not "wide"; and eight feet in length is not "large.

Only those exceeding these measurements are called high, wide, and large beds. Furthermore, there are eight types of beds; the first four are distinguished by their material, and their noble substance is not permitted.
Regarding sitting, one does not distinguish between large and small; this refers to couches made of gold, silver, ivory, or horn. The latter four are distinguished by the person using them:

even if one were to spread out a mat on the ground, it would be improper for these honored persons to sit upon it—namely, the couch of a Buddha, the couch of a Pratyekabuddha, the couch of an Arhat, and the couch of a preceptor or teacher.

Seventh, regarding the distinction of status between the Great and Small Vehicles: The Sarvāstivādins ask, "Is there a *prātimokṣa* precept outside of the seven assemblies? They answer, "The eight precepts [are].

Based on this principle, one who receives the eight precepts is not included within the seven assemblies; however, if one considers their status, they should sit above the *upāsaka* of five precepts because they have received more precepts. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* [states]: ... [text continues] ... Regarding the seventh point, the distinction of the stages (*avasthā*) between the Great and Small Vehicles: The Sarvāstivādins inquire whether there exists a *prātimokṣa* discipline outside of the seven assemblies. They reply that the eight precepts do exist. Inferring from this principle, a person who has received the eight precepts is not subsumed under the seven assemblies. Nevertheless, if one considers their rank, they ought to sit above the *upāsaka* of five precepts, as they have received a greater number of precepts. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*...

He is like a valiant general. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "An upāsaka who observes the eight precepts" (*aṣṭāṅga-upāsaka*)—in the language of Qin, this means "one who dwells well" (*śubha-vāsa-puruṣa*).
This person, through a virtuous mind, dwells apart from the breaking of the precepts.
Chapter Thirty-one on Receiving the Ten Precepts.
This chapter has eleven sections, titled: 1. Explanation of Names; 2. Requisites for Leaving Home; 3. Receiving Precepts and Exerting in Practice; 4. Receiving and Discarding Robes and Alms Bowls;
5. Purification (Śuddhi); 6. Forfeiture (Naiḥsargika); 7. Recitation of the Prātimokṣa; 8. Summer Retreat (Varṣā); 9. Receiving the Days; 10.
Self-Examination (Pravāraṇā).

First, regarding the explanation of the name: the *Yesheshi zhuan* (Biography of Yaśas) states that "śrāmaṇera" is translated in the Sui period as "one who is weary and young," referring to the weariness of practicing the Way.
It is also translated as "ceasing [evil] and [practicing] benevolence" (*xici*), meaning to cease worldly defiled emotions while using benevolence to save all beings.
Furthermore, because ordinary worldly sentiments still persist when first entering the Buddha-dharma, one must cease evil and practice benevolence.

Regarding the second [category], those who rely on others for their renunciation, the *Renunciation Merit Sūtra* (*Chujia Gongde Jing*) states: "If one grants male or female slaves, or common people, the merit of renunciation is immeasurable;

it is like filling the four continents with Arhats and providing them with offerings for a hundred years—this does not equal the boundless merit of someone who, for the sake of Nirvāṇa, renounces the world for a single day and night. Furthermore, it is like this:

The *Benyuan jing* (Sutra on the Original Causes) states that building stupas made of the seven treasures reaching as high as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is not equal to the merit of going forth [into homelessness].
Because of going forth for even one day and one night, one will not fall into the three evil realms for twenty kalpas.

The *Saṃghīti-sūtra* states that by going forth for one day and one night and practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one leaves behind the sufferings of the three miserable paths for sixty-six thousand and sixty years; such is the merit of going forth.
The *Sūtra of Virtue* states: "If one creates obstacles or suppresses those who have left the household life, such a person severs the seeds of the Buddha;
all manner of evils accumulate within their body like the great ocean. They will presently suffer from leprosy and die, entering the Black Darkness Hell with no prospect of release.
The *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "There are two kinds of fetters for those who leave the household life: first, the fetter of views; second, the fetter of gain and offerings. There are these two.

An abscess has two characteristics: first, seeking out the faults of others; second, concealing one's own transgressions. A sutra states that there are two poisonous arrows that pierce the mind simultaneously:
first, wrong livelihood for the sake of profit; second, attachment to robes and alms bowls. The *Wubai wen shi* (Five Hundred Questions) says:

"In the past, there was a bhikṣu who delighted in fine clothing and was obsessed with them day and night. He died of illness and was subsequently reborn as a snake, which returned to coil around his robes."
When the community of monks had finished burying the deceased bhikṣu and taken his robes to perform the ritual, a snake suddenly extended its neck and spat venom.

As the monks watched it together, those who had attained the Way contemplated the snake and caused it to depart; it then entered the grass. When the poison became intense, fire erupted from its body, and it died, falling into hell.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one who is seven years old and understands good and evil should be granted ordination; [the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*] says eighty.
Those over ninety are too old, and those over seventy require assistance for rising and reclining; therefore, their ordination is not permitted.

However, if they are able to cultivate various practices, they may be allowed to leave the household life and become *śrāmaṇeras*. If one is too old or too young, or if they have already left the household life, they should not be expelled.

Regarding the *Bhikṣu-vyaya-śānti* (The Sūtra on the Expiation of Transgressions), it says that an old woman sought ordination from the Buddha; the Buddha spoke a verse to stop her, saying: "You now..."
When one has grown old and the time for renunciation has already passed, one should simply rely on deep faith and find solace within the Dharma.
In the Vinaya, when King Śuddhodana requested that the Buddha allow him to renounce the world, the Buddha said: "Simply contemplate impermanence; this is sufficient for attaining the Way;

there is no need to renounce the world. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Regarding those without sexual organs or with dual sexual organs, according to the Vinaya, they do not attain the Way because they lack the [necessary] faculties."

Therefore, it is not permitted to grant ordination [to those who seek it by force]. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that if one seeks ordination and is denied, yet desires to burn down the monastery, permission is granted [to ordain them] even without informing their parents.
The *Pañcaśata-praśna* states that if one steals [a person] for ordination when forbidden by their parents or by royal law, it constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*).

According to the *Śāstra*, if one obtains ordination despite such prohibitions, it merely violates the royal decree and constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding those who come of their own accord, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that they may not be ordained.
One may keep many śrāmaṇeras, but it is permitted for only one person to have up to three;

if a bhikṣu of great virtue has many sons and urges others to ordain them so they may transcend suffering, yet they still do not comply, he may send them to other people. He himself may instruct these śrāmaṇeras, who are of three grades:
from seven to thirteen years of age, they are called "crow-driving śrāmaṇeras"; from fourteen to nineteen, [they are called] "great śrāmaṇeras."
Regarding the name "Dharmic Śrāmaṇera," from those aged twenty to seventy, the *Śrāmaṇera-nāma-pañcaśata-praśna* states:
"If, after having gone forth, one steals property from one's original household, one commits a *pārājika* offense. Why? Because at the time of initial going forth, one renounces everything;
it is not one's own property. This applies equally to principal deposits and interest on debts. If a practitioner wishes to go forth..."

First, one should go inside the *saṃghārāma* and stand in a place where one can see but cannot hear, performing a formal motion (*jñapti*) identical to that of a single-announcement procedure (*ekakarmavācanā*) to inform the Saṃgha.

This is done so that the formal inquiry and response may be established without fault. Thus, in the lower section of the Vinaya, it is recorded that [the Buddha] privately ordained two children of another person as monks;
the Saṃgha was unaware of this, and later when their parents came searching for them, [the monks] all said they had not seen them. Subsequently, when the children were found, the various [monks]...

The Bhikṣu felt ashamed in every way. The Buddha said: "From this day forward, if you are to ordain another as a renunciant, you should perform a *jñapti* (a formal motion) to harmonize the Saṃgha and ask the Saṃgha:
'Now that the Saṃgha is in harmony, what shall we do? To answer this, the *jñapti-karman* for one who has undergone tonsure is as follows:
'Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! This person, [Name], is having their hair shaved by [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] [Name]. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha..."

"Please listen as I inform [the community] that [so-and-so] will have their hair shaved by [the bhikṣu/bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so; thus it is announced. If [the community] does not know [who this is], they should go from room to room to inform them;
once known, they may proceed. Next, one requests the preceptor, saying: "Venerable Sister, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, so-and-so, now request the Venerable Sister to be my preceptor. May the Venerable Sister act as my preceptor. By relying upon the Venerable Sister, I shall obtain the shaving of my hair."
"Shave my hair for the sake of compassion, going forth from home" (recite three times). Next, request the preceptor, saying: "Venerable Sister, please attend to me, [Name].
I now request the Venerable Sister to act as my preceptor. May the Venerable Sister act as my preceptor for me;
through reliance upon the Venerable Sister, I shall shave my hair and go forth from home for the sake of compassion" (recite three times). Both masters should respond together, saying: "Very well."
The *Śraddhavat Puruṣa Dharmanirdeśa Sūtra* states: At the place where the hair is to be shaved, sprinkle fragrant water on the ground within a circle of seven feet;
hang banners at the four corners and set up a high seat for the one intending to leave the household life. Furthermore, provide two superior seats for the two masters.
Once the one wishing to leave the household life has put on his original lay garments and finished prostrating and taking leave of his parents and honored relatives, he shall recite this verse:
Wandering through the three realms, one cannot escape the bonds of affection; yet to abandon affection and enter the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the true way of repaying kindness.
Having recited this, one discards secular clothing. According to the *Sudarsana-sūtra*, one should bathe with fragrant water to remove the scent of the white-robed laity.

The *Duren jing* states that although one wears the robes of a renunciant, one may only wear the *nivāsana* (inner robe) and the *saṃkakṣikā* (undershirt); one is not yet permitted to wear [the full set of formal robes].
When donning the *kāṣāya* at the site of the human path of practice, one should approach the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and kneel with the right knee on the ground.

The preceptor should regard the candidate as a son and must not harbor thoughts of contempt or lowliness toward him. The disciple, in turn, should regard the teacher as a father. According to the *Saddarśanasamuccaya*, it says:

"One should explain [the nature of] hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, and so forth. Why is this explained? Because there are those who have previously contemplated these five things, and now, for the sake of shaving their heads, they are reminded of them.
Immediately upon the arising of his past karma, he attained enlightenment.

Just as Rāhula attained arhatship before his tonsure was even complete, or as a ripe boil awaits the needle and a lotus flower awaits the sun to bloom—having thus expounded the Dharma in various ways, he came and sat before the Ācārya.
According to the *Sudarsana*, he was consecrated with perfumed water, and it was praised, saying: "Excellent! Great Man!"
One who is able to realize that the world is impermanent, renounce the mundane, and take up *nirvāṇa*—such a person is rare and inconceivable.

Having finished paying homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, he further spoke a verse, saying: "I take refuge in the Great World-Honored One, who can deliver beings from the suffering of the three realms of existence;

may all sentient beings likewise universally enter the bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thereupon, the *ācārya* shaved his hair and ordained him. As the *Duoren jing* (Sūtra on Ordaining Persons) says: "For..."
When his hair was being shaved, those nearby recited the *pravrajyā-gāthā*: "Deforming one's appearance to maintain the vow of integrity; severing attachment to have no kin;
abandoning the home to propagate the Holy Way; may all people be delivered. At the time of shaving the hair, he was instructed to leave three or five strands of hair on the crown of his head.
Upon arriving before the Upādhyāya, he knelt with his right knee on the ground. The Upādhyāya asked him, "Now, for you, I shall remove the hair from the crown of your head."
Having granted permission and replied, "Excellent," the Upādhyāya then shaved his hair. He knelt before the Upādhyāya, who bestowed the *kāṣāya* upon him;
he received it by placing it upon his head and returned it to the Upādhyāya. This was repeated three times. Then the Upādhyāya dressed him in it.
While it was being properly adjusted, the *Sudarsana-sūtra* spoke this verse: "How great is the robe of liberation, the signless field of merit!"
Having offered his robes as an act of service, he extensively practiced the precepts to deliver all sentient beings.

Having finished prostrating before the Buddha according to the *Duren jing* (Sutra on Delivering Humans), he circumambulated the path three times and recited this verse of self-congratulation: "How fortunate is he who encounters a Buddha! Who would not rejoice? May blessings and vows meet with their proper time;
I have now obtained the benefit of the Dharma. He then prostrated before the assembly and his two teachers, and sat down in the lower row to receive the six [precepts].

Having personally paid homage, one receives the intention to leave the household life and depart from the secular world; with a heart full of joy, the parents and all relatives perform prostrations to them, delighting in their resolve for the Way.

It is most excellent to shave the head before midday. According to the *Vinayamātṛkā*, once the hair has been shaved and the kāṣāya robe donned, one should then confer the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.

Third, regarding the exertion in cultivation through receiving the precepts, this is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the formal procedure (*vidhi*) as the primary body; second, distinguishing the remaining auxiliary practices.

Within the first part, after the assembly has been gathered and the candidate for ordination has been seated in a place visible but out of earshot, the formal act is performed according to the *jñapti-caturtha* (one motion and three proclamations) so that the Sangha may know they have obtained the dharma.
One asks the Sangha: "The Sangha is now in harmony; what is being done? The answer is given.

The procedure for the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) is as follows: "Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen. This person, so-and-so, wishes to go forth from the household life under the guidance of the Bhikṣu (or Bhikṣuṇī), so-and-so.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent that so-and-so go forth under the guidance of the Bhikṣu (or Bhikṣuṇī), so-and-so. This is the motion.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*, one first confers the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*) and subsequently confers the ten precepts (*daśa-śīla*). This is the rule in this Vinaya.

It is best to follow the practice even in the absence of a formal text; however, one must not receive the precepts directly [from an individual]. Receiving the Ten Precepts from the Saṃgha results in a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"One should be made to prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha and then proceed to the place of the Ācārya. Having prostrated, one kneels with palms joined, and the teacher instructs:
'You should follow my words as I confer the Three Refuges upon you. He replies, 'So be it' (*evam astu*). The text does not specify that this must be performed in the presence of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the method of receiving [the precepts], one should receive them in a separate location; if one wishes to generate the feeling [of the vow], it is best to receive them properly before a large assembly of the Saṃgha.

Prior to formally receiving the precepts, one must inquire about the obstacles and difficulties (*antarāyika-dharma*); although not fully detailed in the Vinaya text, it is logically necessary to ask because if such obstacles exist, one cannot receive the precepts.
The circumstances for inquiring about these obstacles are largely the same as those explained above in the section on the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The essence of the precepts for taking the Three Refuges is as follows: "I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Saṃgha.
I now follow the Buddha into the homeless life. [Name] is my Upādhyāya. The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One.
(Recite three times. "I, [Name], have completed taking refuge in the Buddha; I have completed taking refuge in the Dharma; I have completed taking refuge in the Saṃgha. I now follow the Buddha..."
Having gone forth, [Name] is my preceptor; the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One. (Recite this three times.
Once the precepts have been received, one should next explain the characteristics of the precepts: "For as long as life lasts, one shall not kill living beings.

Is this the precept of a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī? Can you uphold it? Answer: "I can. "For as long as life lasts, one shall not steal. Is this the precept of a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī? Can you uphold it? Answer: "I can."

[The preceptor asks: "Can you answer that you will, for as long as life lasts, refrain from sexual misconduct? This is a precept of the śrāmaṇera and śrāmaṇerī; can you maintain it? [The candidate] answers: "I can. [The preceptor asks: "Can you answer that you will, for as long as life lasts, refrain from drinking intoxicants?
This is a precept of the śrāmaṇera and śrāmaṇerī; can you maintain it? [The candidate] answers: "I can. [The preceptor asks:

"Can you answer that you will, for as long as life lasts, refrain from wearing flower garlands or anointing the body with perfumes? This is a precept of the śrāmaṇera and śrāmaṇerī; can you maintain it? [The candidate] answers: "I can. [The preceptor asks: "Can you answer that you will, for as long as life lasts... [The candidate] answers: "I can."
"Throughout one's life, one shall not go to watch or listen to singing, dancing, or performances; can you, [novice monk/novice nun], uphold this precept? He/She replies, "I can.
"Throughout one's life, one shall not sit upon high or wide beds; can you, [novice monk/novice nun], uphold this precept? He/She replies, "I can.
"Throughout one's life, one shall not eat at improper times; can you, [novice monk/novice nun], uphold this precept? He/She replies, "I can."

"Can you, for as long as life lasts, refrain from grasping raw gold, wrought gold, silver, or precious objects? This is the precept for *śrāmaṇeras* and *śrāmaṇerīs*. Can you uphold it? They reply, "I can. Regarding "raw and wrought":
the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* state that "raw color" refers to natural color, while "wrought" refers to processed color;

thus, raw gold and wrought silver are both clearly identified. Having finished explaining the characteristics of the precepts, he announces: "These are the ten precepts for *śrāmaṇeras* and *śrāmaṇerīs*, which are now complete."

As long as one possesses this physical form and life, one must not transgress [the precepts]. Having already understood the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*), one should explain for them that the merit of leaving the household life (*pravrajyā-guṇa*) is higher than Mount Sumeru, deeper than the great ocean, boundless like the four quarters, and vaster than empty space.

Furthermore, one should explain for them the five virtues, the ten recitations, the practice of maintaining the robes and bowl, and the six remembrances (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), etc.—which are largely the same as those within the Saṃgha, yet different from those of worldly people—namely, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
Regarding these six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), because they apply universally even to *śrāmaṇeras*, when one reaches the third recollection, it says:

"I am so many years old; on such a month, day, year, and time, I received the ten precepts. According to the Vinaya regulations, both the sequence of one's birth year and the sequence of the year of ordination must be known.

Fourth, regarding the acceptance of the robes and bowl: according to the Sarvāstivāda school, once a śrāmaṇera has received the ten precepts, he should possess two sets of robes, one upper and one lower:

first, the *uttarāsaṅga*; second, the *antarvāsaka*. (The remaining materials and their methods of preparation, as well as the regulations for the loss of robes, are the same as those for the bhikṣus;
only the wording for the formal acceptance differs slightly. Holding the upper robe in his hands, he faces one who knows the Dharma (a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī) and says: "Venerable Sir" (or "Sister").

With single-minded attention, [Name] (śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī), please attend to me: this *maṇḍala-uttarāsaṅga* has been made according to the prescribed measurements; I now accept it. (Recite three times.

The procedure for accepting the lower robe follows the same pattern. The text for relinquishing: Great Virtuous Sister, with single-minded attention, please attend to me: [Name] (śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī), this *maṇḍala-uttarāsaṅga*, which was originally accepted, I now relinquish.

(Recite three times. The procedure for relinquishing the lower robe follows the same pattern. The text for accepting the bowl: Great Virtuous Sister, with single-minded attention, please attend to me...

"Venerable [Sister], please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name] (a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī), now accept this *pātra*, a vessel of proper measure. (Recite three times; the formula for relinquishing it may be understood accordingly).

The text for accepting the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) is extensive: "Venerable [Sister], please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name] (a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī), now accept this *niṣīdana*, made of proper measure.

(Recite three times; the formula for relinquishing it may be understood accordingly). The *Pañcaśata-praśna* states: "If there is no novice (*śrāmaṇera*), a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) may perform the same."
The Ritual Procedure (*karmavācanā*) (the preceding texts for receiving and relinquishing robes are not found in this Vinaya; their meaning is based on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*).

Fifth, regarding the declaration of purity (*viśuddhi-uddeśa*): if one obtains extra robes, alms bowls, or medicine, one should first request a member of the fivefold assembly who knows the Dharma to act as an intermediary pure donor (since a true donor is rare, they are not discussed here). "Venerable Sister, please attend to me with single-mindedness. I, the novice [or] novice nun, [name],..."

"I, [Name], now request the Venerable Sister to act as the intermediary pure donor for my robes, medicine, and bowl. May the Venerable Sister act as my intermediary pure donor for robes, medicine, and the bowl out of compassion. (Recite this three times.

Subsequently, regarding long robes and other items, one should perform the *śuddhi* (purification) before a single *śrāmaṇera* who knows the Dharma, following the same procedure as the rules for the Saṃgha;

however, change the name accordingly. If one obtains money or precious objects, one should declare them to a *śuci-puruṣa* (pure person), just as in the midst of the Saṃgha. If one keeps money or precious objects and wishes to relinquish them in order to repent, one must first relinquish them to a *śuci-puruṣa*. The offense is then to be confessed before a single *śrāmaṇera* who knows the Dharma.
The text for the confession is the same as that for a *pāyattika*, with the only difference being the designation of the offense as a *dukkaṭa*.

Regarding the sixth category, the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: if one commits an offense such as possessing extra robes (*atirekacīvara*) or staying overnight apart from one’s robes (*cīvaravippavāsa*), one must likewise go outside the boundary (*sīmā*) and confess and relinquish [the robe] before one who knows the Dharma (such as a *śrāmaṇera* or *śrāmaṇerī*).
If the ritual is performed within the boundary, those who have not received the full precepts do not constitute a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).

First, one should relinquish the robes and articles; next, one should invite a preceptor for confession (*kṣamāpaka*). If there is subsequent regret, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). This is the same as within the community of monks, with the sole difference that the name of the offense is changed.

If one commits an offense belonging to the first category [the *pārājika*], all three groups of practitioners commit a *sthūlātyaya* (grave wrongdoing), yet they must still undergo banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*).

If one commits an offense from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the community) downward, up to the hundred rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*), whether concealed or fundamental, one must perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.
Seventh, regarding the one who recites the *Prātimokṣa*, there are two types: general and specific. (The general method is the same as that for the *saṃgha*). Next, concerning the specific practice:

at the time of the *poṣadha*, each group should assemble in its own hall, burn incense, scatter flowers, provide warm water, distribute voting sticks (*śalākā*), appoint a person to recite the precepts, and chant the *brahman* chants;

these are largely the same as the recitation by the *saṃgha*, differing only in the names used. Therefore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one śrāmaṇera is appointed to oversee the proceedings.
When the *śrāmaṇeras* and *śrāmaṇerīs* cast the voting sticks (*śalākā*), those who do not attend shall have their consent (*chanda*) received by a fellow resident.
When the total number is being announced, they should place the sticks they have cast into the midst of the Sangha and entrust them to the *karmadāna*; he shall then announce the total number.

Once the one who delivered the sticks has returned to their original location, another person is appointed to recite the *Prakaraṇa* of the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, the ten precepts for *śrāmaṇeras*, and the five virtues.
When the first person among the group of ten has finished ascending the seat, the Preceptor of the Precepts (*śīla-ācārya*) shall next chant the *Brahma-pūjā*.

Having chanted the *Brahma-pūjā*, he should make the following formal announcement: "Venerable Sisters (or Venerable Brother), listen with one mind. Today is the day of the *poṣadha* for the recitation of the precepts for the *śrāmaṇera* and *śrāmaṇerī*.
We intend to recite the Ten Precepts, the *Āryā-Mahāprajāpatī-sūtra*, and the Five Virtues. The enumeration of the ten members is thus announced."
Venerable Sisters (and so forth), each of you should quiet body, speech, and mind, and listen with single-minded attention while joining your palms.

Venerable Śrāmaṇeras (and Śrāmaṇerīs), there are ten precepts upon which you must rely for study in order to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). What are these ten? (The Śrāmaṇeras recite the first ten precepts;

this is the text from the *Prakaraṇa* of Mahāprajāpatī). Venerable Śrāmaṇeras (and Śrāmaṇerīs), there are five pure virtues that constitute a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), being excellent and sublime. Relying upon them...

The attainment of merit through these [practices] is sufficient for one to become a Buddha. What are the five? First, generating the aspiration to leave secular life and cherishing the Way within one's heart;
second, altering one's physical appearance to accord with the monastic robes; third, casting aside body and life to follow all that is virtuous;
fourth, forever severing ties of kinship and affection so as to be without partiality toward anyone; and fifth, vowing to seek the Mahāyāna for the purpose of delivering all beings.

Therefore, at that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for them: "Altering one's appearance to maintain the will and integrity, severing attachment so as to have no kin, leaving the household life to propagate the Noble Path—may all people be delivered.
Those with the five virtues who transcend worldly affairs are called the Supreme Field of Merit;
by making offerings to them, one obtains eternal peace, for their merit is foremost. (From the *Fútián jīng*) There were several dozen śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās of great virtue.

In order to destroy the ten kinds of false views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and also desiring to enable practitioners to distinguish between the true and the false regarding the monastic life, what are these eleven?

First, all sentient beings depend upon and rely on food (to destroy the non-Buddhist path of self-starvation, such as those who rinse their mouths with bran-water, drink juices, eat wind, or practice breath-sustenance).

Second, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) (to destroy the non-Buddhist path of spontaneity, such as the Vatsīputrīyas who hold that milk is for drinking, thorns are sharp, crows are black, fire is hot, water is wet, wind is light, and earth is heavy; all such views arise from a lack of causal understanding).

1. No-arising without cause (spontaneous birth); 2. The three types of sensation and perception (to refute the non-Buddhists who take Brahmā as the cause, such as those who claim Maheśvara, Brahmā, or the King of Beings is the father and mother of all sentient beings, and that their anger and joy depend upon that deity);
3. The Four Noble Truths (to refute the non-Buddhists who deny causality, such as those who claim that grasses and trees grow spontaneously and that humans are likewise); 4.

The Five Aggregates (to refute the non-Buddhists who cling to a "self" (*ātman*), asserting that within the body there exists a separate self that acts as the sovereign master); 5. The Six Sense Bases (to refute the non-Buddhists who hold to a single consciousness, just as a monkey moves through six windows in a room, so too do the sense faculties).

1. The seventh is the single consciousness that universally traverses [the realms]. 2. The seventh is the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). This is for the purpose of destroying the non-cultivation of outsiders (*tīrthika*); by turning back from and observing in accordance with [reality], one sees beyond eighty thousand kalpas and no longer perceives further objects, which is designated as True Truth (*satyadharma*) and Nirvāṇa.

It is like a ball of thread on a high mountain: when the thread is exhausted, the ball stops. Why then would one need to cultivate the Path? [This view is thus refuted. 3. The eighth is the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). This is for the purpose of destroying the false causes of outsiders;

some maintain the precepts of crows, chickens, deer, dogs, oxen, or hares, while others cultivate the eight dhyānas or cultivate false wisdom and false knowledge, taking these to be the true Path while turning their backs on the eightfold noble path. 4. The ninth is the nine abodes of sentient beings (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*). This is for the purpose of destroying [attachment to] the heavens of form and formlessness.

Furthermore, the non-Buddhists who calculate toward *nirvāṇa* take the two realms—the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the meditative attainment of neither-conception-nor-non-conception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)—as places where the mind is submerged; they claim these represent the ultimate principle. However, these are merely abodes for sentient beings. Tenth are the ten totalities (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*). These are established to refute the non-Buddhists who hold to the extremes of form and emptiness:

using form to refute the existence of the desire realm and using emptiness to refute the existence of the form realm. They claim that emptiness is the ultimate limit. Now, the establishment of the ten bases is merely the operation of one's own mind to a greater or lesser degree; in reality, there is only the single consciousness, and fundamentally no external objects exist.

Because they falsely establish notions of right and wrong and do not eliminate the view of self, they continue to undergo birth and death. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Non-Buddhists can produce the boat of dhyāna-concentration to cross the ocean of the desire and form realms, but they cannot cross the formless realm, which is like a vast and deep sea, because they do not break [through their delusions]."

[This is] my heart’s intention. [The section on] the "Ten Counts" appears in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. O Venerable Sisters, I have finished reciting the Ten Precepts, the Five Virtues, and the Ten Counts.
If there is anything further regarding the Buddha-dharma, all should study it together therein. Having finished the recitation of the precepts, each person recites a verse of self-congratulation:
"The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is the foremost joy; hearing the Dharma and practicing it with devotion is joyful; the harmony of the great assembly is joy."

The joy of union with tranquility is the bliss of sentient beings being free from defilement; the joy of peace is like that of the Great [Saṃgha]. When the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) by the monks and nuns has not yet concluded, the śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs shall temporarily recite sūtras and preach the Dharma.

They shall wait until the *karmadāna* strikes the wooden mallet three times, at which time they shall all come to the hall and enter the assembly in order, kneeling on their right knees (*hukuei*) with palms joined according to their usual seating positions. The Precept Master on the high seat shall then perform [the ritual].

Having finished the explanation regarding those who can protect the precepts and so forth, [if there are] fewer than four—namely three or fewer [śrāmaṇeras or śrāmaṇerīs]—one should recite the precepts face-to-face with each person, saying:
"Virtuous elder sister (or brother), attend closely; today is the day for the recitation of the precepts.
I, [name], am pure. [This is to be said] three times. If there is only one person, one should perform the recitation of the precepts through mental reflection, saying: "Today..."
