On this day of the *Poṣadha*, I, the śrāmaṇera [or śrāmaṇerī] so-and-so, am pure (three times). Regarding the eighth point on the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*):
according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the five groups of practitioners observe the retreat and receive the formal authorization for travel;

however, within the "precept against wandering during the three seasons" of this Vinaya, the three groups of practitioners also incur an offense. This must be understood. [This is] called "different" (viśeṣa).

Regarding the ninth day for receiving [the robe], although there is no explicit teaching in the Vinaya when seeking the text, it is permissible to apply it by analogy to the seven-day rule (*saptāha-vidhi*).

However, this is not the case; one may also directly [apply it] within one's own boundary (*svasīma*) to monks, novices, nuns, female novices, laymen, and so forth, even when they have gone outside the boundary.

Regarding the tenth point, the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for correction), there are two approaches: the general and the specific. If following the general procedure, once the Saṃgha has completed its *pravāraṇā*, those possessing the five virtues come to the place where the śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs are located;
they kneel facing one another and recite the *pravāraṇā* formula of the Saṃgha, as both [the monks and the novices] are subject to being charged with offenses.

If following the specific procedure, at the time the mallet is struck, each group assembles in a separate hall to burn incense, scatter flowers, distribute voting tallies (*śalākā*), provide hot water, and so forth.

As detailed in the *Poṣadha* (Recitation of Precepts) for the Great Saṃgha, once the counting sticks have been distributed and returned to the Great Saṃgha, one person should be appointed to perform the *cāruka* (the formal motion).
Next, the Elder shall orally designate two persons as the *pañca-varga-dharmas* (the five virtuous witnesses), after which the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) is performed.

(The term "Saṃgha" is changed to "Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha" in the *Shuowen*). If there are fewer than five—namely, four or less—the *śrāmaṇeras* and *śrāmaṇerīs* perform the *pravāraṇā* face-to-face, addressing them as "Venerable Sister."
With single-minded mindfulness, one should think: "Today is the day of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) for the community of monks;

I, [the śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī] so-and-so, am pure. (Recite this three times. One person should think with single-mindedness: "Today is the day of the *pravāraṇā* for the community of monks; I, [the śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī] so-and-so, am pure. (Recite this three times.
For those who are not pure, they should mentally confess their transgressions. From this point downward, the *Vinayamātṛkā* clarifies miscellaneous rules of conduct.
A śrāmaṇera should know shame and remorse, dwelling well within the dharma of serving his teacher;

he should not be indolent or unrestrained, but should guard his own body and speech, humble himself, and respect others. He should always delight in upholding the precepts and take no pleasure in frivolous play.
He should not rely on the cleverness or strength of his own mind, nor should he be flighty; he should know the sense of shame and constantly follow his two teachers to recite and study.
In all matters performed within the Saṃgha according to the sūtras and the Dharma, nothing may be contravened; thus one should understand extensively that the Sarvāstivādins hold this view.
A śrāmaṇera commits an offense by digging the earth without a purpose related to the Three Jewels.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that for the three lower groups [of monastics], committing an offense without cause constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. The *Caturvargika-vinaya* explains that "without cause" refers to having no [valid] reason.
Regarding injuries, as well as matters such as eating leftovers, consuming food kept overnight, or cooking for oneself—these are permitted when no one else is present, but forbidden when others are.
As for the punishment of a śrāmaṇera, even if one has previously spoken to his teacher, one should not unjustly assist the śrāmaṇera;

rather, if a punishment must be administered, it should consist of various forms of hard labor, such as sweeping the ground, clearing away filth, pulling carts, or working on stone steps and pathways. If...
One should not be made to serve as a messenger for the upādhyāya, the ācārya, or other persons; rather, one should speak [to them] and provide service in accordance with the Dharma.

One should perform duties for the upādhyāya and the Saṃgha in their proper order and must not obstruct them. If no offerings or requisites are given from within the Saṃgha, these are the property of the donor and should be given accordingly.
According to this Vinaya, starting from the senior bhikṣus, the rooms, dwellings, bedding, and furniture should be assigned in order to the śrāmaṇeras.
If one cannot cherish and protect [a disciple], one should not grant them material offerings; rather, these should be given according to their seniority.
As for all other requisites for śrāmaṇeras, they are as described in the *Vinaya* of the Five Divisions, the *Three Thousand Dignified Manners*, the *Śrāmaṇera-vidhi-sūtra*, and so forth.

however, they must not explain the lightness or heaviness of the retribution for the offenses, but should instead instruct them by citing specific instances so that they do not transgress in meaning. Chapter Thirty-Two: Receiving the Bodhisattva Precepts. (This chapter, while not included within the primary tenets [of this school], is essential for practical application; were it omitted, one would likely fail to employ it correctly.
This chapter has eleven main sections: 1.
Receiving and relinquishing, as well as the benefits and losses; 2. Distinguishing the virtues of the capable person and the recipient.
1. Requesting the Master’s Instruction; 2. Four Requests for Permission to Hear; 3. Distinguishing the Characteristics of the Precepts; 4. The Method of Washing and Confession;
5. The Method of Formal Reception; 6. The Method of Requesting Witness; 7. The Method of Mental Recitation; 8. The Method of Observing and Violating; 9. The Method of Prostration and Withdrawal.
Regarding the first point, the benefits and harms of receiving and relinquishing [the precepts], the *Ratnavyūha Sūtra* states:
"O Son of the Buddha, I now establish for all Bodhisattvas the root of all precepts, which is the so-called Threefold Aggregate of Precepts (Tri-skandhaka-śīla).

O Son of the Buddha, once one has received the ten inexhaustible precepts, the recipient transcends the four Māras and overcomes the suffering of the three realms; from birth to birth, they do not lose these precepts, and they constantly follow them in practice."

From human beings up to those who have attained Buddhahood—regarding the ten inexhaustible precepts: these refer to the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*) of a bhikṣu as the first four; the fifth is not to sell intoxicants; the sixth is not to disparage or speak ill of lay or ordained bodhisattvas;
following the four additions below, the four *pārājika* offenses of a bodhisattva constitute the ten inexhaustible precepts.

O Son of the Buddha, if any sentient beings of the past, future, or present do not receive these bodhisattva precepts, they cannot be called possessors of consciousness; they are no different from animals and cannot be called [sentient beings].

Those who are constantly separated from the ocean of the Triple Gem—neither bodhisattvas, nor men, nor women, nor ghosts, nor humans—are called animals, those of wrong views, or followers of external paths;
because they do not accord with human sentiment, it is known that the Bodhisattva precepts have a method for receiving them but no method for relinquishing them.
Having been transgressed, they are not lost, persisting until the end of the future. If there is anyone who wishes to receive them...
Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, the Dharma Master first explains them for the practitioner, causing them to take delight in and be attached to them, and only then does he confer them.

Furthermore, if a Dharma Master is able to teach and transform a single person within any land to leave the household life and receive the Bodhisattva precepts, the merit of that Dharma Master surpasses that of one who constructs eighty-four thousand stupas; how much more so if it be two, three, or even more persons?
The merit and retribution of a hundred or a thousand people cannot be measured; yet for such a Dharma Master, his wife, husband, and six kin may mutually serve as teachers.

Those who receive the precepts enter the realm of all Buddhas and the ranks of the Bodhisattvas, transcending the suffering of birth and death for more than three kalpas. Therefore, one should receive them.
Even if one commits an offense, it is superior to not having received them at all; for one who has received them, even committing an offense is what defines a Bodhisattva.

Those who do not transgress [the precepts] are called outsiders; for this reason, there are those who receive one portion of the precepts and are called "one-portion bodhisattvas," and so on up to two, three, four, or ten portions, which is called "receiving the complete precepts. Therefore, when the mind is exhausted, the precepts are also exhausted; because the mind is inexhaustible, the precepts are also inexhaustible.
As for sentient beings of the six realms who receive and obtain the precepts, they obtain them simply by understanding the words, and once obtained, they are not lost.
The *Śīla-sūtra* also states that there are two causes and conditions for losing the bodhisattva precepts: first, regressing from the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*);
second, giving rise to an extremely evil mind. Apart from these two conditions, even if one passes through the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts in future lives, one never loses the precepts.
When one receives the bodhisattva precepts again in a subsequent life, it is not called "newly receiving" them.

To clarify this, the *Pure Brahma Net Sūtra* states: "At that time, after the wise one has chanted the *karmavācanā* for the person receiving the precepts before the Buddhas of the ten directions, all those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions see this person from afar and conceive thoughts of them as a son, a younger brother, or a disciple;
they all extend their hearts toward them with compassion and protective mindfulness. Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas protect and mindfully regard them from afar, [they cause...]"

When one who has received the precepts experiences an increase in merit and does not lose the wholesome dharmas, their every pore from the crown of the head down to the feet feels as if a cool breeze has entered the body, and their entire frame trembles with awe. One should know that the recipient is then endowed with the marks of the precepts.
At that time, there must be Buddhas of the ten directions who, with the eye of the True Dharma, behold this practitioner as possessing them.
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni, with a mind of truth, should proclaim these words within the assembly of noble ones to inform the great multitude:
"In that world, in such-and-such a country, at such-and-such a place, such-and-such a bodhisattva has requested the bodhisattva precepts from such-and-such a wise one.
This person has no teacher; out of compassion, I shall act as their teacher. Furthermore, the Buddha said:
When a Buddha-son bestows the precepts upon others, there are only seven transgressions that prevent one from receiving the Bodhisattva precepts:

in addition to the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), these include killing one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or ācārya, all kings, princes, ministers, and officials, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, laymen and laywomen who have faith,
men and women of the eighteen Brahma heavens, those without sexual organs, those with dual sexual organs, and those with yellow [disorders].
Gatekeepers, slaves, all ghosts and spirits, vajra-deities, animals, and transformed beings—provided they understand the Dharma Master’s speech—all may receive the precepts.
One should instruct them so that the saṃghāṭī robes they wear are all of a discolored hue (prakāśavarṇa), distinct from those of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Furthermore, it says: "If, O Sons of the Buddha, a crown prince wishes to receive the position of a king, or receives the position of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*),"
When the hundred officials receive their positions, they should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts;

all ghosts and spirits will then protect the person of the king and the persons of the officials, and all Buddhas will rejoice. Having received the precepts, they should give rise to a mind of filial piety and reverence.
Upon seeing those of higher rank, preceptors, ācāryas, or fellow students, fellow visionaries, and fellow practitioners, if the Bodhisattva instead gives rise to arrogance—
If, with a mind of delusion or pride, one does not rise to welcome, nor perform prostrations, in each instance failing to act according to the Dharma;

or if, when making offerings, one does not provide for them even by selling one's own body, kingdom, city, sons, daughters, or the seven treasures and various goods—if one does not do so, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
The *Biography of Dharma Master Dharmakṣema* states that there was a Dharma Master named Daojin who wished to receive the Bodhisattva [precepts].
Śīlacaṇa ordered Huìjìn to repent; on the eighth day, Jìn went to Caṇa to receive the precepts. Caṇa then became greatly enraged.

Jìn subsequently exerted himself with diligence for three years, both fearing [retribution] and repenting. Within his state of meditative concentration, he saw Śākyamuni Buddha and various great bodhisattvas bestowing the precepts upon him.
That night, more than ten people simultaneously experienced a dream identical to what Jìn had seen. Jìn went to Caṇa to recount his vision and confession.
Before he had even walked ten paces, Nanchen suddenly started up and said, "Excellent! You have already received the precepts; I shall further bear witness for you.

He then expounded the characteristics of the precepts before the image. Once Daolang had fully understood them, he followed the same dream and advanced together with him, humbly requesting ordination by seniority to become his Dharma brother.

Having respectfully investigated the holy teachings and observed the myriad paths of transmission, I humbly consider the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* to be the most essential pivot.

For now, I have carefully relied upon it to compose this grand track for my own personal use; how could I dare to presume to instruct others? Regarding the reception of the precepts, there are only two types: first, the...
Regarding the second point, within a thousand *li*, all seven assemblies (*sapta-parṣad*) may serve as preceptors. Among these seven assemblies, the bhikṣus should be considered the most superior;
furthermore, among the bhikṣus, those who are senior in years (*vṛddha*) are determined to be the most excellent. Regarding the virtues of such seniors, there are again three kinds:

first, those who are bodhisattvas of the same Dharma who possess the complete lineage (*gotra*); second, those who have already generated the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). As for the latter...

The fulfillment of the three qualities for generating the resolve consists of possessing wisdom, power, and skill in both speech and meaning, as well as the ability to recite and uphold [the teachings].

These manifest the ultimate [attainment]; furthermore, one must possess these three virtues to be fit to serve as a teacher. If one entirely lacks such conduct, they are not qualified to be a teacher.
As for the disciple, they too must possess the spiritual lineage and generate the resolve before they may receive the precepts.

Third, regarding the invitation of the preceptors, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "When one is about to receive the Bodhisattva precepts, one first invites the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to serve as preceptors.

The invitation says: "I, the disciple [Name], together with all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, respectfully invite Śākyamuni Tathāgata to serve as our Upādhyāya (Preceptor), and respectfully invite Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva to serve as our Ācārya (Preceptor). One should thus invite them.
Maitreya Bodhisattva acts as the preceptor; he requests the Buddhas of the ten directions to act as witnesses and requests the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions to be his companions.
Fourth, regarding the request for permission: before the preceptor, he spreads out a *niṣīdana*, removes his leather sandals, and performs a prostration by touching feet.
One should then speak as follows: "I beg the Venerable One to grant me the reception of the Bodhisattva precepts.
If the Venerable One does not find it troublesome, may he compassionately grant his permission. (Recite this three times. The Precept Master replies: "Very well.

Once permission has been granted, one immediately teaches the *Vaipulya-mātṛkā-śāstra*, the *Pañcavidyā-sthāna-śāstra*, and so forth, so that [the candidate] may know what constitutes an offense and what does not, and what is defiled and what is undefiled.
One must first become thoroughly proficient in the soft, medium, and superior grades of the forty-two precepts before receiving them from the Buddha;
this case is not like that of one who has previously studied the Mahāyāna, for whom permission is granted and the precepts are received immediately.

Having received authorization from the preceptor, one may then—whether after three years, one hundred days, or a single day—within the ritual enclosure, bare the right shoulder and perform three prostrations.
One pays homage to all Buddhas of the ten directions and to all Bodhisattvas on the great earth.
Having paid homage to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one recollects the merits of those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas contained within the three aggregates (*tripuñja*).

One then pays homage to the preceptor, kneels with the body bent forward, and speaks these words three times: "I pray only that the Virtuous One will confer upon me the Bodhisattva precepts. Once these words have been spoken, one cultivates purity.
The mind should maintain only the precepts, with no other thoughts.
Fifth, regarding the discernment of the various characteristics of the precepts: the Great Sage’s method for delivering sentient beings relies solely upon the precepts.

Generally speaking, there are three essential points concerning the precepts: first, the precepts for householders, namely the five precepts and the eight precepts; second, the precepts for those who have left the home life, namely the ten [precepts].
The two hundred and fifty precepts are the precepts commonly practiced by the three classes of worldly practitioners; that is to say, they are the three clusters of precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*).

Furthermore, these three clusters are of three kinds: first, the various natures of the precepts; second, the mind of the precepts, which is the bodhicitta and the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*);

and third, the practice of the precepts, which consists of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgraha-vastūni*). As for these perfections and integrations, if one follows their majestic manifestation...
Regarding the formal rules, they are called the Three Aggregates; if categorized according to practice and stages, they are termed the Seven [Categories];

and if considered in terms of qualities and positions, they are designated as the Seven Grounds and the Thirteen Abodes. Any such explanations are all variations within the Dharma of the precepts. Furthermore, for their sake, the four *pārājika* dharmas are taught:
first, one must not, for the sake of gain and offerings, praise oneself and disparage others—a lack of shame constitutes a *pārājika*.

The first *pārājika* is the mind of stinginess, failing to give to those who are poor and lowly; this is a *pārājika* of shamelessness. The second *pārājika* is the mind of anger, striking or reviling others before the assembly;

even when the person apologizes and seeks reconciliation, one does not accept their confession due to a lack of shame; this is a *pārājika* of shamelessness. The third *pārājika* is the mind of delusion, slandering the Mahāyāna;
this is a *pārājika* of shamelessness. By explaining these precepts, it enables the recipient to know for themselves whether their own strength is capable [of upholding them].
Receiving [the precepts] requires that one’s mind be nurtured and purified; thus, one gives rise to a superior internal intention. Sixth, regarding the purification through repentance:
this means that only when the mind is clear can one be fit to receive [the precepts]. The defilements of a defiled mind consist solely of delusion and hindrance.
"Delusion" refers to slandering the Triple Gem; "hindrance" refers to extensively committing the ten unwholesome actions. Now, in teaching repentance, one truly repents of these.
I, your disciple [Name], respectfully address the Buddhas of the ten directions:
from the beginningless past when consciousness first arose until this present body, I may have personally lacked faith in the Triple Gem, or taught others not to have faith in the Triple Gem;

I may have seen such acts and rejoiced in them, or I may have personally disparaged the Triple Gem, or taught others to disparage the Triple Gem, or seen such acts being committed [and rejoiced therein].

Whether rejoicing in [the destruction of] the Triple Gem, or personally destroying or damaging the Triple Gem, or instructing others to destroy or damage the Triple Gem, or seeing such acts being committed and rejoicing;
or whether personally committing killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, or instructing others to commit killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, or seeing such acts being committed and rejoicing;

or whether personally engaging in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous speech, or instructing others to engage in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous speech, or seeing such acts being committed.

Whether rejoicing in them myself, or through my own greed, hatred, and delusion, or by inciting others to greed, hatred, and delusion, or seeing such acts being committed and rejoicing therein—if I have failed to feel shame or remorse regarding these various transgressions, thereby losing the Bodhisattva precepts without realizing it, I now, before the Buddhas, repent with utmost sincerity.
May all my transgressions be forever severed without remainder. With a sincere heart, I pay homage to all Buddhas. (One recitation is sufficient.)
(Three times is even better).
Seventh, regarding the formal reception of the precepts, there are briefly three parts of question and answer: first, the question and answer that determines one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*);

Whether sitting or standing, one speaks these words: "Listen, you, [Name], son of good family or daughter of good family, disciple of the Dharma, sister of the Dharma!
Are you a Bodhisattva? The other replies, "I am. The reason for sitting is that the Preceptor of the Precepts is elderly and lacks physical strength;
the reason for standing is that the Preceptor of the Precepts is young and possesses strength, being free from fatigue. Thus, [Name]...
"Jia" (the first character) likely refers to the name bestowed by one's parents, teachers, or elders; it does not mean to invoke the titles of the Emperor or the Magistrate to honor one's clan.

Even if such titles were used, they would not constitute the taking of the precepts; rather, it would be to turn one's back on the Dharma and follow worldly passions, which is not the ritual for honoring the Way.
Regarding the second question and answer: the question asks whether the Bodhisattva vow has been taken, and the answer states that it has already been taken.

The "aspiration for awakening" (*bodhicitta*) is precisely another name for the mind of the Way. Regarding the third question and answer: it refers to the formal instruction for receiving the precepts, which says:

"O virtuous man or woman, you who wish to receive from me all the bodhisattva vows—the vow of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), the vow of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the vow of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*)—these precepts are those observed by all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present."
"Abiding in the precepts, all bodhisattvas of the past have already trained, all bodhisattvas of the future will train, and all bodhisattvas of the present are now training.
Are you able to receive [these precepts]? He replies, "I am able. (This is said three times. Now, as for the address "good man" or "good woman," this is used when referring to a single person;

Recite three times: "I receive the Bodhisattva precepts; may you act as my witness. (Recite three times. As for the invocation of the Buddhas:

all the Buddhas of the ten directions—beginning from the Buddha Virtuous Virtue (*Śubhavyūha*) in the eastern direction, up to the Buddha Bright Virtue (*Prabhāśrī*) in the lower direction, and including all other Buddhas, the foremost and unsurpassed Great Teachers who currently possess direct knowledge, vision, and awakening—now [bear witness] that this certain Bodhisattva, in a certain world...
"Before this image of [Name] Buddha at the [Name] Monastery in this realm, I, [Name], three times receive the Bodhisattva precepts;

may you act as my witness. (Recite three times. Because of this declaration, before the immeasurable Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of the great earth, there appear auspicious signs according to the Dharma:
either a radiance, or a cool breeze, or a wondrous and extraordinary fragrance. Because these signs appear, [the precepts are established]. Ten.
When all Buddhas regard this [certain] bodhisattva as a son and the great bodhisattvas regard him as a younger brother— because they regard him as a son and a younger brother—
they possess a heart of loving-kindness and affection that causes this bodhisattva, from the time he receives [the precepts] onward, to repent immediately upon transgressing,

to apply himself with diligence and mindfulness, and to firmly maintain them so as not to violate them; thus, until reaching Bodhi, he shall never regress and will be fully endowed [with these qualities].
He was fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty secondary characteristics, all-pure qualities, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses,

the three foundations of mindfulness, the three ways in which he needs no protection, great compassion, the quality of never speaking falsely, the eradication of all habitual tendencies, the wondrous wisdom of all modes,
and the one hundred and forty unique dharmas; riding upon great kindness and compassion, he traveled throughout the ten directions to deliver beings extensively.
Sentient beings do not decline the toil; all sentient beings alike share in this benefit.
Furthermore, regarding the reception of the precepts by men, the ritual for women is likewise the same; the only difference is that one addresses a woman as "Sister.
As for the deportment of baring the shoulders, this is also the same and need not be done.

Regarding the ninth [method], the reception of the precepts through mental recollection: if there is no such person available to receive them from face-to-face, that Bodhisattva should, before an image of the Buddha, personally receive full ordination and cultivate majestic deportment, saying:

"I, [Name], inform all Buddhas of the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas throughout the great earth: I now, before these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, receive the entirety of the Bodhisattva..."

The *saṃvara-śīla* (vows of restraint), the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (vows for gathering wholesome dharmas), and the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (vows for benefiting sentient beings)—these precepts are those in which all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present abide;

they are what all bodhisattvas of the past have studied, all bodhisattvas of the future shall study, and all bodhisattvas of the present are now studying. (Recite three times. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "If from..."
When receiving the precepts from a teacher, one does not require auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*), because the lineage of teachers has been transmitted through successive generations and possesses power.

However, for one who vows to receive the precepts before an image of the Buddha, it is necessary to request auspicious signs before the ordination can be conferred; this is because, as one is not receiving them from a teacher, one lacks such inherent power.

Tenth, regarding the characteristics of upholding and transgressing: A disciple of the Bodhisattva precepts, [Name], on such-and-such a day, month, year, and hour, received the Threefold Pure Precepts of a Bodhisattva from Master [Name] based upon the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. What are these three?

First is the precept of restraining conduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), which involves abstaining from all that is unwholesome and initiating the practice for realizing the Path; this is the cause for the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

Ultimately, it becomes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); cessation is upholding, while activity is transgression. To follow the teaching, practice with reverence, and be cautious so as not to commit [transgressions]—this is the second, the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*śīlaṃ kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhakaṃ*).

There is nothing that does not accumulate and give rise to practices that assist the Path; this is the cause for the merit of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*), which ultimately becomes the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Activity is upholding, while cessation is transgression. To follow the teaching, practice with reverence, and thereby accomplish the merit of conduct—this is the third, the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattvārthasaṃgrāhakaṃ*).

The precepts of sentient beings are such that there is no non-arising that is not saved; they arise as the practice of the non-abiding path. This is the virtue of grace, which ultimately fulfills the manifestation of the *nirmāṇakāya*.

To maintain this is to abide [in the precepts], whereas to depart from it is to transgress them. Regarding the inclusion of the *saṃvara-śīla* (precepts of restraint), there are essentially only four, namely the four *pārājika* offenses mentioned previously.
This comprehensively clarifies the faults to be abandoned within the three clusters (*triskandha*). As for the essence of that which abandons these faults, it refers to body, speech, and mind.

Karma is volition. Regarding the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*): it means that there is no goodness that is not accumulated—namely, the virtues of body, speech, and mind;
the three types of wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; the ten *pāramitās*; and the eighty-four thousand practices conducive to the path.

One follows the teachings and practices them to perfect the virtue of conduct. Regarding the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*): one takes the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) as the mind and the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgraha-vastūni*) as the practice. As for the four immeasurables:

This refers to loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Compassion is able to uproot suffering until it is exhausted; loving-kindness is able to bestow happiness until it is fulfilled;

sympathetic joy means rejoicing when sentient beings are ultimately freed from suffering and attain the fulfillment of happiness; equanimity means causing sentient beings to practice the path of the Buddhas and reach the destination of the Buddhas, at which point one gives rise to the mind of equanimity.

Regarding the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) for the practitioner, they are: giving (*dāna*), kind speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and cooperation (*samānārthatā*).
When a Bodhisattva wishes to gather in sentient beings, he first relieves them from the suffering of their physical forms by means of material gifts;

next, he awakens their minds through affectionate speech, causing them to gain faith and understanding. Regarding the gathering through beneficial conduct: based on that prior faith and understanding, he subsequently causes them to initiate practice.

"Practice" refers to the cultivation of morality, concentration, wisdom, and so forth, leading sentient beings to respectfully undertake these deeds; this is gathering through beneficial conduct. Regarding gathering through commonality: once the cultivation of practice is perfected...
The transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) achieves the three bodies (*trikāya*), as they are realized by the Noble Ones (*ārya*). Thus, the treatise states:

"Generosity and kind speech cause those who have not yet resolved their minds to resolve them; acting for the benefit of others causes those whose practice is not yet matured to reach maturity; and sharing in common benefit causes those who are not yet liberated to attain liberation.
The items listed above are for the recipient of the precepts to recite, so that they may know the timing of receiving the precepts and briefly understand the instructions received from the teacher.

This concludes the section on maintaining awareness of transgressions and offenses, as well as the exhortations, rejoicings, dedications, and vows; for fear of excessive prolixity, these are not described here.

Regarding the eleventh practice, the ritual of bowing to the Buddha and withdrawing: according to the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), one should perform one prostration to the Buddha and one prostration to the Earth Bodhisattva;
it does not mention bowing to the Dharma and the Sangha. However, from the perspective of the underlying principle, it is preferable that the ritual be extended to include them all.
Essentials of the Vinaya, Volume Lower Part, End; Chapter Thirty-Three:
Caring for the Sick and Conducting Funerals.

This chapter has six main sections: 1. Establishing the intent of nursing the sick; 2. Distinguishing between persons who are qualified and those who are not; 3. The methods for providing service and support;
4. Arranging the location; 5. Preaching the Dharma and collecting the mind; 6. The rites for the final burial.

First, regarding the intention behind establishing the rule for tending to the sick: For those with conditioned forms, there are many entanglements; the four elements conflict with one another and the six viscera are difficult to harmonize.
If one does not provide care, life has nowhere to rest. Therefore, the Vinaya states: "If you do not look after one another, who then should?
Thus, even the World-Honored One washed away the excrement and urine of a sick person and swept and sprinkled the area.
He made his dwelling place extremely clean and spread out his robe to lie upon it, then established a rule, saying:
"From this day forward, one should tend to the sick bhikṣu; one should act as a caregiver for the ill. If you wish to make offerings to me, you should offer them to the sick.

How much more so for those who share the same Dharma and precepts—how could we ever abandon one another? The World-Honored One, being a person of the highest station, yet personally tended to the sick; how much more so should those of equal Dharma and righteousness not neglect one another?
Even regarding the intention of attending to the sick, it is the same. If one asks: "What is the meaning of attending to the sick that makes its merit equal to that of making offerings to the Buddha?

The answer is: When one attends to the sick with a compassionate heart, uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness, such practice is identical to that of the Buddha. Furthermore, a treatise states: "To act in accordance with the Buddha’s words is called making offerings to the Buddha."

Second, regarding the discernment of persons as right or wrong: this Vinaya states that if there is one who is ill, it is permitted for the *upādhyāya* to accompany the patient, and the *ācārya* to accompany the patient;
if disciples are available, they should attend from the closest to the most distant.

If there are none at all, the Saṃgha should assign someone to care for the patient. If such a person is unwilling, they should be appointed in successive order; if they still refuse, then as follows...
If there is no bhikṣu [to attend to the sick], śrāmaṇeras, upāsakas, and others should look after them;
if there is no such person, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇerīs, and upāsikās should perform whatever tasks are required, but they must not touch the bhikṣu-saṃgha.
The Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states: "One should dispatch [attendants] according to the number of the sick; if one does not look after them, [there is an offense]. One.

If any member of the Sangha commits an offense and encounters a sick bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī on the road, they should seek out a vehicle to carry them back and provide them with offerings in accordance with the Dharma;
this should continue even until the time of death, when they should perform cremation or burial and must not abandon them.
The same applies to those of the three lower assemblies.
Third, regarding the provision of necessities, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* states that there are nine conditions through which a sick person will inevitably meet an untimely death:
first, knowing that food is not beneficial yet greedily consuming it; second, lacking the ability to exercise moderation; third, eating while previous food has not yet been digested;
fourth, vomiting while food has not yet been digested; fifth, forcibly retaining food that has already been digested and should be expelled; sixth, failing to follow the proper course of digestion.
Regarding the seven types of illness, one should provide food according to the specific ailment without making calculations. Eighth, there is laziness; ninth, a lack of wisdom.
If a patient has a physician’s fee outside of their robes and bowl, it should be taken to provide for them. If the patient has none, the Sangha should provide it.

If the Sangha has none, then from among the patient's own expensive robes and bowl, those of higher value should be traded for items of lower value to be used by the patient, while the remainder should be provided as support. This applies even if the patient is reluctant to part with them.
One should inform the Sangha, saying: "This patient does not understand impermanence; being stingy, he begrudges his robes and bowl and refuses to exchange them.

Having informed the Sangha, one should speak to him with gentle words and teach the Dharma so that he may attain understanding. Only then should one effect the exchange. If there is still nothing available, one should seek it from outside and give it to him.
If one takes fine food from within the Sangha to give to the attendant, one must not be parsimonious regarding one's own resources.

However, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that in places where no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible) is available, it is permitted for a bhikṣu to personally ignite a vessel and place water in it so that the *kappiya-kāraka* may wash rice and put it therein;
the bhikṣu then ignites a fire to cook it, and subsequently receives it from the *kappiya-kāraka* to carry it to the sick person.
If there is absolutely no *kappiya-kāraka*, then as stated in the *Pañcaśata-praśna-vastu*: "If a sick bhikṣu is in the mountains or marshes..."
□□ One must not travel back and forth during the day in a deserted place. A bhikṣu may prepare food for seven days;

having first purified the rice, he may accept it and prepare it. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If one is ill and lacks medicinal decoctions, one may offer flowers, fruits, or food to others to request them in exchange for medicinal decoctions;
this does not constitute an offense. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Whenever the saṃgha distributes gruel, one should ask whether there is anything else [to be obtained]."
If there is no rice gruel for the sick person, one should first give it to the patient and only then distribute it to the Sangha. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"One should inquire according to what the patient requires, ask about the cause of the illness, seek out a physician, and procure medicine. When the day arrives, go to the Sangha kitchen and ask whether there is food for the sick person.
If there is none, take items from the provisions stored in the Sangha's storehouse; if there are no such items, one should seek them externally on their behalf."

If a virtuous, well-renowned, and meritorious bhikṣu requests [medicine] from a sick person, and that person recovers through the medicine obtained, then—provided it was not impure within the Buddha’s Sangha, not leftover from overnight storage, not handled by those who are unqualified to receive it, and not stored overnight—it may be taken and consumed. *Śubhavyūha* states:
"One who attends to the sick should not give rise to weariness. If one has no resources of one's own and cannot obtain [medicine] by seeking it out, one may borrow the property of the Triple Gem."
Having lent [an item], one must return it tenfold according to the Dharma. The *Five Hundred Questions* states:

"If a nurse uses a patient's belongings to provide for the patient's necessities without asking the patient, or if they do so even after the patient has expressed dissatisfaction, these items may not be used.

If they have already been taken, they must be repaid; failure to do so constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). When a bhikṣu is gravely ill, one must not allow him to be deprived of his robes and bowl while attending to him."
If one possesses no robes due to a lack of merit, and yet accepts and maintains worn-out robes and alms bowls, one commits an offense of falling (pāyattika).

According to this Vinaya, one should ask the sick person what kind of robes they require; if that patient receives inferior robes and bowls or sends them to another, the attendant for the sick fears [reproach], and the Buddha said: "It should not be done thus."
Regarding the fourth point, the location for placement, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If a Venerable One is ill, he should be placed in an excellent room in an exposed area so that monastics and laypeople may come to inquire after him, thereby generating wholesome roots.

One must always burn incense, light lamps, smear the ground with fragrant liquid, and provide service to the patient and guests. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "The attendant praises the patient, saying: 'Venerable One, you maintain...'"
Be fully endowed with the precepts and do not be attached to your dwelling, clothing, acquaintances, or friends.
Keep the Three Jewels in mind and contemplate the impurity of the body; within the three realms, be careful never to be indolent.

Act according to the length of your life (if you know you are gravely ill and lose right mindfulness by thinking of wealth, rooms, kinsmen, or friends, move from your original dwelling to a quiet room). As the *Jihuan tu* (Diagram of Jetavana) states: "In the northwest corner of the monastery..."

The place where the sun sets is designated as the Court of Impermanence (*anitya-kuti*). If there is one who is ill, they are placed within the central hall, which is called the Hall of Many Impermanent Births;
those who depart from it are extremely numerous, with only one or two remaining. Inside this hall, a standing image gilded in gold is installed facing west;
the patient should be laid down before the image, and a [cord] should be tied to the hand of the image.
Have five-colored silk banners made, and have the patient hold the ends of the banners with their hands, forming the intention of rebirth in the Pure Land.
Although they may experience the necessities of life such as defecation and urination, the World-Honored One does not consider this unwholesome.

Considering that this land is fundamentally a place of mixed evils, he nevertheless descended his numinous spirit to receive the various classes of living beings and lead them across the sea of suffering; how much more so now, when one with sincere faith entrusts their life to the Buddha?

Regarding the abandonment [of the patient]: the *Zhihuan tu* (Diagram of the Jetavana) states that one should follow whatever object the patient is focused upon—whether it be the forms of Amitābha, Maitreya, Akṣobhya, or others—and arrange them as previously described, burning incense and scattering flowers with various adornments to inspire the patient’s wholesome mind.
Fifth, concerning the preaching of the Dharma and the gathering of the mind: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the caregiver should follow what the patient previously practiced.

Whether it be those training in the forest (*āraṇya*), those who recite the sūtras and uphold the Vinaya, Dharma masters, or those who study the Abhidharma, one should assist them in their communal affairs and praise them according to their understanding and practice;
one must not disparage them, for that would cause them to regress from their original wholesome resolve. Thus, the Vinaya states:
"One should preach the Dharma to the sick so as to bring them joy. The *Vinayamātṛkā* says: "The sick person need not follow the instructions of the attendant."
It is auspicious for people to act contrary to the wishes of those who are ill. The "Chapter on the Wise and Virtuous" (*Bhadrapāla*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"Furthermore, he emits a light named 'Beholding the Buddha. That light awakens those whose lives have ended; through the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, they will certainly behold the Buddha. After their death, they are born before the Buddha.
Seeing them at the point of death, [the Buddha] exhorts them to recollect the wholesome, displays sacred images for them to gaze upon with reverence, and further encourages them to take refuge."
Based on the Buddha as the cause, one attains the vision of the Buddha’s light. The *Wǎngshēng Ānlè Guótù Jiàn Fóguāng Lùn* states:
"If good men or good women cultivate the five mindfulnesses and achieve perfection, they will ultimately be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss to behold that Amitābha Buddha.
What are these five? First, prostration; second, praise; third, making vows; fourth, contemplation."

Regarding the examination of these five points for the dedication of merit toward rebirth in the pure lands of the ten directions according to one’s vows, the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Pure Lands of the Ten Directions According to One’s Vows through the Empowerment of Dedication* states:

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Puguang: "If members of the fourfold assembly, whether men or women, wish to be reborn in the buddha-fields of the ten directions on the day of their death, they should wash their bodies, put on fresh and clean garments, burn various famous incenses, hang silk banners and canopies, and engage in chanting."
Recite and chant the honored sutras of the Triple Gem for the sake of the sick, expounding upon causes and conditions, parables, and subtle words.

The meaning of the sutras is that all things are suffering, empty, and not-self; the four great elements are but a provisional combination, their form like a plantain tree with no core substance within, and like a flash of lightning that cannot remain long.
Therefore it is said: "Form is not fresh for long; it shall surely return to decay. Through sincere devotion and the practice of the Way, one may attain [liberation].
"Crossing over suffering, one obtains every fruit according to the wishes of the mind. The *Sūtra on Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Questions* states:

Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying, "As the Buddha has taught regarding the merits and benefits of Amitābha Buddha, if one can practice mindfulness of the Buddha with ten successive recitations without interruption, one will immediately attain rebirth there.
How should one practice this mindfulness? The Buddha replied, "It is not the mindfulness of the ordinary or the foolish."

If one does not harbor unwholesome thoughts and is free from defilements and fetters, possessing such mindfulness as this, one will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).
What are these eleven? First, one should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings;

one must not disparage the conduct of any sentient being—for if one disparages their conduct, one will ultimately fail to attain rebirth. Second, one should [give rise to] a deep [mind of compassion] toward all sentient beings...

First, give rise to a mind of compassion and eliminate all thoughts of harm. Second, develop a resolve to protect the Dharma, disregarding even one’s own body and life, and never giving rise to slander regarding any phenomenon.
Third, cultivate a mind of firm determination within the practice of patience. Fourth, maintain a profoundly pure mind that is untainted by gain or offerings.
Fifth, generate the mind of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), constantly and daily mindful of it without ever ceasing.
Seventh, one gives rise to a mind of respect toward all sentient beings, eliminates the mind of self-conceit (*māna*), and speaks with humility.

Eighth, one does not develop a mind of attachment to worldly discourse. Ninth, one draws near to the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*), deeply engenders various causes and conditions for roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), and remains free from the distracted mind of clamor and agitation. Tenth, one contemplates the Buddha with right mindfulness and eliminates...

Eliminate all discursive thoughts (*saṃjñā*). (Having given these instructions as before, take the sutras and images to the bedside of the patient. Inscribe the titles of the sutras and the names of the deities upon them, and explain them in detail so that they may open their eyes and behold them, thereby awakening their consciousness.

Furthermore, invite those of virtue and wisdom to recite Mahāyāna scriptures, assist in the chanting of hymns, and cause banners and flowers to fall profusely before their eyes. Let the fragrance of incense be thick enough to permeate the sense of smell, and always speak of wholesome matters while refraining from transmitting evil news. This is because at the time of death, many perceptions of evil karma appear, making it difficult to maintain one’s resolve and cast them aside.

Therefore, when attending to the dying, one must employ skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to guide them toward stillness so that their minds continue in succession without a single moment's pause. By means of this meritorious power, one should form the intention to be reborn in a Pure Land.)
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one performs good deeds from birth but harbors evil thoughts at the time of death, one will be reborn in the evil realms;

if one commits evil from birth but harbors good thoughts at the time of death, one will be reborn in the heavens. Furthermore, a sutra says: "One should recollect the merits one has cultivated and maintain pure livelihood.
Regarding the sixth matter concerning the funeral rites, the *Five Hundred Questions* states: "When the teacher passes away, one must not wail loudly; one should weep softly."

Weeping with small tears is [permissible]; therefore, according to this Vinaya, for a nun to beat her breast and weep with flowing tears constitutes a *pāyattika* offense, whereas for a bhikṣu it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Because love and attachment have not yet been extinguished, one must maintain high integrity and pure resolve, remaining unattached to worldly sentiments. Thus, when crying for the sake of sentient beings for the sake of goodness, what fault is there?

After the Buddha’s final passing at the Twin Trees, the bhikṣus rolled upon the ground like round logs, beating their breasts and crying out loudly with tears falling like rain. Although they had not yet abandoned desire, they did not incur the reproach of outsiders. If outsiders come to offer condolences, they should go to the place where the corpse lies, perform the usual rites, and first—

Having taken the hand of the filial son and silently offered words of consolation, one then proceeds to the place of the Great Virtuous One (Mahādeśaka) to fully express one’s grief and inquire after his well-being.

Therefore, as seen in the *Pañcaśata-praśna* and the *Caturvarga-vinaya*, when the tomb or stupa of the deceased is larger than one’s own, one must pay homage to it. The rituals for filial piety are numerous and cannot be described in full;

other matters that are not exhaustive should be supplemented as the occasion requires. The *Pañcaśata-praśna* states that one should first inform the Sangha, using the deceased’s *nirvāṇasaṃghāṭī* (outer robe) to cover [the body].

One may carry out the corpse for burial, but it must not exceed five *qián* in cost; otherwise, one commits a grave offense. The preceptor, disciples, and fellow students should provide funds to conduct the funeral rites.
If there are no assets available for the funeral, the members of the Saṃgha and individuals should each contribute a small amount of wealth to make offerings to the *śarīra*.

If even this is lacking, one should borrow the deceased’s clothing and belongings to temporarily conduct the burial, with the understanding that the borrowed items will be returned with double the value as compensation once the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is completed.
One may also obtain five portions of the remains by requesting them from the present Saṃgha, provided they are covered with robes so as not to expose the private parts.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that the Tathāgata himself lifted one corner of his mother’s bier, while Ānanda and Rāhula each lifted a leg;

he did not allow others to act on his behalf out of gratitude for their kindness. By this standard, since the preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and instructors (*ācārya*) who nurtured my Dharma-body and my elder brothers and sisters who nurtured my physical body have both bestowed such profound kindness and virtue, it is appropriate that I personally carry and escort [the remains] myself.
[Regarding] "no fault": The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that one may not escort the funeral of a layperson (*avadātavasana*) for the purpose of contemplating impermanence (*anityatā*);

thus, there is no offense. If one personally carries the corpse of one's mother for burial, there is no sin. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states that when a bhikṣu dies, the entire community of monks (*saṃgha*) should escort him to the burial site, following the funeral customs of the Western Regions (*pāścāttya*).
These consist of four methods: fire, water, earth, and forest. The Vinaya primarily clarifies the method of fire.

Regarding the second point concerning burial in the forest: if the body is divided into five parts according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it should be buried; if it is cremated, it should be placed upon stone and not set upon grass.

This *Vinaya* states that for both the Tathāgata and a Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*), cremation is performed. The *Ekottarika-āgama* says that the bhikṣus scattered fragrant flowers over the corpse of Maudgalyāyana;
the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is likewise. According to this *Vinaya*, the World-Honored One permitted the five assemblies to erect stupas.
Novice śrāmaṇerīs and those above their rank are all permitted to pay homage at the stūpas of their preceptors. The *Five Hundred Questions* states that one may erect an image for a deceased teacher.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that a master of the Vinaya, a bhikṣu who manages monastic affairs, or a bhikṣu of great virtue and reputation should have a stūpa constructed;
its harmikā and spire should be adorned with hanging banners and canopies, and it should be installed in a secluded location, not in a place where monks practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*).

One should construct it in a place frequented by many people; if one acts contrary to this, an offense is incurred. If the Sangha does not permit it, one should instruct them to act in unison to have it built.
According to various sutras, vinayas, and the Biographies of Eminent Monks, there are many instances of burial within monasteries.
Chapter Thirty-Four: The Rules for Receiving Lost Robes.
This chapter has eleven main sections: 1. The principle of items entering the Sangha; 2. The method of distribution according to the individuals concerned;
3. Whether shared property among co-residents is common or not; 4. The propriety of entrustments; 5. Determining the lightness or heaviness of items; 6. The repayment of debts.

Regarding the first point concerning the establishment of the intent: it is asked why, after the death of members of the five assemblies, all property enters the Saṃgha, and furthermore, [the question arises] regarding those who have been reborn.
Question: At that time, one has left the household life in reliance upon the Three Jewels; yet, why is it that certain objects do not enter the Buddhist Dharma? Answer:
Because during one's lifetime, these objects were obtained through the Sangha, and whatever actions one performed were not without being encompassed by the Sangha.

Therefore, when there are objects donated to the Buddha-Dharma for which a bhikṣu has no share, once the person has passed away, those objects are subsequently assigned to the Sangha. This is what makes them so.

The Sangha possesses the means for enjoyment, while the donor receives the moisture of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); since [the deceased] has entered neither the Dharma nor the secular world, neither side has a claim.
Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When Upāli’s maternal uncle, Upananda, died, the value of his belongings was four hundred thousand taels of gold.
The king, the Kṣatriya clan, relatives, and others all desired to take possession of them. The Buddha said: 'The King shall bestow these goods upon his ministers and officials.'"
A bhikṣu must not divide [the property], even down to that gathered by relatives; if he does not see it called for, both the monastic wealth and the Dharma must be shared equally.
It is improper for laypeople to claim this, as it belongs to the Saṃgha. All relatives say: "It is just as the World-Honored One has decreed."
Regarding the second pair—whether the belongings of a deceased person may or may not be divided—there are ten different points of adjudication.

First, concerning scavenged items (*pāṃśukūla*): according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if a corpse’s clothes are washed away by water and hung upon a tree branch within the boundaries of a monastery, anyone who first sees them may take them.
The meaning is that if there is no one else within the boundary according to this Vinaya, one may take them based on that rule. If...
If there are two or more persons, one must perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to divide them into two groups.

At that time, the *sāṃmukhībhūta-saṃgha* (the assembly present before one's eyes) is like the case in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* where a *śikṣādattaka-śrāmaṇera* dies (who is equivalent to a *śikṣādattaka-bhikṣu* according to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*). When a monk who has been expelled (*pravāsanīya*) dies, if there is no one of the same category among the monks who maintain the precepts, they may take [his effects] from one another.
Within the boundaries (*sīmā*), the *saṃgha* of shared view is like the two factions of the heterodox and orthodox, each being distinct.
Because those who cling to "right" and "wrong" die in this world and in the next, they all see the same thing; they see their own four bases of power (*catvāri ṛddhipādāḥ*).

In such a case according to this Vinaya, when a monk who has been subject to a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) dies, his robes and requisites go to the community of monks who performed the formal act of suspension;
these are the five cases. When one from the two communities of monks dies, as described in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is like the case of a solitary monk who dies.
Regarding death between the two realms according to the *Sarvāstivāda*: this Vinaya has no fixed rule for such cases, such as dying in the house of a layperson.

It follows whichever of the five assemblies first sees [the deceased]; one obtains the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) facing toward the Saṃgha. As in the *Sarvāstivāda*, in the case of death between the two realms, it depends on which direction one is facing;
one should take the seven sense bases (*saptāyatana*) from wherever that may be. For a close relative who is a layperson, it is as explained in the *Madhyama-āgama* of the *Sarvāstivāda*.

When a bhikṣu who has been expelled dies, his robes and bowl are handed over to those with whom he had a prior connection; this is because at the time of birth, one does not share in the community's property or the Dharma.

Regarding the eighth point, wherever the monk may be, the Saṃgha obtains [the items]; as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "There was a bhikṣu who entrusted his robes to Ānanda. A dispute arose among three parties:

This refers to the Upādhyāya’s classification of the nature of the property: because the teacher’s items are assigned to the teacher and the disciple’s items are assigned to the Saṃgha, when a śrāmaṇera dies, all his inner and outer robes are granted to the caregiver through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. Regarding the Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense involving heavy or light items that enter the possession of the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha*, according to the *Śubhavyūha-sūtra*, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* because the number of people involved does not reach five.

Fourth, within the section on the correctness and incorrectness of entrustment (*anuśrāvaṇa*), there are three parts: (1) correct and incorrect entrustment; (2) repeated entrustment and repeated bestowal.

Regarding the three types of entrustment—whether they are accomplished or not—there are four points in the first section. First, the entrustment called "good" means that one recognizes for oneself that all hoarding of things contrary to the Dharma from the past has been exclusively unwholesome;

now that a virtuous mind has arisen, one abandons these material goods and gives them to places where goodness is cultivated, thereby breaking the seeds of stinginess and greed. This is called "good. Second, the entrustment called "unwholesome" refers to the fear that this...
After death, the Sangha shall receive the property; yet if avarice arises and one falsely entrusts it to a layperson, this is called unwholesome.

Third, not making such an entrustment is called wholesome: when one is gravely ill, reflecting that these false riches can give rise to unwholesomeness, one follows the Buddha’s established judgment that they need not be divided by me, but should instead be managed by oneself, maintaining right mindfulness toward the Triple Gem with a continuous flow of mind.
To pass away suddenly without interruption from moment to moment is called "not having entrusted [one's wealth] with goodness.

Fourth, "not having entrusted [it] with goodness" means that while the preceding thought desires to relinquish [wealth], the succeeding thought is stingy and begrudging, fearing that one might return to life and thus lacking the means to support oneself.

When such a mind of stinginess continues uninterrupted from moment to moment, preventing one from practicing giving, and one consequently passes away, this is called "not having entrusted [it] with goodness."
Furthermore, regarding the second category of entrusting and bestowing, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one entrusts it to many people, the last person receives it;

if one bestows it upon many people, the first person receives it. The meaning is that according to this principle, committing a grave offense occurs when one resolves in one's heart to entrust property to another, or utters the words from one's own mouth, or says to someone: "I have already granted such-and-such wealth to so-and-so."
Later, encountering circumstances that led to a lapse, the owner either failed to hand it over to another or instead entrusted it to someone else;

in such cases, the owner incurs a grave offense (*pārājika*) because he has resolved to give it away with the intention that it be transferred to another. If, after this resolution, the original intent is contradicted and the thief steals this property and redirects it to a subsequent person, does the thief not incur a grave offense?
The subsequent recipient who accepts the gift according to the Dharma commits no offense. Regarding items obtained from a thief, the Buddha permitted their taking.
Regarding this, Śīlapālita says: "If one first promises a garment to another person and later, when other venerable ones arrive, transfers it to them instead, one incurs the offense of stealing.

According to the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, once the resolve to relinquish [the item] has been made, one does not commit the offense of keeping an excess [robe]. Third, as for whether the formal entrustment (*anuśrāvaṇā*) constitutes completion:
the meaning is that in discussing formal entrustment, it is essentially the relinquishing of property; it must be accompanied by a virtuous mind and require a firm resolution.
If it is for a place where merit will be generated, there is certainly no regret; these cases all constitute a valid entrustment.

If one says, "After my death, give this object to me to purchase a grave, buy a coffin, create an image, or copy a scripture," it does not constitute a valid entrustment. If one has resolved that whether living or dying they shall have no regrets, it is valid.
This also applies to those who have violated the king’s law and know they will certainly die tomorrow, yet entrust their belongings today.

All [cases] are established provided that before death one thinks, "I am the owner of this object," and having entrusted the wealth [to another], instructs them to quickly create an image, copy a scripture, or make offerings to the Sangha so that I may see it with my own eyes;
if one then passes away, it is established. If one says, "Let it be made after my death," it is not established, as previously stated.
Below this, taking the texts of various schools, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If, while alive, one has already given it to another..."
If the robe has not yet been taken away, the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one proclamation) to grant it to him. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If the property has not yet been delivered, or if it has been received but not purified (*pariśuddha*) and is placed back beside the patient, it does not constitute [the gift]. If it has been purified and placed beside him, it constitutes [the gift].
If one says, 'I shall give this after my death,' or 'I shall relinquish it if I recover,' the previous agreement is not valid; only a definitive decision [is valid]."

Regarding the formal entrustment (*niyata-dāna*), it is largely consistent with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, except that one should not personally dispose of the three robes and six requisites. This Vinaya states:
"If, at the time of death, one entrusts property to the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha, saying, 'After my death, give this to them,' the Buddha said:
'All such things belong to the Saṃgha. Thus, one knows that if the mind is not resolved, the entrustment is not accomplished. The rest is as previously explained.
Fifth, regarding the determination of gravity and lightness: the various schools differ in their urgent or relaxed judgments concerning the distribution of the deceased’s clothing and belongings.

The masters of this region each harbor divergent views; some, out of personal attachment to the *sthavira* (permanent resident) Sangha, employ expedients to categorize items as grave, while others, out of partiality toward the *sammukhībhūta* (present) Sangha, distort the principles to draw them into the category of light.
Such inverted explanations deviate from principle and reality and fail to accord with the teachings, thereby giving rise to disputes and litigation.

It is truly difficult to ascertain the facts; once it is known that this is not easy, if one wishes to settle a dispute, one should first ask the deceased which Vinaya lineage they received their precepts under, taking that as the definitive standard of their own school.

If they were obscurely ignorant of this, one should further inquire which sect the temple has traditionally followed in its practice, so that from beginning to end the matter is settled with precision and no mutual confusion occurs, thereby avoiding defiling one’s own mental conduct. Furthermore, these are merely the practices of remote and uncivilized regions.
As customs gradually diverge, the necessities of life, vestments, insignia, forms, and names become unequal;

it is therefore essential to distinguish between what is light and what is heavy according to the teachings, so that various categories may follow one another with clear textual evidence to prevent private errors. Furthermore, to provide for cases where disputes have not yet arisen, we now establish the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) as the foundation;
where the Four-Part Vinaya is insufficient, we shall supplement it with other schools (*nikāyas*). Within this chapter, we shall provide a brief classification.
First, there are items permitted by one Buddha for the sake of sustaining the body and cultivating the Path, such as the three robes and six requisites for monks and the five robes for nuns;
these the Buddha classified as light offenses. Second, there are items not permitted by one Buddha, such as fields, gardens, slaves, and livestock;
because these obstruct the Path and invite public reproach, the Buddha classified them as heavy offenses. Third, there are items permitted by one Buddha, such as extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*).

Regarding items such as alms bowls, money, jewels, and heavy objects: although these things may hinder physical growth, because they are essential for sustaining the Path, the Buddha permitted their possession.
This principle encompasses both light and heavy categories, which are further divided into three distinctions.

First, those that are "heavy by nature" refers to all gold, silver, money, jewels, wooden or stone jars, bottles, cauldrons, pots, carts, litters, and the sixteen types of pastoral equipment; these are considered heavy because their very substance is inherently heavy.
Because it is suitable for the practice of the path, it is established as entering the category of "heavy" (guru); however, those of "light" nature (laghu) are twofold.

First, all one hundred and one types of requisites that may accompany the body—such as cloth, silk, thread, and so forth—are, regardless of their quantity, all established as entering the category of "light. Third, regarding lightness or heaviness according to usage:
some matters are light according to their usage, such as a razor for shaving, a stone for cleaning bowls, a container for alms bowls, a chest for the three robes, and items for personal use.
Regarding needles, syringes, bowls, cups, ladles, and chopsticks—regardless of whether they are made of copper, iron, ceramic, or wood—they are all classified as light.

However, if the nature of the object is light but its function is heavy, such as large and small curtains, screens, pillows, fans, rugs, carpets, bed-curtains, and the like, these are all classified as heavy.
Fearing that this may not encompass everything, they are further organized into seven categories to definitively determine their weight; one should judge accordingly.

First, regarding items made of silk, hemp, wool, or cotton: this Vinaya states that "seated rugs" (*āsandi*) and "bedding rugs" (*mañca*) constitute a heavy offense (referring to those with outer and inner cloth layers stuffed with cotton).
A *kūrpa* (rug) measuring five cubits in length and three cubits in width, with a pile of three finger-widths, was ruled by the Buddha to be a light offense;
this principle applies by extension to blankets and single-blankets as well. If these exceed the prescribed dimensions—specifically exceeding eight feet—they constitute a heavy offense.
A woolen rug that is thin, soft, and of standard measurement is classified as light, because it is fit for weighing and is used as clothing.

A rug of eight chi or more that is thick and well-made is classified as heavy. Although it may be a small rug, if it has old straps sewn on and is fastened to a treadle or a loom, it is included among the heavy items by virtue of its function.
A *qūyīn* (woolen carpet) with distinct colors of embroidery and brocade is classified as heavy; a large-patterned silk (*dàlíng*) is also classified as heavy.
Regarding small quantities of silk, fine cloth, coarse silk, raw silk, woven fabrics, and so forth—whether large or small—they are all categorized as light items.
For this reason, this Vinaya permits the acceptance of highly valuable robes from kings, various kinds of fine garments, and expensive coarse fabrics. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"It is permitted for the bhikṣus to wear moth-patterned cloth; however, it may not be used as one of the three formal robes (tricīvara), though it may be made into other types of clothing."

Regarding other uses: as for the *vṛṣika-cīvara* (ant-robe), it is like the secular custom of the *vṛṣika* garment; that people commonly use the character "yì" (ant) instead of "é" (silkworm) is incorrect. The ancients borrowed "é" for "yì," hence this confusion. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the *vraṇa-praticchādana-cīvara* (sore-covering robe), *varṣā-śāṭī* (rain-bath robe), water-strainer, two kinds of waist-bands, bedding, and so forth, were judged by the Buddha to be included among the light [offenses]. In the lower section of this same Vinaya, it says that when a bhikṣu inverted his *nirvāṇaka-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) while entering a layperson's house, his body was exposed. The Buddha... [text ends]... judged this to be a light offense. Therefore, the *nirvāṇaka-saṃghāṭī* is not a separate category from the *antarvāsaka*. Furthermore, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that the *nirvāṇaka-saṃghāṭī* is a type of *antarvāsaka*.
