It is stated that making belts, as well as attaching toggles (*guṇaka*) and so forth, are to be treated accordingly as light offenses. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"Kappāsika cloth used as a single-layered inner garment, needle-cases, bowl-bags, leather-shoe bags, and the like were judged by the Buddha to be light [offenses].

Brocade, silk, woolen rugs, and mosquito nets and the like are heavy; according to this principle, those in the *Caturvargika-vinaya* that fall below the prescribed measure are light, provided they are measured against the standard."

Those that are thick are subject to the heavy category because they cannot be worn; this differs from *kūrpa* (woolen rugs), which are thick and soft and may be worn. *Tappara*-like items are similar to brocade and silk;

although they are small *cīvara*, those belonging to beds or desks are included in the heavy category. Those patched with needle-cotton bags or various mixed silks are also included in the heavy category.
The five major colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—are considered light, and therefore [garments of these colors] are included in the light category.
This Vinaya states that one may dye superior-quality cloth or superior silk to the color of a *kāṣāya* and keep it.

When people judge true vermilion and the like as belonging to the "heavy" category, what is their intention? Since yellow, black, and so forth are likewise among the five primary colors, if these garments are all judged to belong to the "light" category, then since the Buddha prohibited white robes for the *tricīvara*, yet even those were judged to belong to the light category, by this same principle, blue, red, and the others should also be included therein.
Light materials such as fine silk, thread, and cotton—regardless of their quantity—are all classified as light because they are used by the relative to make robes.
Conversely, coarse silk, hemp, black wool, and raw cocoons are all classified as heavy because they are not used by the relative to make robes.

There are also some masters who classify them as light, but this is likely not in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding the bag for the three robes, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is classified as light.

Items such as long bags and the like, if they are heavy, are classified as "heavy" [offenses]. If they are the multicolored thread boots or shoes of laypeople, or the dyed clothing of laymen or laywomen, they are "heavy";
if they are not dyed, they are "light. This is because when they were originally given and received, it was with the intent to exchange them for robe-material.
Therefore, in the lower section of the Vinaya, when a bhikṣu wore various lay garments, the Buddha said: "Avoid me."

Regarding the prohibition against making other items out of [forbidden] materials: from this time forward, one should not wear any of the articles belonging to the class of laypeople (*avadātavasana*).

Thus we know that if one originally received them for their monetary value but did not intend to wear them oneself, they fall into the category of light offenses (*laghu-āpatti*) and there is no transgression.

However, if one originally wore secular clothing such as garments with low collars, robes, tunics, or long-sleeved coats, because these were strictly prohibited by the Buddha, they are all judged to fall into the category of heavy offenses (*guru-āpatti*). If they are secular...

Regarding human clothing that has been torn or damaged: regardless of whether it is colored or plain, it is all classified as entering the category of light [offenses], such as fine brocades and silks.
Even if torn or damaged, if it is still colorful and ornate, it enters the category of heavy [offenses]. If it was first dyed and subsequently damaged, it enters the category of light.
Second, regarding copper, iron, pottery, and wood: this Vinaya states they include copper jars, basins, rope beds, wooden beds, water jars, washing vessels, and tin [vessels].
Staffs, fans, axes, chisels, lampstands, pillows, carriages, and implements made of iron, leather, bamboo, wood, or pottery—these five types of tools are all capable of creating objects;
they are likewise classified as heavy [offenses]. Thus, this Vinaya states that for the sake of avoiding clutter where there is no place to set them down, one should have them placed in leather bags;
it does not refer to the objects being created. This Vinaya also mentions "hair-cutting knives."
Regarding the classification of light and heavy offenses concerning money, gems, and so forth: as stated below, obtaining money from among graves is permitted if one breaks it to use it as copper.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that all iron or wooden vessels, cauldrons, and the like, if they hold less than two *dōng* (斗), fall under the category of light;

if they exceed this, they fall under the category of heavy. This includes items such as scrapers for sweat, tubes for nasal irrigation, irons, incense burners, incense bowls, hooks for walls, meditation weights, spoons, bowl-rests, and large [vessels].
Small bowls, half-bowls, tongs, pincers, scissors, cloth-cutting knives, door-latches, curved door-hooks, and the like are all judged to belong to the category of light [offenses].
If vessels made of crystal, ivory, horn, bone, or shell exceed half a *sheng* in capacity, they belong to the heavy category;
if they are less than that, they belong to the light category. All dyed materials—whether boiled or unboiled—should not be divided. The meaning is as follows: all... [text ends].
Regarding the category of dyeing implements, those listed above from the "heavy" (guru) offenses downward are not permissible according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya).

However, if they are standard-measure vessels such as alms bowls (*pātra*) and other small items, they may be permitted according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten-Recitation Vinaya) as minor offenses (*laghu*).

Aside from these, items such as cauldrons, pots, and wooden vessels—even if they are small—cannot be carried on one's person; therefore, they all fall under the "heavy" offenses according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. If, however, [one follows] the... [text ends].
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is stated that those who receive the precepts may rely on [the teacher] to resolve doubts, lest they err in their application; thus, there is a separate commentary.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that items such as money, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, coral, crystal, *karketana*, agate, jade, and so forth, as well as heavy beds, sitting benches, wooden trays, wooden jars, wooden vats, bamboo baskets, and the like, constitute grave offenses. The *Sammītiya-vinaya* states that needles [also fall under this category].
The *Lengqie jing* (Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra) states that for the purpose of cutting and tailoring the *kāṣāya*, one is permitted to keep a four-inch blade with a crescent-shaped edge;
this is judged to be a minor offense (*laghu-apatti*). Exceeding the prescribed measure for white iron, ceramic, or earthenware bowls and the like is judged to be a grave offense (*guru-apatti*).

Furthermore, if during one's lifetime one constructs coffins, outer caskets, or various funeral requisites intended for the rites following death, these are all judged to be grave offenses. If, during the days of one's life... [text truncated]

Regarding the items used by one's preceptors, parents, or others—such as the objects entrusted by the deceased, including chests, screens, partitions, and locks—all are judged according to their inherent value;

however, they are classified as "heavy" (grave) because they obstruct long-term [use]. As for what this Vinaya calls *kūpya* (valuable) vessels, tradition holds that these refer to bowls, bronze basins, and the like.
Whether they conform to the standard measurements or not, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, they are classified as "light" (minor). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: [omitted text].

The term *kañcī* (鍵[金*咨]) refers to a small cup; thus, the latter part of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "The *kañcī* enters the small bowl (*kṣudra-pātra*), the small bowl enters the medium bowl (*madhyama-pātra*), and the medium bowl enters the large bowl (*mahā-pātra*).
The *Yao-lü-yi* (要律儀) further explains: "*Kañcī* is an accessory utensil for food; in the language of Qin it is called a 'shallow iron bowl'.
Regarding its meaning, it is said to refer to implements for making offerings, such as scripture racks, Buddha-beds, tables, desks, and fly-whisks.

Regarding miscellaneous incense, incense tables, sutra cases, and the like—if these were made without a specific intent, being merely intended for the offering to the Buddha, they shall enter the property of the Buddha-Dharma according to the deceased person's wishes;

they must not be confiscated and assigned elsewhere. However, if they were definitely made as one’s own personal property, or if they were gifts from others with no other designated purpose, such as incense burners and scripture racks, they are classified as minor offenses (dukkaṭa) according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states: Regarding ritual implements for making offerings, they should be given to whoever is capable of making the offering. If there are precious objects used for adornment that cannot be dismantled, they are classified as heavy;
those that can be dismantled, if they are precious objects, are classified as heavy, but if they are not precious objects, they are classified as light.
As for other miscellaneous incense and incense stands, they are to be assigned according to the weight of the incense burner. Apart from these, there are the curved legs of the Buddha’s bed.
A footstool, a knee-strap, a *ruyi* scepter, a desk, a whisk, and a sutra casket—these items belonging to the deceased are not fixed as belonging to the Buddha-dharma while they were alive;

therefore, after death, they should be judged as belonging to the heavy category (*zhòng*). However, if it is certain that they belong to the Buddha-dharma, one should follow the deceased's intention.

A spittoon belongs to the heavy category. Wooden *niumo* beads, rosaries, beans, flour, and gourds, being essential personal items, are logically permitted to enter the light category (*qīng*), as they are definitively assigned to the deceased.

Regarding the meaning of "other people's property," it refers to money for casting bells and the remaining materials from casting bells. If the donor has specifically designated these as belonging to the bell, they shall be returned to the use of the bell.

If the original gift was not specifically designated, then the money for casting bells and the remaining materials from the casting of bells shall all be entered into the common property of the resident monks (*sāṃghika*).
Third, as for fields, houses, dwellings, gardens, and groves, these are included in the category of "heavy" property; this Vinaya states that monasteries (*ārāma*) and...

The *jambū* fruit tree belongs to the specific room; likewise, items belonging to a specific room refer to cases where silk or cloth was relinquished for the purpose of constructing a room for oneself.
If these have already been exchanged for heavy valuables, they enter the category of "heavy" property; at the time of death, if they remain light items, their distribution is permitted.

If they are specifically used to adorn the dwelling—such as curtains, canopies, or ceiling hangings—they are subsumed under the category of "room-articles. If [the distribution occurs] during the spring of that monastery...
Regarding the division of quarters during summer and winter, there are no fixed guests or hosts; one should simply settle them according to their original locations.

These items must not be divided, as they are for the common use of guests and hosts and are not restricted to any individual. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, earth and clay are considered heavy;

by extension, realgar, yellow arsenic, and white plaster are also considered heavy. Fourth, regarding articles made of leather: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, "leather articles" refers to oil-sacks and so forth.
Items weighing half a *dou* or less—such as leather sandals, leather boots, leather baskets, processed leather, leather for the soles of shoes, and leather for the toes—should be divided.
Any portion exceeding this weight is included in the *Saṃghāṭī* (heavy) category; leather sandals are treated according to this same principle.

Regarding shoes and boots, the *Qīngyì* (Light Meaning) states that flat boots, slanted boots, and the like all enter the heavy category because they are not monastic robes (*dharma-vastra*). Those that are in accordance with the Dharma follow the *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* and enter the light category.
This Vinaya states that no leather garments whatsoever may be worn; it is also judged to fall under the *Guru-vinaya*. The *Vinayamātṛkā* says:

"Regarding the places to which the Sūtras and Vinayas were originally entrusted, one should rely on those original entrustments. If there is no such entrustment, they should be bestowed upon whoever is capable of upholding them.
All secular books, plain paper, silk, and the like are logically permitted to be included under the *Guru-vinaya*. Fifth, regarding animals, the *Vinayamātṛkā*...

Camels, donkeys, horses, and the like are to be used by the resident monks of the monastery for transport. Regarding the sixth category, namely the monastery attendants and slaves, this Vinaya states:
"If the monastery attendants enter [the monastery] with private property, regardless of whether it is heavy or light, it all belongs to that person.
If a slave of the Sangha dies, his clothing and belongings are given to his relatives; if he has no relatives, they are offered [to the Sangha]."

Regarding the property used for the permanent Sangha, if a private slave dies, the principle allows for two interpretations. If the deceased was one who shared food and clothing with the master, all their assets may be taken by the master himself and disposed of as he pleases.
If they did not share such provisions, the value of the property must be paid as a tax, or the laborer’s services may be assigned in rotation to offset the loss.
As for the assets themselves, they go to the relatives; if there are no relatives, the matter is handled according to the specific circumstances.

One may take possession of and use items that have no owner. Regarding the seventh [category], the four types of medicine—whether taken at the proper time, at improper times, for seven days, or for life—all are classified as belonging to the heavy [offense].
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one who has been invited to eat within the Saṃgha dies after the food has entered their possession, it is treated like the distribution of robes and bowls.
The *Yìyì* (義) states: "The present Saṃgha should be ordered to distribute it; it belongs to the heavy [offense]. If [the person] has already died...
Afterwards, those who obtain food may return to their original places. What has been listed above is based on one particular school;

it is not exhaustive, and matters not covered therein should be decided according to the circumstances as they arise. It is not strictly necessary that everything must conform to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya).

For instance, items such as a water pitcher, needles, awls, or shears that are currently needed for personal use—provided they are categorized as minor offenses (*dukkaṭa*) according to other vinayas—involving no fault.
Regarding the sixth point, whether debts are to be repaid or not: first, they are distinguished by way of doctrinal categories; subsequently, scriptural citations are adduced to provide proof.

If a member of the Sangha owes property belonging to a deceased person, or if a deceased person owes property—whether light or heavy—to the Sangha or an individual, if such property exists, it shall be returned in kind;
if it does not exist, it shall be settled through a cross-transaction (*vyatikara*). The reason for demanding repayment is that heavy items must be accounted for.

If light property belonging to the permanently resident Sangha (*sthāvarika-saṃgha*) enters the presence of the assembled Sangha (*sammukhībhūta-saṃgha*), and if one previously owed light items from the deceased but now receives heavy items, one must exchange them for light items and distribute the shares.

If one previously owed heavy items from the deceased but now receives light items, these shall enter the permanently resident Sangha; because they were originally heavy items, they ultimately cannot be shared with the general Sangha.
If the permanent monastery (saṃgha) owes heavy goods to the deceased, they need not be claimed back, as they must be returned to the permanent monastery.

If light goods are owed, they should be pursued and entered into the distribution for the present monks (pratyutpanna-saṃgha). If heavy goods have been obtained, they must be exchanged for light goods to be distributed among the present monks.
If an individual owes both light and heavy goods to the deceased, both must be claimed back, because of the heaviness [of the debt].
Regarding the entry of items into the permanently resident (*sthavira*) Saṃgha, light items enter into the *pratyutpanna* (present) Saṃgha; thus the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"When a bhikṣu dies, property belonging to the Three Jewels should be returned to the Three Jewels; as for property borrowed from a bhikṣu, it should be reclaimed and entered into the *pratyutpanna* Saṃgha.

Therefore, one knows that in cases of both reclaiming and borrowing, the judgment is made according to the original basis, even when there is mutual indebtedness between the *pratyutpanna* Saṃgha of the four directions and visiting bhikṣus numbering four or more.

The matter of such items is also explained as above. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There was a bhikṣu who purchased wine on credit; before he had repaid the price, he died. The Buddha said: "If he has [personal] robes and bowls, they should be used to repay him.
If he possesses no property, one should take from the property of the Saṃgha to repay him. This is done for fear that it might bring a bad reputation upon the other bhikṣus. The commentary explains:

"It does not say 'permanent property' (*sthavira*) or 'property currently present' (*pratyutpanna*). When the time comes, one should measure and give what is due; if there is a debt, it must be settled."
If there are other items that do not give rise to censure or fault, they need not be returned, as there were no possessions belonging to the deceased. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If one previously gave the price for a robe to another, and that person dies, one should demand its return. If one took a robe from another but had not yet paid the price, and that person dies, one should return the original robe;

if it is not available, one should return the robe and bowl. Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Regarding debts and interest, if they are in a different location [from the deceased], [they should be settled accordingly]."

There are five distinct cases regarding death: 1. When the robes and bowl are deposited in another location and the person dies in a different location, the Saṃgha acquires [the property] according to the location of the objects.

2. When one dies in a location where they owe a debt, the Saṃgha acquires [the property] from the location of the debt. 3. When one dies in a location where they have provided a guarantee for a loan, the Saṃgha acquires [the property] from the location of the guarantee.
4. When one dies in a location where they have pledged collateral, the Saṃgha acquires [the property] from the location where the money was taken or the object was pledged.

The Sangha obtains [the property] from five places of death: the place where money was received, the place where a promissory note was held, the place where the promissory note was held, and the place where the Sangha obtained it.

The meaning of this should be examined in detail; herein, there is still some lack of clarity. If the interest-bearing goods are with a layperson and have not yet been recovered upon demand, one may, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, seek to collect them based on the promissory note.
If the goods are with the Sangha, after the death [of the owner], the Sangha obtains them according to the location where the goods reside.
In the end, one must not, on account of possessing a written contract, take possession of monks from another boundary, for both parties are equally *saṃgha*.
Furthermore, regarding heavy property, it may not be taken, for it is not permitted to transfer the property of this *saṃgha* to that *saṃgha*.
If goods are owed to a layperson in a village, this is treated the same as the case in the *Caturvargika-vinaya* concerning the five groups of monastics who die without a dwelling place.
If an item was brought in earlier, the one who first took it shall take it; if it is a heavy object, it shall be disposed of according to where it was first seen.

If many people know of it together and dispute it without reaching a decision, it shall be settled according to the five methods for adjudicating *vinaya* found in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:

"If property lent out is located outside the monastery, one shall dispatch a pure attendant (*śuddha-karmakara*) belonging to the *saṃghika* community within the monastery to search for and retrieve it, so that it may enter the permanent property of this monastery's resident *saṃgha*."
The *Śata-praśna* states: When a bhikṣu borrows an object from another person and that person dies, he must inform the Saṃgha before taking back the original item.

If he takes it without informing them, he incurs an offense. If the owner does not return it and he takes it by force, or if the Saṃgha knows of the situation and does not return it to him, both parties incur an offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If one seeks to collect a debt, one should examine whether the debtor maintains the precepts and is trustworthy; if so, one may give [the loan], otherwise not.
One who possesses faith should not be given [the task]; however, one who is trustworthy may be given as a witness, and the opposite of this is not permitted.

Seventh, regarding the distribution of rewards to those endowed with virtue, the Vinaya states that there are two sets of five virtues. The first set of five virtues concerns being able to care for a patient who is difficult to care for;
this signifies the fulfillment of the virtue of attending to the sick. What are these five? First, that which a patient should not do...
1. Having eaten, one desires to eat more and refuses to take medicine; 2. The caregiver possesses a sincere heart but does not speak according to reality;
3. One should act but does not act, or should remain still but does not remain still; 4. The body experiences pain but cannot endure it; 5.
The body has the capacity for action but does not act, suppresses others from acting, and furthermore is unable to sit in quietude to still the inner mind.
Regarding the second set of five virtues, these clarify the virtues that a caregiver must personally fulfill. What are these five?
First, knowing what the patient may eat and what they may not eat, and providing accordingly. Second, not treating the patient’s excrement, urine, saliva, or vomit with contempt or disdain.
Third, possessing a heart of compassion, caring for the patient not for the sake of food or clothing. Fourth, being able to manage the medicinal decoctions until the patient recovers.

If, at the time of death, one is able to preach the Dharma to the patient so as to gladden them, and if one’s own merit in wholesome dharmas increases—possessing these five qualities, one should provide clothing and requisites to the patient.
If one tends to the patient only perfunctorily and lacks a sincere heart, the Buddha judged that such a person is not entitled to receive gifts from the *saṃgha*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are four types of caregivers who do not deserve rewards for their service: first, those who tend to the patient only temporarily; [and so forth].
1. A nurse who lacks long-term commitment; 2. Monks who take turns nursing out of turn; 3. One who seeks personal merit and does not give rise to compassion; 4.

One who acts with wrong livelihood for the sake of gain—none of these are permitted to receive a reward. Furthermore, if one dies while nursing due to an offense against the king’s law, they likewise do not deserve a reward, as this was not due to illness.
However, if one nurses a patient for their benefit in order to hasten their recovery, [a reward is appropriate].

The underlying intent is that even down to the case of one who burns a single lamp for a deceased person, that individual should receive these items. This Vinaya states: "One should not inquire as to the superiority or inferiority of their virtue;

the robes for daily use (*parihārika-cīvara*) should be given. If it is not known which are the robes for daily use, one should assess the virtue of the attendant according to its being superior, middling, or inferior.
If they are of the highest grade, one gives them the three superior robes; if they are of the middle or lower grades, [one gives accordingly].

Regarding the sick person and the three robes of medium and inferior quality, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "First, one must ask which robes and bowl they maintain; each should be asked individually.
If one does not ask, or if [the sick person] does not know or does not believe, then one should give them the six items that are neither poor nor excellent.
According to the *Sarvāstivāda*, the three robes must be double-sewn, but those that have not been reinforced with needle-stitches may not be entered [into the formal assembly].
Regarding the "six items" mentioned for a caregiver in this Vinaya: the three robes constitute the first three;
the alms bowl is the fourth; the sitting mat is the fifth; and the needle case is the sixth. As for the inclusion of the "container for holding robes" and the "storage vessel" in the text:

the container for holding robes refers to the robe-bag and the wrapping cloth for the three robes; the storage vessel refers to the bowl-bag, the bowl-casket, and so forth. These are all included within the general category.

Entering into the distribution of rewards is based on righteousness; it is said that if one possesses the six requisites, they are granted, whereas those who do not possess them and so forth form four permutations:
(1) possessing both virtue and requisites; (2) possessing virtue but lacking requisites—these two cases are granted according to the Dharma;
(3) possessing requisites but lacking virtue; (4) lacking both virtue and requisites—these latter two cases are not permitted.
When a monk falls ill while performing formal rituals and the community wishes to provide him with a special reward, all such items should be gathered and placed before the present assembly of monks.

After the *karmavācanā* (formal motion) has been completed, they should be distributed according to the relative merit and status of the recipients, with three proclamations made for verbal consensus. Then, based on the monks' collective sentiment, they may be given in whatever amount is appropriate.

Next, one should select a person who is fit or unfit to receive them; as stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when a bhikṣu is ill, members of all seven assemblies should attend to him.
Two groups are entitled to receive the robe: bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras; the other five [groups] do not receive it. For a bhikṣuṇī who is ill, three groups are entitled to receive it:
bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs. Even if her parents, brothers, or others care for her, they should not be given [the robe], because their labor does not suffice.
The *Mātṛkā* states that if a layperson cares for her, a small amount should be given.
The same applies to the three groups of nuns. Regarding a *śrāmaṇera* caring for the sick, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that he should be given one-fifth [of the portion].

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that a *śrāmaṇera* caring for the sick is treated identically to the *bhikṣu*. The meaning is as follows: if many *bhikṣus* and *śrāmaṇeras* are caring for the sick, it should be given to those who have reached the limit [of their service];
if they have all reached the limit, it should be given to one person, and then divided equally among those in private places. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "If [one] cares for..."

When a sick person goes out to beg for clothing and medicine on behalf of a patient, they should divide the acquisitions into three portions of the *tricīvara*. At that time, one portion should be set aside and awaited until the person returns, at which point it may be given to them.

Alternatively, this may be included within the "present before the eyes" (*pratyakṣa*) distribution; both the formal proclamation (*udghoṣa*) and the waiting for the person's arrival are permissible. Furthermore, if other monks come from elsewhere to visit this monk, they should also be granted a reward for their labor.
Regarding the timing for the eighth division [of the funeral rites], if the patient has died, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one should not immediately open the door.

If there is a disciple who maintains the precepts and is trustworthy, one should give them the door-bolt; if they are not trustworthy, the door-bolt should be entrusted to the monastery officials (*saṃgha-karmadāna*).
Once the śarīra have been first honored and the arrangements completed, if the disciple is one who maintains the precepts and is trustworthy...

Regarding the distribution of the deceased's clothing and belongings: if the person sent to retrieve them is not trustworthy, one should instead have a *karmadāna* (an official in charge of affairs) retrieve the items before the Saṃgha divides them.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When the bhikṣus were dividing the robes by the side of a corpse, the corpse rose up to guard the clothes. The Buddha said: "Wait until after the corpse has departed;
or, if there is another location [where the body is], it should be divided there."

The ninth section on the distribution of property has three parts: first, formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*); second, distribution in the presence of others; and third, mental recollection. Regarding the first, within formal ritual action: if there are five persons, one may perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation) for the distribution of robes as a reward for service. If there are only four persons, one may only use the method of direct distribution; this is because once the formal ritual action has been performed, the three robes and six articles are distributed through verbal agreement as a reward for service. Thus it is said in the Vinaya: "If there are five persons, one should perform the *karman*. This is because the *karman* must be performed by five persons. Furthermore, the *karman* is not required for those who have already received their share. Therefore, the *karman* is established specifically for the purpose of distributing the three robes and six articles as a reward for service. As for the second part, distribution in the presence of others: this refers to cases where the number of persons is fewer than five, such that the *karman* cannot be performed. In such instances, one should distribute the robes in the presence of the assembly. As for the third part, mental recollection: this refers to cases where the number of persons is even fewer than in the previous instance, such that they cannot even distribute the robes in the presence of others. In such cases, one should distribute the robes by means of mental recollection. As for the fourth part, the method of distribution: this refers to the manner in which the robes are actually divided. There are two types of distribution methods: first, equal distribution; second, unequal distribution. Equal distribution means dividing the robes equally among all members of the assembly. Unequal distribution means that the robes are divided according to specific criteria, such as seniority or merit. As for the fifth part, the procedure for distribution: this refers to the specific steps and protocols for carrying out the distribution. There are two types of distribution procedures: first, distribution by means of a formal ritual action; second, distribution by means of verbal agreement. Distribution by means of a formal ritual action refers to cases where the number of persons is sufficient to perform the *karman*. Distribution by means of verbal agreement refers to cases where the number of persons is insufficient to perform the *karman*, and thus they agree upon the distribution verbally. As for the sixth part, the rules regarding distribution: this refers to the prohibitions and regulations concerning the distribution of robes. There are two types of rules regarding distribution: first, rules concerning the timing of distribution; second, rules concerning the eligibility of recipients. Rules concerning the timing of distribution mean that robes should be distributed at the appropriate time, neither too early nor too late. Rules concerning the eligibility of recipients mean that robes should be distributed only to those who are qualified to receive them. As for the seventh part, the consequences of improper distribution: this refers to the karmic results and disciplinary penalties incurred by distributing robes in violation of the rules. There are two types of consequences for improper distribution: first, loss of merit; second, violation of the precepts. As for the eighth part, the benefits of proper distribution: this refers to the spiritual and practical advantages gained by distributing robes in accordance with the rules. There are two types of benefits from proper distribution: first, the maintenance of harmony within the Sangha; second, the accumulation of merit for both the giver and the recipient. As for the ninth part, the summary of the distribution of property: this refers to a concise overview of the entire process of distributing robes and other monastic goods. It is summarized into three categories: first, the formal ritual action; second, the presence of others; and third, mental recollection. These three categories encompass all aspects of the distribution of property. Therefore, the distribution of property is a matter of great importance, and one must ensure that it is carried out in strict accordance with the Vinaya rules. Any deviation from these rules will result in negative consequences for both the Sangha and the individual practitioners. Thus, it is essential to study and practice the proper methods of distribution with diligence and precision. Only by doing so can the Sangha maintain its purity and the Dharma continue to flourish. This concludes the ninth section on the distribution of property. May all beings attain peace and happiness. May the light of the Dharma shine throughout the world. May all sentient beings be liberated from suffering and realize the ultimate truth. May this merit be dedicated to the benefit of all beings. May the Three Jewels be ever-present and the teachings of the Buddha endure forever. May all who encounter this text gain wisdom and compassion. May they all attain enlightenment and become Buddhas. Thus, the ninth section on the distribution of property is completed. May it be auspicious. May all be well. May all be peaceful. May all be happy. May all be enlightened. May all be liberated.
