Nimu said: "Among four people, one cannot be designated to enter the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), for the remaining three would not constitute a *saṃgha*.
Therefore, those who now establish this rule first have the attendant of the dying person bring both light and heavy items together into the midst of the *saṃgha*.
As for heavy items that cannot be carried, there is no need to bring them; they should simply be handed over to the *saṃgha* treasury exactly according to the standard procedure."
Having closed the door and restricted visiting monks, one uses an object to communicate that, according to principle, there is no private entry.

Once the monk has entered, he gazes upon the sick person by their clothing and belongings, bows at the feet of the Sangha, kneels with his right knee on the ground, and with his hands, offers the clothing and belongings, saying:
"Venerable Sisters (or Elder Brother), may the Sangha listen: [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so has passed away in such-and-such a place. Whatever clothing or non-clothing they possessed—"
"The resident monks of this dwelling place should divide [the property] for me. (The monk or nun) so-and-so now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha. (This is sufficient with one recitation.

Among the assembly, those who are clear in the Vinaya shall immediately adjudicate it. First, they ask within the Saṃgha: "Who knows of the deceased person's debts to the Three Jewels or to individuals?
And who knows of loans received from the Three Jewels or from individuals? Having thus interrogated each one regarding the presence or absence [of such obligations], the matter is concluded.
Thereafter, the items shall be categorized by weight in sequence: heavy items are placed in one location and light items in another.

Furthermore, the attendant shall be questioned as to whether they have transported the deceased’s light or heavy property with the corpse; if such items exist, similar items shall be requisitioned and included in the distribution through *karmavācanā*.
If no such items exist, the recipients shall be rewarded according to their merit and labor. If the five qualities [of the distributor] are not present...
If [the requisites] are already complete, it is improper to take more. If a caregiver privately steals the property of a deceased person to provide for funeral rites, this is also improper;

since it constitutes the offense of theft, one must not seek it. If one were to borrow them temporarily, or take them while maintaining a neutral state of mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), they should be returned as before.
However, those who practice these matters nowadays simply ask the Sangha, "Are the requisites complete? If the answer is that they are complete, they take them based on the external appearance alone.
It is universally acknowledged that those who fail to respond when their conduct is coarse and vulgar have earned their reprimand;
since this is known, if one wishes to uphold the Dharma and bring about the welfare of the world, one must deliberate upon whether a person is capable or incapable of receiving [certain honors].

Furthermore, granting or withholding, promoting or demoting, must originate from within the Saṃgha itself. Why then inquire about "virtue" (guṇa) or "harmony" (sāmagrī)? As for those who tend to the sick, their labor must surely be rewarded.
The *vinayadhara* (preceptor) should say: "Elder, you have indeed rendered great service in tending to the sick; the Buddha has commanded that you be rewarded generously.
If you do not accept it, you may fear you will contravene the Holy Teaching. Elder, you should comply with the Teaching and receive it. The one who tended the sick should then state:
"I have no merit and am unworthy to receive such a reward. The Sangha should then firmly urge him to accept it. Is such an administration of the Dharma not a skillful governance?
Once the assembly has resolved to treat the external objects as belonging to the deceased, the attendant who is caring for the sick should kneel with palms joined.
Then, following the standard procedure for requesting consent from the Saṃgha, he should say: "Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! The bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī), so-and-so, has passed away.
Whatever robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage containers he possessed at this residence..."
The preceding monks should divide [the property]. If it is the time for the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha now gives [it] to the attendant (bhikṣu/bhikṣuṇī), so-and-so.
Thus is the motion. Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen: the bhikṣu/bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, has passed away.

Whatever robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage containers he possessed, these should be divided by the present Saṃgha; the Saṃgha now gives them to the attendant (bhikṣu/bhikṣuṇī), so-and-so.

Whoever among you, Venerable Elders and Sisters, approves of granting the robe, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage container to the [monk or nun] named so-and-so who has attended to the sick, remain silent;

whoever does not approve, speak. The Sangha has already approved the granting of the robe, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage container to the [monk or nun] named so-and-so who has attended to the sick. Because the Sangha approves and remains silent, it is so.

Regarding this matter, the meaning of "holding it thus" is as follows: among the six items, they may not necessarily all be present; one should record them into the *karmavācanā* according to their number, whether many or few.
One must not recite the entire text in its general form, for that which lacks the specific subject matter is not called a valid *karma* and is termed "unlawful" (*adharma*).
Question: Is the *karma* accomplished? Answer: It is accomplished, but because it is unlawful, one incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*), just as when recording two *śrāmaṇeras*.
At one time, regarding the reception of the precepts, there are two cases: one with difficulty and one without difficulty. For one without difficulty, the five factors are fulfilled.

It is said that a *bhikṣu* who nurses a patient outside the boundary may also receive a reward. According to the *Sarvāstivāda*, if the three robes and bowl are sought from another location, they are to be rewarded here.
If these virtues are not complete, then [the reward] follows their respective shares; if the length exceeds three or five cubits, it is distributed according to the excess.
A small amount [of property] should be announced to the Saṃgha so that they may know it is being given in harmony; this is good. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If a śrāmaṇera dies, the inner and outer robes he was wearing are given to the attendant; other light items are divided by the Saṃgha. The *Karmavācanā* states:

"The deceased śrāmaṇera so-and-so has left behind inner and outer robes as well as non-robes and other items; all else is the same as the rules for the great Saṃgha. Next, the division of light items is explained.

Regarding the *karmavācanā*, the various masters explain that one should first perform a formal motion (*jñapti*) followed by a second motion (*dvitīya-karman*) to appoint a monk endowed with five virtues—
namely, one who is free from attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, and who knows what may or may not be divided.

Once such a person has been appointed by the Saṃgha through the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* and entrusted with the task, that monk should then perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to complete the distribution.
Regarding this, one should divide it into these three parts; that the Vinaya text does not mention it is because it is abbreviated. Now, I shall set aside this interpretation to avoid redundancy.

Furthermore, among the rules concerning non-timely gifts received by the Saṃgha, there is no text regarding the appointment of a person; it simply says, "one person should be appointed," and then proceeds with the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one announcement) for the distribution.
Originally, there was no text for the appointment via *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, nor was there even a name for such a procedure.

Furthermore, if there were any intention [to include them], why would they not have been included here in this Vinaya? In the sections above and below, those who assign roles are all presented with their names and identities fully complete;
for what reason are they specifically excluded here? It is not only that there is no text regarding the assignment of roles, but there is also no separate text regarding the distribution of robes.
Is it not the case that this very text concerning the entrustment of robes subsumes the text regarding the distribution? How is this known? Because of the *karmavācanā*.

The monk says: "The Sangha now holds these robes and articles and gives them to him; this is the formal entrustment of the robes. He shall then return them to the Sangha, who shall then take up the distribution of the robes.
Therefore, we know that the absence [of a specific person] does not mean that the formal *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure) itself is omitted.

The monk asks the assembly: "Sangha, you are now in harmony; what is to be done? They answer: "The distribution of light robes belonging to deceased [monks and nuns]. "Venerable Sisters, may the Sangha listen! [Monk...]"
[The name of] the nun [so-and-so] has passed away. Whatever robes or non-robes she possessed, the present Saṃgha should divide among themselves.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent. The Saṃgha now takes these robes and articles and gives them to the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so;

the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so shall then return them to the Saṃgha. This is the motion. Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen: the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has passed away; whatever... [the rest of the text follows].
If there are robes or non-robes present that the Saṃgha should divide, the Saṃgha now holds these items and gives them to [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so,

who shall then return them to the Saṃgha. Those of you, Venerable Elders and Sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha now holding these items and giving them to [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so, who shall then return them to the Saṃgha, remain silent.

Now, who does not approve? Since the Sangha has approved and remains silent, the Sangha now takes these robes and articles and gives them to [the bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī] so-and-so, who shall return them to the Sangha.
This matter is thus settled; the *karmavācanā* is completed. Immediately thereafter, the robes are distributed.
If there are insufficient robes for all, according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, they should be given to one robeless bhikṣu by means of a formal assembly (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*).

If there is only one robe and it is of good quality, one should first harmonize with the Saṃgha and then distribute it according to the *Sudarsana-vinaya* (Shanjian lun), proceeding from the seat of highest seniority in order;
those who need it may take it directly without it reaching those below (according to the Vinaya, it is also permissible to divide it and distribute it). The commentary states:

if the clothing and requisites are extremely abundant and belong to the community as a whole, one should follow the method prescribed by the holy teachings for distribution; there is no need to forcibly request them from the Saṃgha for the purpose of repair or construction.

Regarding the transgression of generating outflows during a *śīla*-assembly: if one who has left the household life applies themselves to the practice of wisdom rather than harboring thoughts of merit, yet their followers possess a mind of generosity, they may perform the ritual at the proper time.

As for those who are absent and unable to attend, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this includes cases such as seeking robes or medicine for a sick person, or managing affairs on behalf of the Saṃgha; even if one is not present at that moment, [the assembly remains valid].

Furthermore, regarding those assigned by the community, it is explained that they receive their portion next. As for the assignment of portions to śrāmaṇeras and attendants (*karmakara*), this Vinaya states:
"If the Saṃgha is in harmony, they should be given an equal share with the śrāmaṇeras. If they are not in harmony, then from among four parts, one part should be given to the attendants;
from among five parts, one part should be given to them. If these are not given, [the property] should not be divided; if it is divided, [they] shall obtain [their share]."

Regarding the *Vinayamātṛkā*, it says: "If five people live together and one of them dies, the three remaining members shall reach a consensus to award the robes, bowl, and so forth to the attendant who cared for the deceased.
As for the other belongings, all four may receive them by performing the *jīrṇavibhāga-karman* (the formal act of direct distribution);
there is no need for a successive distribution. The *jīrṇavibhāga-karman* is as follows: 'Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! [Bhikṣu/Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so has passed away.'"
Whatever property, whether robes or non-robes, belonging to one who has passed away, should be divided among the present Saṃgha.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent that the Saṃgha now divide these robes and articles. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Venerable Sisters (or Brothers), the Saṃgha listen: [the name of] such-and-such a Bhikṣu (or Bhikṣuṇī) has passed away.
Whatever property, whether robes or non-robes, belongs to him, should be divided among the present Saṃgha. Which Elders (or Venerable Sisters) consent to the Saṃgha now dividing this?

Regarding the distribution of robes and requisites: [The proponent] says, "It is silent; who does not approve? Let those who do not approve speak. The Saṃgha has approved. The Saṃgha has now finished distributing these robes and requisites.
Because the Saṃgha has approved by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. As for the second method, the method of the majority:
regarding the *Vinayamātṛkā*, it says that if four people live together and one dies, the remaining three should pass [the items] on to one another in succession.
The text states: "If two venerable sisters (mahātherī) say, 'Venerable sister, please remember that this object should belong to us,' and the other two likewise say the same, they shall obtain it.

Furthermore, if two persons face each other and mutually say, "Venerable sister, please remember that this object should belong to us," according to this Vinaya, if there are three persons and two perform the formal act (*kamma*), the wording is not clearly defined; it simply says: [they shall obtain it].
Regarding the three verbal declarations made between one another for the purpose of receiving and sharing [the inheritance], according to the *Vinayavibhāṣā*, this is considered excellent.
If there is a caregiver who should be rewarded with a portion, two people should reach a consensus and hand over the robes and bowl to them.

The *Vinayamātṛkā* states that when three people live together and one dies, the same principle may be applied by analogy. Third, regarding the method for a single person using mental intimation (*manasikāra*), the *Vinayamātṛkā* says:

Regarding what is called "the dharma of a single correspondence" (when two people live together and one dies): one should mentally reflect and verbally declare, "The property of this deceased bhikṣu should belong to me.

Having made this statement, others who arrive later may not share in it. This Vinaya states: if one person receives a gift, he should mentally reflect and verbally declare, "This is my portion," and it is thereby obtained.
The tenth section, "Clarifying Miscellaneous Matters of Distribution," explains the meaning as follows:
If a bhikṣu dies on private farmland or in a private monastery (*svaka-vihāra*), the property should be divided according to the rules for monasteries. What is meant by a "private monastery"?

It refers to a place built separately by laypeople within a village or settlement specifically intended for the use of renunciants alone, not accessible to householders, and which is surrounded on all sides [by such boundaries].
Fences, hedges, walls, and moats are what constitute a *saṃghārāma*; it is not necessary to perform a formal boundary-delineation (*sīmā-bandha*).

If a monk arrives from afar or if those who were previously there tend to the sick, heavy property goes to the deceased person’s original monastery, while light property goes to the *saṃgha* present there.

If there are four or more persons, the light property is divided by means of a formal ritual motion (*jñapti-karman*). If no boundary had been previously established, three persons or more may divide it after performing the ritual procedure.
Regarding the lower [category], whether within or outside the boundary, one simply divides it face-to-face with the [other] monks, as this differs from the case of death in a layperson's household.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If the robes and bowl of a deceased monk are kept in a nunnery, they should be returned to the monks for division.

If someone saw them first, he may take them into his own possession; if many people know of them, they may be taken collectively within their own boundary. This also applies when a nun has deposited them with a monk.

The case of Kūṭa’s robe and bowl is as previously understood. If there is no one to guard them and those who see them treat the matter according to the household customs of laypeople, then this Vinaya states:
if a bhikṣu dies in a layperson’s house where there is no monastery, a faithful donor (dānapati) should take charge of and record these items.
If members of the five groups of renunciants arrive, they should first be given [the items]; if none arrive, they should...
If one sends [an item] to a nearby monastery, even though one knows it is the property of a deceased layperson, one must physically take hold of it with the intention that it belongs to oneself;

only then does one acquire this object. Conversely, if one does not do so, it is not accomplished. If a layperson has already taken possession of it and determined it as their own stolen property, the legal principle is established and it may not be reclaimed.
If, out of fear of the path of unwholesome karma, one later returns it to them, there is no offense. This applies equally to monks and nuns.
If those who arrive at the same time belong to different groups, the two assemblies must not take [the property] together, as each is a person who knows the Dharma;
nor is it necessary to perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), for by simply taking possession at that moment, it becomes one's own.

This is not the same as in the case of a deserted monastery, where one must necessarily perform a ritual because of its state of neglect. Even if one knows there is clothing or property belonging to a deceased person, before it has been seen—let alone...

If a bhikṣu who arrives later is already under the jurisdiction of a distant [monastery], the light items must still be shared together; as for heavy items, they follow the disposition of those who arrived first.

If it is known that there are heavy items belonging to a deceased person from the original monastery, they should enter the permanent property (*sthavira-saṃgha*) of that original monastery and must not enter the nearby [monastery].
Therefore, this Vinaya states: "Have a layperson take charge of and record the clothing of the deceased."
Regarding objects, if a renunciant comes, one should give them to him; if none comes, they should be sent to a nearby monastery (*saṃghārāma*).
Since it was originally determined that a monk would deliver them, it is known that giving them as one pleases is not an obstacle even for those at a distance. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"After the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed, one should measure the shadow [of the sun] and consider whether visiting monks might enter the boundary; one should know that [the ritual] applies both before and after their entry. This is what is meant by "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*).

Because the *saṃgha* boundary is large, this method is established for questioning regarding the property of a deceased bhikṣu: "Is the boundary of the renunciant realm divided? The answer is that the *Vinaya* states:

"If clothing or requisites are difficult to divide, one should proclaim: 'Come to such-and-such a place at such-and-such a time. Whether someone is sent to fetch them or they come in person, the portions should be distributed.
Regarding what should be obtained, the various schools' formulations of offenses also do not state that it is accomplished. [Question: What about when one is about to die?

When the property of a bhikṣu enters within the boundary, and the bhikṣus therein do not know it, they take it out of the boundary; if it is obtained by a person previously seen [there], the answer is that it may be received.
This is because when the bhikṣus of the original boundary were unaware of the division at the time, and because they share the same dharma.
Chapter Thirty-Five: Precepts on Difficult Practices.

This chapter contains eleven topical sections: 1. Distinguishing the Community; 2. Discerning Community Property; 3. Begging for Food; 4. Ascending the Seat; 5. Expounding the Dharma; 6. Shaving the Hair; 7.
Purifying the Ground; 8. Encountering Robbers; 9. Saving Living Beings; 10. Miscellaneous Matters.

First, regarding the classification of the monastic community (*saṃgha*): the *Bhūmivastu-śāstra* states that a *caitya* is a stūpa (which should be understood as a Buddha-stūpa), while a *vihāra* (meaning "place of pure dwelling") is a monastery.
The *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "That which contains relics is called a stūpa; that which lacks them is a caitya.
A stūpa is also called a *stūpa*, *thūpa*, or *tomb* (*zhǒng*); it is also termed a "square mound" (*fāng fén*). A *caitya* is called a "temple" (*miào*); a temple is...
Regarding the name Ti-p'o-ni-chieh-lo (Devanīgara), the *Mao Ye-she zhuan* states that "tian-you" (heavenly travel) refers to the heavens, while "you" (travel) refers to the monastic quarters.
Because the King established it, it is called "Tian-you. Traditionally, the term "si" (monastery) was used as a substitute for this;

"si" is a public institution established in this land, meaning an office or an administrative bureau. Regarding Kuang-dou-ti-she (Kauṭumbika), the *Sui* commentary states that "si-fang" (four directions) refers to the monastic quarters. This was formerly translated as... [text ends].
*Zhāotí* (招提) is a corruption and abbreviation. In the past, people changed *dòu* (鬪) to *chú* (除), and *shē* (奢) to *zhāo* (招); furthermore, it was erroneously changed to *zhà* (柘).

Because these two characters are similar in form, this error has persisted for a long time. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Building a hall to offer to the monks is called offering to the *Zhāotí* Sangha.

The *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* says: "If a Buddha-stūpa is dilapidated, one may build a better one; one obtains wisdom. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra* says: "One obtains greater merit by building a better one."

The *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra* states: "If one harbors resentment toward stūpas, temples, or various images, and out of obstruction or malice moves them to another location—such an evil person is included among those who commit heinous acts and is subject to the highest grade of retribution. The *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra* states:
"If one destroys a temple or kills a bhikṣu, when that person is about to die, all their limbs will ache with intense pain."
If one dies without having confessed [the offense], one falls into the Avīci hell and undergoes all manner of sufferings.
Second, regarding the exclusion of the property of the Saṃgha: in summary, there are five types of property belonging to the Saṃgha. First, the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions;
that is to say, all heavy items are termed the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions, from Arhats above down to Śrāmaṇeras below—all are included.
1. *Sāṃghika* (shared property): This refers to items that may be sold, purchased, offered to others, or used privately;

it is named according to these specific conditions. 2. *Sthāvira-saṃghika* (property of the resident community): This refers to property that always remains in this particular location and cannot be moved;

when monks from the four quarters arrive, they utilize it right here. It is named after the location. 3. *Cātuddisa-saṃghika* (property of the universal community of monks) [also called *Jiàotíchéshē wù*]: This refers to the property of laypeople... [text fragment].

Regarding the distribution of land to the *saṃmukha-saṃgha* (the monastic community present), individuals each built private dwellings. When monks from the *cāturdiśa-saṃgha* (the monastic community of the four quarters) arrived, there was no place for them to stay.
Consequently, someone took this private land and erected buildings for the *cāturdiśa-saṃgha*, providing all their necessities; it is named after the location itself.

Regarding the property of the four types of *saṃgha*, this is called "the Great Assembly" (*mahāsaṃgha*), as it is held in common by the multitude. This refers to the collective property of the assembly.
Regarding the name: the "five *saṃgha-mālya* items" refers to goods obtained by trading flowers from the *saṃghārāma*;

they are so named because they originate from those flower garlands (*mālya*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a layperson enters the monastery, they should borrow bedding and furniture for their use.
There are five kinds of *saṃgha* property that must not be sold and must not be divided: first, land; second, buildings; third, essential utensils; fourth, fruit."

Regarding the five kinds of flowering fruit trees: because the people of the borderlands do not understand the [Sanskrit] language, if they intend in their hearts to give an object to a bhikṣu but say with their mouths that it is for the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, one may use it at will.

(According to this principle, when laypeople nowadays offer objects, they often say "for the teacher's incense fund"; however, if the intent is to designate it as the price for robes, one may likewise use it at will.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If there is one who has labored in planting fruit trees on monastic land—whether it be a single tree or a single grove—"

Regarding the taking of fruit, if one cannot take all at once, one may take one branch per year; when all branches have been taken, one must stop. Regarding the cutting of melons or vegetables, one may take one [fruit] per year.
If a monk builds a hut on land belonging to the Saṃgha and the Elder (Upādhyāya) comes and does not grant permission, the Buddha said:
"Take the grass and wood and go elsewhere. The *Wubai wenshi* (Five Hundred Questions) states: "If one has first offered a banner to the Buddha, one may take it to perform other Buddhist rites."
If the donor does not permit it, one may not consume it. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"If food has been offered to the Buddha or others, even if one receives and holds it before purchasing it, one may eat it, because at the time of holding it, there was no notion of ownership."
Regarding the third [type of practitioner], the *Yaśas-āvadāna* states that those who practice *piṇḍapāta* (translated here as "going for alms") are those who go from house to house;

"alms" (*piṇḍa*) refers to the food received through begging. (The old translation "fenwei" is an error. According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, "fenwei" means begging for food. If one belongs to the noble ones of the Three Vehicles, all alike beg for their food.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* states that there are many benefits to begging for food, which cannot be fully detailed here.
It is stated that while communal food has its limits, begging for alms is inexhaustible; thus, the disciples of the Buddha cultivate the dharma of the inexhaustible.

When a forest-dwelling bhikṣu of this Vinaya enters a village to beg for alms, he washes his hands at dawn, puts on his seven-piece robe (*saptaka*), folds his great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and places it over his shoulder, and holding a staff to ward off dew, he walks along the road constantly contemplating wholesome dharmas. If he sees...
When people first greet him, saying "Welcome," if he is near a village, he should put on his outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and go to the village gate.

He should observe the characteristics of the streets—the characteristic of the first gate and the characteristic of the seventh gate—and walk along the side of the road holding his staff in his right hand and his bowl in his left hand, begging for food in sequence.
If a layperson brings food to him, he must not go out to meet them and receive it; he may only go to fetch it if they call for him.
One must not forcibly beg; if one knows that food will be obtained, one should stand and wait.

Once the food has been received and even after leaving the village, one should set the bowl on the ground, fold the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), and proceed as before without departing immediately. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When begging for food, one must not say, 'Give me food;
it will bring great merit,' but should remain silent while standing in the place where one is. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* [states] regarding the time of begging for food: [one should remain silent].
Having entered through the triple gate to the courtyard, he snapped his fingers three times; when [the doorkeeper] did not respond, he departed.
The *Saṃghīti-vinaya* states that when Kāśyapa made a vow to beg for food, whatever he first obtained he gave to the monks and nuns, while what he obtained later he ate himself.

The *Ratnamegha-sūtra* states: "Whenever one begs for food, divide it into four parts: give one part to fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*); give the second part to the poor and lowly."
Of what is begged, one-third is given to the various ghosts and spirits, and one-fourth is used for one's own sustenance;

however, one should focus solely on practicing the Way, giving rise to no mind of greedy attachment toward food. When begging for food, one should maintain mindfulness of dignified deportment, never being frivolous or restless, gazing attentively before oneself at a distance of no more than one fathom, and begging from house to house in proper sequence.

Regarding the fourth point, ascending the seat: according to the *Three Thousand Dignified Manners*, when reading a scripture from a high seat, one first pays homage to the Buddha, then to the Dharma of the scriptures, and finally to the presiding elder.
Once seated properly facing the elders, after the sound of the *ghanṭā* has ceased, one first recites verses of praise and chants as prescribed by the Dharma.
According to this Vinaya, two bhikṣus must not preach the Dharma together upon the same high seat. This is because they would... [mutually]... [interfere with one another].

Because they quarreled over seeking each other's faults, the *Five Hundred Questions* states: "If, while preaching the Dharma among the Sangha, one sits upon a high seat and leans against a desk or grasps a fly-whisk (*cūḷāmaṇi*) when not ill, it is an offense of transgression (*pāyattika*).
However, one who uses a whisk made of non-hair materials does not incur this. According to this Vinaya, one may possess a tail-whisk;
the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that because cat-tail and ox-tail whisks were used to sweep Buddha-stūpas, they may be accepted. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "From now on..."

It is already permitted to take twigs, brushes, strips of bark, and so forth to make them; with the exception of cat tails, cow tails, horse tails, and handles made of gold or silver, it is permitted to take all such things.
If they are white, they should be dyed to change their appearance; one must not adopt the coquettish gestures of a courtesan.
This is called the method for the whisk (*vījana*). If one is preparing a lion throne for a Vinaya master, a Dharma master, or a recitation master, one may scatter flowers upon it.
One must not sit upon it if it has not been brushed clean. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states:
"One must not place flowers, incense, necklaces, or other ornaments upon the body of the Buddha; however, it is permissible to scatter them as an offering to the Saṃgha.
Likewise, one must not place flowers or incense upon drinks, food, or meals as an offering to the Saṃgha."
Fifth, regarding the one who preaches the Dharma: this Vinaya concerns preaching the Dharma for the sake of *dānapati* (donors). One may preach the *Sūtras* and explain their analyzed meanings;

it is not an offense to omit the full recitation of the words and phrases. The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If the assembly is large and the text is extensive, there is fear that weariness or aversion might arise. The Buddha said:
'I permit the bhikṣus to cite essential passages and sublime phrases from within the Sūtras to directly reveal their meaning; this does not constitute an offense.'"

Furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, we do not prize flowery and ornate speech; rather, my intention is that even if the words are plain and simple, they must not lose their meaning and must be easy for people to understand.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the assembly delights in the shallow and does not delight in the profound, it is called 'evil exposition' because it does not benefit others;
the opposite is called 'good exposition. Furthermore, one should eliminate the mind of greed, the mind of self-deprecation, and the mind of disparaging others.
The great assembly should establish a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of sympathetic joy, a mind of benefit, and an unshakable mind.
Even for the sake of a single four-line verse, if one causes another to understand it as it truly is, they will enjoy peace and happiness for a long night.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who requested those whose roots of precepts were broken and who were incomplete to preach the Dharma; because of this, these evil persons gained influence and brought shame upon the Saṅgha. The Buddha said: "I permit [this]."

The Dharma Master Tripitaka was asked about the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which states: "If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma with a mind of expectation for the sake of gain and offerings, his followers will likewise emulate this teacher;
such a person thereby destroys his own assembly. The *Wubai wen shi* (Five Hundred Questions) states:

"If one reads, recites, or preaches the sūtras for others with a mind of expectation for material things, one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*); if there is no such mind, there is no offense."

One does not commit an offense through greed when taking [robes] where there are no robes available. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: "A certain Dharma master was permitted to receive the instructions and preach the Dharma to sixty newly ordained bhikṣus.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If one upholds, recites, copies, or proclaims [the teachings], one must not do so at an improper time or in an unsuitable country;
nor should one preach without being requested, with a frivolous mind, by disparaging others, by praising oneself, or by preaching indiscriminately—only then will [the merit] be extinguished."
If the Buddha-dharma even causes immeasurable people to die and fall into hell, it is an evil friend (*pāpa-mitra*) to sentient beings.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are five kinds of persons to whom one should not preach the Dharma or the Vinaya when questioned: namely, those who ask as a trial; those who ask without having a doubt;
those who ask not for the sake of repenting an offense they have committed; and those who ask without receiving [the teaching] yet persist in questioning—none of these may be answered.
Sixth, regarding the purification of the hair: the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that long hair, whiskers, and nails are all signs of one who has broken the precepts;
the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that for an araṇya bhikṣu, hair may grow as long as two inches without violating the *vinaya*;
and the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* explains that those who shave their hair remove only the hair on the head and the beard, as it is improper to remove any other body hair.
Shaving is for the purpose of removing pride and self-conceit; therefore, according to this Vinaya, a bhikṣu must not shave the hair of a layperson or subject them to service.

To do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. This exception does not apply to those who wish to leave the household life. (In the present age, many monks and nuns harbor flattery and seek profit, accepting the service of the laity;

they destroy what is wholesome and increase what is evil—none surpass these in transgression. If the hair becomes extremely long, whether it be two months' growth or longer than two finger-widths [it must be shorn].

When fingernails grow as long as a single grain of barley, they should be clipped; one must not use scissors to clip them. A bhikṣu should trim his hair once every half-month and clip his nails once every half-month;
to violate this rule constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. It is permitted to keep a hair-receptacle (*keśa-bhāṇḍa*). According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, hair should be buried in the ground.

Regarding the seventh stage, the Pure Ground (*śuddhabhūmi*), the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Sweeping a single room of a monastic dwelling throughout Jambudvīpa is not as meritorious as sweeping a palm-sized area of a Buddha stūpa.
The *Saṃyukta-pratyaya-sūtra* (Compendium of the Hundred Causes) states that sweeping the ground yields five merits:

first, removing the defilements of one's own mind; second, removing the defilements of others; third, eliminating arrogance; fourth, subduing the mind; and fifth, increasing merit and attaining rebirth [in a favorable state].

The *Śrāmaṇera-vinaya-sūtra* on Proper Conduct states that there are five rules for sweeping the ground: first, one must not sweep with one's back turned toward others; second, one must not sweep against the grain;
third, one should ensure it is made clean; fourth, one must not leave tracks behind; and fifth, one should immediately clear away the dust so that it is free of impurities.

The *Sūtra on Questions by the Pure-Faithed Upāsikā* states that sweeping the ground where the Buddha resides yields five blessings: first, one’s own mind becomes pure, and others who see this [also] [attain purity].
1. They give rise to a pure mind; 2. they become beloved by others; 3. their hearts rejoice in the heavens; 4. they accumulate karma for physical excellence; 5.
at the end of life, they are reborn in the good realms among the devas.
Regarding the eighth case, "meeting bandits": according to this Vinaya, if a bhikṣu is stripped by bandits and walks about with his body exposed, he incurs an offense.
One should cover one's body with soft grass, tree leaves, or the like, and take up a long robe (*prāvaraṇa*) to wear;
if none is available, one should seek clothing from friends or among the Saṃgha, asking, "Do you have bedding? If there is some, it should be given;

if not, one should personally open the storehouse, take out a thick quilt, tear it apart, and cut it into a robe to cover the body. Having gone outside to beg for clothing, once it has been obtained, one should return and wash it.
If one dyes, sews, or fails to place dyed cloth back in its original location, an offense is incurred.

According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, because of the loss of robes, one may obtain white garments or robes of the five primary colors that have not been cut; even wearing the robes of non-Buddhists does not constitute an offense.

According to the *Vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra*, one should cause the sound of a bowstring to be heard in vain to make the thieves depart. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, when thieves approach, one should strike the bell, ring the gong, and throw stones.

If a thief says, "There is a rock; go down under the rock," one should frighten him away so that he departs. If the robe is subsequently lost, one may wear a *saṃghāṭī* (monastic robe) until it can be returned to its original location.
If there is no one there, one should follow it to a nearby place where monks reside and entrust it to them for return to its original location, standing ready to take it back when it is returned.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If a thief asks, "Where is the property of the *saṃgha*? a *bhikṣu* must not point out a valuable location, nor should he... [text ends].
If one is accused of lying, one should point toward items belonging to the Buddha, such as rooms, beds, and seats, or toward offerings near a stupa.
If traveling on a road where there is rain, let a junior monk go in front; if there is danger from bandits or wild beasts, let the elder be in the center.
If one wishes to inspire compassion in bandits, let the senior monk walk at the head.

The ninth [case], "Saving Living Beings": according to this Vinaya, if one acts with a compassionate mind to release others who have been bound—such as releasing a puppy that has been seized or a piglet;

or releasing cattle and so forth that have been tied up by bandits in an araṇya (wilderness)—none of these constitute an offense. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one uses supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to seize the property of bandits, as well as the people themselves, and releases various birds and livestock, it is said that because the act was performed out of compassion, there is no offense. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if a hunter says, "This deer... [and one intervenes].

When the deer was struck by an arrow, [the hunter] said, "I shall shoot you again to kill you! The bhikṣus avoided the arrows; the deer neither avoided them nor fled, and after being rebuked, it departed.
After it had gone, the deer died. The Buddha said, "One should return [the deer] to the hunter. If one breaks a net or a prison out of compassion, it is merely a *duṣkṛta* offense.
When a pig struck by an arrow entered the monastery, the bhikṣus asked, "Where did this come from, and who is its owner? The pig had none.

There was a pig-herd who departed; after he had gone, [the monks] reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "If there is such a cause and condition, one may employ 'other words' (an-apatti-vāda), and there is no offense.

The *Wubai wenshi* (Five Hundred Questions) states: "When traveling, if one stays overnight in a shrine belonging to spirits, one must not have any intention of disturbing them; to violate this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense."

Regarding the tenth miscellaneous matter, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If in other regions or countries, although it is my teaching, if it is not considered pure there, one may not practice it without fault;
conversely, if it is not my teaching but must be practiced, one must not fail to do so.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There are seven disadvantages to lighting a fire: first, it impairs the eyes; second, it impairs the complexion; third, it causes the body to become weak; fourth, [it damages] the robes..."

1. Defilement; 2. Destruction; 3. Deterioration of the five types of bedding and seating; 4. The sixth [cause], which gives rise to the conditions for violating the precepts; 5. The increase of worldly speech. According to the *Five Hundred Questions*, it says:
"To continue the Buddha’s light so that it never ceases means to extinguish the darkness of the Buddha’s ignorance by means of the limitlessness of fundamental wordless contemplation.
Regarding the lamp before the Buddha, the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha said: "If one takes from the side of the object, the light will not be diminished."

The *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] states that one must not suddenly enter the hall with a lamp while holding it; one should announce, "Venerable sirs, a lamp is about to enter," and so on, until the extinguishing of the lamp.
It is the same for extinguishing the lamp: first, one should cover it with the hand and speak; if they do not permit it, one should not blow it out with the mouth.

One should fan it out with the hand, a garment, or a leather fan. If the head is scorched, the seeds will form. According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, those who have left the household life should abandon the five kinds of stinginess. First...
1. Stinginess regarding material wealth; 2. Stinginess regarding the Dharma; 3. Stinginess regarding one's family; 4. Stinginess regarding one’s dwelling place;

5. Stinginess regarding not praising others. The Sūtra speaks of the "Four Graces," namely: parents, teachers and the Sangha, the king, and donors. The "Five Classes" refers to humans, devas, nāgas, and spirits.
Regarding the taking of an oath in this Vinaya, one should say: "If I do this thing, I take refuge in the Buddha; if you must do it..."

Regarding this matter, one should likewise take refuge in the Buddha (*namo buddhāya*) and not speak of other grave matters such as the hells and so forth. The *Five Divisions* (*Pañcavargika*) states that these are not places for coming and going;
however, when defecating, urinating, or washing one's hands and feet, it is permitted to wear sandals. Furthermore, one must not go to the latrine naked.
The *Three Thousand Dignified Deportments* (*Trisahasra-īryāpatha*) states that one must not sit upon the monastic seats or bedding without having washed the areas used for defecation and urination.
The Elder above [should] pay homage to the Triple Gem; if one pays homage without merit, one should remove the *kaṣāya* (monastic robe). Regarding excrement and urine:
according to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, one must not urinate or defecate upon the bedding of the Saṃgha; if one lies down or sits upon it, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
According to this Vinaya, there are five faults in not chewing a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*): first, the breath is foul; second, one cannot distinguish flavors; third...
1. Heat and shadows do not dissipate; 2. one does not desire food; 3. the eyes are not clear; 4. after chewing, one should rinse [the mouth], because [if not] one dies from being eaten by worms;
5. there are five faults for one who cannot endure insults: 1. being fierce and intolerant; 2. feeling regret later; 3.
being disliked by many people; 4. a bad reputation spreading abroad; 5. falling into the evil realms after death. Thus it is said in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
When a visiting bhikṣu enters a monastery, after resting briefly, he asks for the quarters of the senior resident bhikṣus, pays homage at the Buddha’s stūpa, and only then washes his feet.
Regarding entry into a nunnery, the *Wubai wen shi* (Five Hundred Questions) states that one may enter only if there is a valid reason (*yuan*);

otherwise, one may stay overnight within the nuns’ boundary but not enter their rooms. According to this Vinaya, there are five benefits to walking meditation (*caṅkrama*): first, one becomes capable of traveling long distances; second...
One is able to contemplate; third, having few ailments; fourth, digesting food and drink; fifth, attaining long-term stability in meditative concentration. The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states:
"There is no fault in giving alms to those who beg at monasteries—such as the destitute, infants, prisoners, and pregnant women.
A bhikṣu should study this. The *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "Before five summer retreats (*varṣa*), one relies on others to receive instruction in the Vinaya-piṭaka; after five summer retreats..."
Thereafter, one who possesses full knowledge should train in non-self (*anātman*) regarding persons and phenomena. As the *Śāsanāloka-śāstra* asks: "How does one train in the Vinaya?

It means reading, reciting, and understanding its meaning. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that when making music as an offering to the Buddha, if a mind of desire arises and one becomes attached, one must immediately abandon it.
The *Ekottarika-āgama* says that after King Ajātaśatru attained long-lasting faith, he issued an edict throughout the kingdom forbidding families from serving the Buddha.

Regarding the transport of goods and the welcoming and seeing off [of guests], the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that if one takes items from a hidden treasury for the purpose of providing for the Three Jewels through vegetarian feasts or lectures, there is no offense.
The *Pañcaśata-praśna* says that if one is given military weapons as a gift, they need not be accepted.

The *Trīṇi-sahasra-vidhi* says that when entering another’s room, one should: first, snap the fingers outside; second, remove one's hat; third, perform a prostration; and fourth, stand upright and offer instruction.
Regarding the five matters for which one should not remain as a teacher to a layperson while instructing them in the performance of merit, the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states:
first, one should not reside in the donor’s household; second, one should not fix the mind on greed for profit;
third, one should preach the Dharma to each individually regarding giving, observing the precepts, the eightfold fast, and so forth; fourth, one should not engage in entertainment with them.
There are five ways in which one whose mind is unattached constantly desires to see [the donor]: furthermore, there are five matters by which one is held in high esteem and respected by a donor:
first, not going back and forth to the donor’s former acquaintances; second, not seeking to use one's influence to manage the donor’s household affairs;

Chapter Thirty-Seven: On a Bhikṣuṇī Requesting to Maintain a Following.

Regarding the method for requesting to maintain a following, this Vinaya states: A bhikṣuṇī who has reached twelve years of seniority and wishes to ordain others by conferring full precepts (*upasampadā*) must perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one announcement).

The meaning of this chapter is summarized into two parts: first, clarifying the ritual for confessing before the assembly; second, clarifying the ritual for reciting the precepts.

Third, regarding miscellaneous practices, there are two parts: first, the method of mutual guidance between teacher and disciple, and second, the method of miscellaneous practices. As for the bhikṣuṇīs:

A Concise Explanation. (Regarding the eight heavy rules for bhikṣuṇīs, the first four are the same as those for bhikṣus. In total, there are three hundred and forty-one bhikṣuṇī precepts.

Regarding the precept against physical contact (*sparśana*), it constitutes an offense when six conditions are met: first, there is a man;

Regarding the five cases where physical contact occurs between bodies—excluding the one case where one is clothed and the other is unclothed, or both are clothed, etc.—one does not incur a grave offense (*pārājika*).
Sixth, as for the offense incurred upon experiencing pleasure: a *bhikṣuṇī* incurs a *pārājika* with every instance of contact with the male body, regardless of its extent.

Do not inquire whether she is dead or alive; if a woman merely touches [the organ] and experiences pleasure, it constitutes an offense. Regarding the rule concerning sexual assault, one who causes death does not commit an offense;

thus the Vinaya states that if a man with a defiled mind witnesses her death, he does not commit an offense. As for the two types of Saṃgha (monks), there is no distinction based on the woman's age; they all commit the offense.

For a *bhikṣuṇī*, both parties must possess a defiled mind. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a *bhikṣuṇī* has a sore or abscess in a minor area, she may employ a man [to treat it]."

Eight matters constitute a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). This precept is established through five conditions: first, it is a human male; second, one perceives him as a human male; third, there is a defiled mind;

The Vinaya-offense states: "To seize by the hand" means [seizing] from the wrist upward is light; "to seize by the clothing" refers to seizing the upper garment on the body.

If a son commits the first seven offenses with a mind of defilement against both [women], it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if he does not repent and completes the eighth offense, it is a *pārājika*.

If one man commits eight [offenses] against eight women at once, or commits eight [offenses] against eight women over the course of eight years, it constitutes eight [complete] offenses.
Even if one enters [a dwelling] with eight layers of walls, there is no sequential offense; the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are likewise not violated in such cases.

One does not commit an offense if there is something to be given, or if one is performing prostrations, or passing through, or receiving the Dharma, or entering a secluded place without committing an evil act, because in all these instances there is no defiled mind.

However, one commits a *pāyattika* (offense of falling) by entering a dark room, because although there is no specific purposeful act, it involves the risk of scandal or disgrace. Thus, an offense is committed.
The precept against concealing another’s grave offense is established as an infraction when six conditions are met:

(1) the person is a *bhikṣuṇī*; (2) she has committed a grave offense; (3) one knows that she has committed a grave offense; (4) one forms the intention to conceal it; (5) one does not disclose it; and (6) the dawn appears, at which point the infraction is incurred.

(If one lives alone with no one present, the concealment is not established, as explained in the section on the confession of offenses. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a *bhikṣuṇī* who has been subject to formal suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) becomes deranged in mind..."
If one conceals [a fault], it is not an offense; however, if one stops [the concealment] while still in a state of madness, yet continues to conceal it once recovered, it constitutes an offense.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a nun sees another nun commit a grave offense, she should speak of it to others. If the offender is fierce, evil, or powerful, and there is fear of danger to life or celibacy (*brahmacarya*), she should form this thought:
'The consequences of his own actions and offenses he himself shall know. It is like a fire breaking out that burns a house; one should simply [protect oneself]."
When one is occupied with saving one's own life, how can one attend to other matters? Once the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*) has been attained, one may cease [the confession].

According to this principle, there is no offense in concealing [a fault] with an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind; for although it is not the mind of equanimity, it is an indeterminate state that does not produce the intention to conceal.

Therefore, the mind that conceals must necessarily be an unwholesome (*akuśala*) mind, as it intentionally hides the faults of another so that outsiders do not know or hear of them. If one wishes to confess [the fault], one should do so immediately.
One must seek out a person who is already known to be pure and confess before them; this constitutes a valid confession.

If one confesses before someone who is not yet known to be pure—or before someone who refuses to accept the confession—it is invalid, as both parties must have confessed. Furthermore, if one confesses before someone who has committed an offense, the confession is not accomplished.

If one wishes to confess, one must state the name of the person against whom the offense was committed and record the specific category and nature of the offense; only then does the confession become valid. If these conditions cannot be met...
Regarding the names of persons and the types of offenses, there is no fault of concealment.
If the person before whom one has confessed has already received it, there is no need to speak further; to do so would result in the fault of infinite regress.

If that offender has already confessed of their own accord, others who harbor a mind of concealment do not incur the offense, because the fundamental confession has already been completed. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Bhikṣuṇīs..."
One must not disclose a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) before a bhikṣu and then later repent it before a bhikṣuṇī;
nor should one, if unaware of the specific nature of the offense, go to a bhikṣu to ask general questions for clarification and then return to the bhikṣuṇī to repent. The Vinaya states:

"If a bhikṣuṇī knows she has committed an *aṣṭau pārājikāḥ*, she should confess it at the morning meal; if she knows after the meal, she should confess it at the evening meal. Only in such cases [is it permissible]."

If one fails to speak [the confession] at the appropriate times during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if the dawn light appears, it is a grave (*pārājika*) offense.
Those who do not incur an offense are: one for whom there is no person toward whom to speak; one who intends to speak but the dawn light has already appeared;
or one who, while speaking, fears life-threatening or religious obstacles (*brahmacarya-vighna*). In all such cases, there is no offense.

The second section, a brief commentary on the two *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules for nuns, consists of seventeen offenses. Regarding the two offenses concerning matchmaking and the two concerning false accusation, these are explained in the same manner as the rules for monks.
As for the offense regarding "human speech" (*manuṣya-vāda*), this rule is established through four conditions: first, speaking to a layperson who is an official adjudicating legal matters;

second, speaking toward a lay devotee (*upāsaka*) regarding such matters; third, enumerating those specific matters; and fourth, taking action by drafting a formal document—by doing so, one commits the offense.
Regarding the definition of this offense: it refers to going before an official to dispute right and wrong. If the presiding judge records the matter in writing, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one speaks verbally without specifying names, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:

"If a nun goes with a layperson (*gṛhapati*) to an official's office and says to the layperson, 'You speak first regarding the principle,' if she speaks [first], it is a *duṣkṛta*; if the layperson speaks [first], it is [the same]."

The nun then went to the official and claimed she had been stolen; the layman (upāsaka) likewise claimed he had stolen her. Whether the nun’s claim was justified or not, both cases constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The layman said, "Official, summon both the layman and the nun to the office; let the official himself judge whether the claim is justified or not.

If the nun has no fault, yet goes to the official and says, "The person [who took me] shall be fined by the official," then according to the amount of the fine imposed, she commits an offense corresponding to the value of the property.

If one owes a debt and their property has been seized by another, they may go to the authorities to request protection; however, they must not disclose the person's name, for the authorities will investigate and punish the offender themselves, leaving the petitioner free from blame.
If someone enters a monastery to cut down trees, one must not seize their axe or hatchet; rather, one should demand payment for the value of the wood.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a nun is insulted or oppressed by others, she may speak to her parents, relatives, or those who possess power."

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: If a nun, in the presence of those presiding over a legal proceeding, out of anger and resentment reviles the monk she originally struck, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;
if she reviles the monk she originally struck in the presence of others, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Regarding these four individual precepts, they are combined into one precept.
First, the rule concerning crossing a river alone is explained, which constitutes an offense when four conditions are met: first, it must be a river of water according to the Vinaya.
It is not that one cannot cross water alone; nor is it a matter of the depth or breadth.

Now, according to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, if one crosses water by lifting one's robes—differing from traveling on land—one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This applies even to rivers within a *mahā-sīmā*, as the difficulty of the situation is the same.
It is like entering a village alone within a boundary, which also constitutes an offense. However, if there is a bridge, it is permitted as usual. These are the two points.
If she crosses alone as before, and another nun enters the water quickly, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; when both feet have stepped onto the bank, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If the latter nun enters the water alone and it is a *sthūlātyaya*, at the time she steps onto the bank, if she finds the former nun to accompany her, there is no offense.

If she crosses by means of a carriage, boat, or the like, there is no offense in any case. The Vinaya states: "That nun should seek out another nun to cross together; when entering the water, she should follow [the rules accordingly]."
1. When crossing a deep river, one should lift the hem of the robe until reaching the opposite shore; once there, one should gradually lower the robe and then all at once step onto the bank.

If one does not wait for a companion, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. 2. There is no offense in three cases: when there is no cause or condition; when there is a life-threatening danger or a threat to the *brahmacarya*;

and when a companion has died. 3. To cross alone by oneself constitutes an offense. This means that if there is no possibility of mutual assistance from a companion within the river, one is considered "alone."

Entering a village is established as an offense when four conditions are met: first, it must be a person; second, regardless of whether it is within a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) or within a village or monastery (*nigama-ārāma*), entering alone constitutes an offense according to this Vinaya;
third, if a nun travels alone to a village, she incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for every village she reaches;

fourth, if she travels through a desolate wilderness where there are no paths, even if she hears the sound of a single drum, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; and fifth, if she travels alone within a village, it is an offense for every boundary (*sīmā*).
*Dūṣkṛta* (according to this principle, if one travels alone within a single precinct or alone within a single household, one incurs only *dūṣkṛta*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one travels with a companion to the boundary of a city or town, they should remain within arm's reach of each other as they cross the boundary;
if they are beyond arm's reach and cross the boundary alone, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Second, traveling alone; third, lacking a valid reason; fourth, crossing the boundary. Thus it is said.

Regarding the offense (the Old Commentary states: "If one wishes to enter a village, even if there is a crossroad, merely crossing it constitutes an offense"; however, as there is no such text in the various schools, it should be considered that no offense has been committed).

Therefore, according to this Vinaya, if there is no boundary, one commits the offense only when traveling alone within the range of hearing and sight of one's companions after the single drum-roll has sounded.

If one reaches the gate and does not wait for the subsequent companions, but both feet cross the threshold of the gate, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. If there is already a nun within the village, there is no offense, because the preceding nun serves as one's companion.
If one leaves the village, it is only upon crossing the threshold that the offense of sleeping alone is incurred; this offense is established through three conditions:

first, staying overnight outside the reach of the "extended hand" (śīrṣa-hasta), regardless of whether it is within a monastery or a village; second, sharing a bed even if on separate mats, which constitutes an offense;

and third, one must remain within the reach of the extended hand and maintain mutual vigilance to avoid the fault. If one was originally within the reach of the extended hand but later, due to movement during sleep, suddenly becomes separated, [the offense is incurred].
This does not constitute an offense [for the initial act], because one commits the offense as soon as one turns over with the intention of separating [from the other]. Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"Regarding 'staying overnight together,' if they are out of reach of one's outstretched hand, for every single turning over, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"One should remain within arm's reach; during the night, one should search for each other with the hands three times, but these three times must not be done all at once."
Regarding the investigation during the first, middle, and last watches of the night to ascertain whether [the object] is present or absent, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one does not reach the location during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if the dawn light appears, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Second, there is no offense if there is no underlying cause, such as when life or the Brahma-faring are at risk, or when seeking tranquility. Third, this applies to each instance of lying down.
Regarding the offense of walking alone behind [one's companions], the root rule concerns intentionally separating from one's group while within sight or hearing;

this constitutes an offense even if the companions have no grounds for hardship. The Vinaya states that if one separates from both sight and hearing, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (saṅghādisesa); if one separates from either sight or hearing, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (thullaccaya).
As for cases where there is no offense, it first clarifies that there is no offense when crossing water; furthermore, there is no offense if one proceeds gradually with one's companions.

Crossing [a river] without losing one’s dignified demeanor; crossing by boat, crossing a bridge, or crossing by stepping onto a beam; or when a companion dies, one halts their journey, travels a long distance, or encounters various difficulties—in all such cases, there is no offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the water is shallow, if there is no fear, or if it is in the presence of a man, there is no offense.

Regarding the allowance for entering a village without offense, it is as explained in the aforementioned conditions for allowances. Regarding the allowance for staying overnight without offense, the Vinaya says: "Together with..."

When two nuns stay overnight within reach of each other’s outstretched hands, if one nun goes out to relieve herself, or to receive, recite, or chant the scriptures, or for the sake of seeking solitude to practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), or to cook soup, porridge, or drinks for a sick nun, or due to other such difficult circumstances, she does not commit an offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a nun is ill, or if the city is surrounded by bandits and chaos, she may stay alone overnight."
Regarding cases where there is no offense despite having committed [an act] that would otherwise be a transgression: one should remain within sight and hearing.
If a bhikṣuṇī voids excrement or urine, or encounters various difficulties and the like, there is no offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"One must not leave the boundary of the village, except for traveling on a road, voiding excrement, or unexpectedly losing one's companions; if one has not yet reached the next [village], there is no offense. The same applies to illness. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
If one flees in fear and, due to old age or illness, cannot keep pace with the group, there is no offense.

Regarding the third category [of offenses], such as spinning or weaving, or pulling, stretching, and winding the fibers—each of these constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense entailing forfeiture) for obtaining cloth; it is not permissible to wear it without performing the formal act of confession (*pratikarman*).

Apart from these, the other precepts do not lack distinguishing characteristics; however, some are omitted because the text is overly verbose and lacks essential points, some because the occurrences are rare, and others because their intent is easily understood.

The principles and characteristics of these clarifications are difficult to manifest; had I wished to present them in full detail, I fear it would have resulted in an excessive proliferation of volumes.
I hope that those who uphold this work will rely upon the text for resolution. *Vinayapeṭaka-yāo*, Volume Lower, End (Concluded).
On the twenty-sixth day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Hōei era, this volume was completed through collation at Jishōin by Ryōsei Kan.
